Summary

Tuesday’s preliminary hearing in the cocaine trafficking case against former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor has been pushed to Wednesday, September 2, at 10:00 a.m., after the Ministry of Justice requested a last-minute continuance. The delay comes as questions grow around the state’s timeline linking her to an alleged cocaine network.

Court Grants Continuance Hours Before First Hearing Was Set to Open

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

MONROVIA — The preliminary hearing in the cocaine trafficking case against former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor will not go forward until next as Wednesday, September 2, 2026.

Early this morning, The Ministry of Justice’s Office of the City Solicitor asked the Monrovia City Court for a continuance just hours before the case was due to open, and Stipendiary Magistrate Cllr. L. Ben Barco granted it.

The hearing will now resume Wednesday, September 2, at 10:00 a.m.

In its request, the government said the Supreme Court’s closing of its March Term of Court had pulled several senior lawyers away to attend on their supervisors, leaving the prosecution short of the counsel it needed for the day.

It is a short delay, but it lands at a moment when the state’s own account of the case is drawing closer scrutiny. Howard-Taylor faces nine charges built around allegations that a businessman, Sheikh Bassirou Kante, introduced her to an alleged Croatian-Ukrainian cocaine network in “early 2022,” first at her Congo Town residence and later in Dubai.

What has quietly complicated that narrative is a matter of public U.S. court record: Kante was arrested in Maryland on April 20, 2022, on wire fraud and money laundering charges unrelated to narcotics.

The charge sheet gives no specific date for the Congo Town meeting or the Dubai trip, and no travel records placing Kante in Liberia or the Gulf ahead of his arrest have yet been made public. That gap has left room for a question the defense is expected to press hard on Wednesday: where, precisely, was everyone when this was supposed to have happened?

Howard-Taylor has denied all charges.

Her legal team has called the case baseless and politically motivated and says it will contest it vigorously when the hearing resumes.

FrontPageAfrica will continue to follow this story as it develops.

World.title: Liberia: National Flag Day Oration: “FROM HERITAGE TO HOPE: THE FLAG THAT UNITES US”
World.content:
By Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Minister of Finance and Development Planning

Republic of Liberia On the Occasion of the 179th Anniversary of National Flag Day August 24, 2026

His Excellency the President of the Republic of Liberia;

Members of the Legislature present;

Former Officials of Government,

The Dean and Members of the Cabinet and other officials of Government;

The Doyen and Members of the Diplomatic and Consular Corps;

Traditional and Religious Leaders;

Members of our Armed Forces and National Security Institutions;

Our Teachers and Students;

Members of the Fourth Estate;

Distinguished Guests;

Fellow Liberians at home and throughout the Diaspora;

Ladies and Gentlemen:

I am deeply honored to stand before you on this historic occasion as we commemorate the 179th anniversary of Liberia’s National Flag Day under the inspiring theme:

“From Heritage to Hope: The Flag That Unites Us.”

Today, we gather not merely to celebrate a national symbol. We gather to reflect upon who we are, where we have come from, what binds us together, and—perhaps most importantly—where we intend to go as one people and one Republic.

Our flag is cloth, but it is more than cloth. It is color, but it is more than color. It is history, but it must also be hope. It is a reminder of yesterday, a symbol of our common identity today, and a solemn promise to the generations of tomorrow.

FROM HERITAGE

One hundred and seventy-nine years ago, our forebears gave this Republic a flag to represent the aspirations of a newly independent African nation.

Eleven alternating red and white stripes and a lone white star resting upon a field of blue became the emblem under which generations of Liberians would live, struggle, celebrate, mourn, disagree, reconcile, rebuild, and dream.

That flag has witnessed our finest hours. It has also witnessed our darkest days.

It has flown in times of peace and conflict. It has been raised at inaugurations and lowered in mourning. It has accompanied our men and women in uniform and flown above our schools, public buildings, diplomatic missions, and international gatherings.

Through political transitions; through a brutal civil war that destroyed infrastructure and took countless lives; through public-health emergencies such as Ebola and COVID; through economic downturns and the difficult work of national reconstruction, the Lone Star has continued to fly high over land and over sea.

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen:

As I mount this hallowed podium on this National Flag Day, my mind’s eye races back through time, capturing vivid scenes from my distant past.

I see myself on August 24, 1978, a first grader at Bolahun Public School in Wawoma Clan, Kolahun District, Lofa County, proudly dressed in my school uniform—a white shirt and green short trousers—marching alongside my fellow first graders behind the students in the higher classes. Hundreds of students from village schools across the Clan have also converged on Bolahun for the grand Flag Day parade.

The entire clan has practically descended upon the town. Parents, relatives, friends, and well-wishers throng the streets, or more precisely paths, to witness the beautiful spectacle of schoolchildren marching proudly toward the designated point to salute our red, white, and blue flag.

I can still hear the cheers.

As each drill commander approaches the designated line and gives the salute, the crowd erupts in applause and laughter.

Those moments brought the entire town alive.

For us as children, National Flag Day was never merely a day to salute the flag. It was a day of celebration and fun—a day when students felt especially proud to be in school and parents experienced the joy of watching their children march with excitement and confidence.

Nearly five decades later, those memories remain vivid.

That little first grader marching through Bolahun in 1978—the little boy who would later return to Monrovia and continue his schooling in Logan Town, Jamaica Road, Kakata, and other places—could not have imagined that one day he would stand before his country as National Flag Day Orator, called upon to reflect on the meaning of the very flag he once marched so proudly to salute.

But that possibility should never be unique to one person.

It should be part of the Liberian promise available to every child.

Every Liberian child should be able to look at the Lone Star and say:

My country sees me. The circumstances of my birth do not determine the boundaries of my possibilities.

My dreams matter.

That is the Liberia we must build.

THE FLAG THAT UNITES US

My fellow Liberians:

If the flag belongs to all of us, then loyalty to that flag requires us to seek the common good.

But unity does not mean uniformity.

Indeed, look at what we witnessed during today’s parade: students dressed in different uniforms, coming from different schools, marching in different formations—but all saluting one flag.

There is a lesson for Liberia in that image.

We too may wear different political uniforms. We may come from different counties. We may belong to different tribes, religions, professions, associations, and social groups. We may disagree passionately about policies, personalities, and the direction of our country.

But above all those uniforms flies one flag.

We can disagree and still be Liberians.

And as I said in 2010 at the induction of officers of the Federation of Lofa Associations in the Americas FLAA) :

“Our individual counties exist within a country called Liberia, and while we have our individual county flags that belong to some of us, we have a single national flag that belongs to all of us. So, our county-centricity must never conflict with or undermine our country-centricity.”

Today I would add:

Our party-centricity must never undermine our country-centricity.

There must always be something above everything else.

That something is Liberia.

LET US INDIVIDUATE

We must resist the temptation to stereotype one another negatively because of political, county, tribal, religious, or other associations.

There is nothing wrong with loving the group to which we belong. But while loving our own group, we must recognize that other Liberians have an equal right to love theirs.

Our membership in one group does not make everyone in our group good.

Membership in another group does not automatically make someone else bad.

Every county, tribe, religion, or political party has its good, its bad, its ugly.

Every government has its good, its bad, its ugly.

The media has its good, its bad, its ugly.

The same is true of civil society, religious institutions, the business community, and every other human institution.

Why?

Because institutions are populated by imperfect human beings.

So let us individuate.

Let us assess each Liberian primarily by who that person is, what that person does, the values that person demonstrates, and what that person contributes to the common good.

Being outside government does not automatically confer sainthood on anyone, except if we fall for that feeble argument that the environment outside government is a paradise populated only by angels and cherubim.

Conversely, being in government does not automatically make a person bad, except again if we surrender to the warped argument that government by nature is an evil construct populated only by demons.

There are Liberians outside government who protect the flag every day through their service to country. And there are legions of Liberians in government working diligently and patriotically for the forward march of our nation.

The location of a person matters less than the character and patriotism of the person.

PATRIOTISM MUST BECOME PRACTICE

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen:

In recent years, the celebration of our nation’s Independence Day has taken on a remarkable new momentum. Liberians at home and across the Diaspora are increasingly adorning themselves in our national colors and celebrating Liberia with a passion, pride, and enthusiasm perhaps greater than we have witnessed in generations.

It is as though Liberians are falling in love with their country all over again—renewing their marital vows to our beloved Liberia in symbolic ceremonies of national recommitment taking place across the world every Independence Day.

This growing spirit of patriotism is a beautiful and encouraging phenomenon. It must be nurtured and sustained. Whatever we have done—as a people and as a government—to inspire this renewed affection for Liberia, we must continue to do, and do even better.

But It is easy to dress in national colors.

It is easy to sing the national anthem.

It is easy to wave the flag.

The harder task is to live by what the flag demands of us.

The raising of the flag and the singing of the national anthem should not merely make us teary-eyed. They should extract from us a commitment to take practical actions in the interest of our country.

Patriotism is not only what we say about Liberia. Patriotism is what we do for Liberia.

A public official who protects public resources is raising the flag.

A teacher who enters the classroom prepared to educate the next generation is raising the flag.

A nurse or doctor who faithfully cares for patients is raising the flag.

A member of our joint security forces who resists the tempting overtures of drug cartels and enforces the law regardless of name, status, wealth, or connections is raising the flag.

A businessperson who pays legitimate taxes and treats workers fairly is raising the flag.

A journalist who pursues truth responsibly is raising the flag.

A citizen who refuses corruption even when nobody is watching is raising the flag.

A young Liberian who chooses education, hard work, creativity, entrepreneurship, and service over despair is raising the flag.

The flag, therefore, should inspire more than emotion.

It should inspire responsibility.

Because love of country without responsibility to country is incomplete.

THE FLAG IN THE OFFICE

This responsibility has particular meaning for those entrusted with public office.

When the President, Vice President and other public officials assume office, they take an oath solemnly pledging allegiance to the Republic and undertaking to uphold its Constitution and laws.

That is why the flag is hoisted on all public buildings. That is why the flag is in the offices of public officials.

It is not merely decoration.

The flag represents millions of Liberians at home and throughout the Diaspora. Its presence should remind every public official that a government office is not a private space for advancing personal interests at the expense of the common good.

In a sense, every day that flag in a public office speaks silently to the official seated beside it, saying:

Liberia and Liberians are right here with you.

Liberia is watching you. Liberia is counting on you.

So, think Liberia. Love Liberia. Build Liberia.

THE LIBERIAN ENTERPRISE AND THE RESPONSIBILITY OF LEADERSHIP

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen:

Our country is like a common enterprise in which every citizen is a shareholder.

Those privileged to occupy public office do not possess a greater ownership share in Liberia. On election day, the President in the Executive Mansion or a fisherman in West Point, is entitled to one ballot—not two, not three—one.

Public office therefore does not increase one’s ownership of Liberia. It increases one’s responsibility to Liberia.

And leadership itself extends far beyond public office. Responsibility for country rests on the shoulders of every Liberian, especially those who can rightly be called Liberian leaders. And I use the phrase “Liberian leaders” broadly.

A Liberian leader is anyone whose position or influence can shape the thinking, behavior, and direction of other Liberians—for better or for worse.

Pastors and imams are Liberian leaders because congregations look to them for moral direction.

Principals and teachers are Liberian leaders because they shape impressionable minds.

Political party leaders are Liberian leaders because thousands take cues from their words and actions.

Talk-show hosts, panelists, editors, reporters, bloggers, and influencers are Liberian leaders because they influence what citizens believe to be true or false.

Business leaders, market association leaders, motorcyclist union leaders, trade union leaders, health professionals, sports leaders, community leaders—all exercise influence.

And influence creates responsibility.

A microphone creates responsibility.

A pulpit creates responsibility.

A classroom creates responsibility.

A political platform creates responsibility.

A social-media following creates responsibility.

Wherever influence exists, responsibility follows.

THE TRAGEDY OF THE COMMONS

There is, however, a danger that comes with common ownership.

Sometimes, because Liberia belongs to all of us, we behave as though Liberia belongs to none of us.

Economists describe a related phenomenon as the “tragedy of the commons”—when individuals pursue narrow private interests in ways that ultimately undermine the collective interest.

We say we want clean cities, yet some of us throw garbage from a moving vehicle.

We say Liberia needs a bigger national budget, yet some of us deliberately evade legitimate taxes.

We say we want a crime-free society, but when a friend or relative is lawfully apprehended, some of us demand that the police abandon the law.

We demand accountability from public officials, but excuse wrongdoing when the wrongdoer belongs to our party, county, tribe, church, family, or circle of friends.

That is how the common good is weakened.

Protecting the flag means understanding that what belongs to all of us must be protected by each of us.

FROM HERITAGE TO HOPE

My fellow Liberians:

The theme of today’s celebration does not stop at heritage.

It calls us from heritage to hope.

Heritage tells us where we came from.

Hope tells us where we can go.

But hope cannot simply be a wish.

National hope must be constructed.

It must be planned.

It must be financed.

It must be protected by strong institutions.

It must be powered by discipline, sacrifice, hard work, innovation, and what I call our thinking equity.

Our national development agenda—the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development—is therefore an instrument of hope.

Not empty hope.

Not wishful hope.

But hope translated into plans; plans translated into projects; and projects translated into measurable improvements in the lives of our people.

DEVELOPMENT AS A NATIONAL UNITER

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen:

The Government of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai inherited enormous challenges. But we are not content merely to curse the darkness.

We are lighting candles. We are lifting the flag.

And based on what we are doing, I can now confidently say that this generation of Liberians will in few years be able to drive on paved roads from Monrovia to Harper and from Gbarnga through Zorzor, Voinjama, Kolahun, and Foya toward Mendikorma on the Sierra Leone border, things that previous generations of Liberians since the nation’s founding could only dream of.

We are working to expand reliable electricity, improve schools and healthcare, strengthen institutions, create jobs and opportunities, and connect communities that for too long have remained isolated from the full promise of national development.

Why?

Because one of the most effective ways to unite a country is to develop the country.

The roads we are paving do not ask the political party of the persons travelling on them.

The electricity we are expanding in Monrovia, in Buchanan, in Voinjama and across the country does not ask the tribe of the child studying beneath its light.

The hospitals we are improving or the ones we are building will not ask the county of the patient seeking treatment.

The schools we are equipping, rehabilitating or constructing, including the more than 100 schools for foundational learning that we are about to rehabilitate or construct, will not ask whether a child’s parents voted for the government or the opposition.

Development, when it is inclusive, is one of the most powerful expressions of national unity.

A road connecting two counties connects more than geography—it connects people, markets, opportunities, and hopes.

Electricity reaching a community does more than illuminate houses—it expands possibilities.

A functioning school does more than educate a child—it strengthens the future of the Republic.

This is how we move from heritage to hope.

Under the leadership of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, our government is working with urgency to expand the fiscal space necessary to finance the ever-growing ambitions of our people.

When some critics and cynics considered a billion-dollar national budget a distant and unrealistic aspiration, we chose to pursue the difficult work of expanding domestic revenue and strengthening fiscal capacity. And sometime in September this, we shall hit the historic billion-dollar mark, the first time since the founding of our country.

But a bigger budget is not an end in itself.

Its meaning lies in what it makes possible:

More roads.

More electricity.

Better schools.

Stronger healthcare.

More jobs and opportunities.

Stronger institutions.

And measurable improvements in the lives of our people.

That is the standard by which development must ultimately be judged.

COMPETITION WITHOUT HATRED

But development alone cannot unite a nation if our politics continually tears it apart.

We can compete politically without hating one another.

We can disagree without becoming enemies.

We can seek victory without requiring another Liberian’s destruction.

There is a dangerous form of politics that treats national life as a zero-sum game: for me to live, you must die; for me to rise, you must fall; for me to succeed, you must fail.

We must reject that mindset.

Some may consider such a position naïve or non- Machiavellian.

But we should never become comfortable acquiring our joy through the pain of others or celebrating our advancement through the destruction of others.

We can be competitive without being cruel.

We can succeed without destroying.

We can win without hatred.

A person’s political opponent is not a person’s political enemy. After all, the position or office in contention is not the personal property of political contenders. It is for the Liberian people.

When hatred becomes the organizing principle of politics, eventually everybody loses.

OUR SHARED PATRIOTIC COVENANT

Perhaps one of the challenges of our national life is that we have become very clear about what separates us but insufficiently clear about the minimum values that must unite us.

Liberia needs a minimum Patriotic Covenant—a set of irreducible national values to which government and opposition, Christian and Muslim, young and old, rich and poor can subscribe.

Let that covenant affirm:

That Liberia comes first.

That political power must be pursued peacefully.

That public resources belong to the people.

That corruption is wrong regardless of who commits it.

That truth matters.

That our differences must never justify hatred.

That the Constitution and the rule of law must prevail over personalities.

That no political victory is worth destroying Liberia.

And that every generation, in the spirit of intergenerational equity, has a duty to leave the Republic stronger than it inherited it.

These should not be government values or opposition values.

They should be Liberian values.

PEACE MUST NEVER BE TAKEN FOR GRANTED

Distinguished Ladies and Gentlemen:

Our history has taught us a costly lesson:

Division can destroy in a few years what generations labor to build.

Peace, therefore, must never be taken for granted.

We must guard it.

We must nurture our democracy.

We must strengthen the rule of law.

And we must ensure that our words—whether spoken from political platforms, radio stations, pulpits, community meetings, or posted online—do not reopen wounds that our nation has struggled so hard to heal.

Words matter.

A microphone can educate or inflame.

A radio program can inform or divide.

A political platform can inspire or incite.

A social-media post can build bridges or deepen fractures.

Our children deserve to inherit our progress.

Not our divisions.

Not our hatred.

Not our anger.

WHAT SHOULD THE FLAG SEE?

We often ask what do we see when we look at the flag.

Today, let us reverse the question.

If the flag could look back at us, what would it see?

Would it see citizens committed to building their country?

Would it see leaders placing national interest above personal interest?

Would it see young people equipped with knowledge, skills, and opportunity?

Would it see political opponents who disagree without hatred?

Would it see communities living peacefully despite their differences?

Would it see public resources being transformed into roads, schools, hospitals, electricity, jobs, and opportunity?

Would it see integrity becoming stronger day by day?

Would it see hope becoming stronger than despair?

Those questions cannot be answered by this speech.

They will be answered by our actions.

CONCLUSION: THE FLAG WE MUST LIVE

My fellow Liberians:

The flag we celebrate today came to us from history.

The Liberia beneath which it will fly tomorrow is ours to build.

That is the journey from heritage to hope.

And wherever the Lone Star flies, let every Liberian remember:

This is our heritage.

This is our hope.

This is our home.

This is our Liberia.

But let us also remember:

The flag cannot raise itself.

We raise the flag when we raise our standards.

We raise the flag when we raise our integrity.

We raise the flag when we raise our children with knowledge, discipline, and hope.

We raise the flag when we raise one another.

And we raise the flag highest when we put country above self.

So let us leave this celebration determined not merely to wave the flag, but to live the flag.

Not merely to salute Liberia, but to serve Liberia.

Not merely to hope for a better Liberia, but to build one.

May the Lone Star forever unite us.

May peace remain within our borders.

May hope rise in every Liberian heart.

And may Almighty God continue to bless the Republic of Liberia and save the State.

Happy 179th National Flag Day!

Long live the Lone Star!

Long live the Republic of Liberia!

I thank you.

World.title: Rep. Marvin Cole Rallies Bong County Behind Jewel Howard-Taylor, Alleges Selective Justice in Drug Case
World.content:
MONROVIA – Bong County District #3 Representative Marvin Cole is calling on residents of Bong County to unite in support of former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, urging citizens to seek what he described as a free and fair trial for the former Vice President, who is a native of the county.

By J.H. Webster Clayeh [email protected]

Madam Taylor is facing charges of drug trafficking, money laundering and several related offenses following an investigation by Liberia’s Joint Security agencies.

The charges include alleged unlicensed importation, sale, distribution and transportation of controlled substances, criminal conspiracy, facilitation and solicitation.

She was arrested on August 19, 2026, at Roberts International Airport while attempting to leave Liberia before being taken to the Liberia National Police headquarters for questioning.

On August 25, the Monrovia City Court ordered her remanded to Monrovia Central Prison after rejecting her lawyers’ request that she remain in a medical facility or be granted humanitarian accommodation instead of imprisonment.

Appearing on Sky FM’s 50-50 Talk Show on Tuesday, Representative Cole described Howard-Taylor’s imprisonment as an example of selective justice, arguing that she remains innocent until proven guilty.

“I want to tell the citizens of Bong County, our daughter Jewel as far I know as per the law, she is not guilty, she has not done any wrong, you should not be deterred, you should not cry, we should pray with her, we will stand up to this government to ask for free and fair trial of our former Vice President and our daughter,” Representative Cole said.

Cole also questioned why other individuals linked to drug-related investigations have not faced similar treatment, despite Madam Taylor’s swift prosecution.

“I’m not saying that Justice should be delayed or should not be served when it comes to Jewel, my position on this matter is, if you arrested Jewel and kept her at the Police Station, charged her in six days time, send her to the magisterial court and send her to prison, what happened to Johnny Dean, what happened to the LDEA former Officer-in-Charge that the President just released of his post, what happened to the GLS company to the Roberts International Airport, the company that the drug allegedly passed through,” Representative Cole said.

He continued: “All of them should be behind bars but the government is still doing business with that company. And so, if the government conducts itself like that then we will say the government is selective and they are not fighting drug.”

The lawmaker also raised concerns about the role of Sheikh Bashiru Kante, who is identified in the Liberia National Police charge sheet and the Monrovia City Court writ of arrest as an alleged intermediary between Howard-Taylor and individuals investigators say were members of an alleged transnational cocaine-trafficking network. Those allegations have not been proven in court.

Questioning Kante’s credibility as a potential witness, Representative Cole said: “You can’t have Sheikh passing all around going to night clubs drinking champagne and trying to blackmail other people by giving information. How authentic that the information Sheikh is providing can be proven in court?”

He further argued that prosecutors must prove Madam Taylor knowingly participated in any criminal conduct.

“If Jewel participated, he must prove that Jewel knowing participated. It means that Sheikh has to prove that people were discussing cocaine business in Dubai and Jewel knew that cocaine business they were discussing about and she participated, he got to prove that.”

World.title: Boakai Warns Officials Against Procurement Breaches, Demands Fair Access to Government Contracts
World.content:
MONROVIA— President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has warned government officials against circumventing Liberia’s public procurement laws, stressing that state contracts and purchases must be conducted transparently to safeguard public resources and ensure qualified Liberians have a fair opportunity to do business with government.

By J.H. Webster [email protected]

President Boakai made the remarks Thursday during the opening of the 24th Cabinet Meeting in Monrovia, which focused on procurement and concessions.

The meeting was held under the theme, “Value for Money: Maximizing Fiscal Space through System Efficiency and Government Asset Security.”

The President acknowledged that procurement procedures can sometimes be lengthy and frustrating, particularly when government institutions need to purchase goods or obtain services.

However, he said the requirements are designed to protect public resources and should not be bypassed for convenience.

“Sometimes people get frustrated about all what you have to do to go through to buy this and buy that,” President Boakai said.

He added: “But just imagine if these things were not in place, and even if they are in place, that people there were not implementing them, the resources you are talking about, you will not have them.”

According to Boakai, strict compliance with procurement regulations is essential to preventing the misuse of state resources and ensuring that government contracts are awarded through fair and competitive processes.

He said procurement should not be viewed merely as an administrative requirement, but as an important accountability mechanism capable of expanding opportunities for Liberians while reducing perceptions of favoritism.

“When we say procurement in the sense of procurement, it helps with accountability. It helps with fair play in the market. It also helps with making sure that every citizen has access to rendering services to this country,” he said.

The President also challenged the perception that participating in government requires securing a government job, emphasizing that Liberians and local businesses can contribute to national development by supplying goods and services to public institutions.

“Participation in the government doesn’t mean that everybody will work with the government, but you can serve, you can provide goods and services,” the President stated.

Boakai stressed that access to government business must be determined by competition and established procedures rather than personal relationships, political influence or connections.

“To do that in a competitive society, you need to have a process by which everybody can have access without going around saying, well, they give it to their friend, they have this, they have that,” Boakai said.

The President’s remarks placed accountability and value for money at the center of the Cabinet’s discussions as his administration seeks to improve efficiency in public spending, strengthen the management of government assets and ensure that limited state resources produce greater benefits for citizens.

President Boakai also commended members of his Cabinet for their service, noting that public officials are often judged by their mistakes while their daily efforts receive limited recognition.

“People wait for the mistake you make, but we’re in leadership. So we watch and listen. We want to appreciate you very much,” he told Cabinet members.

World.title: Liberia: ANC Demands Independent Probe Into Narcotics Case, Warns Against Selective Justice
World.content:
Cllr Lafayette E. O. Gould, Chairman of the ANC.

Monrovia — The Alternative National Congress has called for an independent, transparent and impartial investigation into Liberia’s ongoing narcotics probe, warning the government against using the case to selectively target political opponents.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The ANC’s call follows the arrest of former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor amid investigations into a major transnational cocaine operation.

In a statement issued Monday, the opposition political movement said Howard-Taylor, as a former Vice President and opposition leader, is entitled to constitutional protections, dignity, due process and the presumption of innocence.

The ANC, in a statement issued by Secretariat, stressed that her political status should place her neither above nor beneath the law, arguing that allegations against her must be established in court rather than through “public spectacle, political maneuvering, or trial by media.”

The party said it supports efforts by the government and security authorities to uncover the full extent of narcotics networks operating within and through Liberia, describing the movement of large quantities of illegal drugs across the country’s borders as a threat to national security, public health and the future of Liberian youth.

However, the ANC warned that “justice must never be selective.”

The party expressed concern over what it described as a growing perception that the government is targeting individuals associated with the former Congress for Democratic Change (CDC), while questions about alleged involvement of individuals linked to the ruling Unity Party administration remain unresolved.

The ANC noted that the latest major drug bust occurred three years into the current administration and argued that authorities must investigate all individuals reasonably suspected of involvement, regardless of political affiliation or government position.

It also pointed to public comments by Liberia’s Inspector General of Police indicating that senior government officials had been implicated in the investigation.

“If the rule of law is to have meaning, then the law must pursue every person reasonably suspected of involvement—whether affiliated with the opposition, the ruling party, the security establishment, or any other institution—with the same vigor and impartiality,” the ANC said.

ANC Wants Entire Narcotics Network Exposed

The opposition group is demanding a comprehensive investigation aimed at identifying every individual or entity that may have financed, facilitated, protected, transported or otherwise participated in the alleged narcotics operations.

It said no political affiliation, government position, security role or personal connection should shield anyone from accountability.

At the same time, the ANC cautioned the government against turning criminal investigations into instruments of political competition.

“Political opponents must be defeated at the ballot box through superior ideas, competent leadership, and a convincing vision for Liberia—not through the weaponization or selective use of state institutions,” the statement said.

The ANC is therefore calling on the government to establish an independent and credible investigation, follow the evidence regardless of political affiliation or government status, apply the law equally and protect the constitutional rights of everyone under investigation.

The party also wants the government to provide the Liberian public with transparent answers about the scope of the narcotics operation and the identities of those responsible for facilitating it.

The ANC concluded with a direct message to the government: “Justice—not partisan politics—must direct the actions of the state.”

“No one is above the law, and no one is beneath its protection,” the statement added.

The statement was signed by ANC Secretary General Desmond U. Nimely and approved by National Chairman Cllr. Lafayette E.O. Gould.

World.title: Liberia: CDC Rebukes UP Secretary General, Demands Probe into 2023 Campaign Financing
World.content:
CDC Secretary General Jefferson Koijee (left) and UP Secretary General Amos Tweh.

Koijee challenges Amos Tweh to produce evidence of alleged CDC-cartel deal, raises questions over UAE travel and alleged campaign funding

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

Monrovia — The political battle between Liberia’s two largest political parties has intensified, with the opposition Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) sharply rebuffing allegations by ruling Unity Party Secretary General Amos Tweh that the former CDC administration entered an agreement with international drug cartels to use Liberia as a cocaine transshipment point.

The latest exchange comes amid an ongoing investigation into Liberia’s largest cocaine seizure and mounting political demands for transparency over alleged links between drug-trafficking networks, political actors and state institutions.

Tweh made the allegation during the dedication of the Unity Party’s Nimba District #7 headquarters in Saclepea, Nimba County, accusing the CDC administration of facilitating Liberia’s use as a transshipment route for cocaine destined for Europe and other parts of the world.

According to Tweh, the alleged arrangement was made in 2018, when the CDC came to power, and allowed international drug networks to become deeply entrenched in Liberia between 2018 and 2023.

He argued that the Boakai administration has demonstrated greater political will in combating narcotics trafficking, pointing to the arrest and prosecution of more than 30 people allegedly connected to drug-related offenses.

Tweh also cited the detention of former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor as evidence that the government is prepared to pursue suspects regardless of their political status.

He challenged the opposition’s criticism of the government’s drug crackdown, arguing that the CDC could not simultaneously demand aggressive action against drug traffickers while objecting when individuals associated with its political camp are investigated.

CDC: ‘THE MASK IS OFF’

But CDC Secretary General Jefferson Koijee has dismissed Tweh’s allegations as political hypocrisy and challenged the Unity Party official to produce evidence supporting his claim.

In a strongly worded response titled “The Mask Is Off!”, Koijee demanded that Tweh produce the alleged agreement between the CDC and international drug cartels.

“If Tweh has evidence that the CDC ‘signed a deal with Drug Cartels,’ let him produce the agreement, identify the cartel, name the signatories, state the date and place, and submit the evidence to investigators,” Koijee said.

He argued that without documentary evidence, Tweh’s allegation amounts to a political attempt to divert attention from questions surrounding the Unity Party and its leadership.

Koijee specifically called for an independent investigation into what he described as sponsored travel to the United Arab Emirates involving Tweh and Unity Party National Chairman Rev. Dr. J. Luther Tarpeh during the decisive period of the 2023 presidential campaign.

The CDC official alleged that the travel was linked to individuals and interests that the opposition has associated publicly with the cocaine investigation.

He also raised allegations involving President Joseph Boakai’s son, JoJo Boakai, demanding that he account for allegations and associations previously raised publicly in connection with what the CDC calls “Cocainegate.”

The allegations remain contested, and the CDC has not publicly established through a judicial finding that the individuals named were involved in cocaine trafficking or cartel activity.

CDC Demands Investigation into Alleged Campaign Funding

Koijee said the opposition’s demand for an independent investigation extends beyond the recent cocaine seizures to alleged financing of the 2023 political campaign.

He claimed the CDC has previously released what it considers documentary evidence concerning sponsored travel and alleged financial interests surrounding the Unity Party’s campaign.

Koijee called for investigators to establish who sponsored the travel, when and where meetings took place, and whether any individuals or entities connected to the alleged cocaine network provided financial support to the 2023 campaign.

He further referenced an alleged US$25 million in illicit campaign-related funding.

“The entire Government is involved,” Koijee alleged, while calling for investigators to follow the evidence wherever it leads.

‘Produce The Evidence’

The CDC Secretary General framed the dispute as a challenge to the Unity Party to substantiate its accusations rather than trade political claims.

He said the opposition would continue pressing for an independent investigation into alleged connections between political actors and drug-trafficking interests.

“We will continue to mount the pressure wherever it leads to,” Koijee said, adding that the CDC would pursue accountability for anyone it believes may have been compromised by alleged cocaine-cartel interests.

His response follows a broader call by the CDC for an independent investigation into transnational drug trafficking and allegations of cartel penetration of Liberia’s national security and state institutions.

Political Fight Over Cocaine Probe Deepens

The exchange between Tweh and Koijee further intensifies an already bitter political confrontation over Liberia’s cocaine crisis.

The Unity Party has portrayed the Boakai administration’s drug crackdown as evidence of political will and a commitment to equal application of the law.

The CDC, meanwhile, has accused the government of selectively prosecuting political opponents while failing to adequately investigate allegations involving individuals connected to the ruling establishment.

The latest confrontation has shifted the political debate from the handling of the cocaine seizures to questions surrounding campaign financing, international travel, alleged political-cartel connections and the integrity of Liberia’s security institutions.

At the heart of the dispute is a simple but consequential demand from both sides: produce the evidence.

While Tweh has accused the former CDC government of facilitating Liberia’s alleged emergence as a cocaine transshipment point, the CDC is demanding that he produce the agreement and documentary proof behind the accusation.

The opposition, in turn, wants an independent investigation into its allegations concerning the Unity Party’s 2023 campaign financing and alleged links to individuals implicated in the cocaine controversy.

With neither side backing down, the cocaine investigation is increasingly becoming a major political battleground ahead of Liberia’s next electoral cycle.

Secretary to the Cabinet, Patrick Kangwa, has confirmed that the venue for the forthcoming inauguration ceremony for the President-elect, Hakainde Hichilema, is ready for Tuesday, September 1st, 2026.

Speaking during his tour of Heroes Stadium, Mr Kangwa assured that he is impressed with the work done so far by all stakeholders.

Mr Kangwa thanked the combined inauguration committee for a job well done and for sticking to the planned organisation.

World.content:
The Board of Trustees and Members of State55-Afrikan have congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election as President of the Republic of Zambia, describing his victory as a testament to the confidence Zambians have in his leadership.

In a congratulatory message signed by Secretary General Oseni Adeoye and Vice President–Diaspora Baruti Katembo, the organisation said President Hichilema’s continued stewardship offers hope not only to Zambia but to the entire African continent at a time when Africa needs steady hands and bold ideas.

The Board said the win is a clear testament to the confidence people have in his leadership, vision and commitment to prosper all of the Zambian people.

The group reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening bonds of friendship, cooperation and mutual respect with the people of Zambia.

It expressed readiness to work with the President and his administration to advance shared goals of social and economic justice and good governance based on African peer mechanisms.

Further, State55-Afrikan said it believes President Hichilema can enhance the quest for African integration towards a federal state anchored on the ideology of pan-Africanism, by people participation.

The organisation extended the assurances of our highest consideration and best wishes for a successful tenure of office.

World.title: HRC committed to execute functions of the ATI Act
World.content:
The Human Rights Commission (HRC) has assured citizens that it remains committed to executing its oversight function of the Access to Information Act with independence, fairness, and strict adherence to the rule of law.

Speaking during the Access to Information (ATI) engagement meeting at Sali Riverside Resort in Mansa District in Luapula Province, Human Rights Commission Director General, Mbololwa Wamunyima noted that the commission has been designated as the oversight body for the Access to Information Act.

Ms Wamunyima, who was represented by the Commission’s Manager for Compliance and Legal Services, Chilambe Mpanga, stated that the HRC is mandated to ensure the enforcement of the right to access information is protected at all levels, regardless of prevailing circumstances.

“The right to access information in the country is not merely an administrative procedure but a fundamental right guaranteed by the Constitution and protected under Article 11 and other provisions enshrined therein,” he said.

Mr Mpanga explained that when information flows freely, it empowers citizens to hold public officials accountable and enables those officials to operate within the confines of the law.

“I therefore encourage everyone to be open as we engage during this interaction. This is regarded as a safe space to discuss the effective implementation of the right to access information by all citizens,” he added.

He further emphasised that access to information empowers journalists and Civil Society Organisations (CSOs) to verify and share accurate information with the public, thereby ensuring citizen participation in the governance structures of the country.

Meanwhile, Luapula Province Assistant Secretary, John Mwasha commended the Human Rights Commission for organising stakeholder engagement meetings.

“The Human Rights Commission has empowered us with knowledge and understanding of the ATI Act. When we return to our institutions, we will bear in mind that this Act exists to ensure openness, particularly in public institutions,” he said.

Mr Mwasha urged information officers to understand both the limitations and the extent of the information that should be shared with the public.

World.title: Chief Kazembe congratulations President Hichilema on re-election
World.content:
Chief Kazembe of the Chewa-speaking people in Lumezi District has congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema, on his re-election as Republican President in the recently held General Election.

Chief Kazembe said traditional leaders remain resolute in working with the Government of the day to promote development and improve the welfare of their communities.

He was speaking when Lumezi District Commissioner, retired Brigadier General, Patrick Mtonga, called on him at his palace in connection with the Eastern Province Jurisdiction Sustainable Landscape Project.

The traditional leader commended the Government for promoting sustainable forest management through the establishment of Community Forest Management Groups under the project.

Chief Kazembe said the initiative would contribute significantly to the conservation and sustainable management of forests while providing communities with opportunities to benefit from natural resources.

He said such developmental programmes should be supported by all stakeholders, adding that the traditional leadership will continue working closely with the Government to spearhead developmental activities in the area.

And the DC said the Government remains committed to working with traditional leaders in advancing development in Lumezi district.

Rtrd General Mtonga said traditional leaders and Government share a common responsibility of serving the interests of the people.

“We are all part of the Government because we do the same thing, which is serving the interests of our people. Hence, we remain partners in development with the traditional leadership,” he said.

He further described the Eastern Province Jurisdiction Sustainable Landscape Project as a vital intervention aimed at promoting sustainable development, protecting the environment and empowering communities with resources that contribute to their socio-economic development.

World.title: Govt. to strengthen cyber security capacity
World.content:
Ministry of Technology and Science, Permanent Secretary, Brilliant Habeenzu, says Government will continue to strengthen the country’s cyber security capacity.

And Dr Habeenzu says Government recognizes that a secure digital environment is fundamental to the success of Zambia’s digital transformation agenda.

Speaking in Lusaka today at the Fortinet Tech Seminar, Dr Habeenzu said the Ministry of Technology and Science has therefore sustained the strengthening of policy, legislative and institutional architecture for cyber security.

Dr Habeenzu cited the establishment of the Zambia Cyber Security Framework through the Cyber Security Act number 3 of 2025 and the Cyber Crimes Act number 4 of 2025, alongside the Data Protection Act in addition to the Electronic Communications and Transactions Framework.

He said Government , however, needs the help of the private sector in protecting the cyberspace.

“This brings me to the importance of the private sector. The Government can establish laws, policies and standards but the networks, data centres, financial systems, industrial control systems and digital platforms that constitute our economy are operated across both the public and private sectors,” Dr Habeenzu said.

Speaking at the same event, Micronics Consulting Limited, Managing Consultant, Michael Nabutali said digital infrastructure and operational systems have become increasingly connected across the country, a development that poses cyber risks.

“While this connectivity unlocks incredible efficiency and growth, it also exposes our enterprise networks and critical operational technology to evolving cyber risks,” Mr Nabutali observed.

World.title: Commonwealth, Morocco, Namibia Congratulate President Hichilema
World.content:
The Commonwealth, the Kingdom of Morocco and Republic of Namibia have congratulated President Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election as Republican President.

World.title: Kapiri Mposhi man killed by Elephant
World.content:
An attempt to capture a picture of a wandering elephant turned fatal when the jumbo suddenly charged at 53-year-old of Nalituba Village in Kapiri Mposhi District, Central Province.

Abel Mukuni was attempting to photograph the elephant with his mobile phone when it attacked him, killing him instantly.

The incident happened on August 26, 2026, at around 10:00 hours in Misiku Village in the Nalituba area, under Chief Chipepo’s Chiefdom.

Central Province Police Commanding Officer, Lemekani Chirwa confirmed that the deceased was standing about four meters from the elephant when it suddenly charged at him.

Mr Chirwa said the elephant struck Mr Mukuni with its trunk before trampling him thereby inflicting fatal injuries.

He said preliminary investigations suggest that the elephant had strayed from Lunga National Park in neighbouring Ngabwe District.

The Commanding Officer said officers from the Mpunde Patrol Unit responded to the scene and verified that Mr Mukuni had sustained multiple injuries consistent with an elephant attack.

He said the body has since been deposited at Kabwe Central Hospital mortuary, where a post-mortem examination is expected to be conducted.

Mr Chirwa said the Department of National Parks and Wildlife has been notified and is working to track the stray elephant.
