World.title: This house trumpets its history in the face of gentrification. Now it's a landmark
World.content:
This house trumpets its history in the face of gentrification. Now it's a landmark

toggle caption Beth LaBerge/KQED

The house is unmissable. Its colorful exterior, a painted forest of faces.

Latino artists, activists and musicians, suspended mid-motion, grin down at passersby. A spotted jaguar sprawls across the garage door. Around the border of one of its windows, a message is written in all-caps: "It takes the hood to save the hood."

This is the "Latin Rock House," an enduring tribute to the culture and history of the Mission District, one of San Francisco's oldest — and most dramatically gentrified — neighborhoods. Last month, San Francisco lawmakers unanimously declared the Latin Rock House a historic landmark, formally protecting the Spanish-style home from being painted over, altered or destroyed by future owners or developers without the city's permission. The house has been the site of jam sessions and musical creation, community festivals and celebrations and ongoing efforts to engage the city's youth in music. It's also a home, where Richard and Tammy Segovia live.

Sponsor Message

"Now we can say this piece of the city is ours," said owner Richard Segovia, 72, a fifth-generation San Franciscan who was born and raised in the Mission.

"This is for us," he said. "Our culture. Our music. Our people. It's amazing."

Among San Francisco's more than 300 historic landmarks — including the Golden Gate Bridge and colonial-era Mission Dolores church — there are several residences. Most are traditional in style or notable for the historic events that happened within. The city's most recognizable historic homes may be the row of pastel Victorians known as the Painted Ladies, which were included in the opening credits of the sitcom Full House.

None look like Segovia's house of Latin rock.

In a neighborhood that has seen decades of redevelopment, skyrocketing home prices and the displacement of thousands of Latino families, this mural-wrapped home is more than a marker of the Mission's cultural vibrancy. It's a stake in the ground, Segovia said. A sign to tourists and transplants of what this neighborhood has long represented.

"This house is like the whole neighborhood. You see it from the outside and you think wow, such a beautiful painting," Segovia said. "But then you come inside and you spend some time and you realize all the culture and history that was built here."

A changing neighborhood

The Mission District is one of San Francisco's oldest enclaves. Originally the homeland of the Ohlone Indians, the Mission was taken over by Spanish settlers in the 1700s and so named after the Catholic church at its center, now known as Mission Dolores.

Sponsor Message

In the centuries that followed, the Mission went from Mexican farmland to immigrant stronghold as waves of working-class European families moved into the neighborhood following the Gold Rush in the mid-1800s. After the great San Francisco fire of 1906 wiped out much of the city's downtown, the Mission transformed into a commercial district. Over the next several decades, Mexican American families poured in and set down roots.

In 1950, only about 11% of Mission residents would have been considered Latino, according to the California Migration Museum, but by the 1970s, that number had swelled to nearly half.

toggle caption Beth LaBerge/KQED

Segovia's family moved into the house in 1963. He was 10 years old.

"I've seen all of the changes this neighborhood has been through — the good, bad and ugly — and now? My god, I wouldn't even be able to afford to live here today" had he not inherited his home from his parents, Segovia said.

The tech boom that began in the 1990s brought waves of new residents to the city and sent home prices soaring. Eviction rates jumped and some community centers and shops that served a primarily Latino population closed.

Supervisor Jackie Fielder, who represents the Mission neighborhood in San Francisco's legislature, said the area has lost more than 12,000 Latino residents over the last 25 years.

Up and down the block where Segovia's house sits, property values have soared close to $2 million. The Mexican American family that used to live next door, he said, is gone. Graywashed modern homes, like the one next door, have replaced houses painted bright blues and yellows, a stark contrast to the vibrant palette of the neighborhood.

"There's this thing that happens with gentrification where the newcomers tend to ignore whatever conversation is happening in a place aesthetically or culturally because they don't feel like they have to participate," said Sergio De La Torre, a professor at the University of San Francisco who has studied the demographic change happening in the Mission. "In a neighborhood where these gray, muted houses have really multiplied, this guy is doing the exact opposite. This is the other extreme. It's as loud as a house can be."

Sponsor Message

Fielder said she was struck with the idea to landmark the Latin Rock House during a community event there earlier this year.

"It's owned by a native San Franciscan, and it's beloved by the community," she said. "Seeing the mural for myself, seeing the over 87 musicians painted on there alongside traditional Chicano and Aztec motifs, I was like, wow, we have to preserve this. So, that's when we got to work."

San Francisco is the historic birthplace of Latin rock, Fielder added.

As psychedelic rock took over the city in the 1960s, Latino artists blended it with Afro-Cuban beats and percussive sounds more commonly found in jazz and salsa. Artists like Carlos Santana distinguished the genre and brought it to a worldwide audience.

Segovia, a percussionist, has always filled his home with music – playing impromptu concerts for the neighborhood out of open garage doors or inviting friends and fellow musicians over to jam. Eventually, he retrofitted his childhood bedroom into a recording studio.

The cover art for Santana's 1999 record, Supernatural, was created inside Segovia's home, he said.

'I'm holding down my roots'

The petition to preserve Segovia's house was recommended by the Historic Preservation Commission and approved unanimously by the city's legislature after supporters and neighbors testified before the board, lauding its impact and cultural significance to the community.

"What this kind of landmarking does is preserve this part of the neighborhood that has been subject to a lot of displacement and gentrification," Fielder said, adding "it's to preserve an irreplaceable piece of San Francisco's Latino heritage and musical history."

But to some, the preservation effort is a superficial solution to an underlying problem: the erasure of culture and the ongoing displacement of Latino families.

De La Torre, who also lives in the neighborhood, sees the historic designation as lip service: a superficial attempt to preserve the culture and community of the Mission, instead of tackling issues that vex families who live there day in and day out.

toggle caption Beth LaBerge/KQED

Among the things the neighborhood would stand to benefit from, De La Torre said, are financial and legal support for street vendors who keep the commerce district alive, drug treatment programs, and housing assistance.

Sponsor Message

"They could work on more social programs for kids, for example, but they're not doing that," De La Torre said. "It's an easy way out to commit to this thing, to say we care about you guys and we're going to give you things to keep the Latin Rock House alive, but nothing else."

Segovia's house didn't always look like this.

Ten years ago, Segovia received a grant from the California Art Commission to paint a mural on the exterior of his home.

"That's when I decided to make my house the House of Latin rock," Segovia said. "I'm letting the new techie generation know that I'm not going anywhere. I'm holding down my roots."

The walls commemorate artists that have made their mark on the genre, like Santana and jazz percussionist Pete Escovedo, as well as civil rights activists like Dolores Huerta.

Inside the house, new artists are still being molded.

Bands like the all-female salsa group Agua Pura and the young Los Jefes have taken up unofficial residencies in Segovia's home, using his instruments, recording booths and expertise in the industry to help shape their own sound.

Segovia's wife, Tammy, brings them snacks as they jam.

For musicians like Rebecca Rodriguez, 26, the Latin Rock House is a second home, a safe place to experiment and grow as an artist.

"It's just this magical musical house," said Rodriguez, the band leader of Agua Pura. "It's like a museum, but a museum that's still so alive."

On the walls of the performance space are the name and signatures of artists who have come through the house. Rodriguez said she and her bandmates have added their names. So, too, have members of Los Jefes, who were only in high school when they started working together on their first EP at the house.

Sponsor Message

To have their names on the walls, Rodriguez said, feels like being part of something bigger than just the house. It feels like making a mark on the culture, the music she loves and, now, the city itself.

World.title: The Social Security trust fund is running out, and yet it's not a top campaign issue
World.content:
The Social Security trust fund is running out, and yet it's not a top campaign issue

toggle caption Bryan Dozier/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images

Congress has about six years to shore up the Social Security trust fund, which is expected to run out of reserves by the end of 2032.

Enacting a solution is liable to be a significant political battle, likely involving cutting benefits for some Americans or raising taxes on higher earners, or both.

And so far, congressional leaders haven't made it a top-tier issue.

Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno proposed raising the payroll tax for some Americans. Revenues from the tax go into the trust fund. But that bipartisan effort was immediately panned by conservative groups, and little else has emerged as a serious solution.

Sponsor Message

This limited public discussion has created a separate concern, experts warn: that most Americans don't fully understand the problems Social Security faces — let alone be able to weigh in on solutions to the coming shortfall.

"There is a lot of misunderstanding about what all of this even means," Bill Sweeney, senior vice president for government affairs at AARP, told NPR.

Sweeney's group conducted a poll last year that found that just 34% of those surveyed correctly explained that when the trust fund runs out, Social Security will still be able to make payments, but just at a reduced rate.

"That's a failing grade," he said. "So, we've got a lot of work to do, even on just general education about what it means when the Social Security insolvency date happens."

Another 36% of respondents incorrectly believe that when the trust fund is depleted, Social Security would be unable to pay any benefits at all.

Kick the can

If Congress fails to act, payments are expected to be 22% lower, which could be devastating for the millions of seniors who rely on their Social Security benefits to pay for basic necessities.

Sweeney said getting Congress to focus on the Social Security trust fund will be tough because so much else demands their immediate attention.

Sponsor Message

"And so I'm not super confident that they're going to clear the decks and focus on something that's six years away," he said. "It's not very long for regular folks, but for Congress, it can be almost a lifetime."

Sweeney is also concerned that Social Security isn't coming up on the campaign trail, particularly among Senate candidates, who serve six-year terms.

"The people who we elect to the United States Senate in November are almost certainly going to be the ones in the Senate in 2032 deciding what to do with people's Social Security," he said. "And the fact that it's not coming up very often in the debates or in the questions I think is a serious failing. I think we've got to really work on that."

Andrew Biggs, a senior fellow with the American Enterprise Institute, a right-leaning think tank in Washington, said the key problem with Social Security reform is that Congress has the option to do nothing.

"There's no requirement that Congress act at any given time," he said. "They can always choose to kick the can down the road. So you get this cycle where the worse the problem gets, the less Congress wants to talk about it."

What voters don't know

Rich Thau, president of messaging firm Engagious, has been moderating focus groups with swing voters for years. And for the past three months he has asked these voters what they understand about the trust fund's insolvency issues.

Most know very little. He said both major parties need to start doing a better job of educating the public about what is on the table.

"It's impossible for there not to be buy-in from voters in order to get something done," Thau said. "Someone has to pay. And you can't cut benefits without people noticing. You can't increase … taxes without people noticing. So if there isn't buy-in and an acceptance of the looming crisis in Social Security, it's impossible to fix this."

Sponsor Message

Thau said most voters don't understand the basics of the financial challenges Social Security faces, or how the program works. And a lot of individuals, he said, conflate the coming insolvency issues related to the trust fund with longer-term — and long-running — fears that Social Security will not be there for them when they are ready to retire.

Margaret M., 58, participated in one of these focus groups in Pennsylvania. She, like all other participants, agreed to take part on the condition that her last name would not be used.

When asked what currently ails Social Security, she was among those who said she wasn't sure it would be available to her.

"I'm worried not only for myself, but for my son. Is there going to be anything there to help myself or, as I said, my son when it comes time for retirement?" Margaret said. "Luckily, I have some investments put aside, but not everybody does, and they count on that money to live."

Chuck Marr, vice president for federal tax policy at the left-leaning Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, said there's been a longstanding underestimation of the strength of Social Security that he said "has been instilled much too deeply than it deserves."

However, he said, if some of the insolvency issues are dealt with in the coming years, some longer-term anxieties among voters might also go away.

"This will be a way to show people the strength of Social Security," he said. "If you get the Congress on a bipartisan basis … to step up and face the issues."

Benefit cuts vs. eliminating the tax cap

But first, Marr said, voters will need to understand what solutions Congress is considering to address the program's insolvency.

For now, the main considerations are cutting benefits for wealthier Americans or eliminating the cap on Social Security's payroll tax. Currently, wages are only taxed up to $184,500. Eliminating the tax cap would require that all workers, regardless of their salary, pay the same tax rate across the board.

Sponsor Message

Marr said he thinks voters will eventually play a big role in making sure lawmakers don't choose benefit cuts over tax changes.

"I think the public awareness will be critical, and I think it will be there as far as pushing lawmakers not to accept across-the-board, huge cuts in benefits," he said.

AEI's Biggs said fixing a budget shortfall of hundreds of billions of dollars will be a shock to voters, no matter what path lawmakers take.

"To fix that fire, raising taxes would be the largest tax increase in peacetime in U.S. history," he told NPR. "To fix it by reducing benefits would cut benefits by over 20%. To address it by issuing new debt might be more debt than the financial markets are willing to swallow. That could trigger higher interest rates and inflation."

Voters are leaning toward raising taxes on higher earners

So far, AARP's Sweeney said, voters seem significantly more open to raising taxes on some Americans.

"It seems very unfair that somebody who makes, you know, $800,000 a year is paying a smaller percentage of their taxes to Social Security than someone who makes $60,000 or $75,000 a year," he said. "So, I think that that is, you know, without a doubt, the most popular of the options out there."

In his focus groups, Thau has explained proposed solutions to Social Security's insolvency to dozens of voters. Most were hearing the ideas for the first time.

And Thau has found consistent feedback from voters on various options.

When it comes to cutting benefits for upper-middle-class and wealthier retirees, Thau said he has found "close to a 50/50 split."

"Some people think it's reasonable because wealthy people can afford it," he said. "Other people think it's not reasonable because wealthy people paid in and they should just get the benefits back that they deserve."

Sponsor Message

When it comes to eliminating the tax cap, though, Thau said "nearly universally over the last three months, respondents have been in favor of eliminating that cap."

"For them, it's a matter of fairness," he added.

One of those voters was Eric V., a 51-year-old Republican living in Pennsylvania. He was among many voters who learned in the focus group how the payroll tax was structured.

"I always heard and got told growing up, the more you make, the more you get taxed," he told Thau. To "get taxed the same as somebody that's getting a tiny bit of what you make, that's just crazy."

World.title: A melting glacier contributed to the deadly Nepal floods. We can expect more like this
World.content:
A melting glacier contributed to the deadly Nepal floods. We can expect more like this

Loading...

More than a thousand people are missing and at least 400 people are dead after flash flooding tore through Nepal and Tibet early Wednesday. According to initial assessments, a massive chunk of ice snapped off a glacier and tumbled thousands of feet into the valley below. Rock, ice and mud plunged down for miles, washing away communities along the river.

Scientists say glaciers in this region, and around the world, are increasingly unstable because of human-caused global warming. Across the mountains of Nepal and Tibet, climate change is causing glaciers to melt at an alarming rate.

Planet-heating emissions from burning fossil fuels such as oil, gas and coal are the primary driver of climate change. Scientists say that in addition to reducing climate pollution, renewable energy and battery technologies are increasingly price competitive with traditional energy sources.

toggle caption Niranjan Shrestha/AP

"There's no question that this event was made more likely because of climate change and that we're seeing more likely other similar glacier hazards occurring," says Twila Moon, deputy lead scientist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center at the University of Colorado Boulder.

Footage from the Chinese-administered Tibet side of the border with Nepal shared on local media showed a massive gush of water sweeping over a port building as people fled.

Sponsor Message

Loading...

As the water barrelled down, residents filmed it sweeping away a bridge and washing away riverside settlements.

The flooding was made more severe because it happened during the heavy rains of the monsoon season, says Mohammad Farooq Azam, an expert at ICIMOD, an environmental advocacy group that focuses on Asia's high mountains. "Everything is fully saturated already," Azam said. "The rivers are swollen."

This flood is part of a trend, said Arun Bhakta Shrestha, an expert on climate change and the Himalayan glaciers.

toggle caption Niranjan Shrestha/AP

"If you look at the whole Hindu Kush Himalayan region," he said, "it seems like the frequency, the types of those hazards are increasing." Shrestha said everything points to climate change as the reason.

The world will see "more and more events like this," says Alton Byers, a faculty research scientist at the Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research at the University of Colorado Boulder. "Things are getting warmer," he says.

Permafrost on the mountains, the continuously frozen soil and sediment, is now changing, said Byers. He uses the analogy of a stick of butter left out of the refrigerator. "It's going to get softer," he says. "And it's going to lose its structural integrity."

Preliminary reports indicate that Nepal's flood warning system wasn't equipped to handle these floods. That's despite significant government investment in flood warning systems over the last decade in Nepal. Many flood-prone valleys in the country have warning alarms, but as NPR has reported, the government has struggled to keep up with the cost of maintaining the systems.

NPR's Rebecca Hersher contributed to this reporting.

World.title: Canada's economy grew by 3.3% in the second quarter, showing sharp recovery
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's economy rebounded sharply in the second quarter, thanks to a jump in exports and stronger domestic investment, according to Statistics Canada data.

The economy grew at an annualized rate of 3.3 per cent in the second quarter, following an upwardly revised 0.3 per cent in the first quarter, Statistics Canada said. For the month of June, GDP was up 0.3 per cent.

With the first-quarter revision, which ​was previously a slight contraction, Canada was not in a technical ​recession, which is usually two consecutive quarters of contraction.

Exports rose 3.6 per cent according to the data agency, largely because of higher auto exports.

Residential investment also helped boost the economy, as did investment by business owners, who spent more on machinery and equipment in the second quarter. Business capital investment was up 2.3 per cent in the second quarter, snapping a streak of five consecutive quarters of decline.

World.title: Lake formed from debris poses new threat in Nepal, with death toll from floods over 530
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Teams from around the world are pouring into Nepal and Tibet to help rescuers find survivors of a catastrophic flash flood, as more video footage reveals the extent of the disaster.

Rescuers worked through mud and debris Friday in areas devastated by a catastrophic flash flood along the Himalayan border between Nepal and China, continuing the search for hundreds of people still missing as the death toll rose and authorities warned that a newly formed, overflowing lake could trigger further flooding.

Nepalese and Chinese authorities warned of further flooding from a lake that formed upstream after Wednesday's disaster and was already overflowing. They urged people in potentially affected areas to move to safer ground.

Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority says the death toll has risen to 538, while the number of missing people remained at 977 and 3,742 people have been rescued.

Nepali police later put the death toll at 547. At least three people were killed in Tibet.

The missing include tourists from several countries. Global Affairs Canada has said it was aware of 30 Canadian citizens and permanent residents unaccounted for, though it warned the number could fluctuate in the days ahead given the communication challenges in remote areas.

Residents salvage belongings from their destroyed home following flash floods on Friday in Devighat, Nepal. (Ezra Acayan/Getty Images)

Nepalese army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet told The Associated Press that a team had been deployed Friday to the Upper Trishuli-1 Hydropower Project near the Nepal-China border following reports that people were trapped inside a tunnel.

"It is complicated to find the entry and exit points of the tunnel because everything has been covered by mud," Basnet said. "Our first priority is rescuing the stranded people."

People check names of their relatives rescued from villages affected by flash floods in Nepal's Nuwakot district. (Rajesh Kumar Singh/The Associated Press)

Red Cross officials, at a news conference in Switzerland, expressed concern about a secondary flood and said that the organization's rescue operations were temporarily halted after trucks with relief supplies were were blocked ⁠ by further flooding.

"We believe that at ​least 93,000 people have been ​affected and are in great need," said David Fisher, head of delegation for the International Federation ​of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies ⁠in Nepal.

Nepal's Foreign Ministry said on Friday that it appreciated the offers of help from several countries ‌with nationals missing amid the disaster but that it was able to manage the rescue efforts at present.

Flood survivors, including injured people, were taken to Kathmandu and other locations.

The affected areas are popular with hikers and for pilgrimages to religious sites.

Vishnuram Ramaswamy works at a private company in the southern Indian city of Puducherry and said that he last spoke to his mother and two sisters who were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash on Wednesday morning at 9 a.m.

"This was the first time they had gone on this pilgrimage and it was something my mother always wanted to do," he said.

Survivor sees 'black storm'

Customs officer Karbir Gaire is among some of the survivors in Timure, the closest Nepalese village to the border with Tibet.

Gaire reached his office around 8 a.m. on Wednesday and was busy working on his computer when he first felt the ground shake.

"Right after the shake, I noticed a black storm coming towards us," he recalled from Kathmandu, where he is back with family. "We all immediately started running out, and within a few seconds, we were climbing uphill on the opposite side of our office building. I think those 10 or so seconds saved some of us."

The disaster started with a glacier collapse that sent ice and rock flowing downstream, and which registered as a magnitude-5.2 seismic event at the U.S. Geological Survey.

The science behind Nepal's catastrophic flash floods | Duration 2:03 An entire river valley along the Nepal border was wiped out in seconds — but local radar showed no rain, and it wasn't an earthquake. CBC meteorologist Johanna Wagstaffe breaks down how a massive glacier collapse triggered a violent inland tsunami, and why geologists warn this unfolding climate disaster isn't over yet.

Gaire doesn't remember exactly how many people were in the office when the disaster struck, but his 15 colleagues have gone missing.

"It was like a Hollywood movie scene. I don't call it a flood, it was a tsunami," he said.

Gaire described Timure as a vibrant place filled with government offices, hotels, cafes, banks, primary schools, tea shops and residential buildings, where more than 1,500 people were living.

World.title: How teen accounts on Instagram and Facebook are changing after Meta's $18B US settlement
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Changes are coming for teen users of social media platforms Instagram and Facebook.

Parent company Meta agreed this week to make platform design changes for young users and pay up to $18 billion US over the next decade to resolve claims of online harms to youth stemming from nearly every U.S. state and territory.

A coalition of U.S. attorneys general have described it as the largest state consumer protection settlement in history outside of the Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s.

"The writing is on the wall for the social media industry. This is their tobacco moment," said Canadian tech analyst Carmi Levy.

"Things change for Meta and other companies like it from this point forward."

What's changing for teens?

New measures are coming for the Instagram and Facebook accounts of users under 18, including:

Time limits and pauses: a default time limit of two hours daily across both platforms in total, plus prompts and pauses after 15, 60 and 90 minutes of continuous use to disrupt "endless scrolling."

a default time limit of two hours daily across both platforms in total, plus prompts and pauses after 15, 60 and 90 minutes of continuous use to disrupt "endless scrolling." Blackout periods: blocks on most usage between midnight and 6 a.m. and notifications muted between the general school hours of 8 a.m. and 3 p.m. (excluding security or safety alerts).

blocks on most usage between midnight and 6 a.m. and notifications muted between the general school hours of 8 a.m. and 3 p.m. (excluding security or safety alerts). More control over feeds: the ability to choose a non-algorithmic feed by default (along with periodic reminders about this feature) and being able to switch off autoplaying content.

the ability to choose a non-algorithmic feed by default (along with periodic reminders about this feature) and being able to switch off autoplaying content. Limits to social comparison features: hiding "like" counts/reactions and blocking "extreme makeup" filters.

hiding "like" counts/reactions and blocking "extreme makeup" filters. Stronger age verification and age-related content restrictions.

Meta says it will continue existing work blocking strangers from contacting teen accounts and improve reporting tools and parental controls.

It also vowed to toughen some of its new measures — for instance, further reducing the daily time limit to one hour — if rival social platforms Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube also adopted comparable ones.

WATCH | A turning point for social media?: Could Meta’s $18B settlement change social media forever? | Duration 2:33 Meta Platforms agreed to pay up to $18 billion US as part of a settlement to resolve claims brought by states across the United States that the company designed the apps to get children addicted to them, misled consumers about their ‌safety and improperly collected the personal data of children who used its platforms.

Does this affect Canadian teens too?

Technically the settlement applies to the U.S. market — and American teens should expect to see these changes in the next few months, Levy says — but teens everywhere should get ready. Levy says these tweaks will likely spread wider given the concern in so many countries about negative social media impacts on youth.

"Historically, whenever technology companies like Meta introduce significant changes to their infrastructure in a certain region, eventually they do go global," he said from London, Ont.

"I would expect over time Canada will see these changes as well. It's a lot easier for these companies to maintain a common set of tools and features around the world than to have unique features for each country where they do business."

WATCH | What Meta's settlement means for Canada: What could the Meta settlement in California mean for Canada? | Duration 5:35 Meta agreed to a $16.68-billion US settlement over claims it designed its social media platforms such as Facebook and Instagram to make them addictive to children. The settlement was reached Wednesday during a California federal trial. Tech analyst and journalist Carmi Levy breaks down the settlement and what it could mean for Canada.

Does this make social media safer?

The settlement is a step in the right direction, says Jenny Perez, mom of a middle-schooler and founder of the parental advocacy group Unplugged Canada. Yet she sees a much longer list of safety concerns for social media companies to tackle.

Adding a few measures to address what kids experience "is somewhat helpful, but doesn't fix the fact that these products are addictive," she said from Vancouver.

Digital media expert Richard Lachman lauds the interruption to infinite scrolling — a time-suck that's not unlike what researchers of gambling addiction explore, he noted. Yet the computer scientist and digital media professor at Toronto Metropolitan University says he'd rather not solely rely on what a company says it's doing to make itself safer.

"Right now we have Meta's designers saying 'These are the steps we're going to take. Trust us,'" Lachman said. "I would be much happier with an independent, third-party [review]."

WATCH | Meta strikes settlement of up to $18B US in multi-state lawsuit: Meta agrees to platforms changes, pay up to $18B US to settle lawsuit | Duration 4:02 Meta has agreed to pay up to $18 billion US to settle a major lawsuit launched by several U.S. states over social media addiction and security for children. The tech giant has also agreed to make changes to its platforms, including Facebook and Instagram.

Luke Stark, an associate professor of information and media studies at Western University, says the announced measures will help stem some compulsive social media use by teens. Yet he pointed out the measures are limited, noting for instance that older users are also drawn in by addictive platform design.

"These systems affect everybody," he said from London, Ont.

Though Stark calls the settlement "a big example — of which there are not very many — of Meta changing its design under threat of legal action," he thinks it could have gone further.

"The general business model of Facebook hasn't really been touched by this."

What does this mean for proposed regulations in Canada?

Thousands of U.S. state and federal lawsuits still face Meta, Snap (parent of the platform Snapchat), Alphabet (YouTube) and ByteDance (TikTok), but American cases must be considered very differently from those in Canada or internationally, said Toronto tech analyst Ritesh Kotak.

Still, he thinks this week could be a hint of what's to come. "Meta may consider settling and just ending some of these lawsuits once and for all."

The decision to settle "indicates to me that Meta understands that it's got a problem and that it has to kind of get ahead of any kind of regulatory effort," said David Fewer, a law professor at the University of Ottawa.

Fewer suggests Meta's moves could pave the way to fulfilling requirements for Canada's proposed online safety legislation, though there's still "a lot more regulatory clay" to work with, he said, like Canadian calls to tackle addictive algorithm design. "We shouldn't mistake what Meta can live with, with what Canadians deserve."

Back in Toronto, Lachman thinks Meta is eager to resolve its social media woes so as to shift its attention to artificial intelligence.

"They want this to go away so they can focus on AI," he said.

"They don't want to be mired in this. And even though $10, 15, 20 billion US sounds like a lot of money to us, in the size of the potential market for its AI ambitions, with the reach they have into regular daily use by billions of people around the world, this is where [CEO Mark Zuckerberg] wants to play."

World.title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as 'Lake America'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing the interior secretary to rename Lake Ontario to 'Lake America,' as the trade war with Canada continues.

U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Thursday to change the name of Lake Ontario to "Lake America" as tensions with Canada worsen.

Sitting near a map with the name "Lake America" over the body of water, Trump said "entitled" Canada has been difficult to deal with and repeated claims the country was ripping off the United States.

"They want to be treated like a state, but they are not a state," Trump said.

When asked why he was targeting American allies with these types of actions instead of American adversaries, Trump said, "they haven't treated us well."

"The Canadian officials have treated us very badly," Trump said. "They are nasty people."

A map labelling Lake Ontario as 'Lake America' is seen behind U.S. President Donald Trump as he speaks in the Oval Office of the White House on Thursday. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Tensions between the two countries have escalated since trade negotiations fell apart on Friday. Both countries have accused each other of implementing 11th-hour changes.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the agreement became untenable. The federal government unveiled its retaliatory measures, set to go in place on Sept. 8.

Trump first threatened to rename the body of water during an escalating war of words with Ontario Premier Doug Ford.

The two exchanged insults, with Ford calling the president a bully, among other things, and Trump saying the premier was a "less charismatic, intelligent" version of his late brother, Rob.

Boats float on Lake Ontario Tuesday with Toronto's skyline seen in the background. (Adrian Kraus/The Associated Press)

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum — who previously was governor of border state North Dakota — posted on social media "the places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States."

He said he's proud to enact the name change.

'Real foolishness'

In Canada, the move prompted incredulity by officials on social media.

Carney said Canadians will call the body of water Lake Ontario "now and always," while Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said "we're into some real foolishness now."

"It's Lake Ontario, buddy," Houston said.

At an unrelated news conference in Winnipeg, Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew described the situation as an over-the-hill rock star playing old hits at a casino.

"I think that's the part of Donald Trump's presidency we're at now," Kinew said.

"He thought he had a real hit, a real golden oldie with the Gulf of Mexico, and he's trying to bring back that, and he's trying to play the hits for his base. But I think everybody here thinks it's a little sad and it's not his best work."

WATCH | Could his trade war backfire on Trump?: Where Trump’s trade war with Canada could backfire | About That | Duration 2:47 Avneet Dhillon explains how Canada is targeting imports from specific U.S. states with its dollar-for-dollar retaliation against President Donald Trump's 50 per cent tariffs, and how the counter-tariffs could have an impact in key battleground states ahead of the midterm elections. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Lake Ontario — one of the five Great Lakes — is located between Ontario and New York. The province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.

The lake's name comes from the Huron Indigenous people's word "oniatarí:io," which means "lake of shining waters."

Carney said on social media that the name is more than 400 years old, and predates both Canada and the U.S. as countries.

Gulf of Mexico saga

Last year, Trump signed an executive order to change the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America.

It only applies to U.S. federal documents and geographic services, but some online map services also made the change.

The geographic controversy led to the White House removing The Associated Press from certain duties covering the president after the news service did not use "Gulf of America" in its reporting.

The Associated Press took the White House to court in a dust-up that led to Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt ripping many authorities away from the White House Correspondents' Association, the organization of journalists who cover the president.

How are you responding to the tariff war between the United States and Canada? How is it affecting you?

World.title: King Harald V, Norway's reform-minded head of state, dead at 89
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Norway's King Harald, a reformer who emerged from the shadow of his well-loved, extrovert father over more than three decades on the throne, died on Friday at the age of 89, the royal palace said, at a time of multiple crises for the Norwegian royal family.

"King Harald passed away peacefully at Oslo University Hospital on Friday 28 August, 0635 (local time, 0435 GMT)," the royal palace said on its website.

Harald, who was Europe's oldest living monarch, was taken to hospital on August 17. The palace said he was being treated for a bacterial infection in his blood.

In 2024, he had been hospitalized for an infection while on holiday in Malaysia and received a temporary pacemaker at a hospital there. He was flown back home by the Norwegian armed forces and later fitted with a permanent device.

That same year, Harald, Norway's ceremonial head of state since 1991, said he would reduce the number of official engagements in which he took part but ruled out abdication, insisting that his oath as king was for life.

People gather outside the Royal Palace Friday morning, following the death of Norway's King Harald, in Oslo. (Dylan Martinez/Reuters)

Harald's death comes at a tumultuous time for the royal family.

Crown Princess Mette-Marit, married to Harald's son Crown Prince Haakon, is facing intense scrutiny for her friendship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, a relationship for which she has apologized.

Her son Marius Hoiby, born from a relationship predating her marriage to Haakon, was found guilty in June of ​two out of four counts of rape and one count of domestic violence and sentenced to four years in prison after a seven-week trial. Both he and the prosecution have appealed the sentence.

Royal family under scrutiny

Two days after Marius was convicted, the palace said Mette-Marit had undergone a successful lung transplant, without specifying when the procedure took place.

After several weeks of recovery in hospital, she returned home and celebrated her silver wedding anniversary with Haakon in August.

Support for the monarchy dropped to 60 per cent in February 2026, from 70 per cent the previous month, according to a Norstat poll published by public broadcaster NRK, rising slightly to 64 per cent in May.

Harald had constantly remained popular with Norwegians. According to the February poll, he was the royal who best represented the Norwegian royal family, with a note of 9.2, on a scale of 1 to 10.

Descendant of Queen Victoria

A great-great-grandchild of Britain's Queen Victoria, Harald acceded to the throne in 1991 and slowly introduced modern touches that brought a ceremonial post seen mainly as a symbol of national independence into the 21st century.

King Harald and Queen Sonja of Norway at the Milano Speed Skating Stadium during the Milano-Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan, Italy, in February 2026. (NTB/Heiko Junge/Reuters)

The popular king played a crucial role comforting the nation in times of mourning.

When far-right, anti-Islam fanatic Anders Behring Breivik killed 77 people in 2011 in Oslo and on Utoeya island, the king consoled the nation with a powerful televised speech. His voice trembling with emotion, he said that "freedom is stronger than fear."

After floods, storms and other disasters, he would travel to the scene wearing rubber boots and a well-worn jacket to meet those who had lost homes or loved ones.

Embraced openness

Late in life he spoke up for tolerance, declaring in a 2016 speech that Norwegians could have many backgrounds, beliefs and sexual orientations.

In November 2005, Harald and his wife, Sonja Haraldsen, invited 550 Norwegians to a ball to celebrate the centenary of the country's independence from Sweden.

Harald said in an interview at the time that Europe's royal families should not be tempted to reverse moves towards openness and retreat to their palace towers.

"If you've opened the gate it's very difficult to close it again," he told Reuters. "I'm not sure I'd want to close it. So far so good, as far as I'm concerned."

World.title: Why Lindsay Clancy, on trial for the deaths of her 3 children, has so many supporters
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This article contains details about violence against children and suicide.

Outside the Massachusetts courtroom where Lindsay Clancy is on trial in connection with the deaths of her three children — she doesn't deny that she killed them, but jurors must decide if she's criminally responsible — Clancy's supporters have gathered again.

On Thursday, ahead of the closing arguments, they were again dressed in pink. Once again, they were mostly women. And just like during their previous gatherings and in the discourse happening online, a similar message emerged: new moms need help, and they aren't getting it.

"As a physician myself, I’ve been on both sides of this coin when women are dismissed for our concerns, and it’s not fair," supporter Marta Quijano told The Associated Press outside the Plymouth County Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Thursday.

"I don’t think people really understand unless they’ve been through it," said Danielle Buckley, who drove five hours from Maine to watch the closing arguments.

"They just want to see her be punished for what happened to her children."

Aimee Breault of Acushnet, Mass., livestreams a demonstration Thursday in support of Clancy outside the Plymouth Superior Court where she's on trial. (Josh Reynolds/The Associated Press)

Clancy, 36, is accused of killing her three children in 2023 while her then-husband was running an errand. Jurors have heard that Clancy strangled Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and eight-month-old Callan with exercise bands in the basement of their home in the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then attempted to take her own life by jumping out of a second-floor window, which left her paralyzed.

Clancy's defence doesn't dispute the killings. But they argue she isn't criminally responsible because she had bipolar disorder and was suffering from postpartum psychosis, a rare and little-understood mental health condition that can affect a new mom's sense of reality.

Prosecutors argue Clancy is guilty of three counts of first-degree murder, because she plotted to get her husband out of the house so she could carry out the killings.

On Thursday, after lawyers finished their closing arguments in the month-long trial , jurors started their deliberations.

If convicted, Clancy faces life in prison without parole. If she's found not guilty due to lack of criminal responsibility, or by reason of insanity, she would be committed to a state psychiatric hospital.

WATCH | Trial puts spotlight on maternal mental health: The Lindsay Clancy trial and maternal mental health | Duration 2:13 The trial of Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy has put a spotlight on maternal mental health, which some medical experts say may be the only positive outcome in the tragic case. Her legal team argues that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for the murder of her three children because she was suffering from bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis.

'I am Lindsay Clancy'

Court heard that Clancy suffered from hallucinations and delusions that started after her third child was born. On the day of the killings, Clancy said she heard a voice telli ng her, "This is your last chance. Kill the children so you can kill yourself," according to her lawyer during opening arguments.

In addition to the courthouse rallies, there's been a massi ve wave of online empathy. On social media, people have been sharing their own experiences with trying to get mental health support after childbirth. Some have posted statements like, "I am Lindsay Clancy." Others have posted photos of themselves during times of struggle along with the words, "same, Lindsay."

"No matter what we say, nothing useful happens. Many of us lie, fearful of having our kids taken. Those of us who tell the truth are usually met with some combination of stigma, dismissal, and blame — rarely any meaningful support," Zawn Villines wrote on Substack Thursday.

"This Lindsay Clancy trial has hit me so viscerally, and it’s so close to home," Liz Cadeaux said in a tearful TikTok video where she urged other moms having a hard time to seek help.

Conversely, there's also been backlash against the social media campaigns, and opinion pieces and columns that question how so many mothers can possibly sympathize with a woman who killed her children.

Dr. Crystal Clark, the head of psychiatry at Women’s College Hospital in Toronto, says she thinks people are resonating with the trial, but not because they identify with Clancy's final actions.

"They resonate with the suffering, the help-seeking, the distress and despair she was experiencing prior to that, that they recognize in themselves," Clark, also the Canada Research Chair in reproductive mental health, told CBC News.

Because of the overall increased awareness of mental conditions like postpartum depression, Clark says more people are able to identify and name what they have experienced. And that can include not feeling heard.

"Not being heard is very scary."

WATCH | Closing arguments in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial: Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial hears closing arguments | Duration 5:31 Jury deliberations have begun for the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children. Prosecutors say she intentionally killed them, while the defence argues she was suffering from postpartum psychosis.

More support needed: psychiatrist

Jurors have heard that Clancy was prescribed 13 different psychiatric medications across different providers, and her attorneys say Clancy did everything she could to seek help, including going to the emergency room, calling a suicide hotline and checking herself into a psychiatric hospital.

The trial is triggering for many women, who have a long history of having their health and mental health concerns dismissed or misinterpreted, psychotherapist Kaytee Gillis recently wrote in Psychology Today.

"It touches something many women already know intimately: the feeling of asking for help and being unable to find it," Gillis wrote.

A poster sits on the floor in a corner near Lindsay Clancy during her murder trial Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026 in Plymouth, Mass. (John Tlumacki/Pool The Boston Globe/The Associated Press)

In Canada, postpartum depression and anxiety affect almost one-quarter of mothers who recently gave birth, accor ding to 2019 Statistics Canada data. Postpartum psychosis — the sudden onset of psychotic symptoms after childbirth — is much more serious. Researchers estimate that the condition afflicts one to two women per 1,000 after delivery.

Clark, with Women’s College Hospital, says she doesn't believe new moms are ge tting enough support during what can be a very vulnerable and scary time. More needs to be done to identify when moms are suffering and need help, and to provide early intervention, she says.

While the trial has raised awareness of postpartum psychosis, Clark says she's worried about increasing stigma. For instance, Clark says she's seen an u ptick in the number of patients worrying about whether they could be at risk of killing their children, even though it's an extremely rare outcome of a rare postpartum mental illness.

According to a 2024 research paper published in the Archives of Women's Mental Health, untreated postpartum psychosis is associated with an infanticide rate of about four per cent.

"Postpartum depression, postpartum anxiety and postpartum OCD are not associated with postpartum psychosis. It is very unlikely that those illnesses will lead to infanticide," Clark said.

Deliberations in Clancy's trial will resume Friday at 9 a.m. ET.

World.title: Despite Trump's renaming of Lake Ontario, Great Lakes endure as symbol of U.S.-Canada collaboration
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Great Lakes, one of the largest stores of freshwater and a source of water for some 40 million people, have long symbolized how closely intertwined Canada and the U.S. are.

U.S. President Donald Trump took a public sledgehammer to that relationship Thursday as part of his trade war with Canada, signing an executive order directing that Lake Ontario be renamed Lake America.

It's unclear whether Trump can unilaterally rename the lake, whose name predates European colonization of the Americas and has been widely recognized internationally for centuries. But the move comes amid a broader push by the Trump administration that has hindered U.S.-Canada collaboration on scientific research and restoration work in the Great Lakes.

"The way that this current administration in the United States views the environment and views science is demoralizing," said Aaron Fisk, professor at the Great Lakes Institute for Environmental Research at the University of Windsor.

"With the U.S. moving away from evidence-based decisions about the environment … that's a real concern to me because we need them to be a world leader. This really goes against their long term investment in good science," he said.

As part of its massive cuts to the federal public service, the Trump administration has made major cuts to iconic U.S. scientific agencies such as the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the Environmental Protection Agency. Those cuts have, in turn, affected monitoring and research in the Great Lakes.

"The water does not respect political boundaries, and you have to manage it as a water body, as a watershed, not just as a national or state or provincial boundary," said Joel Brammeier, president and CEO of the Alliance for the Great Lakes, a U.S. non-profit that advocates for Great Lakes conservation and restoration.

The Lake Michigan coast in Chicago. U.S.-Canada collaboration is essential to manage and restore the shared waters of the Great Lakes. (Charles Rex Arbogast/The Associated Press)

"Which is why it's always a bit painful when we see somebody out of the U.S. side challenging that collaboration. Because, honestly, the Great Lakes don't get cleaned up and they don't get protected unless the U.S. and Canada collaborate and co-operate."

Bipartisan support saves key Great Lakes program

Even amid the cuts, support for the Great Lakes has crossed political lines. The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative, a two-decade-old program to restore ecosystems and clean up industrial pollution, was targeted for near-total elimination by Trump during his first administration.

In this 2014, file photo the water intake crib for the city of Toledo, Ohio, is surrounded by an algae bloom on Lake Erie. The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative program has funded work in Ohio to slow down Lake Erie's toxic algae. (Haraz N. Ghanbari/The Associated Press)

The U.S. House of Representatives voted to reauthorize the program through 2031, with nearly $500 million US in federal funding per year going to local communities in the region. The measure received both Democratic and Republican support and is now working its way through the U.S. Senate.

"There are few issues that unite political parties like the Great Lakes. The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative has been so successful in doing that," Brammeier said.

The Great Lakes region has been central to industrial growth in both the U.S. and Canada, Brammeier said, hosting major industries such as steel, chemical and aluminum manufacturing. That growth has also left widespread industrial contamination that communities across the region want cleaned up.

"Even though a lot of damage was done across a large part of the Great Lakes, in an odd way that's actually led to this near universal support for the restoration program because so many decision-makers, so many members of Congress have seen the harm in their own communities," he said.

Climate change brings new threats

Historical pollution is not the end of the Great Lakes' problems. Climate change is bringing extreme heat and shifting precipitation to the region, which researchers say requires close study on both sides of the border.

Mike Shriberg, director of the University of Michigan's Water Center, said water availability and access are emerging challenges.

"This summer's a great example. We've had increasing drought and then increasing intensity of precipitation. So water flows have changed because of climate change," he said.

That, combined with future water demand from data centres, power generation and especially agriculture — which is expanding farther north as the climate warms — could create problems in the coming years. Shriberg also said he expects more people to move to the region from parts in the U.S. facing water shortages, particularly in the West, potentially putting further strain on the Great Lakes.

WATCH | Renaming Lake Ontario: Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ | Duration 2:36 U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order directing the interior secretary to rename Lake Ontario to 'Lake America,' as the trade war with Canada continues.

Andrew Gronewold, professor at the University of Michigan, is also thinking about future demand. "I think we're going to face some very difficult choices and questions about how Great Lakes water is used," he said from Hamilton, Ont., where he was meeting with Canadian and First Nations research partners.

Gronewold pointed to efforts by a group of Great Lakes state governors and premiers to "future-proof" the Great Lakes compact and agreement , a set of pacts among U.S. Great Lakes states, Ontario and Quebec governing how the water is used.

"I think over the next several decades, there's going to be increased pressure from outside of the basin for that water, whether it's for agriculture or industry or other uses. That's something that we need to be paying attention to," he said.

World.title: Air traffic controllers allegedly left work early before fatal Air Canada crash at LaGuardia
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The union representing American air traffic controllers has acknowledged allegations that two members left work early shortly before an Air Canada regional jet crashed at LaGuardia Airport in March, killing two pilots.

U.S. media reports suggest the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration is looking to fire the two flight controllers, who allegedly clocked out roughly an hour before their shift ended, leaving a pair of colleagues at the LaGuardia tower without backup.

The National Air Traffic Controllers Association confirmed the allegations, first reported by the Wall Street Journal on Thursday, in an emailed statement.

"NATCA is actively discussing these allegations with FAA leadership. We believe those discussions are the appropriate forum for addressing the matter," the union said.

The U.S. federal agency has not addressed the accusations directly but said it is "committed to holding employees accountable."

"We will not compromise the safety or efficiency of the National Airspace System," the FAA said in an email.

Shortly after 11:30 p.m. ET on March 22, an air traffic controller cleared an Air Canada Express plane to land less than two minutes before green-lighting a fire truck to cross the active runway. The resulting collision left two Canadian aviators dead and sent more than 40 people to hospital.

Footage shows the jet speeding along the rain-streaked strip as the truck crosses its path, veering away too late from an impact that unleashed a trail of smoke and debris as the plane skidded more than 100 metres farther, its cockpit obliterated.

The controller recognized the danger moments beforehand, instructing the truck to "stop" — 12 times in 10 seconds — but receiving no reply.

WATCH | Driver didn't realize 'stop' order was for them: LaGuardia driver didn't know 'stop, stop, stop' warning was for them: NTSB | Duration 1:58 U.S. investigators say the fire truck driver in last month's deadly collision with an Air Canada plane at LaGuardia airport didn't realize the 'stop, stop, stop' radio message was for them, and that a lack of transponders in the truck also played a role.

A preliminary report from the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board in April found that system failures and communication issues played a key role in the accident.

Experts have praised the pilots — Quebecer Antoine Forest and Ontarian MacKenzie Gunther, who flew for Air Canada Express carrier Jazz Aviation — for their quick braking that likely saved lives.

World.title: Film review: Years in the making, Coyote vs. Acme sings a sad toon
World.content:
Article content

There may also be those who are channelling their sympathy for the movie’s very survival. Back in 2023, in a plot worthy of Acme itself, Warner Bros. announced that the already finished film would be shelved as a tax write-off. An outcry from fans caused the studio to reverse that decision and allow Coyote vs. Acme to be purchased and released by Ketchup Entertainment.

World.title: Finance minister presents Colombia’s $203B budget proposal
World.content:
Colombia’s Finance Minister Miguel Gomez presented a budget proposal of COP634.9 trillion ($203 billion) for the coming year, a 14% increase compared to last year.

Much of the increase is due to the government’s debt obligations, which went up 55% to 155.4 trillion ($49.8 billion), almost a quarter of the entire budget.

At a presentation, Gomez told press that an earthquake that left tens of thousands homeless in western Colombia earlier this month also forced the administration of Abelardo de la Espriella to increase spending.

In a video, the finance minister also said that the government “has taken deci

The budget bill, a revision of the one that was presented by the former government of former President Gustavo Petro, will have to be approved by Congress before October 20 or be issued as a decree.

The government will also present a Finance Bill, which determines how the government plans to pay for its spending, before December.

World.title: Colombia claims killing eight suspected EMBF guerrillas
World.content:
President Abelardo de la Espriella said Thursday that Colombia’s armed forces killed eight guerrillas of FARC dissident group EMBF in a joint operation.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella said that the military offensive targeted “camps used by structures of the Jorge Suarez Briceño Block,” a unit of the EMBF, in a rural part of El Retorno in the Guaviare province.

In a precision airstrike followed by an operation carried out by our commandos, the preliminary tally shows that 8 terrorists have been killed so far, 11 rifles and 5 machine guns have been seized, along with a large amount of logistical supplies. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that “Colombia must know we are going on the offensive” against organized crime and illegal armed groups that are all deemed “narco-terrorist” organizations by the government.

“Major ringleaders and their criminal organizations will find no hiding place or sanctuary anywhere in the country,” the president added.

De la Espriella took office earlier this month, vowing to end peace negotiations with illegal armed groups and go on a military offensive with the help of the US military instead.

One of the groups that was negotiating peace with the administration of former President Gustavo Petro was the EMBF, led by former FARC commander “Calarca.”

The group, together with FARC dissident group EMC, controls large swathe of territory in southern Colombia and along the border with Venezuela.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.

World.title: Colombia expands disaster region in 2nd emergency decree
World.content:
Colombia’s government drastically expanded the region affected by the August 10 earthquake in a second decree declaring an economic emergency.

According to the decree, President Abelardo de la Espriella declared the emergency in 15 of the country’s 32 provinces “for a period of thirty (30) calendar days, in order to conjure the crisis and prevent the spread of the disaster’s effects.”

“The territorial scope includes all municipalities listed in UNGRD Situational Report No. 36 and any additional municipalities where direct damage from the August 10, 2026 earthquake is specifically demonstrated,” said the decree.

The emergency decree declared a State of Exception, which allows the government to “adopt, through legislative decrees, all additional necessary measures and budgetary/credit operations to address the crisis” in the emergency region.

According to the decree, the government is considering the following extraordinary measures to respond to the disaster that left more than $9.5 billion in damages.

Tax, credit, and budgetary flexibility to direct new resources to disaster recovery.

Expedited public credit operations bypassing lengthy CONPES/DNP approvals.

Use of the Royalty Savings and Stabilization Fund (FAE) resources as repayable loans.

Expanding the “Works for Taxes” (Obras por Impuestos) mechanism to affected municipalities.

Direct management and monetization of seized assets administered by SAE/FRISCO to fund emergency shelters and humanitarian relief.

Authorizing financial cooperatives to temporarily extend credit and savings services to non-members affected by the disaster.

Streamlining judicial operations, education delivery (remote/alternative spaces), school feeding programs (PAE), housing subsidies, telecommunications repairs, and labor support transfers.

Previously, De la Espriella announced a “Miracle Fund,” which would be used to channel donations from the private sector and international partners.

Since then, Colombia’s elite donated COP1.6 trillion ($526 million) of the $30 billion the government believes it needs for reconstruction.

World.title: Colombia’s government publishes “white paper” on corruption by Petro
World.content:
The government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella gave Prosecutor General Luz Adriana Camargo a white paper with more than 80 complaints over alleged corruption by the previous government.

The 135-page “Book of Truth that was presented by De la Espriella, contained “the result of the work carried out under the coordination of Vice President José Manuel Restrepo during the transition weeks between the presidential election and August 7” when he took office.

De la Espriella suspended the transition process on July 7 after Petro said he refused to recognize the president as his legitimate successor.

Consequently, the book contains mainly political criticisms of the previous “regime” and no evidence of misdeeds that hadn’t been picked by the Comptroller General’s Office, which monitors public spending.

This white paper, my fellow Colombians, does not intend to replace, far less anticipate, judicial investigations or the outcome of actions taken by prosecutors, inspectors, and comptrollers. The book actually represents something simpler and, at the same time, more serious, monumental, and decisive: the fulfillment of my duty as Head of State. I am fulfilling the responsibility that falls upon me by gathering available information and not allowing the facts recorded here in the book I have just delivered to be buried by silence and impunity. The duty of a leader is to bring the truth to the doorstep of justice and stop there, scrupulously respecting the independence and majesty of the judicial system. That moment has arrived. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president blamed the budget deficit on the “sacking” of the Petro administration rather than Congress’s failure to approve the legislation that allowed the previous government to carry out its 2026 budget.

De la Espriella previously said he would extradite Petro if the US Government asked him to.

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.
