What the state announced

Bahia’s tourism secretariat presented the new cruise season on Wednesday 26 August. The venue was the eighth CLIA Brasil Forum, the industry’s annual gathering in Brasília.

The 2026–2027 cruise season runs from October 2026 to April 2027. Salvador’s port terminal has 47 calls scheduled over those seven months.

The schedule spans research vessels to large luxury ocean liners. Together they should bring more than 180,000 Brazilian and foreign passengers to the state.

The economic forecast is R$144 million (US$27.9 million) injected into Bahia’s economy. The estimate comes from the state tourism secretariat working with the cruise industry.

The national context favours the state. Brazil’s current season offers around 670,000 berths on seven ships covering more than 160 itineraries.

Salvador opened the current national season in October 2025, when MSC Preziosa docked there. The city has held a regular place on coastal itineraries ever since.

The forum also heard that cruise lines want more Brazilian homeports. Santos and Rio de Janeiro currently dominate boarding operations in the country.

The MSC Virtuosa factor

The headline ship of the season is MSC Virtuosa. It is the largest and most modern vessel in the MSC Cruises fleet.

The ship entered service in 2021 and carries more than 6,000 passengers at full capacity. Its weekly call gives Salvador a fixed place on the company’s South American map.

Crucially, passengers will be able to embark and disembark in Salvador. The city becomes a starting point, not just a stop on the way.

“Bahia is a very important partner state,” said Adrian Ursilli, the managing director of MSC Cruises in Brazil. He credited joint work with the state and the travel trade for the expanded operation.

MSC confirmed the operation at the Brasília forum alongside state officials. The company has sailed the Brazilian coast for more than two decades.

Why homeport calls pay more

Not all port calls are equal in money terms. A study by CLIA Brasil with the FGV research foundation put the difference in hard numbers.

A passenger on a simple day call spends about R$710 (US$138) in the city. A passenger embarking or disembarking spends about R$920 (US$179), because the trip adds hotel nights and meals.

Homeport status also pulls spending into the airport and hotels around departure day. Travellers typically arrive a day early and leave a day late.

That is why Salvador’s boarding role matters to the forecast. Every traveller who starts or ends a cruise in the city stays longer and spends more.

How last season went

The 2025–2026 season gives the new forecast its baseline. It injected R$115 million (US$22.3 million) into the state’s economy.

About 230,000 cruise passengers came through Bahia’s ports in those six months. Ships called at Salvador, Ilhéus, Itacaré, Porto Seguro and Barra Grande.

The new target implies growth of about 25 percent in money terms. The state is betting on the Virtuosa effect and a wider map of ports to get there.

The cruise season that ended in April already beat earlier years in the state. The segment has grown steadily since coastal cruising restarted after the pandemic.

Beyond Salvador

The state’s plan does not stop at the capital. Smaller ships are the tool for destinations that lack deep-water terminals.

CLIA Brasil’s president, Marco Ferraz, named Porto Seguro, Itacaré, Morro de São Paulo and Barra Grande. “These are operations that do not demand much infrastructure,” he said at the forum.

The southern coast sees cruise tourism as a complement to its beach resorts. Ilhéus already receives occasional calls and wants a regular slot.

If the plan works, the 2027–2028 cruise season could add regular calls south of the capital. Local hotel associations are already lobbying for them.

Bahia told the forum it is investing in nautical infrastructure, destination promotion and service training. Planning already extends to the 2027–2028 season.

What it means for foreigners

For expatriates in Salvador, ship days are the most visible change. Thousands of visitors flow into Pelourinho, the historic centre, within a few hours of docking.

The money lands in a familiar set of hands. Restaurants, taxi drivers, tour guides and souvenir sellers take most of the direct spend.

Foreign residents can also use the season themselves. Salvador’s homeport status means boarding a Brazil coast itinerary without flying to Rio or Santos first.

For visitors planning a trip around the cruise season, one habit pays off. Book Salvador hotels early in the weeks when two ships coincide in port.

The state says its welcome operation will include cultural performances at the terminal. English-language information for visitors is part of the promised service upgrade.

What to watch from here

The first test arrives in October, when the season opens. The pace of early calls will show whether the 180,000-passenger target is realistic.

The second is the Virtuosa’s embarkation numbers. Strong local boarding would justify keeping a ship of that size on the route.

The third is the small-port expansion. If Itacaré and Porto Seguro gain regular calls, Bahia’s cruise map starts to look very different.

Weather rarely disrupts the Bahia leg of the cruise season. The October to April window avoids the rougher southern winter seas.

For now, Salvador holds its place as the cruise capital of Brazil’s Northeast. The next seven months will show how much that position is worth.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Bahia’s 2026–2027 cruise season? The season runs from October 2026 to April 2027. Salvador has 47 ship calls scheduled at its port terminal. How much money will the Bahia cruise season generate? State tourism officials forecast R$144 million (US$27.9 million) injected into Bahia’s economy. Last season generated R$115 million (US$22.3 million). Which cruise ships will call at Salvador? MSC Virtuosa, the largest and most modern MSC Cruises ship, will make weekly calls with embarkation in Salvador. The schedule also includes research vessels and luxury ocean liners.

Sources: Bahia State Tourism Secretariat (Setur-BA); CLIA Brasil; CLIA Brasil/FGV passenger-spending study; MSC Cruises; Brazil Ministry of Tourism.

São Paulo · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Reggae Live Station at Espaço Unimed Friday brings a big one: a roots-reggae festival night at Espaço Unimed in Barra Funda, headlined by Jamaican legends Israel Vibration alongside Brazilian giants Ponto de Equilíbrio and Tribo de Jah. Doors at 8 pm. It’s a rare chance to catch a bill like this under one roof — tickets are on sale through the official seller, so check availability and buy ahead.

Tonight at a Glance —Reggae Live Station · Barra Funda Israel Vibration, Ponto de Equilíbrio and Tribo de Jah at Espaço Unimed. Doors 8 pm, music from 9:30 pm. —Blue Note & JazzB · Paulista / Centro Two sets of jazz on Paulista, plus the jazz basement in the centre. —Canto da Ema · Pinheiros Doors 8 pm, band about 9:30 pm, and a packed dancing floor. —Clubs · Barra Funda The dancefloors are on — D-Edge and the Barra Funda warehouses run late. —Peak night: Friday is São Paulo at full tilt — everything is open, so book ahead and expect surge pricing late.

Tonight, Friday 28 August 2026, São Paulo is at full tilt. There’s a marquee reggae bill in Barra Funda — Israel Vibration and friends at Espaço Unimed — and around it, the whole city is open: jazz on Paulista and in the centre, forró floors in full swing, listening rooms, and the Barra Funda clubs waking up for the weekend. Whatever you’re after tonight, it’s on. Book ahead where you can.

Friday is São Paulo at full tilt — tonight, a roots-reggae bill in Barra Funda. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Reggae Live Station — Espaço Unimed — Rua Tagipuru 795, Barra Funda. A roots-reggae festival night brings together the Jamaican legends Israel Vibration with two of Brazil’s biggest reggae names, Ponto de Equilíbrio and Tribo de Jah, at one of the city’s largest concert halls. Doors open at 8 pm and the music starts at 9:30 pm, with Israel Vibration on at 11. It’s a big, celebratory night — tickets are on sale through the official seller, so check availability and buy in advance. If you’re driving, allow time for parking in Barra Funda; the metro is a short walk.

Jazz on Paulista and in the centre — Blue Note (Av. Paulista 2073) runs its two-set Friday evening; JazzB (Rua General Jardim 43, Vila Buarque) has its intimate basement jazz. Both are seated, both are at their best on a Friday — check tonight’s acts and reserve, as they fill.

Forró and dancing — Canto da Ema (Av. Brigadeiro Faria Lima 364, Pinheiros) opens at 8 pm with the band on around 9:30 pm. If you’d rather dance than sit, this is the one — no experience needed.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Early evening (6–8 pm) — MASP is free from 6 pm on a Friday; doors at Espaço Unimed at 8 pm.

Main event (9–10 pm) — The reggae bill in Barra Funda, jazz on Paulista, or forró in Pinheiros.

Late (midnight+) — The Barra Funda clubs (D-Edge and around) get going; the Augusta bars are busy.

After hours (2 am+) — Barra Funda runs till dawn; some rooms go well past sunrise on a Friday.

Getting home — Rideshare surges after midnight; pre-book or wait for it to settle in a lit, busy spot.

Scenes & Sounds

Reggae — The night’s big draw: Israel Vibration, Ponto de Equilíbrio and Tribo de Jah at Espaço Unimed. Where: Espaço Unimed (Barra Funda).

Jazz and blues — Blue Note and JazzB both run tonight, and Bourbon Street opens most nights, though it had not published tonight’s act. Where: Blue Note (Paulista), JazzB (Centro), Bourbon Street (Moema).

Forró — Canto da Ema’s floor is packed on a Friday. Where: Canto da Ema (Pinheiros).

Electronic and clubs — Barra Funda is the heart of it: D-Edge and the warehouse clubs run till dawn. Where: Barra Funda, Água Branca.

Intimate live music — Casa de Francisca and Centro da Terra run their curated Friday rooms. Where: Casa de Francisca (Sé), Centro da Terra (Perdizes).

Pick Your Night

A big show: Reggae Live Station at Espaço Unimed — the pick of the night.

Jazz lover: Blue Note on Paulista or JazzB in the centre.

Dance: Forró at Canto da Ema in Pinheiros.

Till sunrise: D-Edge and the Barra Funda clubs.

Intimate and seated: Casa de Francisca — the city’s loveliest room.

Where to Go

Espaço Unimed — Barra Funda One of São Paulo’s largest concert halls, in the west-side arena district, hosting big Brazilian and international names. Tonight: Doors 8 pm, music from 9:30 pm: Tribo de Jah at 9:30, Israel Vibration with the Roots Radics at 11, Ponto de Equilíbrio at 1 am. Best time: Arrive near doors for a good spot; it’s largely standing on the floor. Cost: Tickets via the official seller — check availability. Meia-entrada (half price) with valid ID. Address: Rua Tagipuru 795, Barra Funda Getting there: Metro Marechal Deodoro or Barra Funda, short walk. Rideshare surges after the show. Good to know: Book your ride home before the encore to beat the post-show crush.

Blue Note São Paulo — Paulista The São Paulo outpost of the New York jazz club, polished and central, overlooking Avenida Paulista. Tonight: A two-set Friday evening. Check tonight’s act on the site — Fridays sell out. Best time: Wednesday to Sunday. Arrive 30 minutes early — seating is first-come. Cost: Priced per show and published with each booking. Check tonight’s listing before you go. Address: Av. Paulista 2073, 2º andar (Conjunto Nacional), Consolação Website: bluenotesp.com Getting there: Metro Consolação (green line), 200 m from the door. Good to know: Where there are two sets, the later one is usually quieter.

JazzB — República One of São Paulo’s dedicated jazz clubs, an intimate basement room in the centre with a serious, music-first booking policy. Tonight: Doors 5 pm and the show usually around 9 pm. Reserve, as the room is small. Best time: Thursday and Friday from 5 pm; Saturday and Sunday from noon. Cost: Tickets typically R$35 (US$7) to R$60 (US$12). Card accepted. Address: Rua General Jardim 43, Vila Buarque Getting there: Metro República, short walk. Rideshare after dark. Good to know: Small room — reserve online.

Canto da Ema — Pinheiros One of São Paulo’s classic forró houses, going since 2000, with live bands and a floor that fills with dancers. Tonight: A forró class runs about 7 pm, doors are at 8 pm and the band comes on around 9:30 pm. Best time: Wednesday to Sunday; Friday and Saturday are the biggest nights. Cost: The door was R$55 (US$11) full price midweek, half at R$27 (US$5). Check tonight’s listing. Address: Av. Brigadeiro Faria Lima 364, Pinheiros Getting there: Metro Fradique Coutinho (yellow line), short walk. Good to know: No dance experience needed — the crowd is friendly and mixed.

D-Edge — Barra Funda One of São Paulo’s most respected electronic clubs, with a world-class sound system and a serious techno-and-house booking policy. Tonight: A Friday club night — check the line-up and buy in advance for the best price. Best time: Late — the floor fills after 1 am and runs till dawn. Cost: Entry typically R$40 (US$8) to R$120 (US$24) depending on the line-up. Address: Av. Auro Soares de Moura Andrade 141, Barra Funda Getting there: Rideshare is easiest late; Metro Marechal Deodoro is the nearest station. Good to know: Buy tickets ahead and book your ride home before you go in.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Barra Funda / Água Branca: The arena-and-club district — Espaço Unimed and D-Edge. Busy on event nights; travel by car or metro.

Paulista / Consolação: The city’s spine — Blue Note, MASP and a short walk to everything. MASP stays open to 9 pm on a Friday, and entry is free from 6 pm to 8:30 pm.

Pinheiros / Vila Madalena: Bohemian and bar-heavy, with forró at Canto da Ema. Packed and walkable on a Friday.

República / Vila Buarque: Central and lively, home to JazzB. Busy, but keep the usual awareness on quiet streets.

Sé / Centro: Home to Casa de Francisca. Grand by day, very quiet after dark — rideshare door-to-door.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Friday is a big night — the queer parties are in full swing around Augusta, Frei Caneca and Barra Funda. Check listings for tonight’s parties and one-offs.

Everyday-friendly spaces — The Augusta corridor is the hub, buzzing and mixed on a Friday.

Money & How Paying Works Concert tickets: Espaço Unimed sells through the official seller; buy ahead and bring ID for meia-entrada (half price). Couvert and cover: Music clubs add a per-person charge — Blue Note prices each show separately; R$40 (US$8) to R$120 (US$24) at the clubs. Cash, card and Pix: Cards and Pix are widely accepted, but carry R$100 (US$20) for smaller bars and vendors. Tipping: 10% is standard and often added as ‘serviço’. Check before you double-tip.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: Trains run from 4:40 am and the last services leave from around midnight, varying by station. There is no all-night service tonight, so plan on a rideshare.

Rideshare: 99 and Uber surge hardest right after big shows and around 2–3 am. Pre-book, or wait for prices to settle in a lit, busy spot.

Barra Funda at night: Fine around the venues and busy streets, but keep the usual awareness; book a car door-to-door rather than walking to find one.

Phone awareness: Don’t walk with your phone out on quiet streets. Duck into a bar to check maps or call a car.

Pinheiros and Paulista: Busy and well-lit late on a Friday — easier places to find a safe ride.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I still get tickets to the reggae show tonight?

Possibly — it’s a large venue and tickets were on sale through the official seller at the time of writing. Check availability online before you travel, and if it’s sold out, the jazz rooms, forró at Canto da Ema and the Barra Funda clubs are all excellent Friday alternatives.

Where are the late-night clubs?

Barra Funda is the heart of the electronic scene — D-Edge and a cluster of warehouse clubs, running from around 1 am until well past sunrise. Buy tickets ahead and book your ride home before you go in.

I’ve just landed at GRU tonight. Where should I go?

Everything’s open — Blue Note or Bourbon Street for a seated night, Canto da Ema to dance, or Barra Funda to go late. All are about a 30–45 minute rideshare from the airport. Book the show you want ahead.

What’s the dress code?

Casual for the concert and forró; smart-casual for the jazz rooms; the clubs are relaxed but stylish. Comfortable shoes if you’re standing or dancing.

Sources: Espaço Unimed, bluenotesp.com, d-edge.com.br, Ao Vivo (agenda)

World.title: Brazil’s Senate Advances the End of the 6×1 Work Schedule as the Election Clock Ticks
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened: Senator Omar Aziz delivered a favorable report on the 6×1 amendment to a Senate committee on 27 August 2026.

— The strategy: He kept the Chamber’s text untouched, so the amendment can be promulgated without returning to the lower house.

— The opposition: All 12 amendments were rejected, including bids to keep the 44-hour week and to stretch the transition.

— What the text does: It sets a 40-hour week and two paid rest days, reaching full effect one year after promulgation.

— The catch: Industry lobby Fiesp calls it the “Exit-Poll Amendment,” saying the electoral calendar has kidnapped the debate.

— What comes next: The committee votes next week, and a pre-election floor vote depends on Senate president Davi Alcolumbre.

The end of Brazil’s 6×1 work schedule cleared its first Senate hurdle on 27 August, with rapporteur Omar Aziz keeping the Chamber’s text and rejecting every opposition amendment. A floor vote before the October election now depends on a political deal.

What Omar Aziz delivered on Thursday

Senator Omar Aziz presented his report on the 6×1 work schedule amendment to the Constitution and Justice Committee on 27 August. He recommended approval of the text exactly as the Chamber of Deputies passed it.

The choice is a strategy, not a courtesy. An unamended Senate vote means the proposal skips a return to the lower house and goes straight to promulgation by Congress.

Speed matters because Brazil elects a president on 4 October. Every week of delay makes a pre-election vote on the 6×1 work schedule less likely.

The committee is expected to vote on the report next week. Senate president Davi Alcolumbre unlocked the bill after drawing closer to President Lula in recent weeks.

How the proposal got here

The current campaign began in the Chamber of Deputies, driven by Deputy Erika Hilton of the PSOL party. Her signature drive turned a fringe demand into a floor vote.

The Chamber approved the amendment earlier in August. It reached the Senate’s Constitution and Justice Committee on 21 August, with Aziz named rapporteur the same week.

The 44-hour cap itself dates to the 1988 constitution. The six-days-on, one-day-off pattern grew up around it in the decades that followed.

A separate Chamber proposal, from Deputy Reginaldo Lopes, goes further and targets 36 hours over ten years. Public hearings on it have run through the year.

Twelve amendments, twelve rejections

Aziz threw out all 12 amendments filed by fellow senators. Three of them, from Izalci Lucas of the Liberal Party, sought to keep the current 44-hour week.

Others tried to stretch the transition period to as long as four years. They came from Hermer Klann, also of the Liberal Party, and Oriovisto Guimarães of the PSDB.

The fiercest counter-proposal had surfaced earlier in the Chamber. A group of deputies offered a ten-year transition, a cut in the employer severance-fund rate and productivity targets as conditions.

The rapporteur argued that the changes would disfigure the proposal. Some, he wrote, were unconstitutional or would create legal insecurity for employers and workers alike.

The Liberal Party of Flávio Bolsonaro opposes the end of the 6×1 work schedule. The senator and presidential candidate has co-signed a rival amendment for hourly pay with flexible hours, which is stalled.

What the amendment would actually change

Brazil’s standard work week has stood at 44 hours for decades. The amendment cuts it to 40 hours, keeping the eight-hour daily limit.

The bigger change is rest. Workers gain two paid rest days per week with no salary reduction, and one of them should preferably be Sunday.

The 6×1 work schedule is the default in retail, call centres, private security and much of health care. Its workers are disproportionately poor and disproportionately female, union studies show.

The transition runs in two steps. The weekly limit falls to 42 hours two months after promulgation, then to 40 hours within a year.

Aziz cited data from the Institute of Applied Economic Research showing the 6×1 work schedule falls hardest on low-income workers. Cutting it, he wrote, is an act of distributive justice, not merely labour policy.

Fiesp’s “Exit-Poll Amendment” attack

Brazil’s most powerful industry lobby has chosen its ground. The Federation of Industries of the State of São Paulo, known as Fiesp, says the electoral calendar has kidnapped the debate.

In its latest statement, the federation branded the proposal the “Exit-Poll Amendment”. The phrase argues that the timing serves the campaign, not the worker.

Employer groups have warned for months about higher payroll costs and staffing gaps. Retail, health care and services rely most heavily on six-day rotations.

Fiesp took the same cost argument to a Chamber public hearing in May. Its president, Josué Gomes, was among the industry leaders called to testify.

Unions answer that similar cuts abroad did not destroy jobs. They note that a 40-hour week follows the trend in most large economies.

The narrow road to a floor vote

A constitutional amendment needs approval in committee, then two rounds on the Senate floor. Senate rules normally demand five working days between those rounds.

Lula’s allies argue that political will can compress that calendar. They cite past amendments whose two rounds were voted one after the other.

Each round requires three-fifths of the Senate, or 49 of 81 votes. The same supermajority has already carried the proposal through the Chamber.

Alcolumbre met Lula and Chamber speaker Hugo Motta on 26 August to discuss the agenda. He did not guarantee a floor date for the 6×1 work schedule after that meeting.

If the Senate changes even a comma, the text returns to the Chamber. That is the journey Aziz’s report is designed to avoid.

Why the vote lands in the middle of an election

The 6×1 work schedule has become one of the campaign’s defining divides. Lula’s party program endorses the 40-hour week, while the Liberal Party calls it a burden on business.

That is precisely Fiesp’s point about timing. A vote in September forces every senator candidate to pick a side weeks before the ballot.

If the Senate approves the text unamended, Congress can promulgate it without the president’s signature. Constitutional amendments in Brazil do not pass through the presidential desk.

The government sees the bill as a deliverable for its union base. The opposition sees a cost shock landing on small business first.

Watch the committee vote next week first. A strong margin there is the signal that the floor deal with Alcolumbre is real.

For readers abroad, the practical date is promulgation plus two months. That is when the first cut, to 42 hours, would bite.

The government’s whips are already counting votes day by day. They know the margin for error on the floor is thin.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Omar Aziz decide on the 6×1 work schedule amendment? He delivered a favorable report on 27 August 2026, keeping the Chamber’s text unchanged to speed passage. He rejected all 12 amendments, and the Senate committee votes next week. What does the 6×1 amendment change for Brazilian workers? It cuts the standard week from 44 to 40 hours and guarantees two paid rest days with no salary cut. The limit falls to 42 hours two months after promulgation, then to 40 within a year. Why does Fiesp call it the “Exit-Poll Amendment”? The São Paulo industry federation says the electoral calendar has kidnapped the debate. It argues the pre-election timing serves the campaign rather than workers.

Sources: G1 (27 August 2026), Agência Senado, Estadão, Poder360 and the Fiesp statement as reported by Brasil 247 (28 August 2026).

World.title: Brazil’s Senate Puts Critical Minerals Bill on Fast Track With Braga as Rapporteur
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened: Senate president Davi Alcolumbre named Eduardo Braga to steer the critical minerals bill, with a floor vote next week.

— How big the package is: About R$7 billion (US$1.36 billion) in public support, split between a guarantee fund and tax credits.

— The real story: President Lula personally pressed the Senate to unblock the bill, which has sat there since May.

— The catch: The tax credits only start in 2030, and the guarantee fund does not lend money directly.

— Who is involved: Rapporteur Eduardo Braga is an Amazonas senator, and his state holds the giant Autazes potash project.

— What comes next: Braga and Alcolumbre meet on Monday 31 August to set the vote procedure, probably under urgency.

Brazil’s Senate is preparing to vote on the critical minerals bill, with Senator Eduardo Braga of Amazonas as rapporteur and about R$7 billion (US$1.36 billion) of public support on the table. A parallel decision this week cut the cost of state-backed credit for the sector to 3 percent a year.

What moved this week

We reported on 27 August that President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was pressing the Senate to act. The Senate has now answered, and quickly.

Senate president Davi Alcolumbre named Eduardo Braga, leader of the MDB party in the Senate, as rapporteur of the minerals bill. The choice came on Wednesday 26 August, right after Alcolumbre met Lula and Chamber speaker Hugo Motta.

The bill is PL 2780/2024, approved by the Chamber of Deputies in May. It has waited in the Senate for almost four months.

Alcolumbre has committed to a floor vote next week, during a concentrated voting effort. One option is to send the text straight to the floor under an urgency regime, skipping committees.

Braga had already signalled the bill was a priority. He announced earlier that his party had chosen it among the priority matters to approve this year.

Braga and Alcolumbre meet on Monday 31 August to define the procedure. Negotiations over the text are expected to concentrate directly in the plenary.

The R$7 billion on the table

The public support inside the bill adds up to about R$7 billion (US$1.36 billion). It comes in two very different instruments.

The first is the Fundo Garantidor da Atividade Mineral, a guarantee fund with R$2 billion (US$388 million) of federal money. Private quotas could take it to R$5 billion (US$971 million).

The fund does not lend. It guarantees loans made by others, which lowers the perceived risk and the cost of financing for smaller mining companies.

The second instrument is a tax credit programme worth up to R$5 billion (US$971 million). It rewards companies that process and transform these minerals inside Brazil.

The bill also gives priority to promising areas in National Mining Agency auctions. Mineral research authorisations get a maximum, non-renewable term of ten years.

Here is the fine print. Those credits are scheduled between 2030 and 2034, and only companies headquartered and managed in Brazil qualify.

Two texts, one fight

Braga will not start from a blank page. The Senate has its own bill, PL 4443/2025, presented by Senator Renan Calheiros.

Both texts create a national policy and a council to coordinate the sector. The differences sit in two sensitive points.

The Chamber text lets the council screen and block deals involving strategic assets. It also opens the door to an export tax on those minerals, or an equivalent mechanism.

The Senate text avoids both devices. Government officials fear senators will dilute the council’s powers, which would force the bill back to the Chamber.

In the Chamber, rapporteur Arnaldo Jardim defended the tougher version. Brazil cannot remain a mere exporter of raw minerals, he said, and must industrialise its geological wealth.

The Amazonas window

The rapporteur’s home state is part of the story. Braga is a former governor of Amazonas and one of its three senators.

Amazonas holds one of Brazil’s most strategic mineral projects, the Autazes potash mine. Potash is the core ingredient of potassium fertiliser.

Brazil imports about 95 percent of the potash it consumes. The Autazes project, with planned output of 2.2 million tonnes a year, could cut that dependence by about a fifth.

A rapporteur from Amazonas gives such projects a direct channel in the final text. The state government has treated mineral development as a priority for years.

Cheaper credit arrives before the law

The executive branch did not wait for the Senate. On Thursday 27 August the National Monetary Council cut the cost of credit for the sector.

Loans from the Plano Brasil Soberano for investments in the sector now cost 3 percent a year. The previous rates were 8 percent and 6.5 percent, depending on the purpose.

Brasil Soberano is the programme Brazil created in 2025 to support companies hit by United States tariffs. The council also opened its working-capital lines to the fertiliser chain.

That inclusion covers fertiliser makers, producers of fertiliser inputs and miners of minerals used in fertilisers. Potash projects like Autazes fit exactly there.

The deadline to file financing requests at the BNDES, the national development bank, was extended by twelve months. Applications now run until 31 December 2027.

The Finance Ministry said the changes widen support for sectors hit by higher American tariffs. It also cited other effects of international instability.

What to watch next week

The first signpost is the Monday meeting between Braga and Alcolumbre. It will show whether the bill skips committees entirely.

The second is the fate of the council’s veto power and the export instruments. If senators strip them, the text returns to the Chamber and the calendar slips.

The third is the list itself. The new council will define which minerals count as critical or strategic, and every state with a deposit will lobby for inclusion.

The names expected on it include lithium, cobalt, niobium and graphite. Rare earths get the most attention, and Brazil holds the world’s second-largest reserves, behind only China.

Those elements go into magnets, electric motors, wind turbines and military equipment. That is why Washington and Beijing watch this vote as closely as Brasília does.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Brazil’s critical minerals bill? PL 2780/2024 creates a national policy for critical and strategic minerals, with a guarantee fund of R$2 billion (US$388 million) and up to R$5 billion (US$971 million) in tax credits. The Chamber of Deputies approved it in May 2026, and the Senate plans a floor vote in the week of 31 August 2026. What did the National Monetary Council change for the sector? On 27 August 2026 it cut Plano Brasil Soberano loan rates for investments in the sector to 3 percent a year, from 8 percent and 6.5 percent. It also extended the programme to the fertiliser chain and pushed the BNDES application deadline to 31 December 2027. Why does the rapporteur’s home state matter? Eduardo Braga is a senator and former governor of Amazonas, which hosts the Autazes potash project. Brazil imports about 95 percent of its potash, and the project could reduce that dependence by about a fifth.

Sources: CNN Brasil and Metrópoles on the rapporteur choice and the vote calendar; Valor Econômico on the National Monetary Council decision of 27 August 2026; Agência iNFRA; Senate and Chamber records on PL 2780/2024 and PL 4443/2025.

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Lapa at Full Strength Friday is when Lapa runs at full strength, and three of its best rooms sit within a few blocks. Rio Scenarium opens at 8 pm across three floors, Carioca da Gema puts its main show on at 8:30 pm, and TribOz plays two jazz sets. Buy the Scenarium ticket online and walk between the three.

Tonight at a Glance —Pedra do Sal · Saúde The famous free roda in the old port runs on Mondays, not tonight. —Lapa at full tilt · Lapa Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema and TribOz all open, under the Arcos. —Trapiche Gamboa · Saúde Open tonight, though its women-singers roda, Razões Africanas, is on Thursdays. —Circo Voador · Lapa Ajuliacosta opens her “Novo Testamento” tour at 8 pm — sold out. —Peak night: Friday is Rio at full tilt — the port, Lapa and Copacabana all alive. Rideshare late.

Tonight, Friday 28 August 2026, Rio is at full tilt. Lapa runs at full strength, with Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema and TribOz a few blocks apart, and Trapiche Gamboa open in the port. There’s a big gig at Circo Voador too, though it’s sold out. From the grand houses to a tiny jazz room, tonight has range.

Lapa runs at full strength on a Friday, with three of the city’s best rooms a few blocks apart. (Photo: Internet Reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Lapa is the night — Largo João da Baiana, Saúde. Alongside Monday, Friday is one of the two biggest nights at the Pedra do Sal — a free, open-air samba on the historic stone steps in the old port, the neighbourhood where Carioca samba was born. Musicians set up at the foot of the hill, the crowd spreads across the staircase and the surrounding streets, and beer flows from the bars and vendors around the largo. It runs from around 6 pm into the night. It’s free, cash-based for drinks, and one of the essential Rio experiences — arrive early, as the best spots near the roda fill fast, and keep an eye on your belongings.

Lapa at full strength — A short ride away, Lapa is at its Friday peak: Rio Scenarium (Rua do Lavradio 20) from 8 pm across its three floors, Carioca da Gema (Av. Mem de Sá 79) with its show at 8:30 pm, and TribOz (Rua Conde de Lages 19) for jazz — all within a few blocks, with the street under the Arcos alive with bars and crowds. Buy Rio Scenarium tickets online to skip the queue.

Trapiche Gamboa is open — Rua Sacadura Cabral 155, Saúde. In the same port district as the Pedra do Sal, The house is open tonight, but its women-singers roda, Razões Africanas, runs on Thursdays. Doors are around 6:30 pm with a modest couvert, and it is a seated, indoor alternative to Lapa.

One that’s sold out — At Circo Voador in Lapa, the rapper Ajuliacosta opens her “Novo Testamento” tour at 8 pm, but the show is sold out. Worth knowing if you spot resale, but not one to turn up to on spec.

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Early evening (6–6:30 pm) — TribOz plays its early jazz set; doors at Trapiche Gamboa in the port.

Doors (7:30 pm) — Carioca da Gema opens; Rio Scenarium follows at 8 pm.

Main event (8:30–10 pm) — Carioca da Gema’s show starts and Lapa’s houses hit full stride.

Late (from 11 pm) — Stay in Lapa for the street and the houses, or head to Copacabana for Blue Note Rio.

Getting home — Rideshare door-to-door; surge is highest after midnight. Wait in a lit, busy spot.

Scenes & Sounds

Street samba — Not tonight. The free Pedra do Sal roda on the stone steps is a Monday night. Where: Largo João da Baiana, Saúde (Mondays).

Samba houses — Lapa at full strength: Rio Scenarium and Carioca da Gema, plus Trapiche Gamboa in the port. Where: Rio Scenarium (Rua do Lavradio 20), Carioca da Gema (Av. Mem de Sá 79), Trapiche Gamboa (Rua Sacadura Cabral 155).

Jazz and MPB — TribOz in Lapa and Blue Note Rio in Copacabana. Where: TribOz (Rua Conde de Lages 19), Blue Note Rio (Av. Atlântica 1910).

Big gig — Ajuliacosta at Circo Voador, 8 pm — sold out. Where: Circo Voador (Lapa).

Copacabana — Bip Bip is open, though its signature roda nights are Thursday and Sunday. Where: Bip Bip (Rua Almirante Gonçalves 50).

Pick Your Night

The full house: Lapa is the night — the pick of the night.

The full house: Rio Scenarium — three floors of samba and gafieira.

Samba in the port: Trapiche Gamboa in the port, indoors and seated.

Something quieter: Jazz at TribOz in Lapa, or Blue Note Rio in Copacabana.

The reliable bet: Carioca da Gema — intimate live samba, running late.

Where to Go

Pedra do Sal — Saúde (Pequena África) The stone steps in the old port where Carioca samba was born, and the city’s best-known free roda. It runs on Monday nights, so it is one for the start of next week rather than tonight. Tonight: Not on tonight. The roda runs on Mondays, from about 7 pm. Best time: Monday, from about 7 pm. Get there early for the atmosphere before the crush. Cost: Free to attend. Drinks from bars and vendors on a cash basis — carry small bills. Address: Largo João da Baiana, Saúde Getting there: VLT to the port, or metro Uruguaiana and a short walk/ride. Rideshare after dark. Good to know: Wear comfortable shoes and keep an eye on your belongings in the crowd.

Rio Scenarium — Centro/Lapa A magical three-floor 19th-century mansion packed with antiques and seven distinct spaces — one of Rio’s great samba-and-gafieira houses, at its liveliest on a Friday. Tonight: Live samba, gafieira and choro across the floors, 8 pm to 3 am on a Friday. Best time: Wednesday to Saturday; Friday and Saturday are the fullest — arrive earlier for a table. Cost: Tickets via the venue’s site; price moves with the line-up (from about R$30 (US$6), rising with the line-up). Address: Rua do Lavradio 20, Centro Website: rioscenarium.com.br Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, short walk to Rua do Lavradio. Rideshare after dark. Good to know: Buy online and arrive on the early side on a Friday.

Trapiche Gamboa — Gamboa/Saúde A reference point for traditional samba since 2004, in a restored port-district townhouse. Its women-singers roda, Razões Africanas, runs on Thursdays. Tonight: Open tonight, with doors around 6:30 pm. The women-singers roda is a Thursday night. Best time: Tuesday to Saturday; Thursday for the women-singers roda. Cost: Modest couvert, around R$25 (US$5) to R$30 (US$6). Usually 18+. Card and cash. Address: Rua Sacadura Cabral 155, Saúde Getting there: VLT to the port (Parada dos Museus), or rideshare. Near the Pedra do Sal. Good to know: A seated, indoor alternative to the largo, a few streets away.

Carioca da Gema — Lapa Lapa’s most awarded samba house, going since 2000. Live samba, chorinho and MPB in an intimate, air-conditioned room. Tonight: Doors 7:30 pm and the main show around 8:30 pm on a Friday. Best time: Friday and Saturday for the late, full-house nights. Cost: Couvert around R$30 (US$6). Card and cash. Address: Avenida Mem de Sá 79, Lapa/Centro Website: barcariocadagema.com.br Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, short walk into Lapa. Rideshare to the door at night. Good to know: A few minutes’ walk from Rio Scenarium — an easy pairing.

TribOz — Lapa A tiny, Australian-run jazz room and the city’s dedicated home for the genre. Intimate and serious about the music. Tonight: Two Friday jazz sets (typically around 6 pm and 9 pm). Confirm tonight’s act. Best time: Wednesday to Saturday. Two sets a night. Cost: Couvert roughly R$15 (US$3) to R$30 (US$6). Card and cash. Address: Rua Conde de Lages 19, Lapa Getting there: Metro Cinelândia, short walk into Lapa. Rideshare to the door. Good to know: Small room — reserve ahead, especially on a Friday.

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Centro / Saúde / Gamboa: The old port, home to Trapiche Gamboa and, on Mondays, the Pedra do Sal roda. Quiet otherwise, so travel by car.

Lapa: Rio’s nightlife heart under the Arcos, at its Friday peak — Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema, TribOz and Circo Voador. Busy and buzzing; rideshare door-to-door late.

Copacabana: Home to Blue Note Rio and Bip Bip, and an easy beachfront base. Walkable and lively.

Botafogo: A buzzy bar and cinema scene, a relaxed alternative to Lapa’s crowds.

Santa Teresa: Bohemian hilltop of cobbled lanes and artist bars. Charming for an early dinner; rideshare up and down.

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Friday is a big night — Rio’s queer parties are in full swing, many around Lapa and the Centro. The Farme stretch of Ipanema is the daytime hub; check listings for tonight’s parties.

Everyday-friendly spaces — Lapa’s houses and the port rooms are broadly mixed and welcoming.

Money & How Paying Works Cash still matters: street bars and small vendors around Lapa run on cash. Carry about R$150 (US$30) in small notes. Cover and couvert: Rio Scenarium starts about R$30 (US$6) and Carioca da Gema charges about R$30 (US$6); Trapiche and TribOz less. Buy Rio Scenarium online. Cards and Pix: Accepted at the houses; assume cash at the largo and street vendors. Tipping: 10% is usually added to the bill as ‘serviço’. Check before adding more.

Getting Home Safe

Metro: MetrôRio runs roughly 5 am to midnight Monday to Saturday. For a later night, plan on rideshare.

Rideshare: 99 and Uber are the safest way home from the port and Lapa late; surge is highest after midnight. Wait in a lit, busy spot.

The port at night: Quiet after dark — book a car door-to-door rather than walking to find one.

Phone awareness: Don’t walk with your phone out on quiet streets, and keep it away in a crowd. Duck into a bar to check maps or call a car.

Lapa on a Friday: Busy and policed on the main strip, but keep your wits about you and rideshare door-to-door.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Pedra do Sal roda on tonight?

No. The free roda on the stone steps is a Monday night, and we could not confirm a Friday edition, so save it for the start of next week. Tonight, Lapa is where the music is.

Pedra do Sal or Lapa — which should I choose?

Lapa, without much doubt. Rio Scenarium, Carioca da Gema and TribOz are within a few blocks of each other, so you can move between a grand samba house, an intimate room and a jazz bar in one night.

I’ve just landed at GIG (Galeão) tonight. Where should I go?

Lapa is the easy answer, about a 30–40 minute rideshare from Galeão, with three rooms a short walk apart. Take a rideshare door-to-door and carry some cash.

Do I need to speak Portuguese?

Not at all. The music does the work and the crowds are welcoming. A smile, a cold beer, and cash for the drinks are all you need.

Sources: Visit Rio (Pedra do Sal), rioscenarium.com.br, barcariocadagema.com.br, Trapiche Gamboa

World.title: Quaest State Polls Map Brazil’s Divide: Flávio Bolsonaro Takes the North, Lula the Northeast
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened: Quaest published first-round presidential numbers for 23 states plus Brasília on 27 August 2026.

— Espírito Santo: Flávio Bolsonaro leads Lula 37% to 30% there, with 15% of voters still undecided.

— The far north: Flávio wins Acre 42% to 25% and posts his best score anywhere in Roraima, 52% to 17%.

— Lula’s fortress: Lula takes Bahia 50% to 17% and sweeps the Northeast, reaching 58% in Maranhão.

— The catch: National polls show a near-tie, but the state map reveals two separate regional elections.

— What comes next: Brazil votes on 4 October, and Goiás is the rare state where a third candidate, Ronaldo Caiado, leads.

New Quaest state polls give Flávio Bolsonaro Espírito Santo, Acre and Roraima, while Lula crushes the Northeast with 50% in Bahia. The national tie hides a map split cleanly in two.

What Quaest published on Thursday night

The pollster Quaest released first-round presidential numbers for 23 Brazilian states plus the Federal District on 27 August. The wave was produced for Grupo Globo and its regional affiliate stations.

Field work ran from 23 to 26 August in most states. Samples ranged around 800 to 900 interviews per state, with margins of error near three points.

The Quaest state polls are registered with the Superior Electoral Court, as Brazilian law requires. Each was commissioned and paid for by a regional Globo affiliate.

Each poll tested two scenarios, one with the disqualified candidate Pablo Marçal and one without. The numbers below use the scenario without him, unless noted.

It is the broadest single-day state wave of the 2026 campaign. The releases ran through Thursday evening on Globo’s g1 portals, state by state.

Quaest is directed by political scientist Felipe Nunes and polls for Globo and for the Genial bank. Its national series has tracked this race since last year.

Espírito Santo: Flávio Bolsonaro ahead in a swing state

The headline number came from Espírito Santo. Flávio Bolsonaro leads there with 37% of voting intentions, against 30% for President Lula.

Renan Santos of the Missão party takes 4%, and Ronaldo Caiado of the PSD holds 3%. A full 15% of voters say they are undecided.

With Marçal on the ballot, the state tightens slightly. Flávio falls to 34%, Lula slips to 29%, and Marçal himself takes 3%.

In a runoff simulation in the state, Flávio reaches 48% against Lula’s 42%. Voters there disapprove of Lula’s administration by 53% to 41%.

Espírito Santo has become a reliable Bolsonaro stronghold. Jair Bolsonaro carried it in both 2018 and 2022.

Blank and null votes account for another 7% in the state. That is a low figure for this stage of a Brazilian campaign.

The poll heard 804 people between 23 and 26 August. It was registered with the electoral court as ES-04444/2026 and paid for by TV Gazeta.

The far north delivers Flávio Bolsonaro’s biggest wins

In Acre, on the Bolivian border, Flávio scores 42% against Lula’s 25%. With Pablo Marçal in the mix, the senator rises to 44% and Lula slips to 24%.

Acre has followed the same path for years. The state voted for the elder Bolsonaro in 2018 and again in 2022.

Roraima is his best state in the entire country. He takes 52% there, against just 17% for the president.

Roraima gave Jair Bolsonaro one of his widest margins anywhere in 2022. His son now inherits that loyalty almost intact.

The pattern repeats across the Amazon and the Centre-West in the Quaest state polls. In Mato Grosso do Sul, measured earlier in the week, Flávio leads 33% to 27%.

Bahia and the Northeast remain Lula’s wall

Bahia tells the opposite story. Lula takes 50% of voting intentions there, against only 17% for Flávio Bolsonaro, in a poll of 900 people.

Caiado managed only 4% in Bahia, despite his national profile. The Northeast remains the hardest region in Brazil for any centre-right candidate.

The president’s dominance runs through the whole region. He scores 53% in Sergipe against 19%, and 54% in both Pernambuco and Rio Grande do Norte.

Maranhão gives Lula his best number of the wave, at 58%. He also leads in Alagoas, where the race for governor is far tighter than the presidential one.

Bahia has backed the Workers’ Party in every presidential election since 2002. Nothing in this wave suggests that streak is in danger.

The one state where neither man leads

Goiás breaks the two-man pattern. Former governor Ronaldo Caiado leads the presidential first round in his home state, ahead of both national frontrunners.

Caiado governed Goiás until this year and remains its dominant political figure. His lead at home does not travel, as the Bahia numbers show.

Romeu Zema, the former Minas Gerais governor, takes only 2% in Espírito Santo. His support remains concentrated in the Southeast.

Everywhere else, the map belongs to Lula or Flávio. The earlier part of the Quaest wave had already put Santa Catarina at 45% to 20% for Flávio.

Paraná gave the senator 41% in that same round of releases. The South is now his most uniform region outside the Amazon.

The big electoral colleges stay knife-edge. São Paulo reads 30% to 29% for Flávio, and Minas Gerais 31% to 30%.

Rio de Janeiro, Rio Grande do Sul and Brasília are all tied in the first round. In the southern runoff simulation, Flávio wins Rio Grande do Sul by 52% to 42%.

Why the state map matters more than the national tie

Nationally, the race remains a statistical tie. The last national Quaest, from 14 August, put Lula ahead 38% to 31% in the first round.

The runoff in that poll read 43% to 40%, inside the margin of error. The Quaest state polls show how that national tie is built.

Two solid regional blocs cancel each other out. The Southeast’s giants then decide the election, state by state.

In Quaest’s national readings, both men carry rejection rates above 50%. The blocs hold together as much by dislike as by loyalty.

That is why both campaigns will spend September in São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro. Those three states hold roughly 40 million voters between them.

The electoral court still has to decide whether Marçal can run at all. His few points, drawn mostly from the right, could matter in the tightest states.

Undecided voters are the other variable. Their share reaches 15% in Espírito Santo, more than double the current gap between the frontrunners there.

Brazil votes on 4 October, with a runoff on 25 October if no one takes a majority. Free television advertising for all candidates begins this weekend.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who leads the presidential race in Espírito Santo, according to Quaest? Flávio Bolsonaro leads with 37% against Lula’s 30% in the first round. The poll heard 804 voters between 23 and 26 August 2026, and 15% remain undecided. Where is Lula strongest in the 2026 race? In the Northeast. The Quaest state polls give him 50% in Bahia against 17% for Flávio Bolsonaro, 53% in Sergipe and 58% in Maranhão. Where is Flávio Bolsonaro strongest? In Roraima, where he takes 52% against Lula’s 17%, his best state in Brazil. He also leads in Acre, 42% to 25%, and in Espírito Santo, 37% to 30%.

Sources: Quaest state polls released 27 August 2026 via G1 (Bahia, Roraima), Poder360, UOL, Estadão and CartaCapital; national Quaest of 14 August 2026 via G1.

World.title: Brazil’s Ceará Wins Largest New Export-Zone Investment With Voltalia Data Centre
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened Brazil approved five new export-zone projects on 25 August, led by a R$181.7 billion (US$35.3 billion) Ceará data centre.

— How big The five projects total R$206 billion (US$40 billion) across three Northeastern states.

— The real story Ceará’s export zone now hosts Brazil’s two biggest data centre bets, Voltalia’s and TikTok owner ByteDance’s.

— The catch The approval authorises the project but no operator is named yet, and the investment money has not flowed.

— Who else gained Maranhão won a R$18.5 billion (US$3.6 billion) green-steel project, while Piauí gained a green pig-iron plant.

— What comes next The projects should add R$40 billion (US$7.8 billion) a year to Brazilian exports from 2029.

Brazil’s export-zone council has approved a Voltalia-linked data centre worth R$181.7 billion (US$35.3 billion) for Ceará, the largest single investment among the country’s new export processing zones and the second mega data centre for the Pecém complex.

What the council approved

Brazil’s National Council of Export Processing Zones approved five new projects on Tuesday 25 August. Together they carry estimated investment of R$206 billion (US$40 billion).

The largest by far sits in Ceará. A Voltalia-linked data centre carries an estimated R$181.7 billion (US$35.3 billion) at the Pecém Industrial and Port Complex.

Export processing zones are duty-free industrial districts for firms selling abroad. Brazil created the regime in 2007 but had only two working zones for years.

The other approvals went to Maranhão and Piauí, two neighbouring Northeastern states. Their projects cover green steel, biofuels and green hydrogen.

The industry ministry says the five projects should add R$40 billion (US$7.8 billion) a year to Brazilian exports from 2029. That would make this the most valuable single round of approvals in the programme’s history.

Inside the Voltalia project

Voltalia is best known in Brazil as a wind and solar power producer. Its plan pairs the data centre with dedicated renewable plants to feed it.

The company signed a contract with the national grid operator in June for 322 megawatts of connection capacity at Pecém. It called that deal a milestone in becoming a partner for power-hungry digital infrastructure.

Voltalia says it is in advanced talks with several potential operators for the site. No technology company has been named as the anchor client.

Local reporting puts the build-out at about 2,300 jobs during construction. The figure for permanent operations staff will be far smaller, as is normal for data centres.

The approved estimate covers servers, buildings and the energy parks behind them. It is one of the largest private investments ever announced for the Northeast.

A second giant next door

The Voltalia approval lands seven months after works began on the zone’s first mega data centre. That project, led by Omnia with TikTok owner ByteDance as client, broke ground in January.

ByteDance took full control of that hub with federal approval published on 8 January. It bought the project from wind developer Casa dos Ventos to accelerate its data export plans.

The Omnia complex carries an estimated R$200 billion (US$38.8 billion) over four phases to 2033. Its first phase alone is budgeted at R$55 billion (US$10.7 billion).

Construction was about 8 percent complete in July, according to the state industry federation. More than R$350 million (US$68 million) in contracts had already gone to local firms by then.

The ByteDance site is designed for 300 megawatts of power draw and operation from 2027. It will run entirely on renewable energy supplied by Casa dos Ventos, a local developer.

Why Ceará keeps winning these bets

The state’s pitch rests on geography. Fortaleza is the closest major Brazilian city to Europe and Africa, and 18 submarine fibre cables land on its coast.

Officials describe their state as the second most connected region in the world by that measure. The cables carry data to Miami or Lisbon with only minimal delay.

The export processing zone adds the tax angle. Companies inside pay no federal taxes on export revenue, provided they sell at least 80 percent of output abroad.

The port itself is the second draw. It gives hardware imports a direct dock and already handles steel, iron ore and coal for the zone’s industries.

Ceará opened Brazil’s first working export zone in 2013, anchored by a steel mill. Banco do Brasil projects the state’s economy will grow 3.8 percent in 2026, the fastest in the Northeast.

What Maranhão and Piauí gained

Maranhão took three of the five approvals, worth R$23.2 billion (US$4.5 billion) in the Bacabeira export zone. The biggest is a R$18.5 billion (US$3.6 billion) green-steel venture from Vale and Green Energy Park Global.

The zone also gained a R$2.7 billion (US$524 million) bamboo biorefinery and a R$2 billion (US$388 million) green hydrogen plant. The three projects promise 10,000 construction jobs.

Bacabeira’s approvals mark that zone’s arrival as an industrial address. The Maranhão site was created in the programme’s recent expansion and lacked an anchor project until now.

Piauí’s Parnaíba zone won a R$1.1 billion (US$213 million) green pig-iron unit. It will use renewable hydrogen instead of coal in its furnaces.

What it means for foreigners and investors

For foreign companies, the approvals confirm the export zone as Brazil’s most aggressive investment regime. Tax-free export revenue plus abundant renewable power is a rare combination.

For expatriates in Fortaleza, the more visible effect is on jobs and services. Construction waves of this size lift demand for housing, schools and private healthcare.

The state invested a record R$4.8 billion (US$931 million) of public money in 2025. Officials argue that infrastructure spending is what makes private bets of this scale possible.

Currency plays a role as well. With the real near 5.15 per dollar, Brazilian power and construction look cheap to foreign backers.

What to watch from here

The first marker is the anchor client. Voltalia’s project only becomes real money when a technology company signs on as operator.

The second is the ByteDance build. Hitting its 2027 start date would prove the zone can deliver on the timelines it advertises.

The third is energy. Both data centres together will need more than 600 megawatts, and the wind farms to supply them are still being built.

For now the scoreboard favours Ceará. Its two data centre bets alone approach R$382 billion (US$74 billion) in announced investment.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Brazil approve for Ceará’s export zone in August 2026? The national export-zone council approved a Voltalia-linked data centre with estimated investment of R$181.7 billion (US$35.3 billion). It is the second mega data centre authorised for the Pecém complex. What is a ZPE in Brazil? A ZPE is an export processing zone, a duty-free industrial district for companies producing for foreign markets. Firms inside pay no federal taxes on exports but must sell at least 80 percent of output abroad. When will the Voltalia data centre start operating? No date has been announced. Voltalia secured 322 megawatts of grid capacity in June and says it is in advanced talks with potential operators.

Sources: Brazil’s National Council of Export Processing Zones (CZPE); Ministry of Development, Industry, Trade and Services (MDIC); Voltalia; Ceará Economic Development Secretariat (SDE); Ceará industry federation FIEC; Banco do Brasil Resenha Regional.

World.title: Brazil’s Federal Public Defender Sues Braskem Over Abandoned Maceió Salt Mines
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

BRAZIL · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened: The federal public defender sued Braskem on 27 August 2026 over R$5 billion (US$971 million) in mineral losses.

— How big the loss is: The suit says 29.4 million tonnes of rock salt, 52 percent of the deposit, were left underground.

— The real story: The case rests on a 2024 Senate inquiry that accused Braskem of predatory mining outside approved plans.

— The catch: The suit also targets the federal government itself, accused of failing to protect its mineral patrimony.

— Who else it touches: About 60,000 people left five Maceió neighborhoods, and 15,000 properties were emptied.

— What comes next: The defender wants any payment to fund urban recovery under social control, not the federal treasury.

Brazil’s federal public defender’s office has sued Braskem for at least R$5 billion (US$971 million) over the salt deposits abandoned beneath Maceió. The unusual part is the second defendant: the federal government itself.

RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. What the federal defender is asking for

The Defensoria Pública da União, Brazil’s federal public defender’s office, filed the public civil action on Thursday 27 August 2026. It went to the Federal Court in Alagoas, the state whose capital is Maceió.

The suit asks the court to condemn Braskem for the loss of the Maceió salt mines. It values the damage to federal mineral patrimony at no less than R$5 billion (US$971 million).

The figure comes from Braskem’s own mine closure plan of September 2019. Shutting the mines early abandoned 29.4 million tonnes of rock-salt reserves.

That volume is 52 percent of the deposit’s potential. Under Brazilian law, mineral resources in the subsoil belong to the federal government.

The action is signed by federal public defender Diego Bruno Alves. Braskem did not respond to requests for comment from Brazilian media.

Predatory mining, in the Senate’s words

The legal base of the suit is a 2024 Senate parliamentary inquiry into the disaster. That inquiry accused Braskem of what Portuguese calls “lavra ambiciosa”, or ambitious extraction.

The term means mining outside the plan approved by public authorities. It also covers extraction that destroys the future economic use of a deposit.

The suit says Braskem shrank the safety distances between its extraction wells. It also interconnected underground cavities, which destabilised the ground.

A second accusation is concealment. The company allegedly withheld technical information and sent selective risk reports to federal and state inspectors.

Braskem drilled 37 wells under Maceió from the early 1970s onward. Mining ran uninterrupted until May 2019, when sinking streets were officially linked to it.

The salt fed the company’s PVC factory, which opened in 1976 under the name Salgema. Rock salt is the raw material for caustic soda and PVC plastic.

What Braskem does. Braskem S.A., together with its subsidiaries, engages in the manufacture, sale, import, and export of chemicals, petrochemicals, and fuels in Brazil. The company supplies electricity and other inputs to second-generation producers; sells utilities, such as steam, water, compressed air and industrial gases; industrial services; and engages in the production, supply, and sale…

Why the federal government is also a defendant

The second target of the suit is the União, Brazil’s federal government. The defender says it failed to protect its own mineral patrimony.

Despite the Senate inquiry’s conclusions, no lawsuit or administrative charge was ever filed over the mineral damage. The suit calls that an unlawful omission.

Two federal bodies are cited by name. The National Mining Agency declared it has no competence to judge extraction done over the past five decades.

The Attorney General’s Office opened an internal information-gathering procedure. It never moved beyond the preparatory phase and set no timetable for collection.

The defender asks the court to declare the omission and order action. The government would have to investigate, constitute and collect the credit owed for the lost reserves.

The federal defender has worked on the case since 2018. It opened an administrative procedure on the government’s own responsibility and gave legal aid to victims.

Where the money would go

The suit makes an unusual request about any future payment. The money should not go to the federal treasury.

Instead, the defender wants a collective reparatory fund under social participation and control. It would finance urban recomposition and support the affected communities first.

The filing warns of a concrete risk that the money would follow a purely revenue-collecting logic. That, it says, could irreversibly destroy the practical purpose of the case.

The suit names communities such as Flexal de Baixo, Flexal de Cima and Quebradas, home to about 2,700 families. They border the exclusion zone and lost health posts, schools, public transport, security and local commerce.

It also records that insurers now refuse to issue housing policies nearby. Financing for properties outside the official risk area has dried up as well.

The disaster behind the case

The Maceió salt mines sit under five city neighborhoods, including Pinheiro, Mutange and Bebedouro. Cracks appeared in 2018, and the ground kept sinking.

The exclusion zone forced out about 60,000 residents and business owners. Some 15,000 properties were emptied, and most have been demolished.

In November 2023 the city declared a state of emergency over an imminent mine collapse. Once stabilised, the area is meant to become an agroforestry zone and a park.

The criminal front is moving too. Braskem and 13 people, including directors and public servants, are already defendants in the Federal Court.

Other civil claims are running in parallel. In July 2025 the Alagoas state public defender filed a separate R$4 billion (US$776 million) action over devalued homes.

Studies commissioned by the Alagoas government in 2023 put total losses at R$20 billion to R$30 billion. That is US$3.88 billion to US$5.82 billion at today’s rate.

The Maceió salt mines stopped producing in May 2019. Seven years later, their full cost is still being counted in court.

Why the timing matters

The lawsuit landed at a delicate moment for Braskem. The company filed for extrajudicial recovery on 24 August, seeking to renegotiate US$10.9 billion of debt.

Hours before the suit became public, Braskem’s stock had jumped almost 21 percent. Investors were cheering an enlarged Petrobras credit line, not the legal front.

The company already carries R$15.6 billion (US$3.03 billion) of provisions for the Maceió disaster. A new R$5 billion (US$971 million) claim would sit on top of that.

How a fresh public civil action interacts with the recovery is now an open legal question. Creditors and victims will be watching the same court dockets.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Brazil’s federal public defender suing Braskem? The Defensoria Pública da União says Braskem’s early closure of its Maceió salt mines abandoned 29.4 million tonnes of rock-salt reserves, 52 percent of the deposit. It values the loss to federal mineral patrimony at at least R$5 billion (US$971 million). Why is the Brazilian federal government also a defendant? The defender argues the government failed to charge Braskem for the mineral damage despite a 2024 Senate inquiry. It wants the court to declare that omission and order the government to collect the credit. Where would the money go if Braskem loses? The suit asks that any payment go to a collective reparatory fund under social control, not the federal treasury. The fund would prioritise urban recomposition and support for the communities affected by the Maceió disaster.

Sources: UOL column by Carlos Madeiro with the full text of the DPU action, 27 August 2026; Reuters via UOL Economia; Migalhas on the parallel Alagoas state defender action.
