World.title: Costa Rica Supreme Court President Won’t Seek New Term
World.content:
Costa Rica will soon have a new president of its Supreme Court after Orlando Aguirre announced that he will not seek another four-year term leading the country’s Judiciary. Aguirre confirmed his decision Wednesday, August 26, one month before his current term expires on September 26. He will not leave the Supreme Court entirely. Instead, he plans to remain as a magistrate in Sala Segunda, the chamber that handles labor and family matters.

His decision comes at an unusually tense moment between Costa Rica’s government and its Judiciary. President Laura Fernández and other senior government figures have repeatedly criticized the courts over crime, the speed of criminal cases and the handling of high-profile investigations. The Judiciary, meanwhile, has pushed back against government budget cuts and warned against political interference with the courts.

Those disagreements have become increasingly public in recent weeks. Last week, Aguirre declined to participate in a security meeting proposed by Fernández under the conditions established by the Executive Branch. Aguirre said cooperation between the branches of government is necessary but objected to a proposal that would have established goals, deadlines and responsibilities for each branch.

He argued that allowing political authorities to help establish targets or evaluation systems for the Judiciary could interfere with judicial independence. The government subsequently canceled the meeting. The dispute has also moved into the national budget. The Finance Ministry recently ordered another ₡23.72 billion reduction to the Judiciary’s 2026 budget. The Supreme Court has said it will pursue administrative and legal measures to challenge the reduction.

Against that backdrop, Aguirre used his announcement Wednesday to emphasize the importance of keeping Costa Rica’s courts independent. He said the Judiciary faces important challenges and needs to become faster, easier for the public to understand and more open to new technology. But he also stressed that judicial independence, impartiality and due process must remain protected.

Aguirre has led the Supreme Court since September 2022. His election four years ago was anything but simple. Supreme Court magistrates needed five sessions and 19 rounds of voting before he finally secured the 12 votes required to win. The process to choose his replacement will now begin.

Candidates will have an opportunity to formally enter the race, after which their names will be made public. They are also expected to participate in a public discussion about their plans for leading the Judiciary before the 22-member Supreme Court votes. That election could become especially important given the current political climate.

The president of the Supreme Court is not simply Costa Rica’s highest-profile judge. The position also serves as the institutional leader of the Judicial Branch and represents it in discussions with the Executive Branch and Legislative Assembly. Whoever replaces Aguirre will immediately inherit disputes over judicial funding, organized crime, public security and the relationship between the courts and the Fernández administration.

Aguirre, 83, has spent decades in Costa Rica’s judicial system and has been a Supreme Court magistrate since 1989. His current appointment as a magistrate runs until 2029. For the next month, however, he remains president of the Supreme Court. The more consequential question now is who Costa Rica’s magistrates choose to replace him, and whether that person can ease one of the most visible institutional disputes without compromising the Judiciary’s independence

World.title: US Embassy Says Tourist Visa Appointments in Costa Rica Are Not Affected
World.content:
If you have an appointment in San José for a US tourist or business visa, keep it. Nothing has changed for you. The US Embassy in Costa Rica confirmed today that it is not suspending appointments for nonimmigrant visas. Tourism, business and other nonimmigrant categories are going ahead exactly as scheduled.

One group is affected, and it is a small one. If your interview is for an immigrant visa — the kind that leads to permanent residence in the United States — your appointment may have been moved. The embassy said those interviews were rescheduled only for the final days of August.

That matters because the news that reached Costa Rica this week sounded far worse than what is actually happening here. The story started with reports that the United States had halted visa appointments at its embassies and consulates worldwide. Applicants in several countries received emails telling them their scheduled interviews were cancelled and would be rescheduled later, with no new date attached. Some of the international coverage described it as a freeze on all visa interviews.

Other reporting described it more narrowly, as a pause affecting immigrant visa interviews only. In Costa Rica, the embassy has now drawn that line clearly. Nonimmigrant appointments stand. Immigrant appointments in the last stretch of August do not.

The reason behind the pause is a training programme. The State Department began an in-depth course for consular officers worldwide in early August, and appointment schedules are being adjusted to make room for it. A department spokesperson said the aim is to make sure every officer evaluates applicants the same way, no matter which embassy they work in.

What the officers are being trained on is a rule known as public charge. It is not new. Under US immigration law, an applicant can be refused an immigrant visa if the officer concludes they are likely to end up dependent on public assistance after arriving. The training is about how officers reach that conclusion, and the expectation is that they will apply it more strictly than before.

The State Department has not said how long the training will run, or when normal scheduling resumes. That is the part nobody can answer yet. There is a separate legal fight running alongside all of this, and it is easy to confuse the two. On August 21, a federal judge in Manhattan struck down a different policy that had suspended immigrant visas for applicants from 75 countries, ruling that the State Department had gone beyond its legal authority.

Costa Rica was not on that list, and that ruling has nothing to do with this week’s scheduling changes. So what should you actually do? If your appointment is for a tourist or business visa, go. Bring what you were told to bring and do not reschedule on your own. If your appointment is for an immigrant visa in the next few days, check your email, including the folder your provider dumps promotional mail into.

Rescheduling notices are going out by email, and a missed message is the most likely way someone ends up at the embassy gate on a day they no longer have a slot. Check your appointment status directly through the official appointment system before you travel to San José. People come in from Guanacaste, the Southern Zone and the Caribbean for these interviews, and a five-minute check is cheaper than a wasted day and a hotel night.

Anyone starting a new application can still file. The pause concerns interviews, not the submission of paperwork. The wider picture is worth keeping in view. The United States is tightening how it screens people who want to live there permanently, and the training now underway is part of that.

Wait times, refusal rates and the level of financial documentation officers ask for are all likely to shift over the coming months. For anyone with a case in progress, the safest assumption is that the process gets slower before it gets faster.

World.title: The one treasure the rich world cannot buy, Belize has a nation full of it
World.content:
The one treasure the rich world cannot buy, Belize has a nation full of it

By Horace Palacio:

Let me show you a number that the wealthiest nations on earth would trade fortunes for, and cannot purchase at any price.

Twenty seven.

That is Belize’s median age. Half of this entire country is younger than twenty seven years old. Only about one Belizean in twenty has reached sixty five. Nearly seven in ten of us are of working age, right now, today.

Now lift your eyes and look at the countries we call rich. Japan’s median age is pushing fifty, a nation famously buying more adult diapers than baby diapers, with villages of empty schools and a pension system groaning under the weight of its elders. Italy sits near forty eight. Germany close behind. South Korea’s birth rate has collapsed to the lowest ever recorded by any nation, each generation nearly halving the one before it. Even mighty China is now aging and shrinking, growing old, as their own economists whisper, before growing rich.

Those countries have money, technology, and power. What they are running out of is the one resource no treasury can print. Young people. And Belize, cash-poor, import-dependent, problem-ridden Belize, is sitting on a vault of exactly that.

Economists have a name for our position. The demographic dividend. It is the golden window when a nation’s workers vastly outnumber its dependents, when energy is abundant and pension bills are light. It is the same wind that filled the sails of the Asian tigers on their climb from poverty to wealth. That wind is blowing through Belize at this very moment, sixty eight working-age Belizeans for every five elders, a ratio the old world can only dream about.

But now the honesty this column owes you, in two hard truths.

First, a dividend is a window, not a gift, and windows close. Our own fertility rate has already fallen to around replacement level. Run the arithmetic forward and the picture is plain, the babies not born today are the workers missing in 2050. Belize itself begins aging within a generation. We hold this advantage for roughly twenty five to thirty years. Then it is gone, forever.

Second, and sharper, a young population is only a dividend if it is skilled and employed. Untrained and idle, it is not a dividend at all. It is dynamite. The very youthfulness we boast about is what feeds the gang pipeline I have written about, the boys recruited between eight and fourteen, and the departure lounges full of our brightest. A blessing unclaimed becomes a burden armed.

And here is the threat almost nobody in Belmopan is discussing. The aging rich world is not going to sit quietly in its emptiness. It is already hunting. Japan, Germany, Canada and the rest are actively recruiting young workers, nurses, caregivers and technicians from around the planet, because their societies literally cannot function without imported youth. Every young Belizean is about to become a globally traded asset, courted by nations desperate for what we have. If home offers them nothing, Houston and Toronto will offer them everything, and Belize will end its golden window having subsidized the old age of rich nations with its own children. That would be the cruelest export in our history.

So how does Belize actually cash this dividend? Five moves, and the clock is running on every one.

Move one, train for the world’s shortage, deliberately. The aging planet will pay premium prices for exactly what young Belizeans can become, health workers, caregivers, technicians, digital service providers. So build those skills at scale, but structure the trade wisely. Wherever possible, sell the service, not the citizen. The nurse consulting via telehealth support, the young Belizean managing systems remotely for a graying company abroad, the digital services floor serving old-world clients from Belize City, that is the dividend earning foreign exchange while sleeping at home. This is the whole reason the BPO to digital-services climb I keep writing about matters so much. We sit two hours from the largest aging market on earth, speaking its language natively.

Move two, where our people do go abroad, make it a circle, not a leak. Formal work programs with return incentives, diaspora investment channels, the Cabo Verde lesson this column taught during the World Cup, a scattered people treated as deployed assets rather than lost ones. The passport leaves, the wealth and skills flow home, and the door back stands wide open.

Move three, make staying rational. Everything in this column’s ownership agenda, the land titled, the first home financeable, the business registrable in days, the light bill survivable, is really youth policy in disguise. Young people do not leave countries. They leave dead ends.

Move four, sell to the old world instead of just supplying it. An aging, wealthy planet will spend trillions on warm places to retire, recover and be cared for. Belize already has a retirement program and the climate heaven demands. Build the care economy here, retirement communities, wellness, recovery tourism, staffed by trained young Belizeans earning global wages at home. Let their sunset finance our sunrise.

And move five, fix the pension math now, while the ratio is golden. Today many workers support each retiree. Within a generation that ratio tightens like a noose, ask Japan. The Social Security Board must be guarded, funded and reformed in the fat years, because demographic winter forgives nothing and reschedules for no one.

Here is the whole argument in a single breath, Belize.

We spend our days counting what we lack, capital, scale, energy, and it is all true. But we are rich, genuinely rich, in the one currency the mighty are going bankrupt in. Time. Youth. Tomorrow, walking around in school uniforms.

The old world would pay anything for one generation of what fills our classrooms this morning.

The window is open. It closes once.

Claim the dividend, Belize, before the world claims it from us.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: BEL announces Tentative load shedding for tonight!
World.content:
BEL announces Tentative load shedding for tonight!

By Zoila Palma: Belize Electricity Limited (BEL) has announced a tentative load shedding schedule for tonight as the country’s power grid faces possible supply constraints due to high demand in Mexico.

BEL said Comisión Federal de Electricidad (CFE) has informed the company that it may need to curtail power because of high demand on its system. As a result, load shedding may become necessary in several sections of Belize to maintain stability of the national grid.

The tentative schedule indicates that power interruptions may occur between 8:00 p.m. and 11:00 p.m. in sections served by the San Pedro Feeder 2, Corozal Feeder 3, San Ignacio Feeder 1, Dangriga Feeder 1 and Ladyville Feeder 1 Zones 1 and 2.

In San Ignacio, affected areas include the downtown area, Kontiki, Swamyville, Mosquitoville, Boiton, Bradley’s Bank, Cahal Pech, Trapiche, Branch Mouth Road, New Area Santa Elena and portions of 2nd and 3rd Streets.

In San Pedro, areas include San Pedrito, the Airstrip area, San Pablo, San Marcos, DFC, Eiley Subdivision and surrounding communities.

BEL emphasized that the schedule is tentative and may change depending on energy demand and generation levels.

The company explained that load shedding involves deliberately disconnecting feeders or sections of feeders from the grid to match available generation and prevent a wider collapse of the electricity system.

World.title: NICH launches “Belize @45 Magical History Tour” with historian Assad Shoman
World.content:
NICH launches “Belize @45 Magical History Tour” with historian Assad Shoman

By Zoila Palma: The National Institute of Culture and History (NICH) is inviting Belizeans to explore the country’s history through the “Belize @45 Magical History Tour,” featuring historian Assad Shoman.

The initiative forms part of activities surrounding Belize’s 45th anniversary of independence and aims to encourage deeper reflection and discussion about the nation’s past.

The tour will include engagements with high school students, giving young Belizeans an opportunity to examine the country’s history critically and explore aspects that may not always be covered in traditional textbooks.

Public forums will also be held in the evenings, allowing community members to participate in discussions and ask questions about Belize’s historical development.

NICH said the tour will visit communities across the country, with activities scheduled at the Ignacia Cacho Public Library in Corozal on August 28.

In September, the tour will continue at the San Ignacio-Santa Elena House of Culture on September 3, Benque Viejo House of Culture on September 4, and the George Price Center for Peace and Development on September 7.

Additional sessions are scheduled for the Belize City House of Culture on September 11, Banquitas House of Culture in Orange Walk on September 15, and the Corozal House of Culture on September 16.

The tour encourages participants to reflect on Belize’s journey to independence and consider whether independence fully ended the social, economic and historical influences inherited from the colonial era.

NICH is encouraging Belizeans, particularly students and community members, to participate in the tour and engage in what it describes as an opportunity to ask difficult questions about the country’s history.

World.content:
Team Belize represent at Gran Premio Panamá

By Zoila Palma: Belizean cyclists proudly represented the country at the Gran Premio Panamá, earning recognition from the Belize Olympic and Commonwealth Games Association for their efforts on the international stage.

World.title: Rare red northern lights could appear alongside Red moon during Lunar eclipse
World.content:
Rare red northern lights could appear alongside Red moon during Lunar eclipse

By Zoila Palma: Skygazers could be treated to a rare double spectacle tonight as a partial lunar eclipse is expected to turn much of the Moon a deep coppery red while a geomagnetic storm could produce vibrant northern lights across parts of North America.

The partial lunar eclipse will be visible in the Americas, Europe, Africa and Western Asia.

The Moon will pass into Earth’s shadow, with about 96 percent of its surface expected to be covered during the deepest stage of the eclipse.

At the same time, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has issued a moderate G2 geomagnetic storm warning, raising the possibility that auroras could be visible as far south as parts of the northern United States.

Astronomers say observers in Canada and Alaska may have the best chance of seeing the aurora and eclipsed Moon at the same time.

The two phenomena are unlikely to appear in exactly the same part of the sky, but viewing conditions could allow the glowing auroral bands to appear alongside the reddish Moon, particularly for observers farther west.

The potential aurora display follows a powerful M-class solar flare recorded on August 25, which was followed by a coronal mass ejection—a large cloud of charged solar material traveling toward Earth.

NOAA forecast G1 and G2 geomagnetic storm conditions between August 27 and 28, coinciding with the lunar eclipse, which is expected to begin at around 9:23 p.m. EDT, reach its peak shortly after midnight and end around 3 a.m. Friday.

The eclipse will not technically be a total lunar eclipse, since a small portion of the Moon will remain outside Earth’s darkest shadow.

However, it is expected to be the deepest lunar eclipse visible worldwide until December 2028.

The Moon’s red appearance occurs because Earth’s atmosphere filters and bends sunlight toward its surface, while auroral colors are produced when charged particles from the Sun interact with gases in Earth’s atmosphere.

World.title: 29-year-old man busted with amount of cocaine so small it didn’t move the scale; jailed for outstanding $105 fine
World.content:
29-year-old man busted with amount of cocaine so small it didn’t move the scale; jailed for outstanding $105 fine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Belize City man who pleaded guilty to possession of an undetermined amount of cocaine has been sent to prison after he was unable to pay an old outstanding court fine.

Jamal Alexander Jones Jr., 29, a Waste Control worker, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Thursday, where he pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled drug.

Jones was busted on Saturday, August 22, 2026, on Administration Drive in Belize City with an amount of cocaine reportedly so small that it could not register on the gram scale.

For the drug offence, Jones was fined $130 plus $5 cost of court and was given until October 30, 2026, to pay. In default, he faces one month imprisonment.

However, the court also discovered that Jones had an outstanding $105 fine stemming from a 2023 conviction. The Magistrate ordered that the outstanding amount be paid immediately before he could be released.

Jones was unable to pay the $105 and was subsequently escorted to the Belize Central Prison on a warrant to serve prison time in default of the outstanding fine.

World.title: International News: Trump orders Lake Ontario renamed ‘Lake America’ due to escalating U.S.-Canada Trade War
World.content:
International News: Trump orders Lake Ontario renamed ‘Lake America’ due to escalating U.S.-Canada Trade War

By Zoila Palma: U.S. President Donald Trump has signed an executive order directing his administration to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” escalating tensions with Canada as the two countries remain locked in a worsening trade dispute.

Trump signed the order in the Oval Office today, instructing the U.S. Department of the Interior and the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to formalize the name change within 30 days.

During the signing, Trump compared the move to his decision last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America,” joking that the next step could be renaming one of the Atlantic or Pacific oceans.

The name Lake Ontario dates back centuries and is derived from an Iroquois word meaning “lake of shining waters.” The lake forms part of the shoreline of Toronto, Canada, while most of its volume and its deepest areas are on the U.S. side.

White House staff secretary Ben Moss described it as an “American lake” as he presented the order to Trump for signing.

The renaming comes amid a sharp deterioration in U.S.-Canada trade relations.

Trump recently imposed tariffs of up to 50 percent on a range of Canadian goods after trade negotiations broke down, while Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded with tariffs on U.S. exports ranging from 15 to 50 percent. Trump has also threatened to increase tariffs on Canadian automobiles and auto parts from 25 to 50 percent.

Canada has rejected the proposed name change and indicated it will continue referring to the body of water as Lake Ontario.

World.title: Honduran construction worker jailed after failing to pay $1,000 fine for entering Belize illegally
World.content:
Honduran construction worker jailed after failing to pay $1,000 fine for entering Belize illegally

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 25-year-old Honduran national who told immigration authorities he had been living in Belize since 2023 has been sent to the Belize Central Prison after he was unable to pay a $1,000 fine for an immigration offence.

Franklin Estralin Guerra Jacinto, a construction worker of the Gungulung area, appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate on Tuesday, where he pleaded guilty to failing to produce a valid permit upon demand by an Immigration Officer.

Jacinto was fined $1,000 plus $5 cost of court, which he was ordered to pay forthwith. In default of payment, he was ordered to serve six months in prison.

According to the facts presented in court, police at the Raccoon Street Police Station contacted the Immigration Department on Sunday, August 23, after Jacinto was detained.

Immigration officers interviewed Jacinto and requested identification. He reportedly produced a Honduran passport, but checks revealed that it contained no Belize entry stamp.

Jacinto allegedly told authorities that he entered Belize through the Mopan River area near Benque Viejo, Cayo District, in October 2023 and had remained in the country since then.

Immigration officials subsequently searched the Migration Information and Data Analysis System, or MIDAS, using Jacinto’s name, date of birth and passport number, but reportedly found no record of his entry into Belize.

He was informed of his irregular immigration status and later charged.

Jacinto was unable to pay the $1,000 fine and was escorted to the Belize Central Prison to begin serving the six-month default sentence.

World.title: Courage under fire
World.content:
Firefighters battle the inferno at Super Parts Limited on Hagley Park Road on Thursday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Employees of Superior Parts Limited and a taxi driver battled to save millions of dollars worth of motorcycles and cars on Thursday as a raging fire tore through the company on Hagley Park Road in St Andrew, while firefighters were hampered by a lack of water amid the severe drought that has triggered water restrictions in sections of the island.

Although firefighters from seven stations in Kingston and St Catherine responded, the majority of the stock was destroyed in the midday inferno that sent thick black smoke into the air and created traffic snarls on Hagley Park Road and adjoining thoroughfares.

In the midst of the chaos and destruction, 71-year-old Leroy Terlon used a forklift to remove numerous wooden boxes from the premises and placed them on the road.

“I had to put out the energy and the effort to get certain things saved. I have been here for 20 years and I helped to build the company to where it is now, with labour and loyalty. This event shouldn’t have happened,” Terlon told the Jamaica Observer as he sipped a cold beer at a nearby gas station following his heroics.

He said he was cooling off after his exposure to the intense heat.

“This hurts me. This company is like mine. If I talk about it, tears will come to my eyes. I have been there for so long. It hurts me. I don’t have liquid cash in the business, but I have years of service,” he added as he received congratulatory messages from friends for his bravery.

Other employees also rushed to move stock from the building, while taxi operator Kemal Dunn used his car to tow motor vehicles from a car mart adjoining the burning property.

“I just saw it and said I had to help. I knew it would spread because Superior has a lot of boxes,” he told the Observer.

“I was just driving past. My uncle owns a car dealership up the road. This car dealership just started. For a trying man, I decided to just assist him as best as I could,” Dunn explained.

“Only one car got damaged out of more than 30 that were there. I helped them rescue a good 20 of them. I used my car to pull out some. We used a wire to jump-start others because they were parked for a good while and they had no power to start. I am glad I helped them to minimise the loss.

“I was just watching the electric wire. The fire, you just have to know how to stay a good distance because you are going to feel the heat. The wires were sparking and gashing.”

“I love to help a person and he can pass it on to a next person. I am not going to take my phone and video when I can help,” he added, taking an apparent jab at the many onlookers who stood recording the fire with their cellphones.

Dunn said he banged on the windows of neighbouring houses to ensure that no humans were inside.

“All of these things are material things that can be replaced. A lot of people won’t have a job tomorrow, but they still have life,” Dunn reasoned.

As the fire raged, people in a number of adjoining residential and commercial premises moved out as many supplies and furniture before the flames spread.

One Superior Parts employee, who wished to remain anonymous, speculated that welding sparked the blaze.

“There was welding going on around the back. The fire started around that side. Nobody is allowed to smoke on property, so we believe it started with the welding. We don’t see any other way the fire could have started,” the worker said.

Amid the devastation wrought by the fire, police were kept on their toes by onlookers who wanted to get close-up shots to post on social media. Cops were heard repeatedly telling them to remove from the area for their safety.

Other onlookers were heard venting that the motorbikes were being destroyed and the police did not allow them to go in and grab one for themselves.

Throughout the ordeal, power lines caught fire, sending sparks flying and forcing people to take cover. At the same time, numerous loud explosions were heard coming from the premises.

Three firefighters were reportedly injured during their attempt to put the blaze out.

The Observer was told that the Jamaica Fire Brigade had received a call alerting it to the fire at 12:08 pm. Units from Trench Town initially responded, but according to a firefighter who requested anonymity because he was not authorised to speak to the media, the magnitude of the fire was so great that units had to be requested from other stations.

“There were units from York Park, Half-Way-Tree, Rollington Town, Port Royal, Stony Hill, Portmore, and Spanish Town,” the firefighter said, while pointing to the difficulty they experienced accessing water at the scene.

“The water challenges were expected because of the drought conditions. A lot of the hydrants have no water or low water pressure and it was a massive fire,” he added.

Up to 6:00 pm, the fire had not been fully extinguished.

World.title: Sandals Foundation head Heidi Clarke honoured with 2026 Skift IDEA Trailblazer Award
World.content:
CLARKE... I believe the success of any business should also be measured by the opportunities it creates for others to rise, empowering generations and strengthening communities

IN recognition of her far-reaching impact, Sandals Foundation Executive Director Heidi Clarke has been selected to receive the prestigious ‘Trailblazer Award: Women Shaping the Future of Travel,’ as part of the 2026 Skift IDEA Awards.

The Skift IDEA Awards are the travel industry’s way of recognising excellence in design, creativity, and innovation with winners being a beacon of where the industry is heading.

Presented in partnership with Women Leading Travel, the Trailblazer Award honours a woman whose career demonstrates exceptional leadership, resilience, and influence in shaping the future of travel.

Clarke, who heads the philanthropic arm of Sandals and Beaches resorts, has harnessed the power of tourism to strengthen communities and expand opportunity across the Caribbean.

Since the launch of the not-for-profit Sandals Foundation in 2009, Clarke has led initiatives that improve lives across the Caribbean, with a focus on education, community development, and environmental conservation in the nine islands where Sandals and Beaches resorts operate.

Under her care, the foundation has touched more than 1.8 million lives, supporting more than 2,600 schools, close to 200 large-scale conservation initiatives, and mobilising more than 32,500 volunteers across the region, among other extraordinary projects.

“It is truly an honour to be recognised, and I am immensely proud of what our team, together with our incredible partners, has made possible,” said Clarke.

“I believe the success of any business should also be measured by the opportunities it creates for others to rise, empowering generations and strengthening communities. Tourism has an extraordinary footprint, and when we harness that reach with purpose it can be a tremendous force for positive change across our Caribbean region,” added Clarke.

Her work has championed tourism as a force for positive, lasting change, bringing together communities, governments, non-profit organisations, businesses and travellers to address local needs and strengthen the destinations that sustain the industry.

Born and raised in Jamaica, she has spent nearly two decades developing programs that strengthen communities, expand economic opportunity and advance environmental stewardship throughout the Caribbean.

“Heidi is a true champion for the Caribbean and has dedicated her career to creating opportunities for its people and building a stronger future for the region,” said Adam Stewart, executive chairman of Sandals and Beaches Resorts and president of Sandals Foundation. “She leads with tremendous heart and purpose, and with an unwavering belief in the potential of our Caribbean communities. Her work through the Sandals Foundation is at the heart of who we are at Sandals Resorts and Beaches Resorts, and reflects our deep and enduring commitment to the region we call home. This recognition is incredibly well-deserved, and we could not be prouder of Heidi and the contributions she continues to make,” added Stewart.

The Skift IDEA Awards are now in their eighth year. The 2026 winners were evaluated through an initial review by the Skift Editorial Team, followed by an independent judging panel of travel and business leaders representing top hospitality organisations.

World.title: Dancehall gets recognition from the JUNO Awards
World.content:
2025 JUNO nominee Skystar.

AHEAD of the 2027 staging of the JUNO Awards, Canada’s equivalent to the Grammys, the Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (CARAS) has introduced a series of category and eligibility updates.

These updates, according to CARAS in a press release shared with the Jamaica Observer, are designed to better reflect Canada’s music community and to provide clear, meaningful pathways for artistes to have their work recognised.

The category Reggae Recording of the Year has been renamed Reggae/Dancehall Recording of the Year. The reggae category was first instituted in 1985 as Best Reggae/Calypso Recording. For the 1994 staging, the category was renamed Best Reggae Recording, with the name Reggae Recording of the Year coming into effect in 2003.

Canada-based dancehall artiste Phenique is pleased with the evolution of the JUNO Awards.

“I’m excited to see the JUNO Awards continuing to evolve and recognise the diversity within today’s music. I think these changes create more opportunities for artists across different genres to have their work recogniSed and celebrated. It’s definitely a positive step forward,” Phenique told the Jamaica Observer on Tuesday.

Recording artiste, broadcaster and curator of the weekly Reggae North Canadian Reggae/Dancehall Top 20 chart, Tony Anthony, believes that the inclusion of dancehall is long overdue.

“The inclusion of Dancehall in the JUNO Awards’ Reggae/Dancehall Recording of the Year category is a significant and long-overdue step forward for our community. Industry professionals and supporters within the reggae and Dancehall community have advocated for Dancehall to be properly recognised on one of Canada’s biggest music stages. This announcement is not just a change in the name of a category—it is an acknowledgment of the cultural impact, creativity and contribution that Dancehall has made to Canadian music and to the broader music industry. This is an important milestone, but also a reminder that our community must continue to advocate for both genres and ensure that its artists receive the respect, visibility and opportunities that come with being recognized as a vital part of Canada’s music industry,” Tony Anthony disclosed.

2025 JUNO nominee dancehall artiste Skystar, who is originally from the Kingston 20 area, sees the revamping of the reggae category to include dancehall as a step forward.

“I’m excited to see the JUNOS expanding the conversation to officially recognise dancehall. Reggae is deeply rooted in Jamaican culture, but Dancehall has grown into a powerful global movement that continues to influence music, fashion, language and youth culture around the world,” he noted. “For artists like myself who represent the next generation of Jamaican music here in Canada, this recognition matters. It tells us that the sound, culture and evolution of our music are being seen and valued. I believe this is a great step forward, and I hope we continue creating space for the many different sounds and generations that make Reggae and Dancehall so powerful. Respect to the JUNOS for recognising the culture.”

However, Carrie Mullings, former chair of the Reggae Committee for the JUNO Awards, says dancehall music was always submitted for consideration.

“During my time with the JUNO’s (17 years, 12 as a chair) the category already consisted of dancehall submissions when you read the category description. As much as it is nice for the word Dancehall to be included in the category title it was never excluded. I feel these small steps are good but the bigger conversation in my opinion is the fact that an album body of work and a single can be submitted in the same category. We should be addressing the reason the category has not been split into 2, 1 for Reggae/Dancehall Recording of The Year (for single submissions) and 1 for Reggae/Dancehall Album/EP of the Year. As our music grows, collectively we should express our needs for expansion and recognition. Reggae/dancehall has walked the JUNO Red Carpet since 1985, please acknowledge our culture’s growth and award it accordingly,” said Mullings.

Other category changes for the 2027 JUNO Awards include:

Rap: Melodic Rap Recording of the Year and Rap Recording of the Year will replace Rap Album/EP of the Year and Rap Single of the Year.

Electronic/Dance: Electronic/Dance Single of the Year and Electronic/Dance Album/EP of the Year will replace Electronic Album of the Year and Dance Recording of the Year.

Contemporary Christian/Gospel: Contemporary Christian/Gospel Recording of the Year will replace Contemporary Christian/Gospel Album of the Year, with singles, EPs and albums now eligible.

The submission for awards and songs for consideration for the 2027 staging of the JUNO Awards will open on September 21 with November 5 being the final submission date.

The 56th annual JUNO Awards will be broadcast live from Canada Life Centre in Winnipeg, Manitoba, on Sunday, April 4, 2027. JUNO Week runs from April 1 to 4, 2027.

World.title: Nation’s Choice makes $1-billion hotel bet
World.content:
Nation’s Choice chief executive Donald McDonald shows pallets of frozen products inside the company’s Clarendon cold-storage facility, part of a roughly $1-billion investment aimed at expanding capacity for the hospitality sector.

Nations Choice has invested about $1 billion in new cold storage capacity as the Jamaican food company positions itself for increased demand from the hotel sector while preparing to export locally manufactured products across the Caribbean.

Guyana is expected to be the first export market early next year, Chief Executive Officer Donald McDonald said, with Barbados, St Lucia and the Cayman Islands also among the countries being targeted.

The Clarendon-based company imports and distributes frozen and chilled seafood, meats, poultry and vegetables, but has been steadily increasing manufacturing as it builds the Nations Choice name into a consumer brand.

“We are preparing ourselves now to start exporting from Jamaica some of the products that we manufacture,” McDonald told the Jamaica Observer in an interview on Wednesday. “We have gone into some markets, done some market surveys, and there is a lot of interest in some of the products that we do manufacture.”

The planned exports would include burgers, bacon, ham and pickled products made in Jamaica. Nations Choice already moves some branded products into other Caribbean countries but McDonald said those goods are produced or packaged outside Jamaica. That activity accounts for only about one to two per cent of the company’s business.

Nations Choice has invested an estimated $4 billion since starting in 2011 with two containers and five products, McDonald said. The company now employs more than 300 people and handles about 200 stock-keeping units.

The larger cold storage facility represents an investment of about $1 billion and can hold about four million kilogrammes of product. A separate picking room, which is not included in that investment, has capacity for about 1,500 pallets. The operation runs around the clock.

McDonald said the investment was made with Jamaica’s expanding hotel pipeline in mind. Hospitality already accounts for about 20 per cent of Nations Choice’s business, with the remaining 80 per cent coming from the wider local market, including institutions and consumers.

He expects between 8,000 and 9,000 hotel rooms to come on stream over the next two years, which he believes will create additional demand for food suppliers.

Government filings reported in July identified 13 hotel projects facilitated by Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro), that are expected to add 8,943 rooms, although the developments have varying completion timelines and some have been delayed.

“I think that presents a great opportunity for growth in servicing that sector,” McDonald said. “That is why we’re interested in building this new cold storage, positioning ourselves to be able to service the hospitality sector.”

The bet on hotels comes while that part of Nations Choice’s business is still recovering from Hurricane Melissa. McDonald estimated that the company’s hospitality business was down about 30 per cent in November and December as a number of properties closed, particularly in western Jamaica.

The impact was partly offset in the months that followed as hotels that remained open operated at high occupancy because fewer rooms were available. Nations Choice also supplied protein and frozen vegetables to Central Kitchen during its hot meal operations following the hurricane.

McDonald said the company has not yet fully re-established its hotel business because some properties remain closed while others are only now reopening.

Nations Choice is also putting more weight behind products it makes itself. Manufacturing began in 2017 with pig tail and mackerel and has since expanded to burgers, ham, bacon and other processed foods.

McDonald said the company now produces about 29,000 burger patties each week, while locally manufactured products account for roughly 15 per cent of what it distributes.

Over the past three years Nations Choice has also increased the number of products sold under its own brand in supermarkets, moving beyond its traditional business-to-business model supplying hotels, restaurants, wholesalers and institutions such as schools, hospitals and prisons.

Its locally manufactured range includes curried goat and jerk pork burgers, with chicken bacon due to be added in early September.

“We are launching a chicken bacon,” McDonald said.

Those locally made products are also being lined up for the regional push. Nations Choice already supplies Guyana with goods sourced from other jurisdictions, McDonald said, but is now preparing to supply the market with products manufactured in Jamaica.

“I would say we have broken in already because we are already moving products there from other jurisdictions,” he said. “It is just a matter of moving products now from Jamaica there, which is what we are preparing ourselves to start doing.”

World.title: MORE WITH LESS
World.content:
WELLINGTON... it is even more important that the fans come out and support the competition (Photo: Joseph Wellington)

DESPITE ISSA working with one of its smallest sponsorship budgets for schoolboy football in recent times, President Keith Wellington believes this season could be one of the best yet, thanks to a revamped structure across the various competitions.

The launch of the prestigious under-19 high school football season was held on Wednesday, with the daCosta Cup set to begin next Saturday while the Manning Cup kicks off four days later.

However ISSA will execute the competitions with less sponsorship dollars this year, which Wellington says is down to a little over $40 million.

Long-time sponsor Wisynco, which supported the competition for more than a decade through its various brands, has not returned this year after investing $37.3 million in last year’s season. Bert’s Auto Parts has also not returned after coming on board in 2025.

KFC; Kirk Distributors through its brands Kendel and Cetamol; and Charles Chocolate, through its brand Ping Pong, have remained on board while Happy Ice has joined as a new sponsor, just weeks after former Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) Operations Manager Omar McFarlane was named CEO.

While grateful for the current partnerships Wellington says fan support will be crucial this season to help offset the sponsorship shortfall.

“It has and will have a significant impact on schoolboy football in terms of what we are hoping to do. That is why it is even more important that the fans come out and support the competition,” he said. “This is their thing; it’s the fans’ thing. They want to see schoolboy football each year, they want to see their schools participate, and their support in coming and paying $500 at the gate, those little contributions will help to support their schools.”

“We provide all the schools with playing gear, we provide the referee fees for everybody, and obviously we have to find venues when it comes to the latter stages of the competition so we need the support of the general public.”

This season will be one of the most unique in the near-120-year history of schoolboy football. The top 15 teams from both the Manning Cup and DaCosta Cup have earned byes into the second round, with nine teams from the Manning Cup first round and 21 from the daCosta Cup first round advancing to join them.

Wellington says this could lead to a more competitive season compared to previous years.

“We are hoping that the first round — where the teams we believe are more equally matched — will be a lot more competitive and the best teams will advance. And they advance having played [5, 6, 7 games already] to compete against the more established programmes who may have played a lot more practice matches.”

The formats of the knockout competitions, the urban area Walker Cup, and the rural area Ben Francis Cup have also changed, with the top 32 teams now competing. For the past seven years the semi-finalists of the Manning and daCosta Cup were unable to compete.

The all-island knockout tournament, the Champions Cup, will have its format decided during the season.

“We are happy that most persons are comfortable with the changes and are happy to see the changes. What we need to do now is to ensure that we execute properly and that we get the support, not just from the teams involved but from the supporting cast — the students, the general public, and corporate Jamaica, to ensure that we have a successful season,” said Wellington.

Excelsior High will look to defend their Manning Cup title while St Elizabeth Technical (STETHS) will look to retain their daCosta Cup title. Clarendon College are the only team from either competition to have successfully defended their title since 2018.

Manning Cup seeded teams: Excelsior, Jamaica College, St Catherine, Wolmer’s Boys’, Campion College, Charlie Smith, Calabar, St Jago, STATHS, Kingston College, Tivoli Gardens, St George’s College, Eltham, Mona, Vauxhall.

daCosta Cup seeded teams: STETHS, Glenmuir, Clarendon College, Dinthill Technical, Cornwall College, Kemps Hill, Maggotty High, Old Harbour, Garvey Maceo, McGrath, Ocho Rios, Christiana, Manchester, Manning’s, William Knibb

World.title: BYD welcomes ATTO 8
World.content:
The 2027 BYD ATTO 8 was launched over two days — Saturday, August 22 at Kingston Polo Club and Sunday, August 23, with a test drive day at the Police Officers’ Club, St Andrew.

BYD JAMAICA, the arm of ATL Automotive Group responsible for the BYD line of new energy vehicles, rolled out the red carpet for the latest addition to its model line-up, the ATTO 8, with two days of activities this month.

“It’s a dream come true to have the ATTO 8 on Jamaican shores,” Sloane Jackson, head of business, BYD Jamaica, told the Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

The vehicle was launched on Saturday, August 22, at Kingston Polo Club with the opportunity to test-drive it the following day, Sunday, August 23, at Police Officers’ Club, St Andrew.

Jackson explained that the ATTO 8 was not a given, and that it was a process to bring it to market from China, having seen it last April at Auto Shanghai 2025. He and his team were privy to a special and private unveiling of the vehicle.

“One of the things they showed us that wasn’t unveiled at the show, but unveiled to us as the BYD team, was the new Tang. What they told us was that it would be called the Sealion 8 in some markets, and the ATTO 8 in our region, available as a full EV and as a hybrid. We were initially told that we might get it,” Jackson said.

After the revelation that it would be available in right-hand drive, as it was going to be sold in the Australian and South African markets, Jackson felt it would be a great fit for the Caribbean region and his Jamaica portfolio.

The ATTO 8 is a mid-sized SUV, using BYD’s hybrid technology. Currently, it is only available in one trim level, DM-p, which makes it an all-wheel-drive plug-in hybrid vehicle. The drivetrain is similar to the BYD Shark pickup. Under the bonnet of the ATTO 8 is a 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder engine. The petrol engine is paired with two electric motors — front and rear — for a total power output of 536bhp. The 35.6kWh battery is rated to deliver 152km of pure electric range, with a combined range up to 1,400km. It can be charged externally at 11kWh for AC, and DC fast-charged at 72kWh using the CCS2 port. The ATTO 8 can also do Vehicle-to-Load to run attached electrical devices.

On the performance front, 100kph can be reached in under five seconds, with a top speed of 200kph.

Beyond its speed and range as a seven-seat SUV, the ATTO 8 is packed with the technology expected from BYD. There’s wireless charging and USB ports throughout a spacious cabin that features integrated multi-colour ambient lighting, premium materials, double-layer glass for the front doors, and a 21-speaker sound system.

For family use, there is a maximum 1,960-litres of cargo capacity, powered seating — including the ability to control the front passenger from the second row, and even amenities such as a massage function for the second row. There are driver aids for safety and convenience, while the BYD infotainment offers up its usual wide range of interactivity.

Jackson said that the sales numbers of the ATTO 8, to date, have justified its addition to the showroom floor, as it comes at a time when rising fuel prices are driving the automotive consumer’s buying habits, gaining BYD’s line-up of electric vehicles and hybrids even more attention. This was a sentiment mirrored by Mark Dommisse, managing director, ATL Automotive Group.

“We are exceptionally lucky to host this brand in our portfolio. I would say that BYD is the heavyweight champion of the Chinese brands around the world, and that has definitely shown today. When we took on the brand two years ago, I think there was a lot of curiosity from the general public and a lot of questions. Every time the name BYD was asked, it was always with a question mark; nowadays it’s a mainstay brand that everybody knows. It’s trendy, it’s sexy, and they’re bringing out new products left, right, and centre. We’re certainly very happy with the sales volume. We’re very happy with the return on investment, and we’re honoured to hold the brand,” he said.

Beyond the launch, guests were given free rein to examine the ATTO 8’s features to the fullest, while being treated to food, drink, and activities, including creating a signature car fragrance.

The 2027 ATTO 8 DM-p is now available from BYD Jamaica at $15 million, with the EV model expected to arrive next year.

“All that is available to us in right-hand drive is the hybrid. The EV model should be coming in the middle of 2028, which will have the most powerful single electric motor ever built, with the option of 1,000 bhp,” said Jackson.

World.title: Fire engulfs Superior Parts dealership on Hagley Park Road
World.content:
A fire has engulfed the Superior Parts dealership on Hagley Park Road in St Andrew. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Firefighters are now battling a blaze that has engulfed the Superior Parts dealership on Hagley Park Road in St Andrew.

The cause of the fire is not yet known but the incident happened around midday. At least two units from the Jamaica Fire Brigade are on location.

There have been no confirmed reports of casualties.

More to come.

World.title: Waiting for water
World.content:
SOME school leaders are cautiously optimistic as they welcome the Government’s promise to provide water to schools ahead of next month’s reopening, but two of them have made it clear that the assistance must be more than an announcement but a reliable flow of support.

“The principals across all levels of the system are elated that the move is being made to secure sanitation across the schools… If water is provided at no cost or very low cost to schools, this is a move that we not only welcome for our students and our staff but also I am sure the parents would be quite elated to know that their children will be placed in safe and secure school environments because we’ll have the water required for cooking, cleaning and general sanitation,” Anniona Jones, president of the Jamaica Association of Principals of Secondary Schools (JAPSS) told the Jamaica Observer Wednesday.

Her comments came after Water Minister Matthew Samuda assured that the Government will be taking action to ensure that schools, farmers and early-childhood institutions have adequate water supplies amid worsening drought conditions across the island.

The minister’s comments came during official commissioning of the Bunkers Hill Water Supply System in Clarendon on Tuesday. He announced that water trucks will be available to schools while a structured tank programme is being developed to assist early-childhood institutions and farmers with inadequate storage capacity.

Jones, who is also the principal of Haile Selassie High School, argued that while the initiative is welcomed, many institutions across Jamaica would require more than just water assistance. She pointed to the need to have adequate storage facilities.

“It’s one thing to be willing to provide the water, however some schools may need additional support in having tanks and the plumbing costs required for connection to ensure that they will have sufficient water,” she said.

Highlighting the issues faced by her school, Jones said the Government must be ready to commit to frequent water trips, the provision of water tanks to institutions beyond just early childhood education centres, and further assistance with piping systems to minimise water woes come September.

“My school is in a community that has frequent water loss, particularly during the day. We do have some storage facilities, however we are definitely in need of additional tanks. We emptied some of the tanks,” she said, adding that some of the tanks were damaged by both Hurricane Beryl in 2024 and last year’s Hurricane Melissa.

“We would definitely need additional support with additional tanks and, of course, the cost to get those tanks connected to our bathroom facility. We’ve made a move as school administrators generally to secure our canteen, to secure at least one of our bathrooms — and many schools have done that for their staff sanitary facilities. However, given the population, our concern is always the number of tanks available, the number of students, and the frequency of refilling, because that can be quite costly,” she outlined.

Despite these concerns Jones said she is pleased with steps being taken by the Government, and expressed hope that delivery of the initiative will be as convincing as the announcement.

“We welcome not just the statements, but we really are looking for the follow-through. Several comments have been made to reassure the public, however what we will find reassuring at this point is action. We want consistent, clear action that shows that we’re going beyond the sound bites and public relations, but we’re going towards consistent maintenance of high-quality standards for education,” she said.

Sharing similar sentiments was principal of deCarteret College Dr Prim Lewis, who is also fond of the water initiative, and hopeful that the Government actually delivers on its promise.

While acknowledging that her school, located in the parish of Manchester, was not currently experiencing drought conditions due to its climate-resilient infrastructure, she noted that many other institutions are not as fortunate.

Pointing to St Elizabeth, the parish in which she lives and which was severely affected by back-to-back hurricanes, Lewis stressed that the Government will have to make a significant effort to avoid school closures due to empty pipes.

“In St Elizabeth we have not had water in some areas since before [Hurricane] Melissa, and that was basically exasperated by Melissa. Personally, I live in Horizon Park, and at home I have not had water since post-Melissa. I know that sometimes when the NWC operations personnel say that they will bring water, what will happen is that the water may come later than anticipated, based on the number of schools that they have to supply [with] water,” Lewis said.

“The [National] Water Commission has always responded when called, where water is concerned to be delivered to schools. As I said before, it’s just that sometimes the response is not as timely as we expect. I have seen where schools are waiting on water and keeping the school open, expecting that water will arrive at ‘x’ time and the water did not arrive at ‘x’ time and therefore the school had to be closed for that day. [So], I am cautiously optimistic,” she added.

World.title: Former Iceland prime minister to pro-EU voters: Your referendum doesn’t matter
World.content:
“If I become foreign minister or prime minister later, have I fulfilled this simply by asking the EU, ‘what are you willing to give us?’ And is my job done?” wondered Gunnlaugsson. “They can’t explain how to honor the vote if it’s a ‘Yes,’” he said, referring to the current Social Democrat-led government.

The right-wing politician rose to prominence during the 2008 financial crisis as the spokesperson for a campaign against using Icelandic taxpayer money to bail out the country’s largest bank and repay foreign creditors in the U.K. and the Netherlands. He founded the Centre Party in 2017.

Gunnlaugsson describes his party as “small ‘c’ conservative and centrist” — though some of his opponents disagree.

“People sometimes call us populist, and it always annoys me because I always see myself as anti-populist. I’m always talking about things that are difficult to explain, and I’m always annoyed about how politics is becoming all about just the surface and easy ideas,” said Gunnlaugsson.

In June of this year, however, his Centre Party joined the European Conservatives and Reformists group in the European Parliament, which includes right-wing nationalist parties that often receive the populist label, such as Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy and Poland’s Law and Justice party.

A geopolitical vote

On Aug. 29, Icelanders will answer either “Yes” or “No” to the question: “Should negotiations on Iceland’s membership in the European Union start again?”

World.title: Brussels prosecutor fumes at lack of resources to tackle drug violence
World.content:
“As you can see, this hellish streak, which has been going on for several years, continues,” Moinil said, adding that Brussels has already seen 69 gun-related incidents in 2026, against the 102 that took place in 2025.

The incidents reported in Saint-Gilles were linked to a fight between two drug-trafficking gangs. Still, innocent citizens were caught in the crossfire, the prosecutor said: In one attack, clients of a pizzeria had to seek cover from the flying bullets.

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever is convening a meeting with the country’s security services Friday afternoon to discuss drug-related shootings, Le Soir reports.

“Today, as a prosecutor, I am concerned for the citizens, since what I had pointed out — that anyone could get shot — has turned out to be true,” the prosecutor warned.

Since 2025, the police have arrested 93 adults and 14 underage suspects; closed 350 stores; and seized 3,500 luxury cars — which traffickers like to tour Brussels in, according to Moinil — and several thousand users were penalized. By Thursday, the prosecutor’s office had also seized €203 million from criminals in the capital.

“We are working tirelessly with limited resources, since I have not received any additional funding at all despite this crisis,” continued Moinil. He noted that the €10 million in extra resources he’d requested to step up his fight against drug violence was not “excessive” compared with the €203 million already seized.

World.title: Belgium summons US ambassador again over jibe at health minister
World.content:
U.S. ambassador to Belgium Bill White delivers a speech at a press conference on July 15, 2026 in Brussels. | Emile Windal/Belga/AFP via Getty Images

This is not the first time the US ambassador has made controversial personal attacks against Belgian politicians.

Belgium’s Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot has summoned U.S. Ambassador Bill White for a second time this year, after he posted an Instagram story mocking the country’s Health Minister Frank Vandenbroucke.

“Who’s the biggest LOSER in Belgium?” asked U.S. President Donald Trump’s appointee in Brussels on social media, above a seemingly AI-generated picture of Vandenbroucke on a cigar box. In an apparent mockery of the minister’s push to change health warnings used in alcohol advertising, the box reads: “Damages every form of joy in life.”

“It is unacceptable that an ambassador uses such insulting language against a member of government,” Prévot said in a statement to POLITICO. The foreign ministry confirmed the summoning, which was first reported by news agency Belga.

World.title: US probes NATO allies over military support as it mulls further troop cuts
World.content:
Some NATO allies have bridled at the approach. Earlier this month the U.S. sent out a questionnaire, according to two European defense officials, asking allies to detail their views on subjects ranging from defense spending to U.S. foreign policy.

It’s a “scary exercise,” said a NATO diplomat, describing the survey as an attempt to get allies to “pledge their allegiance to the king.”

Colby on Thursday said the questionnaire wasn’t aimed at “dictating” terms nor at obtaining “a complete carte blanche” on U.S. military access, and praised countries for “rebuilding their military strength for collective defense.”

But, he added: “We need to be able to have the ability to operate effectively; we need predictability,” affirming that access to American bases in Europe is a key criterion in Washington’s six-month review of its military presence on the continent.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the review in June partly in response to the airspace and basing restrictions imposed by countries including France, Italy and Spain. President Donald Trump threatened to leave NATO over the constraints earlier this year.

As part of its review, the U.S. sent a “terms of reference” document to allies this month, arguing it would examine issues like defense spending and expanded military access in Europe, according to a person familiar with the matter who was granted anonymity to speak freely. Reuters first reported the document.

World.title: Norway’s King Harald dies at 89
World.content:
Norway’s King Harald V has died at 89 on Friday, ending a 35-year reign and putting Crown Prince Haakon on the throne at a turbulent moment for the country’s royal family. Harald “passed away peacefully” at 6:35 a.m., local time, the Norwegian royal household announced.

Harald’s health deteriorated sharply in his final days. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre on Thursday canceled a trip to Germany, including a planned working dinner with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, to visit the king.

Harald had reigned since 1991 and resisted calls to abdicate despite mounting health problems, repeatedly insisting that the oath he took as king was for life. He is survived by his wife, Queen Sonja.

Haakon, 53, succeeds his father as king automatically under Norway’s constitutional monarchy. His wife, Crown Princess Mette-Marit, becomes queen consort — while facing intense scrutiny over her past relationship with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The crown princess apologized, calling the relationship “simply embarrassing” and saying she had shown “poor judgment.” Her son and Haakon’s stepson Marius Borg Høiby, 29, was found guilty of two counts rape in June. Høiby, who is not an official member of the royal family, has appealed the verdict and is under house arrest.

Harald remained a popular figure in the country despite plummeting support for the broader royal family. A February poll for public broadcaster NRK showed that although support for the monarchy had dropped to a record low of 60 percent, the public had given him an average “grade” of 9.2 out of 10. Haakon was given a grade of 7.9 and Mette-Marit, the new queen consort, 3.7.

World.title: Bas, Klingbeil und die SPD: Lost in Ost
World.content:
Die SPD-Spitze um Bärbel Bas und Lars Klingbeil demonstriert in der Bundesregierung nach außen Normalität. Hinter verschlossenen Türen wächst jedoch die Unruhe vor den drei anstehenden Wahlen in Sachsen-Anhalt, Berlin und Mecklenburg-Vorpommern im September. Rasmus Buchsteiner beleuchtet im Gespräch die internen Szenarien und die wackelnden Stühle der sozialdemokratischen Spitze.

In der Hauptstadt rangiert die SPD in den Umfragen ebenfalls abgeschlagen. Spitzenkandidat Steffen Krach stellt sich im 200-Sekunden-Interview den Fragen von Rixa Fürsen, was die Bundespartei damit zu tun hat und wie er glaubt, an einer Trendwende mitwirken zu können.

Trotz schwieriger Rahmenbedingungen überrascht die deutsche Wirtschaft aktuell mit einem Exportboom. Romanus Otte von POLITICO PRO „Industrie & Handel am Morgen“ analysiert die massiven Zuwächse in den europäischen Nachbarländern. Dieser Wandel auf den Märkten gleicht die herben Verluste in den USA und China momentan aus.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.
