World.title: Could Orbán lead Hungary again?
World.content:
For 16 years, Viktor Orbán exerted an iron grip on Hungarian politics and society. Now it’s being dismantled. Has Hungary finally turned a page on the Orbán era, or could he make one final return?

It’s only a few days before Péter Magyar’s government, which succeeded Orbán, learns whether his anti-corruption reforms have done enough to persuade the European Commission to release €10.4 billion of frozen funds to help the country recover after the Covid pandemic. The money was withheld over breaches of EU law under Orbán, who suffered a landslide defeat at the polls in April.

Host Anne McElvoy talks to János Bóka, who now leads Orbán’s Fidesz party from the opposition benches in the Hungarian Parliament. He was minister for European affairs in the previous government and is seen as a relatively moderate voice tasked with rebuilding a party reeling from defeat. Does he want to cast off an ousted strongman’s shadow – might Orban still be seeking to find a way back?

World.title: Radical left Mélenchon courts Greens as presidential bid gains steam
World.content:
Châtelain attended France Unbowed’s summer event along with seven other party officials, where she told reporters that “there is common ground” between the Greens and Mélenchon. She even appeared before cameras flashing a wide grin beside Mélenchon — a strong political signal given her key role as the party’s top lawmaker in the National Assembly.

“We are at two crossroads at once,” she said, referring to the rise of the far right and the climate change-fueled heat and wildfires that engulfed France over the summer. “What matters now is finding the most effective way for the Greens to put their ideas forward.”

L’écologie est un bien commun. Ravi d’accueillir Cyrielle Chatelain aux #AMFIS2026. pic.twitter.com/laVEhYp4eq — Jean-Luc Mélenchon (@JLMelenchon) August 21, 2026

On paper, Mélenchon has some of the credentials needed to convince the Greens. He has defined himself as an “eco-socialist” for over a decade and stressed the need to “unite the red with the green.” Even Monique Barbut, the former head of WWF France who now serves as ecology minister in France’s current center-right government, said in a recent interview that Mélenchon is the candidate who “incorporates climate issues most fully into his proposals.”

The foreign policy split

There are, however, sticking points. Mélenchon is a vocal critic of the European Union in its current form, which he sees as an engine for unregulated capitalism, while the French Greens have long advocated for European federalism.

“[The EU] is a fundamental issue, because our project conflicts with European regulations,” said Clémence Guetté, who is in charge of writing Mélenchon’s presidential platform. “We know where our disagreements [with the Greens] are.”

Mélenchon and the Greens have also clashed on support for Ukraine. Mélenchon is against Ukraine joining the EU and said his goal was to “bring Russia back into the European family,” while the Greens have been much more adamant in their support for Kyiv in its war against Russia. The Greens also see Mélenchon as too friendly toward China.

World.title: Are the Baltics safe? CIA director's Moscow trip raises more questions than answers
World.content:
If CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s secret trip to Moscow was intended to calm fears of a confrontation between Russia and NATO, it appears to have achieved almost the opposite.

 

His sudden arrival in the Russian capital this week triggered days of speculation over what intelligence could have prompted Washington to dispatch its spy chief to deliver a message to Moscow and whether the Baltic states should be worried.

US media reported that Ratcliffe warned Russia against attacking NATO members, particularly Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, amid intelligence assessments that Moscow could seek to test the alliance as its war in Ukraine remains deadlocked.

American thinktank the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said the circumstances of the visit suggest Washington regarded the intelligence behind it as sufficiently urgent and sensitive to justify Ratcliffe travelling to Moscow in person.

“US Central Intelligence Agency Director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow suggests that Russia may be preparing to conduct an act of aggression against a NATO member in the relatively near term to invalidate NATO’s Article 5,” ISW said.

But the Washington-based organisation also drew an important distinction: there are no signs of the kind of large-scale Russian military build-up around the Baltic states that preceded the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Instead, it said, any near-term Russian action could be considerably more limited: an air, missile or drone strike, or a small land incursion designed not to seize large amounts of territory but to test whether NATO allies would respond collectively under Article 5.

Former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves questioned whether the Baltic states were the reason for Ratcliffe’s trip at all.

In an exclusive interview with Euronews, Ilves said he had “severe doubts” that concerns over the Baltic states were behind the CIA director’s mission, arguing that Washington’s more immediate concern was Russia’s support for Iran.

“What is the real problem for the United States right now? The real problem is Iran, the fact that the Russians are giving targeting information to the Iranians,” Ilves said.

FILE: A poster with an image of Russian President Vladimir Putin is seen on the wall of the Narva Castle opposite Russian border, in Narva, Estonia, Tuesday, May 9, 2023. AP Photo

He was equally sceptical about suggestions of an increased Russian military threat to the Baltic states, dismissing them as “all spin.”

“Why would they do anything in the Baltic states at this time?” he said, arguing that Moscow had little reason to risk a confrontation with NATO while its war in Ukraine remained deadlocked.

Concern in European military circles

A European military source told Euronews that intelligence agencies have been picking up signals for months suggesting that Moscow could seek to exploit the Trump administration’s changing approach to its European NATO allies to launch another attack in the region, as Washington pushes Europe to assume greater responsibility for its own defence.

The source cautioned that this did not amount to evidence that Russia has taken a decision to act. But the concern, they said, was that a distracted Washington, combined with the shift in responsibility towards Europe, could present Moscow with a window of opportunity.

Seen through this lens, Ratcliffe’s trip could have been intended to remove any doubt in Moscow about the consequences of testing NATO at a time when Washington is both heavily preoccupied elsewhere and redefining its role in European defence.

The source described Ratcliffe as one of the Trump administration’s strongest supporters of NATO, Europe and Ukraine, but doubted that Putin would heed his warning. The timing itself may be part of those calculations.

FILE:An Airbus Tiger multi-role attack helicopter flies during a multinational military Exercise Pikne ("Lightning") near Suurekivi, Estonia, Tuesday, Sept. 30, 2025. AP Photo

The source stressed that the Baltic states, particularly Estonia and Lithuania, are considerably better prepared for a potential confrontation with Russia than much of the rest of Europe.

As Europe strengthens its defences, it raises another strategic question: if Moscow is considering testing NATO, why wait until the continent is better prepared and a new US administration that might be more committed to its defence?

A painful memory of 2021

Nearly five years ago, Ratcliffe’s predecessor, William Burns, travelled to Moscow with a warning. When he arrived in November 2021, Russia was already months into a large and increasingly visible military build-up around Ukraine. Less than four months later Russia launched its full-scale invasion.

A European military source drew an uncomfortable parallel between the two missions.

“It is good that the CIA director went to Moscow to deliver a warning," the source told Euronews. “Not that Putin will listen.”

But there is a crucial difference between the two cases. No comparable Russian build-up is visible around the Baltic states today. A Russian attempt to test NATO, however, would not necessarily require one.

A more limited operation could require little of the visible military preparation that preceded the invasion of Ukraine. If the objective is to test NATO rather than seize territory, ambiguity could be the point.

FILE: Vladimir Putin arrives at a wreath-laying ceremony marking the 85th anniversary of the Nazi German invasion into Soviet Union in World War II, Moscow, June 22, 2026. AP Photo

‘Our threat assessment has not changed’

Officials in the Baltic states have spent the days since Ratcliffe’s visit trying to dampen fears that another 2021 may be unfolding on NATO’s eastern flank.

Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the possibility of Russian provocations against NATO must be taken seriously, but insisted that Estonia’s threat assessment had not changed.

Latvian officials similarly said their assessment of the conventional military threat remained unchanged and the risk of a Russian invasion was low.

Yet public reassurance has been accompanied by calls for considerably greater preparedness.

Five European Commissioners from countries on the EU’s eastern flank have urged European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to take additional measures in response to what they described as mounting security challenges in the region.

Their proposals include appointing a high-level coordinator for the eastern flank, strengthening regional stockpiles and civil preparedness, improving the protection of critical infrastructure and accelerating the EU’s Eastern Flank Watch initiative against hybrid threats.

Baltic officials may see no evidence of an imminent conventional invasion, yet preparations continue for sabotage, drone incursions, hybrid operations and more limited Russian military provocations — many of which the region has already faced.

From Kyiv’s concerns to Washington’s warning

In April, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russian preparations could point to further mobilisation and a possible offensive either against Ukraine or the Baltic states.

Estonia publicly pushed back. Tsahkna said the warning did not correspond with Estonian intelligence or Tallinn’s own assessment.

“We do not see Russia concentrating its forces or preparing in any way militarily to attack NATO or the Baltic states,” he said.

By July, however, Lithuania and Latvia were themselves warning about the possibility of more limited Russian action.

Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said intelligence indicated Russia could be planning limited attacks on critical infrastructure, including energy and transport facilities, while Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs warned that Moscow could seek to test NATO’s Article 5 commitment without launching a full-scale invasion.

A week ago during a summit in Kyiv, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said there was no direct conventional Russian threat to the Baltic or Nordic states.

World.title: Skyrocketing windmills: The world’s tallest wind power plant is going to dwarf the Eiffel tower
World.content:
Smalltown Klettwitz lies at the very heart of Germany’s Lusatia region. Lignite used to be mined here for decades. The bucket-wheel excavators have left gaping scars across the landscape.

 

But the country is reaching a turning point: Germany is now getting serious about ending coal burning. And Klettwitz is transforming into a frontrunner in the countrys race to handle the climate crisis in a more sustainable way.

Solar and wind farms now stand on the spoil heaps of the former opencast mine, as far as the eye can see. Among these, one steel structure in particular catches the eye - the GICON high-altitude wind power plant. It is still under construction but already outgrowing the neighbouring giant windmills.

It is a big day for the GICON team: Europe’s biggest and most powerful crane, a yellow monster machine, is lifting a tower segment weighing many tonnes into place. Up there, some 160 metres above ground level, climbers are putting the pieces together.

High above ground level, climbers are putting the pieces together spiderman-style... Hans von der Brelie

GICON employs some of Germany’s finest engineers. The company was founded by Jochen Großmann. Why is the GICON team building such a massive structure in the first place? Euronews wants to know.

Why so high, Professor Großmann?

“Because the wind blows stronger and more steadily the further I get from the Earth’s surface,” Großmann explains on site, while a team of high-altitude climbers is moving up and down the steel struts spiderman-style. “That’s why wind turbines have become taller and taller – because there’s so much wind up there that they generate more than double the output of the turbines standing here in the surrounding area.”

Großmann’s idea: future wind farms should have ‘two storeys’ so that the wind can be ‘harvested’ twice – once at the bottom and once at the top. “Retrofitting existing wind farms with taller windmills alongside regular ones give us two tiers of high-altitude windmills, and allows us to triple the yield from the same area,” Großmann estimates.

Großmann’s idea: future wind farms should have ‘two storeys’ so that the wind can be ‘harvested’ twice – once at the bottom and once at the top. Hans von der Brelie

GICON plans to erect 100 high-altitude windmills by the early 2030s, then the objective is to scale it up to 1,000 plants in a few years’ time. GICON could become a global player, “the opportunity is there”, Großmann tells Euronews.

“All the wind farms in Germany would offer the potential for 4,000 additional high-altitude wind turbines,” the GICON-CEO stresses, “Simply by retrofitting existing wind farms. That’s an incredible amount of potential. This also applies to African countries. We’ve had enquiries from Asia. The Chinese are asking about it. I think there’s huge international potential here.”

World.title: Anna Unger becomes head of Hungary's top anti-corruption body NVVH
World.content:
One of the new Hungarian government's key pledges was to recover state assets and financial instruments that have been unlawfully managed or have gone missing and to prevent further abuses.

 

To this end, a special authority is being set up; its head was elected on Friday by secret ballot, with 145 votes for Anna Unger.

At the same time, the institution's deputy head, Katalin Tasnádi, was appointed as deputy president in charge of investigations. The institution will be run by a five-member leadership, three of whom will be responsible for specific areas of expertise, making it possible to involve the expert who lost the election in its work in an active role.

Background

During the week, parliament's Committee on Justice and Constitutional Affairs finally heard three of the 96 candidates: Anna Róza Unger, a political scientist and lecturer at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE); lawyer Miklós Ligeti, legal director of Transparency International Hungary; and Nicholas Sárvári, a Canadian-Hungarian businessman who runs a company specialising in international asset recovery and crisis management.

At the hearing, Unger warned that it would be unrealistic to expect final judgments in all major corruption cases within six years. In her programme, she spoke not only about uncovering individual cases, but also about dismantling the institutional and political system that makes corruption possible.

In the debate before the parliamentary vote, the prime minister stressed that the government plans to speed up and shorten criminal proceedings in order to prevent delaying tactics and impunity.

The committee eventually recommended Anna Unger to the National Assembly. Miklós Ligeti received four votes in favour and four abstentions; six MPs supported Unger's nomination, one opposed it and one abstained. Nicholas Sárvári did not receive sufficient support.

Anna Unger and Miklós Ligeti X/Facebook

What is its mandate? It can investigate and bring charges

Setting up the NVVH was not, in itself, a precondition laid down in law for the release of EU funds, but there is nonetheless a close political and trust-related link between the two issues, as Brussels withheld a significant share of the money due to Hungary because it did not consider corruption prevention, the monitoring of EU subsidies and the consistent investigation of irregularities to be sufficiently guaranteed.

Together with Hungary's decision to join the European Public Prosecutor's Office, the NVVH is also intended to signal that the new government not only wants to protect future EU funds, but also intends to track down and recover public money that was previously spent unlawfully. The authority will therefore not "turn on the Brussels money tap," but its ability to function, its independence and its effectiveness could provide important proof that Hungary is capable of offering proper guarantees for the lawful use of EU funds.

The office's task is to track down, secure and, where possible, recover money and other assets that have unlawfully been removed from public ownership, but its powers are much broader than that. It can examine state and municipal decisions, public procurement procedures, concessions, subsidies, EU funds, state-owned enterprises, chains of contracts, financial flows and the real beneficial owners behind them.

The NVVH will not simply be a supervisory or advisory body. It will be able to conduct its own investigations and preliminary proceedings, request and cross-match data, initiate action by other authorities, and in the case of certain corruption offences and crimes involving public assets it will be able to carry out investigations itself.

The office may also take over cases that are still pending before an indictment is brought, if it considers that this would allow the state's criminal or financial claims to be asserted more effectively. In such cases it can step into the shoes of the prosecution service, bring charges and then represent the case as public prosecutor before the court. With this, and after the amendment of the Fundamental Law, the Prosecutor General's Office has lost its previous monopoly on acting as public prosecutor.

The institution will be able to use administrative, criminal-law and civil-law instruments in parallel. This is the source of its strength, but also of the main rule-of-law concerns: with such wide-ranging powers, it will be particularly important to see what internal oversight, judicial control and public accountability mechanisms will limit the discretion of its leadership.

Selection process sparked fierce debate

Critics of the nomination procedure objected that while the committee had already selected three candidates to go through to the next round, the Tisza parliamentary group later put forward Nicholas Sárvári as a separate nominee. This raised the question of whether the candidate backed by the group was competing on the same terms as the other participants in the open call.

Many considered Miklós Ligeti to be the most qualified and experienced of the candidates, and therefore described the choice of Unger as outrageous and worrying. Other critics pointed out that Unger is a political scientist and does not have a background as a prosecutor or investigator of the kind usually required to run a law-enforcement body of this size. Supporters, however, argue that the president's primary task will not be to lead individual investigations, but to build and provide strategic direction for an independent institution that brings together different areas of expertise.

MPs from Fidesz and the Mi Hazánk party did not take part in the committee's decision. According to Fidesz, the NVVH has been given excessively broad investigative, prosecutorial and information-gathering powers without adequate external checks, and the authority could therefore easily become a tool for political score-settling. The party has also initiated a constitutional court review.

The success of the new authority will not be determined by how many high-profile proceedings it launches, but by whether its investigations lead to indictments that stand up in court, final judgments and assets actually recovered. Part of the money may be hidden in foreign bank accounts, complex corporate networks, real estate or ownership structures that are hard to identify, and recovering it may require lengthy international legal proceedings.

World.title: Spain wins EU backing for temporary fuel tax cuts as Middle East crisis keeps prices high
World.content:
Spain has received the European Union's green light to temporarily cut taxes on petrol and diesel below the bloc's normal minimum levels to lower fuel prices for households and businesses hit by the Middle East energy crisis, an official European Commission document reveals.

 

The EU normally sets minimum excise-duty rates for petrol and diesel. Countries can tax fuel above those floors, but going below the EU minimum requires specific flexibilities under the EU’s Energy Taxation law, which Spain secured from July to September because of the exceptional energy crisis triggered by the US and Israel's war on Iran and the ensuing closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Excise duties are special taxes added to the price of specific goods, like alcohol, tobacco and fuel. Governments use this tax to raise money and to discourage people from buying harmful or unhealthy products.

"The European Council recognised that targeted solutions are needed in the short term to ensure availability of affordable energy," reads the document, dated 25 August.

The move comes as the conflict in the Middle East continues to drive energy market volatility, with uncertainty about the future of free navigation through the Strait of Hormuz keeping prices above pre-crisis levels.

The impact is being felt by consumers in everyday life. In August 2025, drivers in Spain paid an average of approximately €1.48 per litre for petrol and €1.41 per litre for diesel. As of 24 August this year, petrol is standing at €1.72 and diesel €1.86.

Related EU loosens state aid rules as Middle East crisis hits energy costs

Spain has specifically asked Brussels to let it go below those EU minimums because of the exceptional oil-price shock in a letter dated 28 June.

The Commission sees the measure as justified, citing Spain's particular reliance on cars, buses and road transport for everyday travel and freight. Inaction would lead to higher fuel prices, which could quickly feed into household and business costs.

Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had previously urged EU countries to take "targeted and temporary' measures to address rising fuel prices. Brussels also eased measures like loosening state aid rules as a short-term solution.

"The Commission examined the requested authorisation and found it unlikely to hinder the proper functioning of the internal market," reads the document. "The Commission considers the requested derogation to be adequate and proportionate, given its short duration, the exceptional circumstances linked to the geopolitical situation, coupled with an exceptionally high market price of oil."

What's the deal?

For July, Spain's tax cut is equivalent to about 15 cents per litre compared with the rates that applied before the conflict started on 28 February. The document states that the government can increase the cuts if petrol and diesel prices rise more than 15% above their pre-crisis levels.

In August, the tax cut will drop to 10 cents per litre, then to 5 cents per litre in September.

However, this is the reduction in the tax, not necessarily a 15-cent fall in the pump price, which also depends on the underlying oil price, refining costs, distribution margins and VAT.

Brussels has also warned that cheaper fuel can encourage people and businesses to use more fossil fuels, and that cutting taxes also means governments collect less money.

Against this backdrop, the Commission says the measure must remain temporary and that its impact on fuel consumption and public finances should be monitored.

Other countries have also reduced fuel taxes or introduced fuel-price support, but they didn't receive exactly the same flexibility as Spain, which was explicitly allowed to set its effective rates below the EU floor.

Italy, Portugal, Slovenia, Hungary, Spain and Ireland have reduced excise taxes on petroleum products since the onset of the energy crisis.

Italy has been running excise duty cuts on diesel and petrol until 26 August and the government is seeking a further extension, according to local media.

World.title: Euronews Culture's Film of the Week: 'The Dog Stars' - A smouldering Jacob Elordi can't save us
World.content:
Ridley Scott has had his fair share of hits and misses.

 

For every Alien, Blade Runner, Gladiator and The Martian, there’s a Kingdom of Heaven, A Good Year, whatever The Counselor was, Napoleon, and an underpowered Glad-II-ator.

No bad word shall be said about Alien: Covenant or House of Gucci. The former is a lot better than you remember, and the latter is a camp masterpiece, and that’s that.

Frustratingly, his latest film sits very comfortably in the ‘miss’ category.

Based on Peter Heller’s 2012 novel of the same name, The Dog Stars stars Jacob Elordi as Hig, your ridiculously handsome everyman and former pilot trying to get by in a post-pandemic America. Following a viral apocalypse which wiped out most of the human population, including his wife, our hero survives by scavenging supplies with his dog, Jasper. Which is a lovely name for a dog. Well done there.

Unlike his Marine-turned-survivalist compadre Bangley (Josh Brolin), Hig clings onto hope that humanity will find a way. He flies his Cessna plane looking for signs of life and is drawn to a mysterious radio signal, which leads him to a military base. There, he meets Cima (Margaret Qualley) and her gruff father (Guy Pearce), and starts to think of a life beyond survival.

However, feral gangs of “reapers” threaten any future plans...

The Dog Stars 20th Century Studios

Whatever your past directorial credentials may be and as impressive as it is to still be behind the camera at the age of 88, there’s no excuse for making the post-apocalypse boring and this derivative.

There’s some 28 Days / Weeks / Years Later in The Dog Stars, a bit of I Am Legend, echoes to Mad Max, and even some Fallout for good measure. All great touchpoints, but they don’t coalesce into something remotely interesting. They just make you wish you were watching a film either scary, thrilling or profound enough to retain your attention.

As it is, The Dog Stars wants to be both an introspective character study and a post-apocalyptic actioner, and fails in both respects. It’s too uneventful to be exciting, not scary enough to be impactful, and too puddle-deep to be insightful. Worse, this is a film that doesn’t say much of anything about the apocalypse, societal collapse, or shared grief. Unlike the source material, Mark L. Smith’s script never grapples with its themes and instead chooses to underdevelop the characters every step of the way.

Aside from Erik Messerschmidt's stunning cinematography, the interminably slow pace led me to focus on an unexpected element in The Dog Stars: facial hair. Specifically, Josh Brolin’s goated goatee.

The Dog Stars 20th Century Studios

Boy, can that man do facial follicles.

Few men can. Idris Elba can. Adam Driver cannot. Ethan Hawk is a master. Orlando Bloom is not. Christian Bale can grow a wild one. Timothée Chalamet may get there one day.

It’s a subtle art, and Brolin – and not for the first time – sports a majestic one here, giving grizzled uncle energy that made me think: If it is the end of the world as we know it, I will find solace in staying away from radio signals and keeping close to your scraggly growth, which assures me that I’ll be safe.

So, unless you’re in the market to watch a smouldering Jacob Elordi wearing a Carhartt jacket and staring into the distance - or looking to start a goatee appreciation society like I am seriously considering - stay away from this overlong and bizarrely bland effort from a filmmaker who’ll hopefully give us one last great film before another pandemic hits.

The Dog Stars is out in cinemas now.

World.title: Fight for water: Dried-up lakes and mass fish deaths at one of Hungary's largest fish farms
World.content:
Several hundred tonnes of fish died in August in one of Hungary's largest fish farm complexes at Rétimajor, south of Budapest.

 

This fishpond system, with a water surface of around 800 hectares, is what remains of the former Sárrét marshlands.

Its current owner, Ferenc Lévai, privatised it in 1994 and has since been running it as a continuously developed, integrated agri-tourism estate, although its main source of income is still fish farming.

The fishpond system, made up of shallow, nutrient-rich lakes of varying depth, reedbeds, islands and muddy shorelines, provides a uniquely concentrated and hard-to-replace habitat for water birds.

The Rétszilasi Lakes and their surroundings are among the most strictly protected areas in Europe. In addition to their Natura 2000 status they are, under the Ramsar Convention, a wetland of international importance.

Fish living in just 30 centimetres of water

The owner and chief executive of Aranyponty Zrt., Ferenc Lévai, believes the problem stems from the water management authorities, in this case the Middle Danube Water Directorate, holding back water above the fishponds for irrigation purposes.

"In our view, because of a very poor water distribution regime, very little water reached us here; we could not even reach the water level that Hungary's most protected area would be entitled to, the ecological water level, which stipulates at least 50% water across the whole water surface," Lévai told Euronews.

"We were unable even to maintain that 50% level: the extent of evaporation and the inadequate water supply led to a catastrophe."

"Around 150 hectares of our area are already dry, on another roughly 400 hectares the fish are eking out an existence in 30-40 centimetres of water, because they are not really living, and it is only on about 200-250 hectares that we have more than half the normal depth, where proper fish farming can take place," he added.

Although they did everything they could in Rétimajor to minimise the damage, 300 to 350 tonnes of fish still died, which according to Lévai's calculations means a loss of around 400 to 500 million forints (€1.1-1.4 million).

The low water level meant the water warmed up more easily, which accelerated gas formation. Gases released from the sludge then poisoned the fish.

Lévai says an even greater problem is that the drying out has put protected wildlife at risk, as the fishpond system is home to numerous rare amphibians and birds.

Authority denies witholding water

Euronews contacted the Central Transdanubian Water Directorate and they said they had prepared for the drought situation, but "the summer heat-dome phenomenon, which caused an emergency situation across the whole country, was not yet known at that time."

From 26 July they had to impose regional water restrictions, under which use of water by fishponds could be limited by at most 20% and irrigation by 60%. They said they complied with this rule and did not withhold water.

On the contrary, in August they released 1.18 million m3 of water over two weeks from the Fehérvárcsurgó reservoir, which largely contains Székesfehérvár's treated sewage, to replenish the fishponds.

According to the water authority there is currently barely more water than that left in the reservoir, 1.4 million m3.

The authority estimates that in the extreme heat as much as 100,000 m3 of water a day may have evaporated from the 800-hectare water surface and alongside this the water use of upstream irrigation, restricted under the rules, is negligible.

"In our view, meeting (restricted) irrigation demands does not materially affect the very substantial volume of water requested to compensate for evaporation losses from fish-farming water use," the Central Transdanubian Water Directorate told Euronews.

"The emergency situation may not have been caused by the abstraction of irrigation water, but by the oxygen-depleted state of water heated up by the heat."

Looking for solutions

Ferenc Lévai has previously told Euronews that he is not looking for someone to blame, but for solutions.

He believes the answer lies in crop-growing businesses building their own reservoirs, storing water during wetter periods and, in times of scarcity, not having to compete for supplies, so that livestock farming and wildlife can come first.

The local water authority also concluded its letter by saying that "the Central Transdanubian Water Directorate is examining the hydrological status of the water system in a study, with particular regard to water reserves committed by users holding water-management operating licences within the system."

"The aim of the study is to determine how water demands can be met in future. It is expected that permits and operating practices will need to be reviewed."

World.title: Major US airlines to launch new European routes for 2027 – here’s where they are flying to
World.content:
It’s been a busy time in the US aviation sector with airlines announcing a raft of new nonstop flight routes for 2027, including many to Europe.

 

Among the new flights planned for next year are Alaska Airlines from Seattle to Athens and Paris; American Airlines from Philadelphia to Porto and Vienna; Delta from Austin to Paris; and United from Newark to Luxembourg, Ljubljana and Ibiza.

Here we take a look at some of the new flights which will connect the US and Europe in 2027.

Alaska Airlines

Next spring, Alaska Airlines will launch its first flights from Seattle to Athens and Paris Charles de Gaulle. The Seattle-Athens service will begin on 12 May 2027, operating three times a week, while the Seattle-Paris route will launch on 25 May 2027, flying five times per week. Both seasonal routes will continue until October 2027.

Seattle-Athens: from 12 May 2027 until October 2027

Athens-Seattle: from 13 May 2027 until October 2027

Seattle-Paris: from 25 May 2027 until October 2027

Paris-Seattle: from 26 May 2027 until October 2027

American Airlines

American has confirmed its international schedule for next summer. It will add three new destinations to its network from Philadelphia – serving Porto and Vienna for the first time ever and offering flights to Reykjavik for the first time since 2019. American will be the only US airline flying to Austria’s capital Vienna when its service begins next May.

In addition to the new destinations, American will also expand its network with nonstop routes from New York JFK to Amsterdam and Nice; from Charlotte in North Carolina to Barcelona; while adding a fourth daily flight between JFK and London Heathrow.

New York JFK-Amsterdam: from 28 March 2027

New York JFK-London Heathrow: fourth daily flight starts 28 March 2027

Philadelphia-Porto: from 28 March 2027

New York JFK-Nice: from 6 May 2027

Philadelphia-Vienna: from 6 May 2027

Charlotte-Barcelona: from 27 May 2027

Philadelphia-Reykjavik: from 27 May 2027

Delta

Beginning on 27 March 2027, Delta will launch the first-ever nonstop service from Austin to Paris Charles de Gaulle.

The service from the Texan city will operate daily during the summer season, with passengers able to connect beyond Europe through Delta's joint venture partnership with Air France-KLM and Virgin Atlantic.

During the peak summer months, Delta, Air France and KLM will offer up to 10 weekly nonstop flights between Austin and Europe, with services to both Paris Charles de Gaulle and Amsterdam.

Austin-Paris: daily from 27 March 2027

United

In the largest expansion in its history, United will add 10 cities to its international network in 2027 – including new nonstop European flights from Washington Dulles to Toulouse and from Newark to Luxembourg, Marseille, Ibiza, Valencia, Terceira, Ljubljana, Olbia in Sardinia, and Catania in Sicily.

Beyond the new cities, United is also adding a new three times weekly nonstop service from Washington DC to Milan from 28 May 2027 and a new daily nonstop service from Denver to Paris beginning on 27 May 2027.

World.title: From Caravaggio to Korea: How Malta’s artists are breaking out of the baroque
World.content:
Julien Vinet wants you to picture twilight with him.

 

The sun will lay itself like a crown atop the limestone buildings. Then rivers of red and orange will flood into the shabby studio he shares with his creative partner, Sam Alekksandra. As another day slips into night over Malta’s Three Cities, the warm light will wash over faded pink walls plastered with posters for their pop-up poetry events.

“Sunset is special here,” Vinet says with conviction.

The French artist, transplanted to Malta about a decade ago after eight years in Japan, has a knack for finding unexpected meaning in familiar moments. He likes to mine their depths until he finds a truth worth exposing – or what he calls “obsolete beauty”.

It’s why he and Alekksandra, the duo behind the collective Ponks, are drawn to liminal things caught in the in-between, like their sunset ritual.

And maybe it’s no coincidence that both have found creative freedom in a country defined by its own in-betweenness.

Ponks' 'Poetry from the Future' at Valletta's Rumi cafe during the 2026 Malta Biennale Vladimir Chistiakov

For Vinet, Malta has given him time and space to pursue both sides of himself: the punk and the perfectionist. For Alekksandra, a Maltese journalist turned poet, it has given her a point of reference to develop her own artistic language.

That kind of creative latitude is relatively new to the country.

For years, artists in Malta had few galleries and even fewer pathways to show their work. Now, with new institutions like the Malta Biennale and a growing international profile, the arts scene here is beginning to look very different.

The space between

Malta is an oddity, a small group of islands in the Mediterranean that has spent millennia absorbing one culture after another. Its cuisine spans African, Mediterranean and British influences. It has the only Semitic language written in the Latin alphabet. It has Phoenician boats, Catholic churches and UK crests.

Despite its plurality of influences, Maltese art for many years was stuck in one episode of the past. As a guide would later tell me in Valletta’s Muza Gallery: “Baroque this, baroque that – for many people in Malta, real art is only baroque.”

Now, cracks in the baroque façade are starting to show.

Before meeting Vinet and Alekksandra, I go on a short tour of Valletta’s art scene, starting – as most do – with Caravaggio’s masterpiece, ‘The Beheading of Saint John the Baptist’ at St John’s Cathedral. But there’s more to Malta’s art scene than saints and martyrs.

Apart from Muza and the new MICAS, Malta’s first national museum dedicated to contemporary art, galleries like Valletta Contemporary have provided a space for more daring work – something many artists told me Malta had lacked for years.

Founded by architect and artist Norbert Francis Attard, the gallery has transformed a 400-year-old warehouse in the city’s lower east end into a two-floor showcase for Maltese and international artists. When I visit, it’s showing ‘Still Time’, a 50-year retrospective of photographer Joseph P. Smith curated by Lisa Gwen Chetcuti.

Norbert Francis Attard poses at his studio in Gozo Edward De Gabriele

“In Malta, there are very few private galleries, and they operate differently than they do in London or New York,” Chetcuti tells Euronews Culture. The galleries often don’t own the work, meaning they aren’t taking on inventory they need to sell – and artists don’t necessarily want them to, either.

“In a small country, they don’t want to put all their eggs in one basket,” she explains. “This exhibition was all done through public funding.”

Valletta Contemporary is an answer to the lack of galleries, but Attard’s ambitions extend beyond exhibitions in the Maltese capital. He runs a residency at his home and studio in Gozo that brings artists from abroad and supports collaborative projects and exhibitions.

He is now converting his Gozo home into a public archive, with a café and garden.

“I’m the kind of person who can stop being an artist during my lifetime as a conscious decision,” he says. “That doesn’t mean I stop being creative. There are a lot of ways one can create.”

Breaking with tradition

Back at their studio, Vinet and Alekksandra are thinking about what comes next, too.

They have met up with their friend and collaborator, the sound artist Michael Quinton, to discuss their contribution to Malta’s pavilion at the Gwangju Biennale in South Korea, which runs from 5 September to 15 November.

Called BEJN / In-Between and led by Vinet as artistic director, the pavilion brings together Attard, Ponks and Quinton in a project that connects Malta and Korea through three linked installations.

Sound artist Michael Quinton scours a Gwangju market for field recordings Malta Pavilion Gwangju Biennalie

Attard is creating a spatial installation that draws on Malta’s festa traditions and Korea’s Obangsaek system, using colours, tension and balance to draw attention to conflict and collective memory. Ponks is building the 'Rope Temple', a five-kilometre web of rope featuring poetry by more than 140 Maltese and Korean writers. The concept draws on Malta’s maritime traditions and geumjul, sacred Korean ropes used to ward off evil spirits.

Beneath the temple, the 'Base Polygon' will divide the experience into three rooms exploring different aspects of poetry. In the first, Quinton combines recordings from Malta and Korea to make a soundscape that changes as visitors move through the space.

As Vinet and Alekksandra explain the temple, Quinton plays hauntingly beautiful music from data, of all things. Drawing on his background in exosolar science, he turns data collected in outer space into sound, making patterns invisible to the human eye audible.

“We always look for the start and the end, but we don’t hear the in-between,” Quinton says. “It’s really about enhancing that present moment.”

Malta’s creative scene is in an in-between of its own. It hasn’t overcome the limitations artists have faced, but neither is it confined by them.

“It’s very active,” Alekksandra explains, pointing to the Malta Biennale, which held its second edition this spring, as evidence of how quickly the landscape is changing. “People make do with what they have. And we keep doing that and keep growing.”

She has seen it firsthand. Ponks’ events began with little more than a microphone and a poster. Now more than 100 people regularly turn up to listen and share their work.

“We just offered the space, and that hole was filled,” she says.

Malta goes to Gwangju

The Gwangju Biennale is giving some of Malta’s locally built practices a very different setting. For Alekksandra, the connection is particularly strong because Gwangju has its own history of writers using art to respond to political upheaval.

“Gwangju is known as the city of resistance, and who is at the forefront of resistance? It’s the writers. It’s the poets,” she says. “They’re the ones who give people the courage to continue [fighting] and immortalising whatever happens.”

Alekksandra knows what it means to reach for poetry after trauma. Following the 2017 assassination of Maltese journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia, she says poetry gave her a way to express emotions that couldn’t easily be put into ordinary words.

While reaching out to artists for the exhibition, she asked an older Korean poet to read his work to her. “I couldn’t understand a word, but I just started to cry,” she recalls.

“We underestimate how much we can talk to each other beyond language.”

It’s a truth Vinet and Alekksandra say they have often found in Malta.

“Malta is already an in-between,” Vinet says. Then he peers out the studio window. “For a few rocks in the sea, it has incredible diversity. And that’s a strength.”

World.title: The climate disaster behind 'The Odyssey'
World.content:
New research finds the Bronze Age collapse of civilization emerged from water scarcity. Are droughts today pushing us toward a collapse of our own?

Christopher Nolan's latest blockbuster has drawn tens of millions of viewers into a world of stormy seas and cities on fire.

Minus the monsters, that world is based in reality. "The Odyssey" — a post-Trojan War survival story — is set during the Bronze Age collapse of civilization.

A new study links that collapse to a severe climate shift. And the authors warn of "implications for the future."

Scientists have long known about a mysterious and severe drought that struck more than 3,000 years ago, overlapping with the disintegration of kingdoms and states across the Mediterranean.

Ancient Epic: The Odyssey on Film To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Research published last month sheds light on the potential cause of that drought. A slow drying trend and a quicker natural cycle of dry weather stacked on top of each other.

By the late Bronze Age, the West African monsoon system had been shrinking for thousands of years, turning a green Sahara into desert. Less rain over Africa meant less over the Mediterranean. That trend amplified when the region hit a dry spell caused by natural climate cycles from the Atlantic, which saw the region swing between decades-long wet and dry periods.

Katherine Power, the Stockholm University scientist who led the study, said the environment at the time could explain the mass migration and conflicts of the Odyssey's era.

For decades, scholars have speculated on the reason for the large-scale movement during this time — which is also referred to as the period of the so-called Sea Peoples.

Archeologists argue that climate shifts could help explain the migration and political collapse at the end of the Bronze Age. The new findings add puzzle pieces.

"We don't know necessarily why those people moved," Power said. "But if we can say, 'hey, the climate was getting worse and worse to survive,' that could be a potential reason."

'A perfect storm of calamities'

And that, she says, is relevant to today. Europe's major rivers are at record lows, and drought is creating conditions for devastating wildfires as well as fueling historic crop-loss. That includes France's lowest maize harvest in 50 years.

Heatwaves and drought have wreaked havoc with crops Image: Patricia Huchot-Boissier/ABACAPRESS/IMAGO

The same cycles of wetting and drying from the Atlantic are still at play, but they're now happening in the context of a world that's heating as a result of humans burning oil, gas and coal.

"I think it is even more alarming and even more of a threat," Power said.

But does what happened then give insights into what might happen now?

Eric H. Cline, archeologist at George Washington University, who wrote a book on the roots of the Bronze Age crisis, said drought and disease were part of the "perfect storm of calamities" that led to societal downfall.

He sees parallels to today. In an email to DW, he said "we should be very concerned," about climate change as a stressor for the collapse of civilization. "That fear is not too dramatic at all."

He added that on his most optimistic days, he believes "we will come to our senses and sidestep that possibility at some point."

How climate change is teaming up with 'Super El Nino' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Was there a trigger moment for the collapse?

Power's research sought to explore what patterns might lie behind isolated Bronze Age drought events.

They started by examining plant spores, ice cores, cave stones, and other natural records that pointed to drought. Then, she and co-author, Stockholm paleoclimate scientist Qiong Zhang, turned to modeling to get a broader picture.

Their model looked at the whole planet, overlaid with a grid, each cell covering a roughly 125-kilometer (78-mile) area. A supercomputer then calculated the conditions in each of these cells, for every month, across thousands of years. That let the scientists look at the entire Mediterranean.

"We're not now stuck with just one core or one cave," Power said. "We can see farther afield and build a whole picture."

What they found was not a single event that dramatically and suddenly changed the climate. Instead, shorter cycles of wetting and drying lined up with a longer warming trend.

"When we are looking for connections between climate changes and civilization changes, we often are looking for that big, huge, abrupt, catastrophic event," Power said, adding that it is "slow, gradual changes that push a society over a threshold.”

She said it could have been a steady fall in water supply that led to a slow decline in crops, which prompted people to migrate, triggering conflict.

"It doesn't take very much to push a society over the threshold that they're comfortable with," Power said. "What if you add something more to the mix? Maybe then that pushes you a bit farther, and you can't quite recover from that."



Edited by: Tamsin Walker

World.title: Serbia: Keeping EU, Russia in play ahead of key election
World.content:
As Serbia heads towards an uncertain election, President Aleksandar Vucic is balancing ties with Russia and EU ambitions. But growing geopolitical tensions and pressure at home are narrowing his room to maneuver.

Smoke from the wildfires still hangs over parts of Serbia, but as the flames slowly recede, another debate is taking shape in their wake — one that has less to do with firefighting and more with politics.

In early August, wildfires swept across Serbia, affecting more than 3,500 hectares (8,600 acres) in the Deliblato Sands Special Nature Reserve alone. For days, firefighters, soldiers and helicopters battled the flames.

Serbia turned to Russia for help in fighting wildfires in the Deliblato Sands Special Nature Reserve Image: Marko Dimic/ZUMA/picture alliance

Then a Russian Ilyushin Il-76 firefighting aircraft arrived in the southern city of Nis. Serbia had turned to Moscow for help, making Russia the first foreign country it asked to provide a firefighting aircraft. Pro-government media greeted its arrival with celebratory coverage, dubbing the aircraft the "Russian beast."

"Considering that there are no firefighting aircraft of this capacity available within the European Union, the arriving Russian aircraft will significantly strengthen our capacities to fight the fires," said Luka Causic, head of the Serbian Interior Ministry's Department for Emergency Situations.

A pragmatic choice between EU, Russia — or a political signal?

The episode, however, was already being viewed through a geopolitical lens, as Serbia had sought Russian assistance before activating the EU's emergency mechanism.

When it did, the response was swift. Brussels mobilized four helicopters from its strategic rescEU reserve, based in Czechia, Romania and Slovakia, along with ground firefighting teams from Germany and Romania.

Emergency services, including German firefighters, were on hand to help Serbia battle wildfires Image: Feuerwehr Bonn/dpa/picture alliance

Vucic rejected the idea that turning to Russia first was a foreign-policy decision or a sign of Serbia's political alignment with Moscow.

"As far as equipment and resources are concerned, we are a European giant. The helicopters we received from Europe to fight the fires are less capable than ours and have a lower carrying capacity than our own," Vucic said during a visit to the Deliblato Sands.

Zelenskyy in Belgrade

The wildfire episode came less than two weeks after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy made his first official visit to Serbia.

The two presidents reaffirmed their support for each other's territorial integrity, which is particularly significant for Belgrade because Ukraine does not recognise Kosovo's independence.

But Vucic is also trying to keep the other side on board, says Vuk Vuksanovic , a political scientist and foreign-policy lecturer at King's College London.

Vuksanovic argues that Vucic's engagement with Zelenskyy must therefore be portrayed in Moscow not as a fundamental shift in Serbia's relationship with Russia, but as a response to Western pressure and Serbia's own interests.

"Vucic is now trying to make sure that neither the West nor Russia becomes an open opponent during the election campaign," said Vuksanovic.

"Zelenskyy was primarily received so that the ruling coalition could present itself to Europeans as a great friend of Ukraine. In the same way, Vucic is trying to present himself to the Trump administration as a great friend of Israel, primarily to ensure that neither the European Union nor the United States becomes an opponent of the ruling party during the election campaign," Vuksanovic added.

Vucic's room for maneuver is shrinking

The problem is that the room to maintain these relationships may be shrinking.

The deeper the confrontation between Russia and the West becomes, the harder it is for Serbia to remain close to both without facing pressure to choose.

The European Union increasingly expects candidate countries to align their foreign and security policies with those of the bloc. Serbia's refusal to impose sanctions on Russia remains one of the most visible obstacles to closer alignment.

But Moscow, too, has reasons not to take Belgrade's loyalty for granted, Vuksanovic said. He argues that Russia does not fully trust Vucic, even as Moscow continues to support his narrative about "color revolutions" — a reference to anti-government protests, in this case the student-led protests in Serbia that started last year, which Vucic and Russia portray as Western-backed attempts to destabilize the government.

For Vucic, however, the longer-term question of Serbia's ties with Russia can wait. The more immediate question is whether he will survive the election, tentatively scheduled for October, and remain in a position to preserve that delicate balance himself.

Edited by: Rob Mudge

World.title: Rwanda genocide: Dutch court sentences man to life in prison
World.content:
The Rwandan-born Dutch national was found guilty of involvement in the massacre of around 3,000 Tutsis, including throwing a grenade into a crowd of people sheltering in a football stadium.

A Rwandan-born Dutch national was on Friday sentenced to life imprisonment by a court in the Netherlands for his role in the 1994 Rwandan genocide.

The Hague District Court found that the 66-year-old man, identified only as Eugene N., had taken part in attacks on homes in Tutsi communities and thrown a grenade into a crowd of Tutsis sheltering in a football stadium, and convicted him of war crimes and genocide.

"The conduct of the defendant establishes a significant lack of respect for human dignity and for human life," read a statement from the court issued after the conviction.

"Only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families."

Handing down the verdict, the presiding judge said N.'s actions were committed with "genocidal intent."

Rwandan genocide: How many people died?

During the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, more than 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed in a campaign of mass murder orchestrated by Hutu extremists. Many leaders of the slaughter were tried and convicted by a United Nations war crimes tribunal that has now closed down.

N. was sentenced for his role in the massacre of around 3,000 Tutsis in Mbazi in southern Rwanda in April 1994, in which prosecutors said he was "personally involved."

"If the horrific crimes of the suspect, in which not one but an estimated 3,000 innocent people were literally slaughtered, in which the suspect personally threw a grenade into a stadium, do not deserve a life sentence, then what does?" one prosecutor asked the court.

Survivors remember Rwanda's 1994 genocide To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Defendant denies involvement in 'horrific events'

N., who the court heard had held a position of responsibility in Mbazi, denied the charges, claiming he himself had been a victim who had lost dozens of his own relatives in "those horrific events."

His lawyers had argued that their client did "everything to prevent the genocide" and had called for an acquittal on all counts.

"The case has torn his scars open again," said one defense lawyer. "He is a broken man."

But the court found that the defendant's position of responsibility made his crimes even worse since he was "held in high regard" and "must have been aware of his role" in events.

"Instead of staying on the sidelines, the defendant committed multiple severe crimes," added the court, although it did acquit N. of the charge of incitement to genocide.

Defense lawyers told the Dutch ANP news agency that they will "almost certainly appeal the charges."

N. fled to the Netherlands in 1998 and had since obtained Dutch citizenship, meaning Dutch authorities were unable to extradite him when Rwandan prosecutors issued an international warrant for his arrest back in 2014.

Dutch prosecutors opened their own investigation in 2020. They have since interviewed dozens of witnesses in Rwanda and arrested N. in 2024.

Last month, German prosecutors also announced the arrest of a man suspected of being an accomplice in the Rwandan genocide.

Rwandan genocide suspect prosecuted in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
