World.title: PM Magyar announces headquarters of new asset recovery office
World.content:
Hungary’s newly established National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH) will be based in Budapest’s Markó Street, in the building currently used by the Supreme Court, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced in Parliament on Friday.

The announcement came as MPs prepared to vote on the institution’s leadership, marking another step in the new government’s plans to strengthen the recovery and protection of public assets.

Magyar said the office would initially move into the Markó Street building after Supreme Court judges leave the premises. The building will have a number of vacant offices available, allowing the new institution to begin operating there.

The prime minister described the location as a symbolic one, as the building is situated next to the headquarters of the Prosecutor General’s Office.

Why is the Supreme Court leaving?

The Markó Street building, known as the Palace of Justice, was constructed between 1913 and 1918 for the then Ministry of Justice. It is currently used by the Supreme Court, the Prosecutor General’s Office and the Criminal Division of the Budapest Court of Appeal.

However, the Supreme Court will eventually move to another historic Palace of Justice opposite Parliament on Kossuth Square.

That building was constructed between 1893 and 1896 for the former Supreme Court and is currently undergoing renovation. Once the refurbishment is completed, the Supreme Court will relocate there, freeing up space in the Markó Street building for the new asset recovery office.

Magyar said the NVVH’s permanent headquarters should be ready within the coming weeks.

New office to receive HUF 2.3 billion

The government has also decided to transfer HUF 2.3 billion (around EUR 6.3 million) remaining from the budget of the former Sovereignty Protection Office to the new institution. Magyar said HUF 6 billion had originally been allocated to the now-abolished body, but only HUF 2.3 billion remained.

The money will be transferred to the budget line of the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office, providing funding for its initial operations.

Four deputy heads to work alongside the president

Parliament is voting on the head of the NVVH on Friday following a selection process carried out by the relevant parliamentary committee. The committee nominated Anna Unger for the presidency after hearing her presentation and questioning her about her plans for the institution.

MPs will vote by secret ballot on the president and one deputy president. If approved, they will take their oaths after the vote.

Magyar stressed that the new institution would not be run by its president alone. Four deputy heads will also work alongside the president, with three expected to be prosecutors and one a financial investigator. He described the structure as a collegiate body in which responsibility would be shared among its senior officials.

Magyar promises faster criminal proceedings

The prime minister also used his parliamentary speech to criticise the length of criminal proceedings in Hungary.

Magyar acknowledged that under the current system, some criminal cases can take as long as six years. He said the government would work to create a system in which most cases would not take five, ten or even 15 years to conclude.

He promised to provide investigators and prosecutors with the tools needed to speed up investigations, while also seeking faster court proceedings. The changes, he said, would apply not only to cases brought forward by the new asset recovery office but to criminal cases more broadly.

Political clash in Parliament

The announcement also triggered a political exchange between the government and opposition representatives.

Magyar argued that the previous Fidesz government had had 5,827 days to put Hungary’s affairs in order, but had failed to do so. He said the Tisza government had been in office for 107 days and had not performed a miracle, but had simply begun “looking after Hungarian people’s money”.

KDNP parliamentary group leader Bence Rétvári responded by pointing out that Magyar had himself been a member of Fidesz for 5,098 of those 5,827 days. Fidesz parliamentary group leader János Bóka compared Magyar to the captain of the Titanic, arguing that no matter how he turns the wheel, he cannot avoid the iceberg.

World.title: Tragedy in Hungary: Seven-year-old boy dies after falling from 10th-floor flat
World.content:
A seven-year-old boy has died after falling from the window of a tenth-floor flat in Szeged, southern Hungary, on Wednesday morning.

The tragic incident happened at a ten-storey block of flats on Szamos Street. Police officers and emergency services were called to the scene following a report from a member of the public.

According to the Csongrád-Csanád County Police Headquarters, the boy fell from an upstairs window under circumstances that have not yet been established. Attempts to resuscitate him were unsuccessful and he died at the scene. Police are investigating the circumstances of the death with the involvement of experts.

Seven-year-old boy reportedly the victim

Local media have reported that the victim was a seven-year-old boy who lived with autism. According to information reported by Délmagyar and RTL, the child was at home with his mother and younger sister at the time of the tragedy.

The precise circumstances leading up to the fall have not been officially established, and authorities have not publicly confirmed all of the details reported by local media.

Police cordoned off the area around the building at the junction of Szamos and Retek streets while investigators examined the scene. A temporary tent was erected at the location, and forensic investigators remained at the building for more than an hour after the incident.

Emergency services could not save the child

The National Ambulance Service confirmed that the child had suffered injuries so severe that his life could not be saved.

According to local reports, the child’s father arrived at the building around the time of the incident and went into shock when he saw his son. RTL reported that the parents live separately and that the children had been staying with their mother that week.

The reports also suggest that the boy may have fallen through a kitchen window, while the property’s balcony was protected by bars. However, these details have not been confirmed by police.

Investigation underway

The circumstances of the child’s death are under investigation. Police said they are examining the case with the involvement of experts to establish exactly what happened before the fatal fall. The tragedy has shocked residents of the Szamos Street area, where police maintained a cordon around the building as the investigation continued.

World.title: Missing Hungarian football star Buzsáky breaks silence after 10 days
World.content:
Former Hungarian international footballer Ákos Buzsáky has broken his silence after being reported missing, reassuring worried friends and supporters that he is safe.

The 44-year-old former midfielder posted a message on Facebook on Thursday, around ten days after his disappearance was reported to the Hungarian authorities. Buzsáky explained that he had deliberately withdrawn from his everyday life following what he described as serious changes in his personal circumstances over recent months.

“Unfortunately, serious changes have happened in my life over the past few months, which have tested me. The waves closed over my head, and I reached the point where I felt I needed to remove myself from these everyday circumstances,” he wrote.

We also reported on Buzsáky missing: Former Hungary international footballer Buzsáky missing, concern grows in England

His mother reported him missing

According to Buzsáky, his mother became concerned about him and contacted the police following a misunderstanding. He said that once he learned what had happened, he ended his period of withdrawal and the authorities were informed.

“I would like to thank you very much for worrying about me and thinking of me. As soon as I became aware of the situation, I ended my retreat and we notified the authorities,” Buzsáky wrote. He also thanked people for the support and affection they had shown him during the period.

“It felt very good to receive so much love,” he added.

The Hungarian police had published Buzsáky’s details among missing persons on 18 August following a report from his mother. His profile was still visible on the police website on Friday morning, although his latest message indicates that the authorities have since been informed that he is safe.

His former club was also worried

The case attracted attention beyond Hungary, with Buzsáky’s former English club Queens Park Rangers (QPR) also expressing concern for the former player. The London club, where Buzsáky spent several years, posted a message asking for information and expressing its concern after news of his disappearance emerged.

Buzsáky joined QPR after moving to England following his spell at FC Porto. He became a popular figure at the club and remained there until 2012.

A career spanning Hungary, Portugal and England

Buzsáky began his senior career at MTK Budapest and also captained Hungary’s under-21 national team. In 2003, he moved to FC Porto, where he won the Portuguese league title and the UEFA Cup with the club.

He subsequently moved to England, initially playing for QPR in the second tier. He later also appeared in England’s third tier before returning to Hungary, where he played for Ferencváros. Buzsáky ended his professional playing career in 2015. From 2018 to 2019, he worked as sporting director at III. Kerületi TVE.

World.title: Átlátszó: Hungarian government building Paks bottom sill without environmental permit
World.content:
The controversial bottom sill being built on the Danube near Hungary’s Paks nuclear power plant is reportedly being constructed before the necessary environmental operating permit has been obtained. Authorities have until the end of September to apply for the permit, but the project could already be completed by then.

Environmental permit could arrive after construction

The Hungarian government is building a so-called bottom sill on the Danube near the Paks nuclear power plant without currently holding an environmental permit for the project, investigative outlet Átlátszó reports.

The issue is particularly controversial because a government decree issued on 12 August gives the authorities until 30 September to submit an application for an environmental operating permit. By that time, however, the bottom sill could already be finished. The application is expected to be based on an environmental review that also includes an assessment of the project’s impact on Natura 2000 protected areas.

According to information from the Bács-Kiskun County Government Office, which has been designated as the environmental authority, preparing the necessary impact assessment documentation is the responsibility of the developer.

The National Directorate General for Water Management (OVF) said that the state-owned VIZITERV Environ Kft. is carrying out the work on its behalf and that the “preparatory tasks related to the authority procedure are ongoing”.

The project was launched after exceptionally low Danube water levels raised concerns about the operation of the Paks nuclear power plant. The bottom sill is intended to help maintain sufficient water levels around the plant’s cooling-water intake.

Economy Minister István Kapitány in Paks. Photo: Facebook/Kapitány István

Was there really an emergency?

Átlátszó also questioned whether the project could legally benefit from an exemption from normal environmental permitting requirements. Certain projects serving defence purposes or responding to emergencies threatening the civilian population can be exempted from some licensing obligations.

However, according to Átlátszó, no separate government decision granting such an exemption was issued in the case of the Paks bottom sill.

Perger András, programme director at the Energy Club (Energiaklub), told Átlátszó that he did not consider the situation an acute emergency, although Hungary’s electricity supply was under considerable pressure earlier in August.

“There was no acute emergency, but it was quite close in early August to having enough electricity for every period, including when the sun was no longer shining.”

Perger stressed that a potential shortage of electricity would not necessarily mean Hungary being plunged into darkness. Instead, larger consumers could be asked to reduce their consumption or, if necessary, temporarily disconnected from the grid.

He also described a complete shutdown of the Paks plant as a manageable situation from a nuclear safety perspective, although restarting the reactors would have presented difficulties.

Living, working or doing business in Hungary?

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Permit could reportedly be refused even after completion

The environmental licensing issue may not disappear simply because construction is completed. A lawyer from the EMLA Association for Environmental Management and Law told Átlátszó that classifying the project as a public-interest investment does not remove the environmental obligations set out in Hungarian law.

This means that, according to the legal expert, the environmental authority could potentially refuse to issue the permit even after the bottom sill had already been completed.

The distinction is significant: construction being physically finished would not necessarily mean that the project had secured all the environmental approvals required for its continued operation.

Government says environmental rules were followed

Átlátszó contacted the ministries responsible for environmental protection and energy, as well as the Prime Minister’s Office, for clarification. The ministry responsible for environmental protection responded that, in its view, the investment was carried out in compliance with environmental and nature conservation regulations.

World.title: Péter Magyar’s political cudgel or rule-of-law safeguard: what exactly is NVVH?
World.content:
The National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office was one of Péter Magyar’s major election promises. But what will its real role be?

Only a few months ago, it was still an election promise. Now it exists in Hungarian law: the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office, or NVVH, has been formally established, with its own chapter added to the central budget in August. The process of selecting its leadership has also entered its final stage.

On Thursday, 27 August, the parliamentary Justice and Constitutional Affairs Committee nominated political scientist Anna Róza Unger as president of the new office and Katalin Tasnádi as deputy president responsible for investigative matters. Parliament is expected to decide on their appointments by secret ballot on Friday. If approved, the office could begin operating from 1 September.

The question, however, is becoming increasingly intriguing: is Hungary getting a new independent safeguard for the protection of public wealth, or is Péter Magyar’s government creating a powerful political cudgel?

The answer matters because NVVH is potentially one of the most powerful institutions created by the new government. It could become a formidable weapon against corruption. But precisely because of the breadth of its powers, it could also become one of the most sensitive institutions in Hungary’s new political system.

This is not simply another government office

NVVH was not created merely to become another state agency occupying a few floors of an office building in Budapest.

Under the new law, its purpose is to uncover unlawful management of public assets, protect public wealth and identify, secure and recover assets that have unlawfully left public ownership. Its remit can cover public procurement, subsidies, concessions, European Union funds, state and municipal assets, public-service financing and the financial flows surrounding state-owned companies.

The legislation goes considerably further than a conventional auditing body.

NVVH can conduct investigations into public-asset risks, order certain forms of asset protection, initiate proceedings before other authorities and bring civil actions. Most importantly, under the criminal procedure framework, it can conduct investigations and, in specified circumstances, exercise the powers of a public prosecutor, including bringing charges and representing the prosecution in court.

That makes the office something considerably more consequential than a traditional supervisory authority.

And it immediately raises the uncomfortable question: who watches the watchdog?

The “Péter Magyar’s political cudgel” accusation is not entirely baseless

The perennial problem with supposedly independent authorities is that independence on paper does not automatically guarantee independence in practice.

A great deal depends on who is appointed to lead the institution, how cases are selected, what safeguards apply to investigations and how effectively courts and other institutions can review its decisions.

This is why the selection of NVVH’s leadership has itself become a political and constitutional test.

The process has already attracted controversy. Ninety-six applications were reportedly submitted for the presidency, with the parliamentary committee initially selecting three leading candidates. The Tisza parliamentary group subsequently sought the hearing of Nicholas Sárvári as an additional candidate, describing him as a professionally suitable applicant who had received the fourth-highest score. Sárvári himself said he had learned from the press that the Tisza group had nominated him. The following day, the Tisza group clarified that none of the candidates was formally a party or parliamentary faction nominee.

Meanwhile, Fidesz members boycotted the selection process.

None of this proves that the office is politically controlled. But it does illustrate why the credibility of its independence will be tested from its very first day.

A rule-of-law safeguard or a political accountability machine?

Perhaps the most important question is therefore not what NVVH is called, but how it behaves.

The law goes out of its way to describe the institution as independent and subject exclusively to the law. It also explicitly requires it to operate according to the principles of legality, independence, objectivity, impartiality, proportionality and respect for fundamental rights.

On paper, these are significant safeguards.

If the office genuinely follows professional criteria, operates according to transparent procedures, gives reasons for its decisions and remains subject to meaningful judicial scrutiny, it could become one of the most important institutions of the government’s promised political transformation.

Its purpose would not simply be to punish decisions made by previous governments. Rather, it would create a permanent institutional mechanism for following public money: where it came from, where it went, who benefited from it and whether the process was lawful.

That could represent a major change in Hungary’s approach to public-sector corruption.

But the opposite scenario is equally easy to imagine.

An authority with extensive investigative powers, access to financial information and the ability to initiate criminal and civil proceedings could become a formidable instrument of political accountability — or political retaliation — if the institutional safeguards prove too weak.

Anti-corruption policy is credible only when the same rules apply to everyone.

If an alleged abuse committed by a former Fidesz government is treated as a serious matter, while a similar case involving the new governing party is quietly ignored, NVVH would quickly lose the very legitimacy it was created to establish.

The first appointments will matter enormously

The choice of Anna Róza Unger therefore carries significance beyond the appointment of another senior public official.

Unger, an associate professor at ELTE’s Faculty of Social Sciences, emerged from a field of candidates that included Transparency International Hungary legal director Miklós Ligeti and sociologist and corruption researcher Dávid Jancsics. Jancsics later withdrew his application.

The fact that Ligeti was among the leading candidates was particularly notable because he had publicly stressed the importance of keeping the institution independent and warned against turning it into a political “witch hunt”.

That distinction is crucial. There is nothing inherently undemocratic about establishing a powerful anti-corruption institution. In fact, an effective system for recovering stolen or unlawfully transferred public assets can strengthen the rule of law.

The danger begins when the political leadership of the country starts treating such an institution as an extension of its own political agenda.

So what will NVVH actually become?

The answer will not ultimately be found in the title of the law, but in the first major cases.

The Hungarian Parliament has already taken the formal steps needed to establish the office, including creating its own budgetary chapter. The legislation gives it an unusually broad mandate, covering everything from public procurement and EU funding to state assets, financial transactions and criminal proceedings.

Now comes the difficult part: proving that these powers can be used without becoming political weapons. For Péter Magyar and the Tisza government, this is an opportunity to demonstrate that asset recovery is not about revenge against the previous political establishment, but about building a functioning system in which public money is genuinely protected.

For the opposition, meanwhile, the test will be straightforward. Will NVVH investigate only the alleged abuses of the previous government? Or will it show the same determination if questionable decisions emerge on the government’s own side?

That is ultimately what will decide whether the new institution becomes a political cudgel or a genuine rule-of-law safeguard. Not what Péter Magyar says about it, not what Fidesz says about it, and not even what the legislation promises.

The real test will come when NVVH has to choose between protecting the government of the day and protecting the public purse. If it chooses the latter — regardless of who is in power — Hungary may indeed be entering a new era. If it does not, the grand promise of a new system may simply have produced another powerful political weapon.

World.title: Bucharest Stock Exchange-listed tech company AROBS posts 121% higher net profit in H1
World.content:
AROBS Transilvania Software (BVB: AROBS), one of the largest entrepreneurial technology companies listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange, recorded consolidated turnover of RON 292 million in the first half of 2026, up 36% compared to H1 2025, EBITDA of RON 40 million, a 29% increase, and net profit of approximately RON 23 million, up 121% compared to the same period of last year.

The first six months of 2026 represented the AROBS group’s best first half of the past three years in terms of turnover, EBITDA, operating profit, and net profit. The positive momentum accelerated in the second quarter, when the group generated turnover of approximately RON 148 million, EBITDA of RON 22 million, and net profit of over RON 15 million, twice the level recorded in Q1 2026 and almost four times higher than in Q2 2025.

“In 2024 and 2025, we increased the scale of the group and added capabilities through the acquisitions we completed. In 2026, our focus is on integrating these capabilities through One AROBS and transforming this structure into an organization that operates as one, both commercially and operationally,” stated Voicu Oprean, founder and CEO of AROBS.

Of the consolidated turnover recorded in H1 2026, RON 242 million, representing almost 83% of the total, was generated by activities classified as organic, while RON 50 million came from companies included in the M&A scope.

At business segment level, Software Services generated turnover of approximately RON 186 million, up 31% compared to H1 2025. Software Products recorded turnover of RON 54 million, 17% above the level reported in the comparable period, while the segment’s gross margin increased from 52% to 54%.

The fastest growth was recorded by Integrated Systems, where turnover advanced by 88% to RON 52 million, mainly as a result of the implementation of projects for the National House of Public Pensions and the Ministry of Health. Furthermore, after the end of the first semester, AROBS Systems signed a contract with the Agency for Payments and Intervention for Agriculture (APIA) with a total value of approximately RON 70 million, excluding VAT, of which approximately 61% is attributable to the company.

In the first half of the year, AROBS achieved 53% of the turnover, 49% of the EBITDA and 65% of the net profit envisaged in the 2026 Consolidated Revenue and Expense Budget, which provides for turnover of RON 552 million, EBITDA of RON 82 million and net profit of RON 35 million. The budget approved in April was prepared based on prudent estimates regarding the contributions of GESS and QUEST, companies acquired by AROBS in November 2025 and January 2026, respectively, and does not include contracts signed after its approval, including the contract concluded by AROBS Systems with APIA in August.

“The results for the first half of the year provide the first financial confirmation of this model. For the second half of the year, our objective is for the increase in turnover to translate to a greater extent into EBITDA. Looking ahead to 2027-2030, the group’s development will be supported by expansion in international markets, the organization of our activities around the verticals in which we have expertise, the development of proprietary products and the integration of AI into the solutions and services we provide,” he added.

World.title: Romanian digital education infrastructure provider Ascendia posts 50% higher net profit in H1
World.content:
Ascendia (BVB: ASC), a Romanian benchmark and provider of critical learning infrastructure, announced its financial results for the first half of 2026. According to the press release, the company recorded the best first half in its history, marking accelerated growth supported by the completion of previous projects, its own product portfolio, and efficient capital management.

The financial performance in H1 2026 was directly supported by the increase in operating revenue. This advance was driven by robust turnover of more than RON 20.6 million, generated mainly by services and sales associated with its own educational software products (CoffeeLMS, LIVRESQ and eJourneys), as well as contracts financed through the PNRR.

At the same time, the company achieved a net profit of RON 8.11 million, up 49.52% compared with the same period in 2025, achieving a solid operating margin of 44.09%. The evolution confirms the efficiency of the integrated business model and the scalable use of in-house products.

“The first half of 2026 was the best first half in the company’s history. After the very good results recorded in H1 2025, we managed to achieve significant growth both in terms of revenue and net profit. We have a solid financial position, with cash of around RON 25.8 million. This flexibility allows us to consider the possibility of early repayment of the ASC27 bonds to reduce financing costs,” said Cosmin Mălureanu, CEO and co-founder of Ascendia.

As of June 30, 2026, equity doubled to RON 37.95 million, representing 71% of total assets of RON 53.45 million. The current liquidity ratio strengthened to 4.56, giving the company the capacity to finance future expansion stages without the pressure of an immediate need for external financing.

World.title: CTP delivers 3,000 sqm of built-to-suit temperature-controlled warehousing in Bucharest
World.content:
Developer and operator of logistics and industrial real estate CTP has delivered nearly 3,000 sqm of built-to-suit temperature-controlled warehouse space to Frigonet Logistics at CTPark Bucharest South, according to a press release published on Friday, August 28.

Frigonet Logistics provides integrated cold chain logistics services, including refrigerated warehousing and handling, national dual-temperature distribution for chilled and frozen goods, picking, and cross-docking. The company selected CTPark Bucharest South for its strategic location and excellent connectivity to Bucharest and key regional hubs, enabling more efficient distribution routes and supporting the continued expansion of its operations.

Frigonet Logistics has signed a long-term lease for its new facility, which it will use to expand its temperature-controlled storage operations for refrigerated and frozen food products, supporting its growing logistics network across Romania.

CTPark Bucharest South is strategically located with direct access to Bucharest’s ring road and major national transport corridors, providing excellent connectivity to the capital, the A0, A1 and A2 motorways, and key destinations across Romania and Southeastern Europe. The park comprises nearly 140,000 sqm of built space across a nearly 37-hectare site.

“Beyond the operational advantages, the location at CTPark Bucharest South provides excellent connectivity to Bucharest and our key regional hubs, helping us optimise distribution routes and improve logistics efficiency. This investment gives us the capacity and flexibility required to support our continued growth and to provide our customers with temperature-controlled transport and logistics services that meet the highest standards,” explained David Stoian, Executive Director of Frigonet Logistics.

The facility incorporates dedicated frozen storage operating at -20°C, a 0-4°C buffer area, a refrigeration plant, and the infrastructure required to safely handle and store temperature- sensitive products while maintaining an uninterrupted cold chain.

“We are pleased to welcome Frigonet Logistics to CTPark Bucharest South and to support the company’s next stage of expansion,” said Cristina Manea, Business Developer at CTP in Romania.

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: Mastering the Music Business brings over 100 speakers to Bucharest
World.content:
The 11th edition of the Mastering the Music Business (MMB) conference will take place at Hotel Caro in Bucharest from September 1 to 3. More than 100 speakers from 16 countries will participate in 27 panels, workshops, and discussions on building careers in the music industry.

The lineup includes Romanian artists and industry figures such as Grasu XXL, Nicole Cherry, Marius Moga, AFO, Bean of Subcarpați, and television host Cătălin Măruță, who also manages singer Andra.

They will be joined by professionals representing European festivals, booking agencies, record labels, and music organizations. Speakers include European Music Exporters Exchange president Corinne Sadki, ESNS junior booker Janneke de Boer, SoAlive Music Conference founder Ruth Koleva, Music Glue business development head Marion Sosnowicz, and Future Echoes festival director Peter Åstedt.

For the first time, the conference will host representatives of music export offices from 11 European countries: Poland, Latvia, Lithuania, Switzerland, Belgium, France, Italy, Ukraine, Austria, Greece, and Germany. Discussions will focus on festivals, touring, and the professional networks that could help Romanian artists reach European markets.

The program will cover topics including artificial intelligence in the creative process, independent music economics, ticket fraud, songwriting, artist selection by European bookers, mental health, fan communities, copyright, and crisis management.

AFO and Bean will discuss Subcarpați’s development on the opening day, while Marius Moga will participate in a panel about how brands choose music projects. The final day will feature a conversation with Măruță about managing Andra and a keynote address by Grasu XXL.

The conference will also include three small-group accelerators focusing on music marketing, booking, and music business fundamentals. They are open to ticket holders through separate registration, subject to availability.

Each conference day will be followed by concerts at Club Expirat as part of the MMB Showcase Festival. Twelve acts from Romania and elsewhere in Europe will perform during the three evenings, with admission free, subject to venue capacity.

Further details are available here.

World.title: Romania’s population drop slowed by migration but still ongoing
World.content:
Romania’s resident population reached 19.041 million people on January 1, 2026, 1,829 fewer than a year earlier, according to provisional data published Friday, August 28, by the National Institute of Statistics.

The decline was largely limited by migration. The number of immigrants exceeded that of emigrants by 102,200, but the difference did not fully offset the natural decrease of 104,100 people.

Overall, the positive international migration balance increased compared with previous years and covered almost the entire difference between the number of deaths and the number of births.

Among people who left Romania, men accounted for 57.9% of the total. They were also the majority among those who came to the country, with a share of 58.6%.

The urban population reached 9.792 million people at the beginning of 2026, up 0.2% from the same period in 2025. The female population stood at 9.744 million people, down 0.1%.

Beyond the decrease in the number of inhabitants, INS data indicate an intensification of demographic aging. People aged at least 65 accounted for 20.5% of the population on January 1, 2026, compared with 20.3% a year earlier. At the same time, the share of children aged 0 to 14 fell from 15.4% to 15.1%.

The demographic aging index therefore rose from 131.3 to 135.9 elderly people for every 100 young people. In other words, at the beginning of 2026, Romania had almost 136 people aged at least 65 for every 100 children under 15. The demographic dependency ratio fell slightly, from 55.6 to 55.2 young and elderly people for every 100 working-age adults.

INS included foreign citizens in the resident population, as well as stateless people, who usually live in Romania for a period of at least 12 months. During the war in Ukraine, the statistics also include Ukrainian citizens benefiting from temporary protection in Romania.

World.title: Tour of Romania brings together 23 cycling teams from 16 countries
World.content:
The 2026 Tour of Romania will bring together approximately 150 cyclists from 23 teams representing 16 countries between September 9 and 13. Italian Olympic champion Elia Viviani will also attend the race as manager of Italy’s national team.

The five-stage competition will cover more than 800 kilometers, beginning in Chișinău, Moldova, and ending with a final circuit in Bucharest. This will be the first edition of the race to start outside Romania.

“The presence of 23 teams from 16 countries confirms the growing interest in the Tour of Romania,” Romanian Cycling Federation president Cătălin Sprinceană said. “We are pleased that the public will be able to see athletes from so many countries at the start.”

The lineup includes ten UCI continental teams, eight club teams, and five national teams. The participating countries are Albania, Austria, Belgium, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Moldova, Monaco, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Romania, Turkey, and the United States.

The national teams of Romania, Italy, Moldova, Albania, and Bosnia and Herzegovina will compete in the race.

Elia Viviani won the Olympic omnium title at Rio 2016 and is a three-time Olympic medalist and three-time track world champion. He has also won stages in all three Grand Tours and claimed the European road race title in 2019. After a 16-year professional career, the Italian cyclist is beginning a new role as manager of his country’s national team.

The participating teams will be officially presented in Chișinău on September 8. The first stage, from Chișinău to Ungheni, will take place the following day.

The race will then continue in Romania with stages from Iași to Piatra Neamț on September 10, Piatra Neamț to Băile Balvanyos on September 11, and Brașov to Ploiești on September 12. The final stage will be held on a circuit in Bucharest on September 13.

The race will be broadcast live by Prima Sport and on the official Tour of Romania and Auchan Romania Facebook pages, while TVR Sport will air daily highlights. Further details can be found here.

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: NASA Space Apps Challenge opens registration for Bucharest, Cluj-Napoca events
World.content:
NASA Space Apps Challenge, the world’s largest hackathon, will return to Romania on November 14-15, with simultaneous events in Bucharest and Cluj-Napoca. Registration for the 48-hour international event is open until November 13.

Under the theme The Next Frontier!, participants will form teams of up to six members and use NASA’s open data to develop solutions to challenges related to Earth and space exploration. The challenges will be announced on September 17.

The competition is open to programmers, scientists, engineers, designers, students, storytelling specialists, and other people interested in technology and innovation, regardless of their age, experience, or professional background.

“Romania has people with ideas and skills who can compete at the highest international level, and this competition is an extraordinary opportunity to bring them together and connect them to one of the most innovative global communities,” said Diana Iosu, founder of DiFine PR and organizer of the Bucharest edition.

The Bucharest event will be held at the Romanian-American University, while the Cluj-Napoca competition will take place at ClujHUB. Registration for Bucharest is available here, and for Cluj here.

Two winning teams will be selected from each city to advance to the global competition and compete against thousands of teams worldwide. Global winners will be invited to visit a NASA center or facility, attend an event celebrating their projects, and meet representatives of the US space agency.

Participants will also receive free access to the Google AI Professional Certificate course offered through Coursera.

People under 18 may participate only with the consent of a parent or legal guardian, who must accompany them throughout the event.

The 2025 edition attracted 200 registrations in Romania. Winning projects included an algorithm assessing the environmental effects of business decisions, a visual platform for learning about physics and astrophysics, and an AI solution that converted air-quality data into real-time information.

Launched globally in 2012, the NASA Space Apps Challenge has brought together more than 487,000 participants from 190 countries and territories. The Romanian editions are organized by ROTSA and DiFine PR.

irina.marica@romania-insider.com

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: IKEA opens first Plan and Order Point in Iași
World.content:
IKEA will open its first Plan and Order Point in Iași on Monday, August 31. Located in Egros Shopping Center, the studio will be the retailer’s sixth such facility in Romania.

The location will offer personalized planning services for kitchens, wardrobes, and storage solutions. Customers will be able to work individually with IKEA specialists to select configurations, products, and finishes suited to their homes and budgets, the company said.

The studio will feature three kitchen layouts, three wardrobe solutions, two planning desks, and more than 1,400 IKEA products. Around 50 everyday products will also be available to purchase directly.

Customers can collect their orders free of charge from the location, arrange home delivery, or use another IKEA pick-up point. Furniture assembly services will also be available.

The new facility replaces IKEA’s existing pick-up point at Egros Shopping Center, with collection services integrated into the expanded format.

IKEA opened its first Romanian Plan and Order Point in Constanța in 2024. More than 4,500 planning sessions have since taken place across its locations over the past year, with kitchens attracting the most interest.

The company’s other Plan and Order Points operate in Constanța, Bucharest, Cluj-Napoca, and Brașov.

World.title: Week in Review: Hopes and Dilemmas
World.content:
The question of who owns Bosnia and Herzegovina’s state property is a major point of dispute and an unresolved issue on the country’s path away from supervision by the Office of the High Representative and towards membership of the EU. Not surprising, perhaps, in a country where the core issue of sovereignty is contested.

Intractable though the issue may seem, might there be movement towards resolving it? Washington’s newly-discovered interest in energy, mining and infrastructure projects in the country is putting the spotlight on this issue. Now the question is whether Bosnia will solve the issue of state property on Washington’s terms or its own.

World.title: Mladic is Dead, and My Serb Grandfather Was Right About His Fate
World.content:
“You will answer for this disgrace and make the entire Serbian people bear the blame,” my grandfather said, punctuating the sentence with a curse as he walked out of the house to calm himself down in the yard. On the television screen, Ratko Mladic was handing out sweets to children gathered in Srebrenica as cameras from the wartime Serb television station SRNA filmed him.

I could not quite understand what the problem was. I had just turned 15. I had grown up in a Serb family and a predominantly Serb community. Mladic was a hero and a liberator. A source of national pride. Fortunately, I had grown up with a grandfather for whom truth and facts mattered more than any other identity. Especially the national one.

At the beginning of the war, my grandfather was subject to military conscription. He did everything he could to avoid taking part in the aggression. We lived in the hills above Sarajevo, and every day and every night we watched shells falling on the city.

My grandfather kept repeating that they would be held to account. I did not give it much thought. Not until I turned 20, returned to Sarajevo, enrolled at the Media Plan School of Journalism and saw footage of Eduard Limonov, the Russian poet, and Radovan Karadzic, the Bosnian Serb leader, firing a machine gun from Zlatiste, near Mount Trebevic. During pauses, they passed a bottle of rakija from hand to hand, sharing it with the soldiers and taking swigs.

World.title: Tribute Gatherings for Ratko Mladic Held Across Bosnia’s Republika Srpska
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp



Bosnian Serb political leader Milorad Dodik (C) attending a church service for Mladic in Banja Luka. Photo: SNSD/Facebook.

Crowds of Serbs gathered in towns and cities across Republika Srpska on Thursday evening to pay tribute to convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic after his death, with hundreds marching through Zvornik chanting his name and senior entity officials attending a memorial service in Banja Luka.

Mladic, the former commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, died on Thursday aged 84 at the UN Detention Centre in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.

The gatherings were attended by members of the public, war veterans and government officials, while some of the events featured open glorification of Mladic and his wartime role.

In Republika Srpska’s administrative centre, Banja Luka, Milorad Dodik, the president of the ruling Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, SNSD, and Republika Srpska prime minister Savo Minic attended a memorial service at the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour, where they lit candles for Mladic.

The service was also attended by representatives of the entity authorities, veterans’ organisations and many members of the public.

Dodik said Mladic had and demonstrated “how to defend one’s people” in what he described as “an unstable, difficult period”.

“Some want this [Serb] people not to remember him, but people have feelings. You cannot ban them, you cannot erase feelings,” Dodik said.

Similar gatherings were held in Trebinje, Bijeljina, Prijedor, Srbac, East Ilidza and elsewhere. In Trebinje, former Bosnian Serb Army members, families of deceased soldiers and local officials lit candles in front of the town’s memorial room and monument to its defenders.

In Bijeljina, Bosnian Serb Army veterans, veterans’ organisations and members of the public gathered, while a memorial service was held in Prijedor.

The head of East Ilidza municipality, Marinko Bozovic, Banja Luka mayor Drasko Stanivukovic, Republika Srpska National Assembly MP Jelena Trivic and Bosnian Serb delegate to the House of Peoples of the Parliamentary Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina Zelimir Nes­kovic attended a memorial service for convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic at the Monastery of St Nicholas on Mount Ozren.

In a social media post, Bozovic wrote of the convicted war criminal: “Eternal remembrance, General, and may you enter the Kingdom of Heaven.”

The memorial service was attended by a significant number of local residents, as well as Branko Blanusa, president of the opposition Serb Democratic Party.

The attendance of ruling party and opposition politicians marked a shared approach between them to commemorating Mladic, despite his convictions for wartime atrocities.

However, scenes from Zvornik in eastern Bosnia drew particular attention. Several hundred people, including a large number of young people, gathered and marched through the town chanting Mladic’s name. According to footage circulating online, participants also carried flags and symbols associated with the Army of Republika Srpska.

Republika Srpska vice president Camil Durakovic condemned the gathering, recalling that Zvornik was the site of mass persecution and killings of Bosniaks during the war.

“This is Zvornik – this is the town where Mladic’s dogs of war carried out his orders. This is the town of mass graves of my people. This is the town from which tens of thousands of Bosniaks were expelled,” Durakovic said.

He questioned whether state institutions existed that would respond to such scenes, warning that, in his words, this represented the “final stage of genocide”.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, the public glorification of convicted war criminals is prohibited under the state-level Criminal Code, following amendments imposed in 2021 by then-High Representative Valentin Inzko after domestic authorities failed to adopt legislation addressing genocide denial and the glorification of war criminals.

Mladic was sentenced to life imprisonment in 2021 under a final verdict, as the UN war crimes court upheld his responsibility for genocide in Srebrenica, persecution, extermination, murder, deportation, forcible transfer and terrorising civilians during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

World.title: Serbia to Organise Genocide Convict Ratko Mladic’s Funeral with State Honours
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Serbian Justice Minister Nenad Vujic told Republika Srpska’s Alternativna Television on Thursday evening that Bosnian Serb genocide and war crimes convict Ratko Mladic will be buried with state honours in Serbia.

“General Mladic is a general, and there are protocols that apply. His role is known, as is what is due to General Mladic, and that will certainly be respected,” Vujic said.

He added the location of Mladic’s burial will depend on the family’s decision.

Mladic was a general of the Yugoslav People’s Army at the start of the Yugoslav wars, and then became a general with the Bosnian Serb Army and the commander of its Main Staff, waging a campaign of ethnic cleansing that ultimately led to his indictment by the Hague Tribunal.

When he died on Thursday in detention in The Hague, aged 84, Mladic was serving a life sentence for committing genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Vujic’s statement is one of the only signs of the Serbian government’s position on Mladic so far. After the news on his death on Thursday, Serbian officials remained silent, although pro-government media mourned his death and accused the Hague Tribunal of neglecting his health.

Vujic told Republika Srpska’s public broadcaster RTRS that he spoke with Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic on Thursday and that they agreed Serbia would provide any assistance needed to organise the transportation of Mladic’s body and arrange to fly it to Belgrade on a “special aircraft”.

“I will probably also travel with the family so that we can complete the formalities related to the transfer of the body,” Vujic said.

“This is sad news for all of us, for the entire Serbian people,” he told RTRS, stressing that Serbian authorities had done everything in their power to urge the early release of Mladic due to his illness.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Crypto Scandal Returns to Haunt Poland’s Right Ahead of Election Year
World.content:
Slovakia foils arson plot on Ukrainian drone factory; Fico pulls plug on transaction tax

Slovak police foiled an alleged arson attack on a Ukrainian drone factory located near Presov, in what appears to be one of the first serious sabotage plots targeting Slovakia’s growing defence industry. The target was Skyeton, which produces sophisticated surveillance and reconnaissance drones at its plant in eastern Slovakia; Skyeton’s Slovak plant does not export its drones eastwards. Police, acting on information from the civilian SIS and Military Intelligence, arrested three men – reportedly two Latvians and a Ukrainian – who they say were preparing the attack “on commission”. One was detained in Germany. The suspects had allegedly gathered petrol mixed with polystyrene, commonly known as napalm, as well as tools, phones, an action camera and a hand-drawn plan. Some 70 employees could have been inside the plant, where equipment is worth tens of millions of euros. Who commissioned the attack remains the big unanswered question. An anti-war group whose name references George Orwell’s novel 1984 purportedly claimed responsibility for the planned attack in a letter sent to Dennik N. Skyeton itself pointed towards Russia, saying Moscow had repeatedly tried to destroy its facilities in Ukraine and damage its reputation. The company said the Slovak plot showed Ukrainian defence manufacturers had become “a real thorn in their side”. The Russian connection has not been established by investigators, however. Slovak police have so far made no public attribution. The case is sensitive given mounting concerns over suspected Russian sabotage operations elsewhere in Europe. A Slovak pro-Russian influencer had filmed himself outside the Skyeton plant weeks earlier and called it a “legitimate target of the Russian army”. There is no evidence his video was connected to the alleged plot. Deputy Speaker Tibor Gaspar of the ruling Smer party echoed the influencer’s view in a recent interview.

In other news, PM Robert Fico announced that Slovakia would scrap its controversial transaction tax from January 2027, reversing course on one of his government’s main measures to restore the public finances. Fico said he had instructed Finance Minister Ladislav Kamenicky to prepare the necessary legislation. The announcement came as something of a surprise. Only last year, Fico described the tax as effectively impossible to abolish because the government needed the revenue for its fiscal consolidation. The tax, introduced in April 2025 and inspired by a similar levy in Hungary, quickly became a headache for the government. Businesses complained that it penalised ordinary payments to suppliers and employees, encouraged a return to cash and made Slovakia a less attractive place to do business. Criticism eventually spread to Fico’s own coalition. Andrej Danko’s nationalist SNS party, which originally voted for the tax, later pushed to water it down, while politicians from the other coalition party, Hlas, also began calling for changes. The bigger problem was that the tax did not bring in as much money as Kamenicky had hoped. Initial estimates spoke of around 700 million euros a year. In its first year, the state collected only 340 million euros, and official forecasts suggest this year’s target will also be missed. That leaves one rather important question unanswered: where will the government find the missing hundreds of millions? Fico did not say. Instead, he predicted that abolishing the tax would lead to unusually strong economic growth. Slovakia’s independent fiscal watchdog is more cautious, estimating the benefit at 0.1-0.15 percentage point.

World.title: Every Fifth Woman in Montenegro Has Suffered Domestic Violence: Report
World.content:
Protest march in Podgorica marking International Women’s Day. Photo: BIRN/Samir Kajosevic.

One in five women in Montenegro has experienced some form of intimate partner violence, and more than half of them victims have not sought help, according to an analysis published by the Ministry of Social Welfare, Family Care and Demography.

“One in five women surveyed (19.7 per cent) reported experiencing some form of violence from their partner or spouse, which, given methodological limitations and the tendency of non-reporting, suggests that the real percentage is significantly higher,” the ministry said in the report

“About 58.6 per cent of victims who experienced violence did not seek help from anyone. Of those who sought help, only 35 per cent contacted the relevant institutions,” it added.

Analysts say that victims often remain silent due to fear of retribution from their partner, economic dependence or concern about stigmatisation.

The ministry’s report was based on a survey of attitudes and perceptions of violence against women and girls in the family and intimate relationships. The survey was conducted last August but the report released by the ministry this month.

In other findings likely to cause alarm, 76.8 per cent of respondents agreed with the statement that “a man should be the head of the family”.

Twenty-two per cent of respondents said they believe that sexual intercourse within marriage cannot be rape, while 44 per cent were willing to justify men who “lose control because of women’s behaviour”.

The ministry’s analysis highlights the need for better protection for women from Montenegro’s Roma and Egyptian minorities, women with disabilities, and those living in rural areas.

It also points to the need for specialised services for victims and mandatory training for professionals who come into contact with them.

According to data from the Police Directorate, 968 criminal offenses related to domestic violence were committed in Montenegro last year, the report states.

World.title: German AfD Figure Behind Alleged Serbian Node in Russian Cyber Meddling
World.content:
A Belgrade firm sanctioned last year by the United States for aiding an alleged Russia-based cybercrime service provider was founded in 2022 by Kazakh-born German citizen Andreas Maul, who has since become a city councillor for the far-right Alternative for Germany party, AfD, BIRN can reveal.

Maul, 38, opened Smart Digital Ideas D.O.O. in a dilapidated nineties-era shopping mall in the New Belgrade district of the Serbian capital in October 2022, according to the Serbian Business Register.

The company was registered as an IT retailer, but the US Treasury says its real activities are more sinister.

On November 19 last year, the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control, OFAC, announced it had ‘designated’ Smart Digital Ideas for abetting Russia-based Aeza Group LLC, which was sanctioned four months earlier as a so-called ‘bulletproof hosting service provider’, a term used for companies that sell access to specialised servers and other IT infrastructure specifically designed to evade detection and conceal cybercrime activities.

OFAC said Smart Digital Ideas had been utilised by Aeza “to evade sanctions and set up technical infrastructure that is not publicly associated with the Aeza brand”.

Currently, the company has no registered employees and, according to Serbia’s central bank, has been unable to access its bank deposits since December 2025. The bank did not specify why.

On November 1, a little more than two weeks before his Serbian venture was hit by US sanctions, Maul became a city councillor in the German town of Selm, some 20 kilometres north of Dortmund, on behalf of AfD, the second biggest party in the German parliament.

Maul did not respond to requests for comment.

His connection to Smart Digital Ideas, and by extension to Aeza Group, will only fuel accusations from some German MPs about the AfD’s perceived ‘loyalty’ to Russia and its intentions should the party come to power.

World.title: War Criminal or ‘Serb Hero’: Reactions to Ratko Mladic’s Death Reflect Balkan Divisions
World.content:
In Serbia, this divide was further reinforced by the stance of pro-government media outlets, which glorified Mladic’s wartime role while emphasising efforts by the Serbian authorities to secure his release and bring him to Belgrade when he was seriously ill and about to die. In contrast, some opposition politicians have spoken of his death as the passing of a convicted war criminal.

When he died, 84-year-old Mladic was serving a life sentence for committing genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He has suffered severe health problems for several years and was being treated by medics at the UN Detention Unit.

Serbian pro-government media amplified claims by nationalist politicians that Mladic was “killed” by the UN court in The Hague because he was not brought to Belgrade for medical care, as his lawyers had repeatedly requested.

“From Gavrilo Princip to Ratko Mladic, the best Serbs are killed while bound,” declared Aleksandar Vulin, former Serbian Interior Minister and ex-head of the Security Intelligence Agency.

Vulin argued that “the Serbian state owes convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic a state and military funeral, as well as a day of mourning”, Bosnian news agency SRNA reported.

Vojislav Seselj, leader of the far-right Serbian Radical Party, also convicted of wartime crimes by the UN court, said that Mladic had long been battling a serious illness and the Hague “villains” had not provided him with proper medical treatment for several years.

Serbia’s public broadcaster RTS and pro-government media outlets highlighted how Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic had appealed to the court the previous week to release Mladic and allow him to come to Serbia.

“I do not understand why they would not allow someone to spend their final days outside a prison cell. But am I particularly surprised? No,” Vucic said at the time, as reported by Informer, one of Serbia’s main pro-government tabloids.

Informer’s high-profile editor-in-chief, Dragan Vucicevic, said that “the real news today should not be that Ratko Mladic has died, but that he was killed in The Hague Tribunal”.

“That is a terrorist organisation whose aim is to convict Serbs of genocide, and now it has killed a general,” Vucicevic said.

Milorad Dodik, leader of the Alliance of Independent Social Democrats, SNSD and former president of Bosnia’s Serb-dominated Republika Srpska entity, also described Mladic’s death as murder.

“This really is a killing, because everything pointed to his poor state of health, and this was an organised approach that was intended to lead to a fatal outcome,” Dodik said, according to Republika Srpska’s public broadcaster RTRS.

No mourning from survivors

World.title: New York TImes, Forbes, Conde Nast Discover New Hvar Sirena Resort
World.content:
August 28, 2026 – It has been open less than a month, but the new Hvar Sirena Resort, set an idyllic secluded bay, is already attracting impressive international column inches of praise.

It only opened on August 4, a soft opening in peak season, but it did not take long for a new rising star of Croatian tourism to attract international headlines, with news of the latest renovation by Suncani Hvar Hotels reaching as far away as New York, with the influential New York Times including Hvar Sirena Resort in its article 5 New Hotels for One Last Sun-Drenched Getaway, from Cape Cod to Croatia.

New York, of course, is very much on the minds of Hvar tourism providers, with the inaugural New York to Split direct flight being an unqualified success this year, reducing the travel time from the Big Apple to Hvar Paradise to just 10 hours, including an impressive speedboat transfer to the island. According to various sources I have come across, this direct flight will be more frequent and last longer in 2027, which is great news for American tourists, who are now the undisputed number one visitors to Croatia’s Premier Island.

While there is no such thing as a private bay or private beach in Croatia, Hvar Sirena Resort come pretty close, located in isolation in a forested bay 1.4km north of the town, with hourly shuttle transfer to the vibe of Hvar Town, meaning tht guests can have the best of both worlds – the transquillity of Hvar, the island, and the internationally famous vibe of Hvar Town, something noted by the Times:

“While Hvar has long been a favourite of boldface names and partygoers, Sirena, set in a cover, says the emphasis is on tranquillity, where a guest can unfurl on the beach or by the pool. The hotel offers ‘silent sailing excursions’ to serene beaches, and each evening a bell signals a ’15-minute’ pause on the hotel terrace during which guests are guided through breathing exercises. The hotel also has a spa and yoga deck and offers weekly cultural activities, like a sunset tasting of honeys and sparkling wine with a local beekeeper.”

The honey theme was picked up by Forbes, which explores an intriguing new trend of bee conservation and honey tasting in luxury hotels around the world in Apitourism Is Buzzing—Is Honey Tasting The New Wine Tasting?, with honey tasting experiences in luxury hotels from Hawaii to New York City and Australia, to Rwanda, Tuscany and Hvar Sirena Resort:

Sunset Honey Ritual, Sirena, Hvar, Croatia

“On an island where bees reportedly outnumber residents 9,000 to 1, Sirena—Hvar’s newest boutique hotel—partners with the multigenerational, family-run Mikletovi Apiary, now in its third generation, dating back to a great-grandmother who supported her family through honey alone. At full summer harvest, the apiary’s 130 hives can produce more than 4,400 pounds of honey in a single week, worked under a zero-waste philosophy that uses everything from the honey to the pollen to the propolis. Guests join a sunset tasting of Hvar’s wild rosemary, sage, and lavender honeys as part of Sirena’s weekly Serene Sessions, with the beekeepers themselves on hand to talk through the island’s ecology.”

And no international tourism media comment on Hvar would be complete without Conde Nast Traveler, the influential American publication which regularly features Hvar among its top destinations in Europe (indeed, its famous Conde Nast Traveler Readers Awards is responsible for the oft-quoted statement that Hvar is among the 10 most beautiful islands in the world).

Sirena: First In – Located on one of Croatia’s prettiest swimming coves, this Havar island newcomer is just right for long summer days

Best for: Solo travelers, groups, or a romantic getaway

Solo travelers, groups, or a romantic getaway Location: Mala Garška Bay, just 1.5 miles from Hvar Town

Mala Garška Bay, just 1.5 miles from Hvar Town Can’t-miss feature: The small turquoise-hued cove is one of Croatia’s most beautiful and a quiet alternative to busy Hvar Town.

The small turquoise-hued cove is one of Croatia’s most beautiful and a quiet alternative to busy Hvar Town. In a nutshell: New 154-room boutique hotel in a secluded, turquoise-hued sea cove, just 10-minutes drive from busy Hvar Town on the hotel’s free shuttle, but a world apart. The dreamy setting is an ideal spot to drop anchor for a relaxing swim, snorkel, and linger over a bottle of local wine under umbrella pine trees buzzing with cicadas.

A really impressive start for this, the latest renovation in the Suncani Hvar Hotels portfolio, which has also added several stars to its hotels in the last 10 years. In addition to the Hvar Sirena Resort upgrade, Pharos, Hvar Bayhill Hotel moved from a 2-star to a 4-star hotel in 2016, which Palace Elisabeth upgraded from a 2-star hotel to the first 5-star hotel on a Dalmatian island back in 2019.

I have not stayed there, but I did visit last week, and, although Hvar Sirena Resort had only been open a few days, it was clear that this is a phenomenal addition to the Hvar tourism scene, offering something a little bit different to the other hotels on the island, with the accessibility of the Hvar Town vibe, but a boutique serenity a whole world away, just 10 minutes by shuttle transfer. One of the best uses of Hvar’s many incredible bays that I have seen in a long time, and I predict a bumper season for 2027 – but do sneak in this autumn to be among the first.

You can learn more about the complete Suncani Hvar portfolio on the official website.

World.title: Ratko Mladić Dead: Before Srebrenica there was Škabrnja
World.content:
August the 28th, 2026 – Ratko Mladic, the butcher of Bosnia and one of the worst monsters of the 20th century is finally dead, but before the infamous Srebrenica massacre, there was Croatia’s Škabrnja.

War criminal Ratko Mladić died yesterday without ever answering for the crimes committed in Škabrnja, even though documents and testimonies presented before the Hague Tribunal point to his role in the attack of the 18th of November, 1991. Index reports that Mladić will primarily be remembered as the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska who was finally sentenced to life imprisonment for the genocide in Srebrenica, the terrorising of the population of Sarajevo, persecution, thousands of murders and other repugnant crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He left a trail of blood wherever he went.

Despite it being the most infamous, his wartime path did not actually begin in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Before Sarajevo and Srebrenica he was one of the key commanders of the JNA in operations based in Croatia, especially in northern Dalmatia. His forces attacked Kijevo, the area of Šibenik, Zadar and Sinj, and he also played an important role in the attack on Škabrnja, after which one of the gravest crimes of the Homeland War was committed.

his role in the crimes against humanity committed in croatia

At the time of the attack, Ratko Mladić was not yet formally the commander of the 9th Corps of the JNA based in Knin, as is often stated. He was actually the chief of its staff and deputy commander, while the corps was commanded by General Vladimir Vuković. Mladić was officially appointed corps commander on the 30th December 1991. Nevertheless, already in November he was one of the most influential people in the chain of command and took part in the preparation of operations.

Škabrnja was located in the zone of responsibility of the 180th Motorised Brigade of the JNA from Benkovac, which was part of the 9th Corps. Alongside the JNA, units of the Territorial Defence and police of the so-called SAO Krajina, as well as volunteer and paramilitary groups from Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, operated in the Zadar area. Documents and statements presented before the Hague Tribunal link Mladić to the preparation of the attack. In the war diary from a meeting held the day before the attack it was recorded that the 180th Brigade was to move an armoured battalion towards Škabrnja and Nadin, with the formulation “that it be wiped out”. A witness who was present at the meeting told the court that this task was issued by Ratko Mladić.

The attack began on the 18th of November at around 07:30 and was carried out from two directions. One column of tanks, armoured personnel carriers and infantry came via Zemunik Gornji, and the other from the direction of Biljane. The JNA used tanks, artillery and aircraft, while members of the Territorial Defence and other Serbian units advanced behind the armoured forces.

“if you withdraw, i’ll shoot you”

Marko Miljanić, the then commander of the defence of Škabrnja, testified before the Hague Tribunal about Mladić’s horrendous behaviour during the attack. Miljanić said that over an open radio channel he heard a conversation between Mladić and the commander of the forces attacking the village. According to his testimony, the commander reported that his ammunition supply had exploded and that he could not continue the attack. Mladić replied: “Continue the attack, you’ll get a reserve of ammunition. If you withdraw, I’ll shoot you.”

After breaking through the Croatian defence the attackers entered the village. Murders of civilians, the abuse of prisoners, looting and the systematic destruction of houses followed. Civilians, among them women, children and elderly people, were dragged out of basements and murdered in houses, courtyards and on the streets. Rape and sexual violence was also committed.

the use of human shields

Captured civilians and defenders were driven in front of tanks as human shields. More than a hundred civilians, mostly women and children, were captured and taken to Benkovac. Adult men were separated from the women and children, and some of them ended up in the Knin camps. According to official Croatian data, on the 18th of November, 43 civilians and 15 Croatian defenders were listed as having been killed in Škabrnja. The crimes continued during the occupation, and the place was looted, burned and almost completely destroyed. During the Homeland War a total of 56 Škabrnja civilians died, and 25 defenders from that place were also killed. After the war another six residents were killed by leftover mines.

why was Škabrnja not included in the hague tribunal?

In the case against Milan Martić, the Hague Tribunal established that units of the JNA, Territorial Defence and SAO Krajina police took part in the attack. Martić was sentenced to 35 years in prison for a wider series of crimes in Croatia, among which were the crimes in Škabrnja and Nadin. The infamous Slobodan Milošević was also indicted for the crimes committed in Škabrnja. His indictment stated that forces composed of the JNA, Territorial Defence and Martić’s police went from house to house murdering civilians. Milošević died before the end of the trial, so no verdict was ever formally delivered against him.

The crime in Škabrnja, however, was not covered by the indictment against the monstrous Ratko Mladić. His Hague case was limited to crimes committed across Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1992 to 1995. There was no legal obstacle to trying him for crimes in Croatia as well. The Hague Tribunal had jurisdiction over them, as confirmed by the proceedings against Martić, Milošević and other accused persons. There is no publicly published official explanation of why the Hague prosecution did not include Škabrnja in Mladić’s indictment. When he was finally arrested back in 2011, the court was already implementing a completion strategy, and the case against him was further narrowed.

The number of individual crimes for which the prosecution intended to present evidence was reduced from 196 to 106, and the number of covered Bosnian-Herzegovinian municipalities from 23 to 15. Nor did the Croatian judiciary complete proceedings against Ratko Mladić for his role in the unimaginable horror that took place in Škabrnja.

The District Court in Šibenik had already sentenced him in absentia in 1992 to 20 years in prison for the attack on Kijevo and the areas of Sinj, Vrlika and Šibenik. Proceedings were also initiated against him for Peruča, the shelling of Zadar and other attacks. Documentation from the Croatian cases was forwarded to the Hague prosecution in 2002. However, in the DORH review of proceedings against Mladić published in 2017, Škabrnja is not formally mentioned.

most of those convicted never did their time

The frequently repeated claim that only one person was convicted for the crime in Škabrnja is also incorrect. The County Court in Zadar in 1995 convicted 18 people: sixteen to 20 years in prison each, one person to 15 years, and Jovan Badžoka to ten years. Most were tried in absentia. Badžoka served his ten-year sentence. Zoran Banić, initially convicted in absentia, after arrest in Switzerland and extradition to Croatia was granted the right to a retrial and was finally sentenced to six years in prison. In some retrials the original verdicts were later quashed and the accused acquitted for lack of evidence. Most of those convicted were never available to the Croatian judiciary nor served the sentences imposed, and numerous direct perpetrators and commanders remained unpunished.

the children growing up today are the greatest victory against this genocidal war criminal

After the news of Ratko Mladić’s death there was no celebration in Škabrnja. Danka Dražina, who was a nurse during the attack, told RTL Danas that she did not feel relief. Instead of Mladić, she said, she wants to think about the fallen comrades and innocent civilians. Dražina believes that “Croatian institutions failed”, especially Croatian politics and the judiciary, because Mladić was not prosecuted for Škabrnja. She said that the children growing up happily today in a free place are “the greatest victory” over the man whom the people of Škabrnja consider one of the main creators of the evil that cloaked their area back in 1991.

World.title: Dominik Livaković Completes Move to Barcelona on Four-Year Deal
World.content:
Croatia’s number one goalkeeper Dominik Livaković has put pen to paper on a four-year contract with Spanish champions Barcelona, the Catalan club confirmed on Thursday. Livaković arrives at Barcelona as a Fenerbahçe player, having spent the second half of last season on loan at Dinamo Zagreb. The deal runs through the end of the 2029/30 season, with Fenerbahçe set to receive a fixed fee of two million euros, plus the possibility of a further two million euros in add-ons.

Announcing the signing, Barcelona posted a photo of the Croatian keeper with the message: “Ready when needed.”

What’s still unclear is exactly how Livaković’s first season in Catalonia will play out. According to reporting from Fabrizio Romano, picked up by outlets worldwide, Barcelona had initially planned to sign Livaković as a long-term option without immediately bringing him into the first-team squad, with the idea being that he’d spend the 2026/27 season out on loan, most likely back at Fenerbahçe, before moving to Camp Nou for good in June 2027 to become primary backup to number one Joan García, once Wojciech Szczęsny’s contract expires. However, a well-connected Barcelona radio programme on Cadena SER has since suggested that plan may have changed, with the club reportedly now leaning toward keeping him with the squad immediately.

Asked about his immediate future upon arriving in Catalonia, Livaković kept it brief: “We’ll see.”

Barcelona used the unveiling to look back on his career path, coming through the youth ranks at Zadar and Zagreb, breaking into NK Zagreb’s first team in 2012/13, before moving to Dinamo Zagreb in the summer of 2016. Over seven seasons in Zagreb, he established himself as one of the side’s most important players, making 295 appearances, conceding 249 goals and keeping 137 clean sheets, while winning seven Croatian league titles among other honors. Those performances earned him a move to Fenerbahçe in the summer of 2023.

Livaković has been a regular for Croatia’s national team since 2017, with his biggest moment on the world stage coming at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, where his heroics in the penalty shootouts against Japan and Brazil helped Croatia to a bronze medal. Four years earlier, he was part of the squad that won silver in Russia. He has featured at the last three World Cups — 2018, 2022 and 2026 — as well as the European Championships in 2021 and 2024.

The move to Barcelona represents the biggest club transfer of his career. The only question now is whether he’ll be fighting for minutes between the posts straight away, or whether another loan spell awaits before his chance at Camp Nou arrives.
