World.title: Georgian minister quits politics shortly after ex-PM’s accusations
World.content:
Georgian minister quits politics

Georgia’s Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze is stepping down from his post and leaving politics. He announced the decision at a briefing at the government administration, saying he wanted to devote more time to his family.

Until April 2026, Mamuka Mdinaradze served as head of the State Security Service. On 21 April, he was appointed deputy prime minister and state minister for the coordination of law enforcement agencies. On 29 July, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze announced that Mdinaradze would take up the post of state minister for regional policy. The new position was due to be created in September, and until then Mdinaradze was appointed regional development minister.

Mdinaradze said his 10 years in politics had been marked by hard work, service to his country and cooperation with the team of the ruling Georgian Dream party. At the briefing, he thanked party members and leaders, including its founder and honorary chairman, Bidzina Ivanishvili.

Mdinaradze said he had been considering leaving politics for the past several weeks and had made the decision on his own initiative before discussing it with Irakli Kobakhidze and Bidzina Ivanishvili. He said they initially disagreed with his decision, but he ultimately managed to convince both that it would be better for him.

Mdinaradze explained his decision to leave politics by saying he wanted to spend more time with his family. According to him, his children, aged nine and 13, had grown up with him largely absent.

The former minister stressed that his decision had not been prompted by any political or personal crisis. He also said there was no need for him to remain involved in regional development, as the ruling team had other leaders capable of overseeing the area.

Mdinaradze did not rule out returning to politics one day, but said he would do so only if necessary.

“I will return only if the team really needs me and there is no other option,” he said.

Mamuka Mdinaradze

As for his future plans, Mdinaradze said he might try his hand in the private sector, including business, although he does not yet have any specific plans.

“Believe it or not, I haven’t thought about it. Perhaps I’ll try my hand in business,” Mdinaradze said.

Reflecting on his 10-year political career, Mdinaradze said its intensity and the level of responsibility had not been easy for him, and that he now wanted to focus on the part of his life that he had put on the back burner for years.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s announcement that he was leaving politics came after his name was mentioned in connection with serious allegations made by former Prime Minister Irakli Garibashvili. Garibashvili, who is currently serving a prison sentence, alleged that he had been pressured “on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders”, with Mdinaradze acting as an intermediary, to confess to a corruption offence in order to prevent him from returning to politics in the future.

On 24 August, Garibashvili was charged with a new corruption offence. The charge carries a prison sentence of 11 to 15 years.

According to investigators, key testimony in the case was provided by former Defence Minister Juansher Burchuladze, who has also been convicted of a corruption offence. According to his testimony, of the 1.5m lari (around $555,000)received as a bribe from businessman Zurab Tukvadze, who won a tender for the Gori Military Hospital, Burchuladze personally handed 750,000 lari (around $277,000) in cash to Irakli Garibashvili in several instalments.

Garibashvili denies the allegations. He says the demand that he admit guilt was politically motivated and intended to limit his ability to return to politics in the future. It was in this context that he mentioned Mamuka Mdinaradze as an intermediary and alleged that the demand had been made on Bidzina Ivanishvili’s orders.

Mdinaradze did not address the allegations against him when explaining his decision to step down.

World.title: ‘No to occupation and de facto annexation’: Anti-annexation platform launched in Georgia
World.content:
Anti-annexation platform launched in Georgia

A new public association, the Anti-Annexation Platform, has been established in Georgia.

Its founders say the group will be non-partisan and apolitical, with its main goal being to oppose Russia‘s occupation and de facto annexation of Georgian territories through legal and peaceful means.

At the platform’s launch at the Tbilisi Marriott hotel, a declaration entitled “No to occupation and de facto annexation – yes to justice, peace and Georgia’s territorial integrity” was adopted.

According to the declaration, the platform brings together Georgian citizens who regard the country’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, the principles of international law, freedom and human dignity as core values.

The founders say that Russia’s occupation in any form, the de facto annexation of the Abkhazia and Tskhinvali regions, support for separatism and forced demographic changes in the occupied territories constitute violations of international law and fundamental human rights.

The declaration also states that the organisation is ready to cooperate with members of any political party, regardless of their political affiliation.

Among the platform’s main objectives are supporting Georgia’s territorial integrity and sovereignty and promoting a legal assessment of Russia’s continuing occupation and de facto annexation.

The group plans to work to protect the rights of internally displaced people and refugees from the occupied territories, prepare legal research and analytical papers, and raise public awareness of developments in the occupied regions.

The platform also intends to cooperate with international partners, think tanks and diplomatic missions. Its activities will include organising conferences, discussions and educational events, as well as helping to protect the rights of people affected by the occupation and de facto annexation.

The platform supports targeted international sanctions against the leaders of the de facto regimes in the occupied regions and individuals involved in the annexation process. The declaration also calls for efforts to initiate international criminal proceedings.

The document stresses that the group’s activities will not be limited to the political agenda.

“We believe that the struggle against occupation and de facto annexation by the Russian Federation is not only a political issue. It is a struggle for justice, human dignity, historical truth and the security of future generations,” the declaration says.

According to its founders, the platform is based on the peaceful and legal resolution of conflicts, respect for international law and the protection of human rights.

“Russia’s de facto or de jure annexation will never become a legal reality, and borders changed by force will never acquire moral or legal legitimacy,” the declaration says.

The declaration was signed by the founders of the Anti-Annexation Platform:

World.title: Lachin meeting: How close are Azerbaijan and Armenia to integrating their power grids?
World.content:
Azerbaijan and Armenia’s power grids

On 25 August, representatives of the energy authorities of Azerbaijan and Armenia met in Lachin. The talks focused on mutual electricity imports and exports, as well as possible options for connecting the two countries’ energy infrastructure at the border.

Just a day earlier, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said that power transmission lines could become the first infrastructure project implemented under TRIPP. Two weeks earlier, Ilham Aliyev said that Nakhchivan was preparing to export significant volumes of electricity.

The sequence of events suggests that energy cooperation is already moving beyond political statements. However, the sides have yet to announce any agreements on the project’s route, capacity, financing or implementation timeframe.

From statements to technical discussions

The meeting in Lachin was attended by representatives of Azerbaijan’s Energy Ministry and Azerenerji, as well as Armenia’s Ministry of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure and the country’s Electricity System Operator.

The official statement consists of just two sentences: the sides discussed opportunities for electricity trade and possible options for connecting the two countries’ power grids at the state border.

The significance of this brief announcement lies primarily in who took part in the meeting. The talks involved not only diplomats but also representatives of the bodies responsible for operating the power grids. This suggests that discussions have moved from political statements to assessing technical and commercial possibilities.

The issue is not new. As early as January 2026, Pashinyan said the two countries’ power grids would be connected on an equal and reciprocal basis. Before that, in Copenhagen in October 2025, Pashinyan and Aliyev discussed the possibility of laying power lines and a gas pipeline along the TRIPP route. However, no technical details were announced in the following months.

During the Soviet period, the power grids of Azerbaijan and Armenia were interconnected, while Armenia supplied electricity and gas to Nakhchivan. These links were severed in the 1990s following the outbreak of the Karabakh conflict.

On 24 August, while presenting the government’s programme to the Armenian parliament, Pashinyan said that TRIPP, which is intended to connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through southern Armenia, would not be limited to railways and roads. The project also envisages pipelines, cables and power transmission lines. According to Pashinyan, a power transmission line could become the first operational element of the project because it is technically easier to build.

Export route for Nakhchivan

Baku’s interest is primarily linked to new generating capacity being developed in Nakhchivan. In an interview with AzTV on 11 August, Ilham Aliyev said the autonomous republic’s current generating capacity stood at around 200 megawatts, exceeding its current level of consumption.

The foundation has been laid for a 300-megawatt thermal power plant in Nakhchivan, while two solar power plants with a combined capacity of 50 megawatts are also under construction. In addition, new solar power plants with a combined capacity of several hundred megawatts are planned on an area covering more than 600 hectares.

According to Aliyev, “the export of very large volumes of electricity from Nakhchivan is also envisaged”.

Azerbaijan is already a net exporter of electricity. According to the Energy Ministry, the country exported around 1.15bn kilowatt-hours of electricity in 2025, while imports amounted to 177.2m kilowatt-hours.

A line through Armenia could connect Azerbaijan’s main power grid with Nakhchivan and, in the longer term, expand opportunities for electricity exports to Turkey. However, this is not the only option. An electricity connection between Nakhchivan and Turkey already exists, while a feasibility study for a new, higher-capacity line is expected to be completed in 2026. The route through Armenia is therefore not Baku’s only option, but it could become part of a broader regional energy network.

What could Armenia gain and lose?

At certain times, Armenia’s nuclear, thermal and hydroelectric power plants generate surplus electricity that could be exported. Opening a route towards Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan could expand its export market and turn the country not only into a consumer but also into a transit and export hub. For Armenia, this would provide an additional route alongside its existing energy links with Iran and Georgia.

However, debate in Yerevan has focused less on the potential economic benefits and more on security concerns. Opposition forces argue that linking strategic infrastructure to Azerbaijan’s power grid could create risks of political pressure and dependence.

Economist Suren Parsyan, meanwhile, says these risks could be mitigated through diversification. In his view, Armenia should maintain its energy links with Iran and Georgia while simultaneously developing electricity trade with Azerbaijan.

At the same time, “connecting” the two power grids does not in itself mean that one country would automatically become dependent on the other. A limited-capacity cross-border line, seasonal electricity exchanges or mutual assistance in emergencies are different models from a fully synchronised common grid. It remains unclear which option will ultimately be chosen.

What stands in the way of an agreement?

The sides are now at the most advanced stage of energy cooperation in the past 30 years. However, technical work on the project is still at an early stage.

They still need to determine the route of the line, its voltage and transmission capacity, sources of construction financing, tariffs, a payment mechanism and the division of responsibilities in the event of accidents. Mutual guarantees for the security of the infrastructure and mechanisms for resolving potential disputes will also be required.

The meeting in Lachin therefore does not suggest that the two power grids will be connected soon, but rather that the sides have, for the first time, moved from general statements to a practical examination of possible ways to implement the project. The next significant sign of progress would not be another general statement, but a technical document setting out the route, capacity, sources of financing and implementation timeframe.

An energy link alone cannot normalise relations. However, if it becomes the first genuinely operational infrastructure project to bring mutual benefits, it could help give the peace process a tangible economic dimension.

World.title: Azerbaijan to transit another Russian wheat and barley shipment to Armenia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 28. Azerbaijan will transit another shipment of Russian grain to Armenia, with wheat and barley to be transported through the country by rail.

Six railcars carrying 420 tons of wheat and four railcars carrying 280 tons of barley are scheduled to depart from Bilajari station toward Boyuk Kasik on August 28.

To date, more than 54,000 tons of grain, nearly 9,000 tons of fertilizer, 1,414 tons of propane, 133 tons of aluminum, 1,114 tons of coal and 334 tons of timber have been shipped from Russia to Armenia in transit through Azerbaijan.

In addition, nearly 15,000 tons of diesel fuel and about 5,000 tons of RON-92 and RON-95 gasoline have so far been exported from Azerbaijan to Armenia.

World.title: Uzbekistan, 500 Global move to expand venture capital opportunities
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 28. Uzbekistan and global venture capital firm 500 Global discussed expanding venture investment, strengthening the country’s startup ecosystem and helping Uzbek technology companies enter international markets, as the sides explore deeper cooperation in the sector.

This was reflected in the statement by the Ministry of Digital Technologies of Uzbekistan, following a meeting between Uzbekistan’s Minister of Digital Technologies Sherzod Shermatov and Pedro Santos Vieira, managing partner at 500 Global.

The talks focused on further developing Uzbekistan’s startup ecosystem, increasing venture capital investment, supporting the international expansion of local startups and coordinating ongoing initiatives in the technology sector.

Representatives of 500 Global shared their experience in the Uzbek market, noting that the firm has invested in Uzbek technology companies and startups since 2021-2022. Its investments have included companies founded by Uzbek entrepreneurs as well as startups established by foreign founders operating in Uzbekistan.

500 Global expressed interest in launching programs in Uzbekistan designed to prepare local startups to attract international investment and strengthen their connections with foreign investors.

“500 Global is interested in implementing programs that can help Uzbek startups prepare for international investment markets and expand their access to foreign investors,” the Ministry of Digital Technologies said.

The company also outlined plans to engage at several stages of startup development as part of its long-term strategy for Central Asia.

The sides discussed measures to create more favorable conditions for venture funds, facilitate the movement of investment capital and improve the operating environment for international investment funds in Uzbekistan.

The discussions come as Uzbekistan seeks to expand access to private capital for technology companies and strengthen the country’s position as a regional startup hub.

The meeting concluded with an agreement to continue cooperation on the systematic development of Uzbekistan’s startup ecosystem, improving conditions for venture capital investment and helping local technology companies access international markets.

The partnership could provide Uzbek startups with greater exposure to global investors and international markets while strengthening Uzbekistan’s broader efforts to develop technology-driven businesses and attract private investment.

500 Global is a global venture capital firm that invests in technology startups across sectors, stages and markets. The firm has backed more than 3,000 startups in over 80 countries and provides entrepreneurs with capital, mentorship and access to international investor networks.

World.title: Murder trial jury sees footage of accused stomping on partner's head
World.content:
A 47-year-old man has faced trial in the Northern Territory Supreme Court this week for the alleged murder of his former partner in Katherine two years ago.

Lindsay Kennedy was charged with Colleen Bradshaw's murder in November 2024, four months after her death at the Royal Darwin Hospital from a traumatic brain injury on July 17.

During the hearing this week, jurors were played footage from two CCTV cameras on Railway Terrace in Katherine's town centre, showing Mr Kennedy punching Ms Bradshaw six days earlier on July 11, and stomping on her head after she fell to the ground.

The footage showed Mr Kennedy walking away twice, before returning to kick the 36-year-old in the head and chest, telling her to "get the f*** out of my life".

The scene on Railway Terrace in Katherine where Colleen Bradshaw was seen being assaulted days before her death in July 2024. (ABC News: James Elton)

He was then seen in the footage leaving her lying on the footpath, crying out in pain.

In her closing address this afternoon, Crown prosecutor Deborah Mandie told the jury they could infer Mr Kennedy's murderous intent from his actions captured in the CCTV footage.

"First he runs intentionally, directly toward the deceased, unprovoked, with fist raised," she said.

"The accused punches her in the head and face and then stomps, and then kicks her head twice more.

"This is not an impulsive, isolated action."

In reply, defence barrister David Hallowes SC told the jury they could use "whatever adjectives you want" to describe his client's actions.

But he said the fact of his assault against Ms Bradshaw, causing her death, did not establish his intent to kill her, and therefore his guilt for the crime of murder.

David Hallowes SC told the jury the most appropriate verdict would be a guilty finding to a charge of committing a violent act causing death, but not murder. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

"She's not dying at that time, you'd think if that's what he wanted — her to die — he would keep on going until he achieved that," he said.

" Say whatever you will about the assault, it was not an intention to kill. "

Mr Hallowes told the jury a guilty verdict to the alternate offence of committing a violent act causing death would be most appropriate, while also accepting that negligent manslaughter might be proven.

Deceased put on bus to Darwin

The court heard Ms Bradshaw and her sister had called Triple Zero (000) four times in the days after the assault before she was eventually seen by hospital staff.

The audio from the first Triple Zero call was also played to the jury, with Ms Bradshaw heard telling the operator "I'm injured" and "I need to press charges".

She was visited the next morning by police, but did not go to hospital against the advice of her sister, who called Triple Zero twice more that afternoon.

The court heard it was only after the fourth Triple Zero call on July 12, in which Ms Bradshaw said she felt "heavy in my head" and "it's killing me", that an ambulance was sent to take her to the Katherine District Hospital.

Deborah Mandie told the court Colleen Bradshaw was declared dead on July 17, six days after CCTV cameras captured her being assaulted. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

But given what the court heard were "unremarkable" vital signs, Ms Mandie said the focus was on an unrelated wound to Ms Bradshaw's wrist that had become infected.

She was kept in hospital overnight before being put on a Greyhound bus to Darwin on July 13, where she presented to Royal Darwin Hospital and was again assessed and given antibiotics to treat her infected wound.

The following day, police attempted to take a statement from Ms Bradshaw, but were told she was too sick.

Ms Mandie told jurors it was another day later, early on July 15, after days of complaining of dizziness, blurred vision and vomiting, that Ms Bradshaw was assessed for "urgent cardiology concerns".

By that afternoon she had been given a CT scan and placed in the hospital's intensive care unit.

On July 16, her family was told that she would not survive and she was declared dead the next day.

Jurors are expected to retire to consider their verdict in the Supreme Court on Monday. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

In her testimony earlier this week, forensic pathologist Salona Roopan, who performed Ms Bradshaw's autopsy, told the court she determined her cause of death to be "blunt force head trauma and consequences thereof".

She said a blunt force trauma suffered by Ms Bradshaw approximately seven to fourteen days prior to her death had started a slow bleed inside her skull.

"Because it's a closed space, the pressure rises because there's more blood than there should be," she said.

"And now there's nowhere for that blood to go, so it starts pushing the brain in order to make space for itself to accumulate."

The court heard that by the time she died, the bleeding around Ms Bradshaw's brain had displaced it by almost a centimetre.

Justice Peter Barr is expected to give his instructions to jurors on Monday before they retire to begin their deliberations.

World.title: Season over for Kangaroos AFLW star after spinal fusion surgery
World.content:
Two-time AFLW premiers North Melbourne have lost midfielder Mia King for the season after she required spinal fusion surgery for a neck injury.

The premiership midfielder reported neck pain following North's win over Brisbane Lions last weekend.

King underwent a thorough medical examination in Brisbane, which revealed a disc injury near her spinal cord.

She remains in Queensland recovering after having successful surgery to fuse together the C5 and C6 vertebrae in her neck.

Roos dominate Aussie AFLW squad North Melbourne has the most players of any club selected in Australia's squad for the inaugural AFLW representative match against Ireland.

The Kangaroos confirmed the procedure would sideline King for the rest of the 2026 season.

"We will continue monitoring Mia in her recovery but we don't expect this type of surgery to stop her from returning to play in 2027," club doctor Victoria Norbury said in a statement.

King was part of North Melbourne's premiership-winning team in 2024, but she missed out on last year's grand final win after an ongoing PCL knee injury.

The Kangaroos are again at the top of the ladder after two rounds this season, with the best percentage in the AFLW.

North Melbourne general manager of women's football Erin Lorenzini said the club would support King as she began her recovery.

"We wrap our arms around Mia," Lorenzini said. "We are devastated for her, but also full of admiration for how incredibly strong she has been this week.

"As a proud Jawoyn woman, she was particularly looking forward to wearing our Indigenous Round jumper in Launceston this weekend.

"We have a very close group of players and staff, and all our thoughts will be with her as we run out against the Bulldogs on Saturday."

World.title: Bathla workers stood down as company struggles to stay afloat
World.content:
Staff of major property developer Bathla group have been stood down as the company struggles to stay afloat.

It comes as the NSW government knocked back a request from the company's administrators for financial support.

The Bathla Group fell into voluntary administration earlier this week, unable to pay debts that topped $3.2 billion.

The administrators stood down staff at the property developer's headquarters on Friday as the firm sought an urgent cash injection of $40 million to see it through until the end of September.

A spokesman for the NSW government said administrators made approaches to it for assistance.

"The government does not yet have a complete picture of the company’s financial position," the spokesman said.

" Given the circumstances, we are not willing to put taxpayers' money on the line to guarantee profits for private creditors. "

Court's quest for justice on white-collar crime Corporate regulator ASIC, and its new boss, is keeping a close watch on Australia's "permissive investment regime".

Several private credit firms have lent money to the developer, some of which have now limited investor redemptions.

About 2,000 homes are under construction across the group, and about 13,000 more are in its development pipeline.

Bathla is one of Sydney's most prolific residential developers, particularly across the city's west.

The company blamed a "perfect storm" of conditions for its collapse, including softening home sales, the federal government's property tax changes and high costs.

World.title: Man who sexually abused daughter and granddaughter jailed
World.content:
A Snowy Mountains man has been sentenced to 22 years behind bars after admitting to sexually abusing his daughter and his granddaughter.

Warning: This story includes references to sexual abuse.

The man, who is aged in his 70s and cannot be named for legal reasons, was sentenced on 10 child abuse charges, including four counts of sexual intercourse with a child.

In Queanbeyan District Court on Friday, Judge Thomas Jones said the man's abuse of children in his care was a "pernicious abuse of trust".

"The offender was able to prey upon both his own daughter and granddaughter's trust and vulnerability," Judge Jones told the court.

"Children in a family situation are virtually helpless against a sexual act by a parent."

Judge Thomas Jones sentenced the man, who had pleaded guilty, to 22 years behind bars, with a non-parole period of 15 years.

The court heard the man's wife had uncovered his ongoing offending against his five-year-old granddaughter when she walked in on him abusing the child at their Snowy Mountains home in late 2024.

The court heard that the man then "voluntarily disclosed other instances of sexual offending", regarding the abuse of his five-year-old granddaughter across three months in late 2024.

The man appeared emotionless and often kept his gaze to the ground as he faced his sentence via audio-visual link from custody on Friday.

During the subsequent police investigation, the man's daughter disclosed that he had sexually abused her between the ages of six and 12 in the NSW Southern Highlands, between 2004 and 2009.

"The offender sexually exploited his biological daughter, in circumstances where she was entitled to feel safe in her own home," Judge Jones told the court.

"The offender was prepared to sexually abuse her [his daughter] when the opportunity arose, even in circumstances when her mother was present in the home."

On Friday, the court heard that the man said he had been sexually abused as a young person and had since been diagnosed with a paedophilic disorder by a forensic psychiatrist.

Judge Jones told the court that the man's criminal history included sexual offences against his son decades earlier, and that he had attempted to castrate himself around 15 years ago, which resulted in "very significant damage" and the man spending 10 weeks in hospital.

He will be eligible for parole in December 2039.

World.title: Pies miss post-siren shot at goal to lose wildcard clash to Dogs
World.content:
Tim Membrey has missed a potential game-winner after the siren at the MCG as Collingwood loses the first-ever AFL wildcard game to the Western Bulldogs by just three points.

Membrey took a mark in the final minute and had a shot from 40 metres out, directly in front, to win the game but left the kick out to the right.

Collingwood players rallied around Membrey as the Bulldogs celebrated their victory, which came after a frenetic final term in which the lead changed repeatedly.

Aaron Naughton and Arty Jones were the gamebreakers for the Dogs with four goals each, while Dan McStay kicked four for the Magpies in a losing effort.

Look back on how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: ICAC finds NSW Health director who faked CV 'seriously corrupt'
World.content:
A former senior NSW Health employee will be referred to the Director of Public Prosecutions after he was found to have engaged in serious corruption, including faking his CVs and nepotism.

In a report published on Friday, the Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) found Zoran Ribicic engaged in serious corrupt conduct over many years.

Mr Ribicic was the NSW Health director of engineering and asset management between 2021 and 2024.

ICAC claimed Mr Ribicic improperly awarded hundreds of thousands of taxpayers' dollars to external contractors, including his sister Mirela Derrin's company Risk Control Consulting (RCC), which received more than $275,000 in payments from Illawarra Shoalhaven Local Health District (ISLHD) across a two-year period.

ICAC found he also favoured RCC over competitors and never declared the conflict of interest to ISLHD.

Wollongong Hospital, which is part of the Illawarra Shoalhaven Local Health District. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

An ISLHD officer reported Mr Ribicic to ICAC in July 2024, and he was subsequently suspended with pay before he resigned in September that year.

Corruption exposed

Mr Ribicic was also found to have engaged in "order splitting", according to the ICAC report.

He was authorised to approve quotes up to $30,000, and requested favoured suppliers to break much larger bodies of work into bundles below that amount.

This allowed him to engage his family and associates without the competition and oversight that would ordinarily apply to substantial contracts.

ICAC Commissioner Helen Murrell presided over Zoran Ribicic's matter. (Supplied: ICAC)

Mr Ribicic told ICAC there were six critical maintenance issues that required attention after the COVID-19 pandemic.

These ranged from malfunctioning lifts and automatic doors to "having to shut down operating theatres because of condensation because cooling and, and, and ventilation wasn't good enough".

NSW ICAC Commissioner Helen Murrell said Mr Ribicic's lack of qualifications to resolve these maintenance issues could have threatened the safety of patients.

"He was not qualified to deal with these problems," she said.

" The things that happened may well be because the whole thing was being managed by somebody who wasn't qualified to do so. "

Mr Ribicic also deliberately failed to declare secondary employment with engineering and consulting firm Lanmar between 2023 and 2024, as required by ISLHD's code of conduct.

He received $210,375 for 10 months' work with the private company that he previously brought on as a consultant to ISLHD.

Alleged fraud

ICAC's report states Mr Ribicic will be referred to the DPP to consider potential fraud offences after he made six job applications to government departments.

These applications contained fake qualifications and used false references to land public sector roles between 2012 and 2025.

He falsely stated he had a doctorate in business administration, a master's degree in project management, a bachelor's degree in engineering and a TAFE Engineering diploma.

ISLHD and five other employers all failed to detect his dishonesty and hired him over a decade.

Public agencies to receive training

ICAC Commissioner Helen Murrell said the explosive findings carry several lessons for organisations to reduce risk of corruption in the workplace.

The recommendations in the report include stronger qualification verification processes, improved conflict of interest controls, enhanced procurement oversight, and improve governance arrangements for consultants.

She said ICAC would deliver training to public agencies like NSW Health in the coming months.

"We'll be leveraging off this report to deliver education to numerous agencies across New South Wales," she said

" It's more important to educate these agencies so that this doesn't happen again or at least the risk of it is minimised. "

Commissioner Murrell would not comment on whether there were any pending ICAC investigations into Mr Ribicic's dealings at the other companies where he was previously employed, but said some of his actions may result in criminal charges.

She lauded processes within the ISLHD that led to the corruption being reported to ICAC.

"It's really great when agencies suspect corrupt conduct and they report it to us," the commissioner said.

"What we worry about is when the internal processes of an agency are such that suspected corrupt conduct is not reported to us, but it's a statutory requirement for it to be reported to us, and that is what happened here."

ISLHD has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Elon Musk's rocket heads home to US after Christmas Island sojourn
World.content:
SpaceX's Starship 40 rocket has begun the long journey home after being retrieved from waters off Christmas Island.

Carrying the precious cargo, heavy duty transport vessel Forte departed the island on Friday afternoon, headed for the United States.

A snorkeller unperturbed by the SpaceX rocket nearby. (Supplied: Extra Divers Australia)

The rocket splashed down in the Indian Ocean on July 24, and spent just over three weeks at sea before being towed to Christmas Island, about 1,500 kilometres off Western Australia's northern coast.

The rocket was retrieved after 24 days at sea and towed to Christmas Island. (Supplied: SpaceX )

The Forte arrived in Flying Fish Cove last Sunday night, with the delicate operation to retrieve the rocket getting underway on Tuesday.

The vessel's ballast tank was filled with water to change the buoyancy of the ship, lowering its deck below the surface.

The rocket was positioned over the Forte with the help of locals before the vessel refloated. (Supplied: Paul Hollier)

Local stevedores assisted in the operation to position the rocket over the Forte before the vessel refloated, lifting the SpaceX cargo out of the water for the first time in more than a month.

Locals farewell SpaceX rocket

The Christmas Island community has been captivated by the rocket, which sheltered just off the coast.

A crew involved in the retrieval effort signed the wall of a local pub. (Supplied)

Local school students followed the Starship's movements, and social media feeds were flooded with images of the rocket, with a local dive company offering 'rocket trips'.

Bird enthusiasts turned rocket watchers on Christmas Island. (Supplied: Lisa Preston)

A local bar even named a cocktail Rocket Fuel in honour of the unexpected arrival, with crew members involved in the retrieval leaving a message on its wall.

Local tourism operator Lisa Preston has been hosting 30 birdwatchers for the island's annual Bird Week, who have been excited to witness the retrieval operation.

The arrival of the Space-X rocket has been a novelty for Christmas Island locals. (Supplied)

Ms Preston said it had been an amazing journey, and the Christmas Island community enjoyed being in the global spotlight.

"The decision being made to tow the rocket here when there's thousands of kilometres of coastline south of us, to be able to fulfil that role, to protect it whilst they did what they needed to do … it shows we've got alternate uses for positive things."

Expensive exercise

The journey of about 20,000 kilometres back to the Starbase rocket development facility in Texas is expected to take several weeks.

University of Sydney Professor of Marine Robotics Stefan Williams said the cost of the retrieval operation would add up quickly.

The retrieval of the Space-X craft from the water took many hours. (Supplied: Paul Hollier)

"We operate pretty regularly on research vessels which can cost $50,000 to $100,000 a day to operate, these are even bigger vessels," he said.

"There's a significant cost involved, both in rescue operations and also in the transport of the equipment from where it's been retrieved, in this case back to the home base in the US."

Rough weather hampered efforts to retrieve the rocket after splashdown. (SpaceX)

Professor Williams said semi-submersible vessels like the Forte were quite common, but using such a large ship was a heavy-duty operation.

"They're used extensively in the offshore industry in oil and gas and increasingly in offshore wind, anywhere you need large bits of equipment to be moved around," he said.

Starship 40's legacy

The 52-metre-long rocket is the first SpaceX upper stage spacecraft to survive a space flight intact and could provide a wealth of information for engineers.

SpaceX is hoping to launch, catch, and reuse its rockets going forward. (Supplied: SpaceX)

One of the goals for the space company is developing a rocket that can return safely to its launch site and be used again.

Astronomer Matt Woods says SpaceX's program is helping to make space exploration more affordable.

SpaceX's Starship 40 is heading back to the US after a controlled touchdown in the Indian Ocean on July 24. (Supplied: Svyatoslav Shanygin)

"Just off the back of the first stage of Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy [rockets], it's dropped the price down on rockets dramatically," he said.

"It's amazing what you can do and how cheap it is for companies and universities to put the satellites up there and continue doing their study of the universe."

World.title: Widow of Adelaide man killed in double-fatal truck crash speaks about prolonged court proceedings
World.content:
The widow of a man killed in a horrific crash at the bottom of the South Eastern Freeway says she is relieved court proceedings are finally over but does not believe the stretch of road is safe enough.

Thomas Spiess, 56, was killed in 2014 after an out-of-control sewage truck collided with his vehicle.

The truck reached speeds of 151.9km/h before ploughing into the busy intersection.

Jacqueline Byrne, 41 was also killed in the crash, and then-Cleanaway truck driver Darren Hicks and motorist Louise Compton were injured.

Mr Hicks — who lost a leg in the crash and went on to become a Paralympic gold medallist — was initially charged over the crash, but the charges were dropped in 2018 and he later gave evidence against Cleanaway.

Darren Hicks (left) leaving court today with his lawyer Mark Twiggs. (ABC News: Rebecca Opie)

Speaking exclusively to the ABC, Jan Spiess said she had not even been able to access a death certificate for her late husband while proceedings were afoot.

"The legal system has dragged it out too long, that's been a disappointment," she said.

" Nobody should have to wait 12 years for a death certificate, that's just inexplicable. "

Ms Spiess said despite safety improvements to the intersection, she believed it was still a very dangerous stretch of road.

"When you're sitting at that intersection at a light or you're driving through it and passing through it, look up," she said.

She said she suffered PTSD as a result of the crash and the way she learned of her husband's death.

Emergency services clean up the site of the fatal truck roll-over at the start of the South Eastern Freeway. (ABC)

In findings handed down on Friday, South Australian Coroner David Whittle made no further recommendations in the inquest into the deaths of Mr Spiess and Ms Byrne but acknowledged the trauma Mrs Spiess experienced.

"Mrs Spiess provided a statement in which she described the traumatising effect of watching live-broadcast news footage of the collision site, in which she could see her husband's car and him being placed on a stretcher, and being unable to obtain information from SA Police when she rang to ask as to his welfare," Mr Whittle wrote.

"It was only later that she was formally advised by police that her husband had died."

Ms Spiess recounted going into shock and the long-lasting impact of the media attention garnered by the case.

She said Mr Spiess's death and the lengthy court proceedings had also greatly impacted her two daughters.

Safety changes implemented

After preliminary findings were handed down in 2014, a speed limit of 60 kilometres per hour for trucks travelling on the downhill track of the freeway was implemented and signage indicating that trucks and buses must use low gear was installed.

Rubble at the base of the South East Freeway after the crash in 2014. (ABC News: Spence Denny)

In his findings, Mr Whittle said the preliminary recommendations made by Deputy State Coroner Schapel in 2014 prior to criminal proceedings commencing were "broad and comprehensive" and had all been accepted and implemented by the government.

"Twelve years have passed since there were multiple deaths on this portion of the Freeway in short succession, without continuation of that pattern," the findings read.

"In short, the improvements made to the Freeway have resulted in a much safer situation than that which presented itself at the time of these deaths."

The coroner considered that other improvements under consideration would likely further improve safety if implemented.

"While road fatalities will never be entirely eliminated, it appears that there are no longer readily remediable systemic safety issues with the particular portion of the Freeway under consideration here," the findings concluded.

In May, national waste management company Cleanaway was ordered to pay a $1.1 million fine for workplace failures that led to the double fatal crash.

The penalty was the largest ever imposed under federal work health and safety laws.

Mr Whittle extended his condolences to the families for their "tragic losses" and acknowledged the lasting impact suffered by Ms Spiess.

World.title: The 38 Australians missing in the Nepal-Tibet floods, and what we know about them
World.content:
Warning: This story contains graphic content. The parents of an Australian woman hiking through Nepal and around the region impacted by the tragic flooding have confirmed their daughter is alive. A majority of the at least 38 Australians still missing after the devastating flash flooding in Nepal and Tibet were pilgrims on a journey to one of the most spiritually significant locations in the world. A woman outside the TU Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu looks at posters of people reported missing after the Nepal flood disaster. Kate Geraghty Through both overtly religious travel groups, or traditional groups offering pilgrimage packages, they were seeking to trek to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar as part of the Kailash Manasarovar Yatra, where they cross into Tibet from Nepal.



Families across the country are reeling in the aftermath of the disaster, as the number of Australians reported missing rises and loved ones at home hold out hope for any good news. Foreign Minister Penny Wong said on Friday morning that at least 39 Australians were now reported missing – up from 35 overnight. However, this is now 38 after the parents of Cara Severino, 26, confirmed she had made contact and was alive. Loading Fifteen of the missing Australians were travelling with the Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel Kailash Group, six others were travelling with the Kailash Journeys tour group, and 11 were on a pilgrimage with non-profit spiritual organisation the Isha Foundation. The whereabouts of one traveller with Kathmandu Holiday Tours and Travel, and six other Australian travellers remain unknown. Indian-Australian community leader Vasan Srinivasan said the other 14 missing Australians from the Himalayan Glacier pilgrimage were Sydney-based members of a cultural and religious non-profit he founded called the Australia Bharatha Brahman Samajam.



“We are all very distressed and trying to track them. I’m just praying.” He said those missing worked in various professions, including the financial industry, and many were his close professional friends. Sumi Adhikari, 41 Sydney woman Sumi Adhikari was travelling with the Isha Foundation on a pilgrimage, her husband Nava Pandey has confirmed to this masthead. According to a Facebook post that was shared by her husband, he last heard from Adhikari just before the floods. Sumi Adhikari is one of the Australians missing in Nepal. Facebook



Her last known location was at the immigration office at the China-Nepal Gyirong border, and was also part of the S3 Isha Foundation group. The Facebook post says Adhikari was in the “same area when the flood happened” and is seeking any information about her. She has two children. Adhikari worked at Optus as a network engineer and studied engineering. Sandeep Mohapatra, 43, and Sidharthi Kumari Sahu, 39 A couple from Melbourne’s east have been identified as being among the 39 Australians reported missing after the catastrophic flash flood in Nepal.



Sandeep Mohapatra, 43, and Sidharthi Kumari Sahu, 39, live in Wantirna South and travelled to the Nepal-China border as part of a trek, their friend Manoranjan “Manu” Nayak told this masthead. Sidharthi Kumari Sahu (left) and Sandeep Mohapatra and live Melbourne and are among the Australians reported missing after the Nepal flood disaster. Facebook He said the couple moved to Australia in 2018 from the Indian state of Odisha, where much of their family remains. Nayak met them through the Odia community in Melbourne. “We’re a very close community of people. We just met during the festive season,” Nayak said. “They didn’t have anyone here to help them. They were just migrants who came here.” Mohapatra and Sahu’s last known location was an immigration centre, Nayak added, but they have been uncontactable since.



Gallery Gallery icon 18 images Floods Photo gallery: Flash flooding devastates Nepal and Tibet “It’s an extremely challenging and difficult situation,” he said. Sandeep’s ​cousin, Soumya Mohapatra, told Reuters: “We last spoke to them on August 23 and received a text message the next day. Since then, we have had no information about their whereabouts. “We have lost hope after hearing about the scale of the destruction and the number of deaths.” Sreedharan Iyer Iyer, 52, Lakshmi Sreedharan Iyer, 50, Rishab Iyer Sreedharan Iyer, 23, and Rudhra Sreedharan Iyer, 20



A family from Cherrybrook, in Sydney’s northern suburbs, is among the missing. Both Rishab and his brother Rudhra study medicine at the University of Newcastle. Their parents Sreedharan and Lakshmi co-own a tour business, Oz Trek International. In a Facebook post, Nisha Khadka said family friends Sreedharan, Lakshmi Iyer, Rudhra and Rishab Iyer were missing in Nepal. Brothers Rudhra Iyer and Rishab Iyer are missing. Khadka said the group was last known to be in Kathmandu before the natural disaster and friends were urgently trying to locate them.



“If anyone has seen them, has any information about their whereabouts, or has found them safe, please contact me as soon as possible,” she said. Chandrasekaran Muralitharan, 47, Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, Ashwin Muralitharan, 14, and Aarush Muralitharan, 11 Another pair of brothers, Aarush and Ashwin Muralitharan, and their parents were travelling with Himalayan Glacier and are currently missing. At 11 and 14, the boys are among the youngest Australians affected by the flood. The younger brother Aarush is involved in junior athletics at Cherrybrook. Ashwin and Aarush Muralitharan and their parents were travelling with Himalayan Glacier and are currently missing. Internet



Kumar Sampath, 61 Melbourne father Kumar Sampath, 61, is also among the missing pilgrims. “He’s a hardworking, successful entrepreneur who came to Australia with nothing and provided his family with everything they wanted,” Kumar’s son Mani told this masthead. Kumar Sampath, from Melbourne’s east, is one of dozens of Australians reported missing. “He loved hiking, nature and recently retired and wanted to explore his faith.”



Sampath ran an engineering business specialising in railways before he retired. His son said his family hoped he would be found alive. Narayan Panthi, 46 Brisbane father Narayan Panthi was on a sacred pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar, embracing the mantra of “living in the present”. Posting about his nine-day journey on social media, he wrote: “May this sacred journey to Kailash bring peace to my mind, joy to my soul, and new energy to my life.” Krishna Prasad Dhakal, the operator of Kathmandu Holiday Tour and Travels, said a group of 17 people who had set out on a bus journey to Manasarovar were missing, including foreign nationals, and it hadn’t been possible to establish contact with any of them.



He said Panthi was part of the travelling group. “It has not been possible to contact him or anyone else yet,” Dhakal said. “I just spoke with family members; they are coming to meet me.” Reshma Bhavin Patel, 46 Reshma Bhavin Patel was confirmed missing by her sister and a family friend in Nepal. Reshma Patel is missing. Facebook/Chin Valsan Her sister, Vaishali, said Patel was part of the Isha Sacredwalks Group, and that they had not heard from her since the floods.



Her group was at the Nepalese border and made contact with another group from the Isha, before going dark. Patel is a mother of two, a 14-year-old girl and a 10-year-old boy, who are leaving for India alongside their family. Her sister confirmed she worked for Canterbury-Bankstown Council. The family friend also confirmed that the Newcastle woman was travelling with a group on the Kailash Manasarovar Yatra pilgrimage. Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and Chitra Venkatraman, 46 Sydneysiders Venkatraman Balakrishnan and Chitra Venkatraman are among the missing. Internet



The son of Sydney-based couple, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and his wife Chitra Venkatraman, 46, told the ABC the last contact he had with them was when they were about 15 kilometres from the Tibetan border. “I’d like to see my parents and everyone who went with them back in one piece, and that everyone else there is as safe as possible,” he said. Uday Shivamurthy, 60, and Kripa Shivamurthy, 56 Sydney-based couple Uday and Kripa Shivamurthy were on a three-week pilgrimage to Mount Kailash – a trip they took every few years – their niece Navya Nataraj said. In a post to Instagram, Nataraj said that the couple had just finished their pilgrimage and were “confirmed to be on the China side of the immigration center in Giyrong at 9:05 AM when flash floods hit the area at 9:14 AM”.



“We are holding onto hope — being on that side of the immigration building gives us reason to believe they may have had a chance to get to safety,” she wrote. “Our family is devastated.” “We have been getting conflicting reports. But then today they released aerial images,” Nataraj told CNN. “We are distraught and devastated.” Uday worked at QBE Insurance and NAB, while Kripa has been an accountant for more than 25 years, according to their LinkedIn profiles. Shivaprasad Rakesh Nayaka



Melbourne-based father Shivaprasad Rakesh Nayaka, a 39-year-old engineer, was at the Nepal-Tibet border heading back to Kathmandu after a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash when disaster struck, his family friends Venkat Narayanan and Nagaraji Navalgatti told this masthead. Nayaka is also from Wantirna South like other Melburnians identified as missing, but his friends do not believe he knew the Victorians caught up in Wednesday’s tragedy. Narayanan has known Nayaka since he moved to Australia in 2008 from the southern Indian state of Karnataka and shared family holidays with him. “He’s such a nice person, humble person, and a jovial-type,” Narayanan said. “I’m so sad … I couldn’t digest it.” Nayaka’s wife and two kids are still in Australia, he added.



“Everyone’s so upset,” Narayanan said. “I’m not in a position to know, but we still believe he is living somewhere.” Other missing Australians Nepalese police have provided a full list of missing Australians, which includes names that were previously reported, names of people from different travel groups, and unconfirmed victims. Further information on their whereabouts and wellbeing is still unclear. Rajeswari Sharma, 64

Sruthi Chandrasekaran

Krishna Sharma

Umesh Sharma

Renee Therese Spry, 51

Bhoomi Mahendrakumar Patel, 41

Ganeshbale Daya

Bharat Mangwani, 41

Michael Ryan Keats, 37

Luke Christopher Costanzo, 30

Agastya Gopi Krishna Naidu, 45



The Isha Foundation said 11 Australians were missing after a building they were believed to be in was destroyed by floodwaters. The last known signal from the group, which had completed its pilgrimage, was after members entered an immigration building on the border, said the Isha Foundation’s founder Jagadish Vasudev, who is known as Sadhguru. “They believe the entire group was in the building,” Vasudev said. “The town where they were entering, almost half the town is carved out of the valley. “At 9.05 we received a message from group leader Praveen. He sent a message saying they had arrived at immigration. This event happened at 9.14am.



“His [Praveen’s] Nepal phone did not become active. If he had crossed, his Nepal phone should have become active but he did not come.” On Thursday night, families gathered for prayers and held a minute’s silence for those lost to the floods, lighting candles beside a hand-crafted display of dyed rice reading “pray for Nepal”. Keshav Kadel was among members of Nepalese community who gathered in north-west of Melbourne at the Australian Nepalese Multicultural Centre, where he serves as vice president. “What’s happening in my town is that bodies are now flowing in the river,” he said. “They have slid all the way down and people are pulling bodies from the river.”



The diaspora was “united in grief, hope and prayer”, centre secretary Sudhir Shakya told the event. “Behind every number is a person – a mother, a father, a son, a daughter, a relative, a friend, and someone deeply loved,” he said. Loading Mourners compared the floods to the 2015 earthquake which devastated Nepal’s capital Kathmandu, killing almost 9000 people. While the death count this time is not as great, Kadel warned that consequences would be more dire at the level of individual towns. He has followed the disaster largely through social media, unable to bring himself to call those in the affected region. “I didn’t have the courage to do that,” he said.



Similar events were held across Australia on Thursday, including a vigil in Rockdale, in Sydney’s south. Australians in need of emergency consular assistance should contact the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre on 1300 555 135, or +61 2 6261 3305 (if calling from overseas). With Josefine Ganko, Eryk Bagshaw, AAP Read more on the Nepal flood disaster:

World.title: Missing Australian makes contact after second flood fears disrupt rescue operations
World.content:
Warning: This story contains graphic content. One of the 39 Australian travellers reported missing after flash floods devastated the Nepal-China border has made contact with her relieved parents, as rescue efforts in the area swung back into action when fears of another major flood dissipated. Cara Severino, 26, called her parents on Friday morning to confirm she was alive and well, but was stranded along the Langtang Trek. People gather to look at posters of people missing in the Nepal flood disaster. KATE GERAGHTY Her parents, Debbie and Frank Severino, said their daughter was hiking the trek with a group, and they lost touch with her because of the floods. But she had subsequently made contact, much to their relief.



Cara Severino, hiking in Nepal, has been able to call her parents. Facebook “We praise God that she has been able to make this brief contact with us. Our thoughts and prayers are with all the families awaiting news,” they said. At least 38 Australians are still missing. Among them is Sumi Adhikari, who went missing near the Kerung border crossing between China and Nepal. “Upon speaking with her husband, we learnt that Sumi went missing while returning from the Mount Kailash-Mansarovar pilgrimage,” Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) NSW state co-ordinator Usha Kiran Bariya said.



“She has not yet made contact.” Earlier, residents in Nepal’s mountainous Rasuwa district, on the border with China’s Tibet, were forced to rush up hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river level as a lake formed by debris from Wednesday’s glacier collapse began to overflow, according to witnesses. Rescue operations continue in the areas of Nepal devastated by the flash floods. AP/Getty The prospect of the lake bursting prompted all Chinese rescue personnel to withdraw to a safe area, state broadcaster CCTV reported. Authorities in Nepal stopped helicopter rescue operations for 90 minutes. The disruption was short-lived after Chinese state media said the barrier lake had stopped overflowing, according to the BBC.



CCTV said rescue operations on the Tibet side were now “continuing as normal” after water levels of the barrier lake “dropped slightly”, the BBC reported. The lake’s reservoir has topped 2.5 million cubic metres of water, up from the estimated 1.5 to 2 million cubic metres that an eight-member Chinese engineering team sent to monitor the site recorded a day ago. Loading The formation ​of the lake had been captured in aerial footage by a Chinese rescue team, showing ⁠masses of brown water accumulating in a basin with no visible outlet. Nepalese police said on Friday afternoon: “Information has been received that the water dam on the Tibetan side has burst again. Therefore, all security personnel, rescue workers involved in rescue and relief operations, and the general public, are requested to remain immediately alert and move to safe locations or notify others.”



The temporary halt came as Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed earlier on Friday that at least 39 Australians were believed to be among those missing, up from 35. However, this has changed to 38 after Cara Severino made contact with her family. “The extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery,” Wong said in a joint statement with International Development Minister Anne Aly. Wong told ABC radio it was “an unfortunate possibility” that more Australians could be reported missing in the coming days as the true scale of the disaster became clear. Nepal’s Foreign Ministry said it did not need foreign assistance for search and rescue operations following the devastating avalanche. Offers of help had come from several countries with nationals missing in the disaster.



But the country’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said Nepal would need at least “a few billion dollars” to recover from the devastation caused by the floods, as he called for international funding for a massive reconstruction effort. The Australian government announced it would provide $5 million in humanitarian assistance as Wong prepared to speak to her Nepalese counterpart on Friday afternoon to discuss how Australia could support the recovery effort. Loading Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a post on social media: “Australia is sending crisis and humanitarian response specialists to help after the devastating Nepal-China floods. We’re also providing humanitarian assistance including food, emergency shelter and medical support.” Greens senator David Shoebridge said the $5 million pledged by Australia would “not come close” to meeting the need for recovery and repair efforts.



“I think Australia needs to step up and really commit to helping rebuild. This is a country with minimal spare resources,” he said. Gallery Gallery icon 18 images Floods Photo gallery: Flash flooding devastates Nepal and Tibet Fast-moving waters swept through villages, wiping out bridges, roads and entire settlements in a Nepalese valley near the border with China on Wednesday, killing at least 547 people in Nepal and five in China’s Tibet, although that number could rise dramatically. More than 1500 people are missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals from two dozen countries, including India, the United States, Britain and Canada. There was more good news on Friday, when 883 locals and labourers were rescued in the Rasuwa district in an effort that included an “extremely dangerous and challenging” rescue mission that freed 350 people trapped in the tunnel of a hydropower plant.



“The troops are still gathering to safely evacuate more than 100 people trapped in the same tunnel,” the Nepalese Prime Minister’s Office said. Footage released by the office showed a team of Nepalese soldiers crawling through thick mud up a steep passageway to enter the tunnel and save those trapped inside. United Nations under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs Tom Fletcher said aid teams were experiencing major difficulties trying to reach the areas most affected by the floods due to the extent of damage to roads and bridges in the area. “It’s a very, very challenging terrain for them to be navigating right now,” Fletcher told CNN. “We’re having to use air assets to reach them. The immediate priority is saving as many lives as we can.”



Footage released by the BBC showed a giant boulder being swept along by the flood, underlining the force of the torrent. Fear of further flooding Nepal and China had both warned of the risks of further flooding in the Himalayas as debris from the initial glacier collapse formed a lake straddling their border. “Residents of the lower banks … passengers, rescuers engaged in rescue operations, and all concerned are requested to exercise special caution and stay in safe places away from the river banks and risky areas,” Nepal’s disaster authority said.



One of the engineers, Chen Hanxiao, said the general approach to reducing the lake’s threat was to excavate a drainage channel at a lower point of the dam, but the width and depth of that channel needed calculations based on how fast the water would flow and how quickly the lake would fill. Related Article Updated

Floods The 38 Australians missing in the Nepal-Tibet floods, and what we know about them China on Thursday said 3 million cubic meters of water, the equivalent of about 1200 Olympic swimming pools, was expected to flow into the lake over the next three days. Peak flow was expected around September 1. Chinese President Xi Jinping dispatched his second-in-command, Premier Li Qiang, to visit the devastated areas of Tibet, demonstrating the severity of the disaster, which may be the worst since an earthquake in 2015 killed about 9000 people. Li inspected emergency rescue and relief operations, and visited first responders and displaced people in temporary shelters, according to the official Xinhua News Agency.



Assessments based on seismic and satellite data indicate the initial flood was triggered by the collapse of a glacier and underlying bedrock in the Himalayan region between Nepal and Tibet on Wednesday, causing a 5.2-magnitude seismic event that sent water, ice, rock and debris downstream. Images and videos circulated online show the extent of the water’s force. Walls of grey water swept through villages and valleys, pulling down trees, pushing boulders and sweeping over masses of people attempting to flee. The aftermath from a tidal wave of mud, rock and water that devastated towns and villages along the Lhende River. AFP The flood is a major test for Nepal’s fledgling government and its new leader, former rapper Balendra Shah, who rode to power on a wave of Gen Z enthusiasm. He will need to work closely with regional neighbours China and India. China has deployed at least 574 rescuers to the land crossing, and India says it is co-ordinating closely with Kathmandu on rescue and relief efforts. The country’s tourism industry, which supports over 1 million jobs, will take a hit in a peak period, and it will be anxious about the future given Nepal’s frequency of extreme weather events.



Which regions were hit? The Bhote Koshi River flooded about 9am on Wednesday (1pm AEST), destroying several villages as well as roads and hydropower projects, officials said. Warnings were issued in several districts urging people to stay away from the banks of the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers. Loading The flood triggered a mudslide that hit Gyirong Port, a major land crossing with neighbouring Tibet, cutting roads, communications and power links to the area.
