World.title: Manly thump Dragons, but fumble denies fans moment they were waiting for
World.content:
Manly 44 Dragons 10 SportNRLNRL 2026 Manly thump Dragons, but fumble denies fans moment they were waiting for Christian Nicolussi August 28, 2026 — 8:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

4 Pines Park: The one thing Manly fans were looking forward did not happen on Friday evening. The Sea Eagles thumped a woeful St George Illawarra 44-10 to keep their slim finals hopes alive. Loading Manly simply need to beat the New Zealand Warriors next weekend and rely on South Sydney or the Cowboys losing both of their final two games to qualify. The Sea Eagles have the firepower and confidence to cause some headaches should they make it to September.



Who would want to stop Haumole Olakau’atu in full flight? Tom Trbojevic is two games back from a hamstring injury and also bound to strip fitter. And what about Clayton Faulolo, who bagged a try, set up another three and is proving arguably the best utility on the northern beaches? But the 13,957 supporters inside 4 Pines Park one last time this season, including members of the club’s 1996 premiership team, rose to their feet for the kick-off in the 74th minute when Nathan Brown was ready to launch himself off the back fence. Brown was playing his 200th NRL game and his last at home before finishing his career in the Super League next year. What Brown lacks in size he makes up for in heart, and quickly earned the reputation for his kick-off carries, not to mention the nickname “Back-fence Brown”.



The TV cameras captured Brown’s eyes light up when the Dragons kicked to his side of the field. The Italian international started to steam on to the ball, got excited, then realised the pass from Jamal Fogarty was never coming because he had dropped the ball. Brown let out a giant sigh, as did the supporters. Departing Manly forward Nathan Brown celebrated his 200th NRL game with a big win. NRL Photos “I felt for him because I saw him wind up about three or four times, he wanted to have one of those carries,” coach Kieran Foran said. “He’s been such a warrior, to get to 200 games and the way he’s had to do it – he’s stayed in the fight a long time – it was great to see him go out a winner [at home] tonight.” It was a shame, but it was never going to change the result.



As is the case every year, Manly are the one club teams above them probably do not want to meet in the finals. If they fall short, they will rue a few tight losses, including golden-point defeats to Canterbury and the Cowboys. It is still a success, considering they dropped their opening three games, sacked coach Anthony Seibold, then eventually appointed one of their favourite sons, Foran, to succeed him. Things will become a lot clearer about the September hopes in the next few days. The future looks bright, regardless, when you think of a player like Faulolo, as well as Onitoni Large, who made his debut with 20 minutes remaining, and was given a warm embrace by Trbojevic as he took the field.



Large is just 19, was in the Wests Tigers system before signing a three-year deal with Manly, and was just as handy at rugby. Foran is confident he has a big future: “The thing I love about Onitoni [during] the last six weeks is the growth we’ve seen in his game; we felt like he was so ready if he was called upon. He’s going to be a special player. He’s young, raw, but he works hard on his game.” Josh Feledy keeps the points coming for the Sea Eagles on Friday night. Getty Images The Sea Eagles were given a standing ovation when they led 26-0 at the break against a Dragons side that completed only 10 of their 15 sets. Things did not improve for the men wearing red and white in the second half. The Dragons will finish with the wooden spoon. At least they have recruited well and have plenty to get excited about in 2027. Still, they will want to finish on a high next week on home soil, and send out the likes of the departing Damien Cook on a high.



Daniel Atkinson had a rough night at fullback, spilling a couple, and then being trampled over by Olakau’atu when he scored a brilliant solo try. Olakau’atu is a scary sight in full flight. So is Brown.

World.title: The 38 Australians missing in the Nepal-Tibet floods, and what we know about them
World.content:
Warning: This story contains graphic content. The parents of an Australian woman hiking through Nepal and around the region impacted by the tragic flooding have confirmed their daughter is alive. A majority of the at least 38 Australians still missing after the devastating flash flooding in Nepal and Tibet were pilgrims on a journey to one of the most spiritually significant locations in the world. A woman outside the TU Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu looks at posters of people reported missing after the Nepal flood disaster. Kate Geraghty Through both overtly religious travel groups, or traditional groups offering pilgrimage packages, they were seeking to trek to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar as part of the Kailash Manasarovar Yatra, where they cross into Tibet from Nepal.



Families across the country are reeling in the aftermath of the disaster, as the number of Australians reported missing rises and loved ones at home hold out hope for any good news. Foreign Minister Penny Wong said on Friday morning that at least 39 Australians were now reported missing – up from 35 overnight. However, this is now 38 after the parents of Cara Severino, 26, confirmed she had made contact and was alive. Loading Fifteen of the missing Australians were travelling with the Himalayan Glacier Adventure and Travel Kailash Group, six others were travelling with the Kailash Journeys tour group, and 11 were on a pilgrimage with non-profit spiritual organisation the Isha Foundation. The whereabouts of one traveller with Kathmandu Holiday Tours and Travel, and six other Australian travellers remain unknown. Indian-Australian community leader Vasan Srinivasan said the other 14 missing Australians from the Himalayan Glacier pilgrimage were Sydney-based members of a cultural and religious non-profit he founded called the Australia Bharatha Brahman Samajam.



“We are all very distressed and trying to track them. I’m just praying.” He said those missing worked in various professions, including the financial industry, and many were his close professional friends. Sumi Adhikari, 41 Sydney woman Sumi Adhikari was travelling with the Isha Foundation on a pilgrimage, her husband Nava Pandey has confirmed to this masthead. According to a Facebook post that was shared by her husband, he last heard from Adhikari just before the floods. Sumi Adhikari is one of the Australians missing in Nepal. Facebook



Her last known location was at the immigration office at the China-Nepal Gyirong border, and was also part of the S3 Isha Foundation group. The Facebook post says Adhikari was in the “same area when the flood happened” and is seeking any information about her. She has two children. Adhikari worked at Optus as a network engineer and studied engineering. Sandeep Mohapatra, 43, and Sidharthi Kumari Sahu, 39 A couple from Melbourne’s east have been identified as being among the 39 Australians reported missing after the catastrophic flash flood in Nepal.



Sandeep Mohapatra, 43, and Sidharthi Kumari Sahu, 39, live in Wantirna South and travelled to the Nepal-China border as part of a trek, their friend Manoranjan “Manu” Nayak told this masthead. Sidharthi Kumari Sahu (left) and Sandeep Mohapatra and live Melbourne and are among the Australians reported missing after the Nepal flood disaster. Facebook He said the couple moved to Australia in 2018 from the Indian state of Odisha, where much of their family remains. Nayak met them through the Odia community in Melbourne. “We’re a very close community of people. We just met during the festive season,” Nayak said. “They didn’t have anyone here to help them. They were just migrants who came here.” Mohapatra and Sahu’s last known location was an immigration centre, Nayak added, but they have been uncontactable since.



Gallery Gallery icon 18 images Floods Photo gallery: Flash flooding devastates Nepal and Tibet “It’s an extremely challenging and difficult situation,” he said. Sandeep’s ​cousin, Soumya Mohapatra, told Reuters: “We last spoke to them on August 23 and received a text message the next day. Since then, we have had no information about their whereabouts. “We have lost hope after hearing about the scale of the destruction and the number of deaths.” Sreedharan Iyer Iyer, 52, Lakshmi Sreedharan Iyer, 50, Rishab Iyer Sreedharan Iyer, 23, and Rudhra Sreedharan Iyer, 20



A family from Cherrybrook, in Sydney’s northern suburbs, is among the missing. Both Rishab and his brother Rudhra study medicine at the University of Newcastle. Their parents Sreedharan and Lakshmi co-own a tour business, Oz Trek International. In a Facebook post, Nisha Khadka said family friends Sreedharan, Lakshmi Iyer, Rudhra and Rishab Iyer were missing in Nepal. Brothers Rudhra Iyer and Rishab Iyer are missing. Khadka said the group was last known to be in Kathmandu before the natural disaster and friends were urgently trying to locate them.



“If anyone has seen them, has any information about their whereabouts, or has found them safe, please contact me as soon as possible,” she said. Chandrasekaran Muralitharan, 47, Shylaja Muralitharan, 42, Ashwin Muralitharan, 14, and Aarush Muralitharan, 11 Another pair of brothers, Aarush and Ashwin Muralitharan, and their parents were travelling with Himalayan Glacier and are currently missing. At 11 and 14, the boys are among the youngest Australians affected by the flood. The younger brother Aarush is involved in junior athletics at Cherrybrook. Ashwin and Aarush Muralitharan and their parents were travelling with Himalayan Glacier and are currently missing. Internet



Kumar Sampath, 61 Melbourne father Kumar Sampath, 61, is also among the missing pilgrims. “He’s a hardworking, successful entrepreneur who came to Australia with nothing and provided his family with everything they wanted,” Kumar’s son Mani told this masthead. Kumar Sampath, from Melbourne’s east, is one of dozens of Australians reported missing. “He loved hiking, nature and recently retired and wanted to explore his faith.”



Sampath ran an engineering business specialising in railways before he retired. His son said his family hoped he would be found alive. Narayan Panthi, 46 Brisbane father Narayan Panthi was on a sacred pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar, embracing the mantra of “living in the present”. Posting about his nine-day journey on social media, he wrote: “May this sacred journey to Kailash bring peace to my mind, joy to my soul, and new energy to my life.” Krishna Prasad Dhakal, the operator of Kathmandu Holiday Tour and Travels, said a group of 17 people who had set out on a bus journey to Manasarovar were missing, including foreign nationals, and it hadn’t been possible to establish contact with any of them.



He said Panthi was part of the travelling group. “It has not been possible to contact him or anyone else yet,” Dhakal said. “I just spoke with family members; they are coming to meet me.” Reshma Bhavin Patel, 46 Reshma Bhavin Patel was confirmed missing by her sister and a family friend in Nepal. Reshma Patel is missing. Facebook/Chin Valsan Her sister, Vaishali, said Patel was part of the Isha Sacredwalks Group, and that they had not heard from her since the floods.



Her group was at the Nepalese border and made contact with another group from the Isha, before going dark. Patel is a mother of two, a 14-year-old girl and a 10-year-old boy, who are leaving for India alongside their family. Her sister confirmed she worked for Canterbury-Bankstown Council. The family friend also confirmed that the Newcastle woman was travelling with a group on the Kailash Manasarovar Yatra pilgrimage. Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and Chitra Venkatraman, 46 Sydneysiders Venkatraman Balakrishnan and Chitra Venkatraman are among the missing. Internet



The son of Sydney-based couple, Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and his wife Chitra Venkatraman, 46, told the ABC the last contact he had with them was when they were about 15 kilometres from the Tibetan border. “I’d like to see my parents and everyone who went with them back in one piece, and that everyone else there is as safe as possible,” he said. Uday Shivamurthy, 60, and Kripa Shivamurthy, 56 Sydney-based couple Uday and Kripa Shivamurthy were on a three-week pilgrimage to Mount Kailash – a trip they took every few years – their niece Navya Nataraj said. In a post to Instagram, Nataraj said that the couple had just finished their pilgrimage and were “confirmed to be on the China side of the immigration center in Giyrong at 9:05 AM when flash floods hit the area at 9:14 AM”.



“We are holding onto hope — being on that side of the immigration building gives us reason to believe they may have had a chance to get to safety,” she wrote. “Our family is devastated.” “We have been getting conflicting reports. But then today they released aerial images,” Nataraj told CNN. “We are distraught and devastated.” Uday worked at QBE Insurance and NAB, while Kripa has been an accountant for more than 25 years, according to their LinkedIn profiles. Shivaprasad Rakesh Nayaka



Melbourne-based father Shivaprasad Rakesh Nayaka, a 39-year-old engineer, was at the Nepal-Tibet border heading back to Kathmandu after a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash when disaster struck, his family friends Venkat Narayanan and Nagaraji Navalgatti told this masthead. Nayaka is also from Wantirna South like other Melburnians identified as missing, but his friends do not believe he knew the Victorians caught up in Wednesday’s tragedy. Narayanan has known Nayaka since he moved to Australia in 2008 from the southern Indian state of Karnataka and shared family holidays with him. “He’s such a nice person, humble person, and a jovial-type,” Narayanan said. “I’m so sad … I couldn’t digest it.” Nayaka’s wife and two kids are still in Australia, he added.



“Everyone’s so upset,” Narayanan said. “I’m not in a position to know, but we still believe he is living somewhere.” Other missing Australians Nepalese police have provided a full list of missing Australians, which includes names that were previously reported, names of people from different travel groups, and unconfirmed victims. Further information on their whereabouts and wellbeing is still unclear. Rajeswari Sharma, 64

Sruthi Chandrasekaran

Krishna Sharma

Umesh Sharma

Renee Therese Spry, 51

Bhoomi Mahendrakumar Patel, 41

Ganeshbale Daya

Bharat Mangwani, 41

Michael Ryan Keats, 37

Luke Christopher Costanzo, 30

Agastya Gopi Krishna Naidu, 45



The Isha Foundation said 11 Australians were missing after a building they were believed to be in was destroyed by floodwaters. The last known signal from the group, which had completed its pilgrimage, was after members entered an immigration building on the border, said the Isha Foundation’s founder Jagadish Vasudev, who is known as Sadhguru. “They believe the entire group was in the building,” Vasudev said. “The town where they were entering, almost half the town is carved out of the valley. “At 9.05 we received a message from group leader Praveen. He sent a message saying they had arrived at immigration. This event happened at 9.14am.



“His [Praveen’s] Nepal phone did not become active. If he had crossed, his Nepal phone should have become active but he did not come.” On Thursday night, families gathered for prayers and held a minute’s silence for those lost to the floods, lighting candles beside a hand-crafted display of dyed rice reading “pray for Nepal”. Keshav Kadel was among members of Nepalese community who gathered in north-west of Melbourne at the Australian Nepalese Multicultural Centre, where he serves as vice president. “What’s happening in my town is that bodies are now flowing in the river,” he said. “They have slid all the way down and people are pulling bodies from the river.”



The diaspora was “united in grief, hope and prayer”, centre secretary Sudhir Shakya told the event. “Behind every number is a person – a mother, a father, a son, a daughter, a relative, a friend, and someone deeply loved,” he said. Loading Mourners compared the floods to the 2015 earthquake which devastated Nepal’s capital Kathmandu, killing almost 9000 people. While the death count this time is not as great, Kadel warned that consequences would be more dire at the level of individual towns. He has followed the disaster largely through social media, unable to bring himself to call those in the affected region. “I didn’t have the courage to do that,” he said.



Similar events were held across Australia on Thursday, including a vigil in Rockdale, in Sydney’s south. Australians in need of emergency consular assistance should contact the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre on 1300 555 135, or +61 2 6261 3305 (if calling from overseas). World.title: Missing Australian makes contact after second flood fears disrupt rescue operations
World.content:
Warning: This story contains graphic content. One of the 39 Australian travellers reported missing after flash floods devastated the Nepal-China border has made contact with her relieved parents, as rescue efforts in the area swung back into action when fears of another major flood dissipated. Cara Severino, 26, called her parents on Friday morning to confirm she was alive and well, but was stranded along the Langtang Trek. People gather to look at posters of people missing in the Nepal flood disaster. KATE GERAGHTY Her parents, Debbie and Frank Severino, said their daughter was hiking the trek with a group, and they lost touch with her because of the floods. But she had subsequently made contact, much to their relief.



Cara Severino, hiking in Nepal, has been able to call her parents. Facebook “We praise God that she has been able to make this brief contact with us. Our thoughts and prayers are with all the families awaiting news,” they said. At least 38 Australians are still missing. Among them is Sumi Adhikari, who went missing near the Kerung border crossing between China and Nepal. “Upon speaking with her husband, we learnt that Sumi went missing while returning from the Mount Kailash-Mansarovar pilgrimage,” Non-Resident Nepali Association (NRNA) NSW state co-ordinator Usha Kiran Bariya said.



“She has not yet made contact.” Earlier, residents in Nepal’s mountainous Rasuwa district, on the border with China’s Tibet, were forced to rush up hillsides to escape a possible surge in the river level as a lake formed by debris from Wednesday’s glacier collapse began to overflow, according to witnesses. Rescue operations continue in the areas of Nepal devastated by the flash floods. AP/Getty The prospect of the lake bursting prompted all Chinese rescue personnel to withdraw to a safe area, state broadcaster CCTV reported. Authorities in Nepal stopped helicopter rescue operations for 90 minutes. The disruption was short-lived after Chinese state media said the barrier lake had stopped overflowing, according to the BBC.



CCTV said rescue operations on the Tibet side were now “continuing as normal” after water levels of the barrier lake “dropped slightly”, the BBC reported. The lake’s reservoir has topped 2.5 million cubic metres of water, up from the estimated 1.5 to 2 million cubic metres that an eight-member Chinese engineering team sent to monitor the site recorded a day ago. Loading The formation ​of the lake had been captured in aerial footage by a Chinese rescue team, showing ⁠masses of brown water accumulating in a basin with no visible outlet. Nepalese police said on Friday afternoon: “Information has been received that the water dam on the Tibetan side has burst again. Therefore, all security personnel, rescue workers involved in rescue and relief operations, and the general public, are requested to remain immediately alert and move to safe locations or notify others.”



The temporary halt came as Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed earlier on Friday that at least 39 Australians were believed to be among those missing, up from 35. However, this has changed to 38 after Cara Severino made contact with her family. “The extraordinary scale of this disaster and the remoteness of the affected region mean immense challenges lie ahead for the response and recovery,” Wong said in a joint statement with International Development Minister Anne Aly. Wong told ABC radio it was “an unfortunate possibility” that more Australians could be reported missing in the coming days as the true scale of the disaster became clear. Nepal’s Foreign Ministry said it did not need foreign assistance for search and rescue operations following the devastating avalanche. Offers of help had come from several countries with nationals missing in the disaster.



But the country’s Finance Minister Swarnim Wagle said Nepal would need at least “a few billion dollars” to recover from the devastation caused by the floods, as he called for international funding for a massive reconstruction effort. The Australian government announced it would provide $5 million in humanitarian assistance as Wong prepared to speak to her Nepalese counterpart on Friday afternoon to discuss how Australia could support the recovery effort. Loading Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a post on social media: “Australia is sending crisis and humanitarian response specialists to help after the devastating Nepal-China floods. We’re also providing humanitarian assistance including food, emergency shelter and medical support.” Greens senator David Shoebridge said the $5 million pledged by Australia would “not come close” to meeting the need for recovery and repair efforts.



“I think Australia needs to step up and really commit to helping rebuild. This is a country with minimal spare resources,” he said. Gallery Gallery icon 18 images Floods Photo gallery: Flash flooding devastates Nepal and Tibet Fast-moving waters swept through villages, wiping out bridges, roads and entire settlements in a Nepalese valley near the border with China on Wednesday, killing at least 547 people in Nepal and five in China’s Tibet, although that number could rise dramatically. More than 1500 people are missing, including hundreds of foreign nationals from two dozen countries, including India, the United States, Britain and Canada. There was more good news on Friday, when 883 locals and labourers were rescued in the Rasuwa district in an effort that included an “extremely dangerous and challenging” rescue mission that freed 350 people trapped in the tunnel of a hydropower plant.



“The troops are still gathering to safely evacuate more than 100 people trapped in the same tunnel,” the Nepalese Prime Minister’s Office said. Footage released by the office showed a team of Nepalese soldiers crawling through thick mud up a steep passageway to enter the tunnel and save those trapped inside. United Nations under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs Tom Fletcher said aid teams were experiencing major difficulties trying to reach the areas most affected by the floods due to the extent of damage to roads and bridges in the area. “It’s a very, very challenging terrain for them to be navigating right now,” Fletcher told CNN. “We’re having to use air assets to reach them. The immediate priority is saving as many lives as we can.”



Footage released by the BBC showed a giant boulder being swept along by the flood, underlining the force of the torrent. Fear of further flooding Nepal and China had both warned of the risks of further flooding in the Himalayas as debris from the initial glacier collapse formed a lake straddling their border. “Residents of the lower banks … passengers, rescuers engaged in rescue operations, and all concerned are requested to exercise special caution and stay in safe places away from the river banks and risky areas,” Nepal’s disaster authority said.



One of the engineers, Chen Hanxiao, said the general approach to reducing the lake’s threat was to excavate a drainage channel at a lower point of the dam, but the width and depth of that channel needed calculations based on how fast the water would flow and how quickly the lake would fill. Chinese President Xi Jinping dispatched his second-in-command, Premier Li Qiang, to visit the devastated areas of Tibet, demonstrating the severity of the disaster, which may be the worst since an earthquake in 2015 killed about 9000 people. Li inspected emergency rescue and relief operations, and visited first responders and displaced people in temporary shelters, according to the official Xinhua News Agency.

Images and videos circulated online show the extent of the water’s force. Walls of grey water swept through villages and valleys, pulling down trees, pushing boulders and sweeping over masses of people attempting to flee. The aftermath from a tidal wave of mud, rock and water that devastated towns and villages along the Lhende River. AFP The flood is a major test for Nepal’s fledgling government and its new leader, former rapper Balendra Shah, who rode to power on a wave of Gen Z enthusiasm. He will need to work closely with regional neighbours China and India. China has deployed at least 574 rescuers to the land crossing, and India says it is co-ordinating closely with Kathmandu on rescue and relief efforts. The Sea Eagles have the firepower and confidence to cause some headaches should they make it to September.



Who would want to stop Haumole Olakau’atu in full flight? Tom Trbojevic is two games back from a hamstring injury and also bound to strip fitter. And what about Clayton Faulolo, who bagged a try, set up another three and is proving arguably the best utility on the northern beaches? But the 13,957 supporters inside 4 Pines Park one last time this season, including members of the club’s 1996 premiership team, rose to their feet for the kick-off in the 74th minute when Nathan Brown was ready to launch himself off the back fence. Brown was playing his 200th NRL game and his last at home before finishing his career in the Super League next year. What Brown lacks in size he makes up for in heart, and quickly earned the reputation for his kick-off carries, not to mention the nickname “Back-fence Brown”.



The TV cameras captured Brown’s eyes light up when the Dragons kicked to his side of the field. The Italian international started to steam on to the ball, got excited, then realised the pass from Jamal Fogarty was never coming because he had dropped the ball. Brown let out a giant sigh, as did the supporters. Departing Manly forward Nathan Brown celebrated his 200th NRL game with a big win. NRL Photos “I felt for him because I saw him wind up about three or four times, he wanted to have one of those carries,” coach Kieran Foran said. “He’s been such a warrior, to get to 200 games and the way he’s had to do it – he’s stayed in the fight a long time – it was great to see him go out a winner [at home] tonight.” It was a shame, but it was never going to change the result.



As is the case every year, Manly are the one club teams above them probably do not want to meet in the finals. If they fall short, they will rue a few tight losses, including golden-point defeats to Canterbury and the Cowboys. It is still a success, considering they dropped their opening three games, sacked coach Anthony Seibold, then eventually appointed one of their favourite sons, Foran, to succeed him. Things will become a lot clearer about the September hopes in the next few days. The future looks bright, regardless, when you think of a player like Faulolo, as well as Onitoni Large, who made his debut with 20 minutes remaining, and was given a warm embrace by Trbojevic as he took the field.



Large is just 19, was in the Wests Tigers system before signing a three-year deal with Manly, and was just as handy at rugby. Foran is confident he has a big future: “The thing I love about Onitoni [during] the last six weeks is the growth we’ve seen in his game; we felt like he was so ready if he was called upon. He’s going to be a special player. He’s young, raw, but he works hard on his game.” Josh Feledy keeps the points coming for the Sea Eagles on Friday night. Getty Images The Sea Eagles were given a standing ovation when they led 26-0 at the break against a Dragons side that completed only 10 of their 15 sets. Things did not improve for the men wearing red and white in the second half. The Dragons will finish with the wooden spoon. At least they have recruited well and have plenty to get excited about in 2027. Still, they will want to finish on a high next week on home soil, and send out the likes of the departing Damien Cook on a high.



Daniel Atkinson had a rough night at fullback, spilling a couple, and then being trampled over by Olakau’atu when he scored a brilliant solo try. Olakau’atu is a scary sight in full flight. So is Brown.

World.title: PNG parliament decision on Bougainville still months off at least
World.content:
After an historic day in which the result of Bougainville's independence referendum was finally tabled in Papua New Guinea's national parliament, an eventual decision on the matter is at least months away.

The parliament adjourned after debate on Thursday on the tabling of the Bougainville referendum result from 2019 in which 97.7 percent of Bougainvilleans voted for independence

PNG's members of parliament will have the final say on whether to ratify the result, although it is not clear when that vote will be taken.

A delegation from the Autonomous Bougainville Government (ABG) sat patiently in the gallery and watched on as MPs offered different takes on what everyone agreed was a difficult decision for them to have to make.

As the Joint Consultation Report and the Melanesian Framework documents were also newly tabled, PNG's opposition leader James Nomane pointed out that the MPs could hardly be expected to make informed decisions when they had only just received these documents.

"I ask that the government be very, very clear about when this vote will take place, and make all effort to inform all leaders of the House about: yes, what happens; no, what happens?" Nomane said.

PNG Parliament press gallery monitor shows Opposition Leader James Nomane speaking during debate following the tabling of the Bougainville referendum result, 27 August 2026. RNZ Pacific / Johnny Blades

PNG's Prime Minister James Marape said his government had a plan for the way forward for either outcome of the vote, affirmative and negative.

After the adjournment, he issued a statement saying the PNG and Bougainville governments would meet in October to set the date for the parliament vote on the referendum.

Earlier, he told MPs to go away and digest the report documents before deciding how to vote, and to ponder the Bougainville viewpoint, while also urging Bougainvilleans to consider the perspective of PNG.

"This is not simply a constitutional or political issue. It concerns the lives, hopes and futures of our people, especially those people whose lives have been shaped by the Bougainville crisis and the Bougainville peace process," Marape said.

'Deconflicting'

The regional member for Bougainville in the PNG parliament was the only Bougainvillean to speak in Thursday's debate.

Peter Tsiamalili Jr said history would judge the MPs not only by the decision they ultimately make, but also by the maturity, wisdom, and respect shown in the process.

"It is also at this juncture that I also want to amplify that how fitting are we able to then bring all this journey of both sides of the house, or both sides of our regions and our islands together, all culminating back into this respectful, honourable house, a house of Melanesia."

The MP spoke of the need to embrace constant dialogue as PNG and Bougainville navigated a way forward.

"I strongly believe that the (Bougainville) Peace Agreement, there may have been ambiguity in some parts of the Peace Agreement, but because of the wisdom of the past, who past leaders who created and crafted the peace agreement, those ambiguity speak right to the heart of the Melanesian way of deconflicting.

"We must continue to have dialogue, and that peace will be found, and solutions will be found through constant dialogue," Tsiamalili said.

Transitions

Minister for Bougainville Affairs Manasseh Makiba, who tabled the referendum result and relevant consultation documents, noted that the Melanesian Framework provided for a structured pathway and orderly transition for Bougainville to assume greater powers, in the event of an affirmative vote by parliament.

"At the heart of the framework is concept of a transitional phase that is being termed as self government," he said.

"Under the Melanesian Framework, an affirmative decision by the national parliament would not result in the immediate independence of Bougainville."

Makiba acknowledged that in the consultations, the national government and the ABG had been unable to reach consensus on the pathway in the event that the parliament does not accept the results.

Bougainville Affairs Minister Manasseh Makiba, 27 August, 2026. RNZ Pacific / Johnny Blades

But he said PNG's government still believed a constructive pathway forward was possible.

"The first element of the pathway would be the completion of the drawdown and effective exercise of all remaining autonomous powers available to Bougainville under Part 14 of the national constitution."

'The real seed'

Meanwhile, a senior MP who oversaw national consultations over Bougainville, described arguments that giving Bougainville independence undermined PNG's sovereignty as reductive.

Dr Allan Marat, the chairman of the Bipartisan Parliamentary Committee on Bougainville Matters, said the referendum issue attracted considerable debate on the issue of PNG sovereignty.

"This in turn has attracted considerable debate, and especially on the sovereignty issue of Papua New Guinea, that if we vote in favour of the 97.7 percent and grant Bougainville independence, then some of the other provinces might want to leave Papua New Guinea as well," Dr Marat said.

"I want to express my personal belief ... that this fear is an uninformed knee-jerk reaction and lacks human understanding."

He said it was more useful to bear in mind the development of a particular political mindset of the Bougainville people, "developed from the Paleolithic period during the last Ice Age period, the early European explorers, the missionaries, the colonial period leading up to independence and on to the 10 years of armed conflict, and eventually the peace process and the referendum until today".

Rabaul MP Dr Allan Marat speaks on Bougainville in PNG's Parliament, 27 August 2026 RNZ Pacific / Johnny Blades

"This human history and facts among the Bougainvilleans were the basis of their reasonings, giving rise to, 'the real seed', of discontentment in the minds of Bougainvilleans.

World.title: More details about missing New Zealanders in Nepal - what we know
World.content:
Five New Zealanders are missing following the deadly flash flood at the Nepal-China border.

A list of rescued foreign travellers released by the Nepal Tourism Board late on Friday did not identify any New Zealanders, though the nationalities of three of the 121 people were yet to be confirmed.

The missing New Zealanders are:

Shweta Mhatre

Dejan Kuzmic

Mihir Patel

Kinnari Patel

Suhasini Reddy

Here's what we know about them, as the search for those missing following the disaster continues.

Friends of missing Auckland woman fear for her safety

Auckland woman Shweta Mhatre is believed to be missing, following the devastating flash floods.

Close friends of hers told RNZ that she was currently in Nepal on a pilgrimage.

None of them had heard from her since Wednesday's catastrophic flash flooding on the Nepal-China border. A former partner of hers, as well as her neighbours, had not seen or heard from her.

RNZ understands Mhatre was part of the Isha Foundation's Sacred Walks pilgrimage.

The Isha Foundation told RNZ on Friday that Mhatre's emergency contacts had been notified about her situation.

Sadhguru, founder of the Isha Foundation, posted a video on social media saying two New Zealanders were missing from his pilgrimage group.

Nepal: We get an insight into disaster recovery Afternoons Download MP3 8m

Police confirm name of other missing New Zealander on pilgrimage

Dejan Kuzmic, another New Zealander RNZ understands is missing, was also part of the Isha Foundation's Sacred Walks.

Kuzmic came to New Zealand from Bosnia and Herzegovina as a refugee when he was 10 years old.

Nepal's Tourist Police confirmed Kuzmic's name to RNZ on Thursday morning.

RNZ has also spoken to a family friend, who confirmed the family had been unable to contact Kuzmic since the floods.

Kuzmic's emergency contacts have been notified. The family friend also said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade had opened a consular case for Kuzmic.

Mihir Patel and Kinnari Patel Supplied

Hamilton couple was celebrating 50th birthday

Mihir Patel and Kinnari Patel, who own the Best Value Urlich Ave Dairy in Hamilton, were visiting Nepal to Kinnari's birthday.

Their eldest son, Drishya Patel, told RNZ he was holding onto hope his parents had left the area before disaster struck.

"They're just on a trip to go visit some of the mountains in Nepal. It's like a pilgrimage of sorts," he said.

"They were having a good time."

His mother had messaged him on WhatsApp about 5:30am local time to say they were leaving. The flash flood began unfolding around 8:40am local time.

The couple have not been heard from since.

"As long as like they actually did leave when my mum sent me that message, I'm hopeful," he said.

Suhasini Reddy SUPPLIED

Mother of two 'had this trip planned for a while'

Suhasini Reddy was believed to be in the Dhunche area, heading towards the Nepal-China border, on Wednesday morning local time.

Her brother, Rajeev Reddy, told RNZ his sister was hiking with a group of friends from Australia. The mother of two had been living there for the past four years.

Her brother last spoke to her the night before the floods, while she was in Kathmandu.

"She was all good, excited," he said.

"She had this trip planned for a while."

Reddy said his sister was supposed to be meeting Chinese immigration about 11am local time. They had not heard anything from her since the flash flood.

World.title: Multiple cars damaged, two people injured on rural road near Auckland's Pukekohe
World.content:
Cordons are in place, two people are injured and multiple cars are damaged on a rural road near South Auckland's Pukekohe.

Police said Patumāhoe Rd in Patumāhoe, was closed on Friday evening, between Hunter Rd and Gun Club Rd, following an incident where multiple vehicles were damaged.

One person was in a critical condition and another was in a serious condition, police said.

Members of the public were asked to use an alternate route.

St John said it attended a traffic incident in the area and sent four ambulances, two rapid response units and one operations manager.

World.title: The art of netball signing: Easter eggs, chaos and a little bit of sleuthing
World.content:
In a congested sporting market where every professional league is fighting for your attention, social media teams at netball franchises have gone into overdrive these past two weeks.

Fans looking for a dopamine hit could get their fix simply by following the Instagram accounts of the clubs in Australia's Suncorp Super Netball (SSN) and the Netball Super League (NSL) in the UK.

Over the past couple of seasons, the bar has been set high during netball's signing windows, with clubs devising increasingly inventive ways to tease - and then reveal - which athlete will don their colours.

The anticipation was palpable in the build-up to the 2027 SSN signing window, when new contract offers were finally made official, and many franchises milked the moment for what it was worth.

The most intrigue during any signing period is generated by new player signings and defections to rival clubs. That interest ramped up another level over the past fortnight, with an exodus of New Zealand players predicted to join the Australian league.

A record number of current and former Silver Ferns have been recruited for the 2027 SSN, while five top players have also inked deals in the United Kingdom, amid the ongoing uncertainty over next year's ANZ Premiership.

RNZ netball reporter Bridget Tunnicliffe spent the fortnight trying to keep up with a dizzying merry-go-round of signings, defections and push notifications pinging across two time zones.

The subtle tease

A common method deployed by many franchises is to tease the next signing and tell you exactly when they will drop the announcement, so fans know when they must constantly refresh their browsers.

West Coast Fever hooked people in by posting short reels with a voicemail left by their next signing - except the voice was distorted.

Queensland Firebirds clue that their next new signing was Te Paea Selby-Rickit. Instagram

Melbourne Mavericks had their head coach drop a clue before each announcement, and sat back to watch their comments section explode, as fans tried to decipher what it meant.

In one video, the coach simply said "meow" three times. Some followers concluded it had to be a certain player who liked cats - they were right.

Queensland Firebirds took a more cryptic approach, with fans quickly working out from a pictoword-style clue that former Silver Fern Te Paea Selby-Rickit was about to re-sign.

Adelaide Thunderbirds went with a series of tarot cards that were considerably more open to interpretation.

Humour is also part of the arsenal. In the style of a sombre Netflix documentary, Leeds Rhinos 'media exec' stared at the camera, lamenting: "It's been a nightmare, everyone keeps saying you better do something creative... feeling that pressure."

The point of it all is not simply to make a signing announcement look flashy and exciting. In an increasingly crowded social media landscape, every clue creates another piece of content, another reason for fans to interact with a club and, crucially, another opportunity for the club to stay in their feeds.

Enter the social media sleuths

West Coast Fever teased their next signing with a distorted voicemail message. Instagram

Peak engagement comes when fans start trying to decode the Easter eggs as they are dropped.

One fan used a voice pitch adjustment app to conclude that the distorted voice in the West Coast Fever clue was former Silver Ferns captain Ameliaranne Ekenasio.

Others cracked the case by listening to old reels of Ekenasio speaking on her own social media account.

"Even though it's sped up, that's gotta be Ekenasio's speech rhythm," they wrote. "She loves to emphasise her adjectives in her product promo reels."

Some clubs will tease a new signing by sharing a mostly obscured image of the player. That can send fans down an unexpectedly specific rabbit hole, scanning athletes' social media posts and comparing, say, their nail polish with the manicured hands in the mystery photograph.

A netball content creator sharing the finding of new 'follows'. Instagram

Then there are the 'followers'.

Fans monitor which players have suddenly started following athletes from rival teams and share their findings with the wider online netball community. A cluster of new follows can be enough to turn a hunch into a full-blown theory and that is perhaps the genius of the strategy - the clubs aren't doing all the work.

Once fans become invested in solving the mystery, they create and distribute the speculation themselves.

Engagement you never knew you needed

After setting the bar so high, franchises now face a problem of their own making - fans expect them to put on a show.

One netball content creator on Instagram implored NSL team Loughborough Lightning to up their game.

"This is just boring, they've dragged out their signing window for so long... just post after post of just re-signing. Can they please do something a little bit more interesting?"

Adelaide Thunderbirds used tarot cards that were very open to interpretation. Instagram

The trick with a good Easter egg is getting the difficulty level right. Too easy and there is no satisfaction, too hard and everyone loses interest.

New South Wales Swifts flagged a pending announcement by playing a clip from the movie Matilda, which a six-year-old could figure out in three seconds was Australian defender Matilda Garrett.

Dragging out a signing too long also kills the vibe.

On 15 August, the Swifts thanked Silver Fern Grace Nweke, saying she was departing the club after two seasons.

Australian media had already reported that Nweke was heading across town to Sydney Sirens. Fans then waited 12 days for the Sirens to announce their marquee signing to absolutely no-one's surprise.

Cross-franchise engagement

Sadly for New Zealand netball fans, the folks behind the social media accounts at the six ANZ Premiership franchises haven't had an opportunity to really flex their muscles this year.

The Pulse set off a new trend of cross-franchise engagement in 2025, when Australian teams started recruiting NZ players. Instagram

The Pulse took an amusing approach last year, when it lost Silver Ferns Kelly Jackson and Maddy Gordon to Queensland Firebirds.

When the Tactix then lost Te Paea Selby-Rickit to the same team, the Pulse posted "they got you too huh", accompanied by the image of a shadowy figure.

Cross-franchise comments have become common - some are also not above throwing a bit of shade on rival teams.

Sunshine Coast Lightning couldn't help themselves this year, when a contracting debacle at Melbourne Vixens saw long-time player Kate Eddy miss out on a 2027 deal due to a 'miscommunication'.

In a clear reference to that fiasco, the Lightning patted themselves on the back in an Instagram post for being the first club in the SSN to say "yep, that's the list and mean it".

The non-conformers

One netball fan depicting the dizzying merry-go-round of signings. Instagram

No clues, no countdowns, no elaborate videos, no heads up that they were dropping player announcements... some clubs bucked the labour-intensive trend of making a song and dance about every signing.

Melbourne Vixens and Sunshine Coast Lightning had the audacity to announce each signing with a mere post on their platforms.

Maybe the social media gurus have created a monster and netball fans will never again be satisfied with a simple "Welcome to the club".

As @netballwithchan exclaimed: "SEND HELP! Trying to keep up with the Super Netball signing window has my head spinning." @circlebacknetball replied that they were going "cross-eyed and getting RSI" from all the scrolling.

World.title: Minister Louise Upston denies dodging questions over missed benefit payments
World.content:
Social Development Minister Louise Upston has appeared to avoid reporters waiting to ask about benefit payments being wrongly suspended, using a side corridor to enter Parliament's debating chamber on Friday afternoon.

A spokesperson from Upston's office denied she was dodging reporters, saying she took a different route to speak to officials before entering the House.

MSD said it became aware of the problem and told Upston about it on 13 August, but Upston told Parliament this week wrongful suspensions had not occurred - before changing her answer after further questions to say it had "possibly" happened.

Meanwhile, a beneficiary advocate said the government was playing with their lives.

The benefit payments were incorrectly stopped following a law change that was rushed through Parliament last year.

The new law requires some beneficiaries to re-confirm their circumstances at least once every 52 weeks, to check whether they are still eligible.

MSD said processing delays caused by a high volume of people confirming their circumstances meant some of their paperwork was not checked in time, so their benefit payments stopped.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon apologised on Friday, a week after he said sorry for another related but separate problem which saw thousands of pensioners miss out on their Winter Energy Payment.

MSD said it could not say how many beneficiaries were affected by the processing delays, or for how long, but they had all been backpaid and MSD had apologised.

A spokesperson from Upston's office said the Minister did not dodge questions.

"Minister Upston was about to present important legislation in the House and - as is common practice - needed to talk with officials who were waiting in a side annex before this legislation went up for debate," they said.

What did the Minister know, when?

MSD said it identified the problem and made the minister aware of both problems two weeks ago, and apologised to her.

Upston was asked in Parliament on Tuesday this week whether beneficiaries had payments suspended due to the processing delayed.

She said "no", but after multiple further questions, said "possibly".

Upston later told RNZ she was disappointed about what had happened, and she expected MSD to manage its workloads.

RNZ asked her office to clarify her comments in the House, but was told she would not comment due to an MSD review into the matter.

Reporters waited for Upston on her way to the House on Friday afternoon, but she took a side corridor that avoids areas where reporters can questions MPs.

The Greens and Labour called on Upston to front up.

Green MP Ricardo Menéndez March said Upston was hiding from accountability, while Labour's Willow-Jean Prime said she was throwing her officials under the bus.

Luxon also told Parliament last week he was confident the wrongful payments had not happened.

On Friday he said he would not correct his statement in the House because it was true at the time.

He apologised to the affected beneficiaries.

Govt 'playing with their lives' - beneficiary advocate

Auckland Action Against Poverty (AAAP) volunteer Pip Colgan said it had a number of clients she believed were affected by processing delays.

She blamed ministers rather than officials.

"The government doesn't seem to understand that, when they make these changes, they are literally playing with people's lives and causing them to go into debt through no fault of their own, then they get chastised by being in debt, but it's not their fault," she said.

Colgan first became aware of the problem in May, when a client contacted her after receiving a letter saying her benefit would be suspended the next day because she had not confirmed her circumstances - which she had.

"It just threw her into a complete tailspin," Colgan said.

"She has hugely complex needs, she just had to go to bed."

RNZ has seen a copy of the letter from MSD which said: "We've used an automated process to do this. This means our system has stopped your assistance due to you not completing your Confirming your Circumstances review."

Colgan said her client had done that in advance - she was very particular, completing the review and then phoning MSD and visiting in person to ensure they had what they needed.

RNZ has seen a screenshot of the documents that were uploaded, dated 8 May.

Her client could not pay her rent and got into debt through no fault of her own, she said.

"I rang MSD and they said that they couldn't process it, even though they knew that she had handed it in."

Colgan said she managed to get the payments restarted by picking up the hard copy of the forms from her client's house and taking them to MSD.

Others would not be so lucky, Colgan said.

"If she hadn't had me to help her, I don't know what what would have happened," she said.

"People who are vulnerable often can't work out what to do because it's all overwhelming and too much."

Problem lies with Minister not MSD, advocate says

Colgan said she did not blame MSD staff, who she understood had been working at all hours to clear the backlog and ensure people received their payments.

"I got an email from them at 8 o'clock on a Saturday night, which you don't normally expect to get from [Work and Income]," she said.

"They were working really, really hard to try and sort this out ... it wasn't caused by them, it was caused by the fast, you know, the urgency of decisions that this government seems to be putting through."

Colgan said politicians could apologise - as Luxon did - but that did not mean they understood the harm caused.

World.title: More than 1200 Auckland home support workers' jobs at risk after Health NZ decision
World.content:
Hundreds of home support workers could lose jobs as contracts cut Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

More than 1200 support workers across Auckland could lose their jobs, after Health NZ decided not to award home and community support contracts worth millions of dollars to three non-profit providers.

The affected organisations are Presbyterian Support Northern, which operates the Enliven service, as well as providers Visionwest, and Lifewise.

PSN chief executive Shaun Greaves told Checkpoint his organisation would like to know why they had been ditched.

"It certainly came as a shock and surprise ... it seems sudden and unjustified.

"I had to look my team in the eyes yesterday afternoon, where we stood in front of them and had to tell them [what had happened].

"It is the hardest news we've had to deliver, these are people that have worked hard for us. Thirty percent of our staff at Enliven have been working for us for over ten years," he said.

"We're just sitting here in awe, we do not understand this decision at all."

There had been no complaints from Health NZ about their services, he said.

To his knowledge, PSN's Enliven service, Visionwest and Lifewise had been meeting requirements around sustainability, quality and fulfilling client needs, he added.

"We would hope that Health New Zealand would look at this again.

"We have challenged the decision, they did an internal review following that and came out and said that their procurement process was still valid.

Presbyterian Support Northern chief executive Shaun Greaves. Supplied / Presbyterian Support Northern

"One of the things we have concerns about ... is that they don't take into account tenure of service, the quality of service, our experience, our deep relationships in the community and the not-for-profit edge we offer."

Just a few weeks ago Greaves had presented a 20-year service certificate to a support worker, who had an almost familial relationship with one client they had worked with throughout that time, he said.

PSN had serious concerns for the 4500 clients who would be affected by Health NZ's decision.

Greaves wanted to see the transition safely completed by March - the deadline for current services to end. However, the affected organisations did not yet know who the new support providers would be.

"We can't start a transition process yet, so March to me sounds incredibly close."

The contract loss also represented a significant financial blow to the organisations, with Enliven's contract worth $19 million alone, he said.

Health NZ said a procurement process was underway for home and community support services across the northern region.

Proposals had been assessed against a range of criteria to ensure services were sustainable, of high quality, and able to meet the needs of people in need to support to continue living independently in their homes.

While Health NZ could not comment on individual proposals or assessments, it acknowledged that some longstanding providers had not been successful and recognised they would be disappointed.

World.title: New Zealand says its ties with its Realm countries remain strong and stable
World.content:
Clockwise New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, The Honourable Dalton Tagelagi Prime Minister of Niue, the Honourable Mark Brown Prime Minister of the Cook Islands (pending official results) and The Honourable Petelo Alapati Tavite Ulu-o-Tokelau. RNZ / Nick Monro

New Zealand says its connections to its Realm countries remain strong and stable, after the first of a series of annual "family reunions".

Christopher Luxon met with Cook Islands Prime Minister Mark Brown, Niue's Prime Minister Dalton Tagelagi and the Ulu-o-Tokelau Alapati Tavite in Government House this morning, ahead of the Pacific Islands Forum leaders meeting in Palau next week.

The Realm countries will ride together this weekend to Palau for the Pacific Island Forum leaders summit next week.

"We've got a hundred and forty thousand Cook Islanders, Niueans, Tokelauans, living here in New Zealand," Luxon told reporters.

"We've got deep connectivity between our four countries, and so it's really important, in a volatile and uncertain world.. what more (New Zealand) can be doing."

When the year began, the relationship between New Zealand and the Cook Islands was frosty. The Cooks had struck out in late 2024, signing a security deal with China that New Zealand hadn't approved of.

New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon at The Realm of New Zealand's four leaders meeting in Auckland on Friday. RNZ / Nick Monro

Amidst a myriad of issues, a breakdown in communications led to a breakdown in trust, leading to a cut in aid only restored earlier this year. Now, Prime Minister Luxon said it's sorted.

"We've normalised our relationship, and we sorted the issues of the last year or so out," he said.

Brown said one of the earlier sore points, a Cook Islands passport, has been laid to rest.

"That's no longer part of our discussions at the moment," he said.

"The Cook Islands has pretty well established itself internationally as a country, and as citizens of New Zealand and increasingly Australia, that's where our status is right now."

Prime Minister Tagelagi echoed this sentiment for his own country.

"If anything, we are so grateful for the New Zealand support, but the Pacific needs to reach out further," he said, "so we don't always have to rely on New Zealand."

For it's part, the Cooks are fielding an unprecedented level of interest from another global superpower - the United States.

The US has made no secret of it's deep sea mining ambitions in the Clarion Clipperton Zone. Where this leads their relationship with Aotearoa remains to be seen, but Prime Minister Brown insists he will ensure his country benefits from any future activity.

"Decisions made on our seabed and our resources are made by the Cook Islands for the interest of Cook Islanders only."

The Honourable Mark Brown Prime Minister of the Cook Islands (pending official results) speaking at The Realm of New Zealand's four leaders meeting in Auckland on Friday. RNZ / Nick Monro

"The Cook Islands is looking very closely at how we as a country would benefit if we moved down the road of extraction."

In a far less fortunate position is Tokelau.

The territory was expelled from the lucrative Parties to the Nauru Agreement Vessel Day Scheme in February, and estimates of the ensuing revenue losses are massive. RNZ has previously reported that New Zealand may have a played a role in getting Tokelau kicked out, thanks to interference in Tokelau's fisheries.

Prime Minister Luxon denied this, saying that between them, they were "putting a full court press" to get them reinstated, particularly with an appeal to PNA members in Palau next week.

Following the meeting, only Tokelau's leader was unavailable to speak to media.

World.title: Friends of Auckland woman missing after Nepal flash flood fear for her safety
World.content:
Close friends of an Auckland woman who is believed to be missing amid devastating flash floods in Nepal have expressed growing concern about her safety.

The friends told RNZ that Shweta Mhatre was currently in Nepal on a pilgrimage.

None of them had heard from Mhatre since Wednesday's catastrophic flash flooding on the Nepal-China border, which has killed more than 450 people.

A former partner of Mhatre also told RNZ he had not heard from her since Wednesday.

RNZ visited Mhatre's home and spoke to neighbours, who said they had not seen her at the house in the past two weeks.

One neighbour said Mhatre travelled frequently and was often overseas.

RNZ understands Mhatre was part of the Isha Foundation's Sacred Walks pilgrimage.

The Isha Foundation told RNZ on Friday that Mhatre's emergency contacts had been notified about her situation.

Sadhguru, founder of the Isha Foundation, posted a video on social media saying two New Zealanders were missing from his pilgrimage group.

Dejan Kuzmic, another New Zealander RNZ understands is missing, was also part of the Isha Foundation's Sacred Walks.

Kuzmic came to New Zealand from Bosnia and Herzegovina as a refugee when he was 10 years old.

RNZ has also spoken to a family friend, who confirmed the family had been unable to contact Kuzmic since the floods.

"He was part of the Isha Foundation's walk group S3 and was at the border crossing, which was hit quite heavily within a reasonable time, which makes us believe he may have been involved," said Seyed Sepehr Hosseini, whose mother attends a meditation group with Kuzmic.

Hosseini contacted the Isha Foundation, which told him Kuzmic's emergency contacts had been notified.

He also contacted New Zealand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, which said it had opened a consular case for Kuzmic.

Five New Zealanders are among more than 1400 missing following Wednesday's disaster.

Hamilton couple Kinnari Patel and Mihir Patel are believed to be among the missing, with one community member admiring their passion for Garba, a traditional Gujarati folk dance.

Ketan Joshi Supplied

Ketan Joshi has known the couple for several years, first meeting them at Garba events in Auckland.

"I met them during Garba events in Auckland and their passion for it caught my eye," he said.

Joshi was working for a community newspaper at the time and vividly remembers seeing the couple dressed in traditional clothing.

"They were so enthusiastic about Garba, and they used to play it from the beginning to the end, which is very rare to see these days," Joshi said.

He said the couple were originally from Vadodara in the Indian state of Gujarat.

Kinnari Patel's brother, Chirag, told Indian media on Thursday the family had not heard from the couple for a week.

He said the couple flew directly from New Zealand to Nepal via Singapore and were planning to undertake the Kailash Mansarovar Yatra, a popular pilgrimage for Hindus, Buddhists and Jains.

India's official Kailash Mansarovar Yatra portal describes the pilgrimage as having deep religious and cultural significance.

The couple had booked the pilgrimage through an agent based in Mumbai, he said.

Patel said the couple had been living in New Zealand for 30 years.

He said he contacted the hotel where the couple had stayed, but was told they had stayed for three days before checking out.

"[My sister] said that she would come back for Raksha Bandhan and would go back," Patel said.

Raksha Bandhan is a Hindu festival celebrating the bond between brothers and sisters, which falls today.

Patel said the couple left for the pilgrimage on 21 August.

He said he was speaking with officials in India about the missing couple.

RNZ understands members of the Indian community in Hamilton have come together to support the couple's children with food and other assistance.

Hamilton couple Kinnari Patel and Mihir Patel are believed to be among those missing in Nepal following Wednesday's catastrophic flash flood. Namaskar Gujarat NZ News

The New Zealand Nepal Society, one of the largest Nepali community organisations in the country, has planned a candlelight vigil on Saturday to remember the victims of the flash floods in Nepal.

Roshan Khadka, president of the New Zealand Nepal Society, told RNZ they had cancelled the Teej Festival, one of the community's largest annual festivals, which was originally scheduled to be held on Friday.

Instead, the community has organised a vigil.

"I've spoken to multiple Nepali organisations in Auckland and with many Indian and Chinese organisations and they've told me that they will all be attending to remember the victims," he said.

Khadka also said they were raising donations at the event, which would be put towards the Nepal Prime Minister's Disaster Relief Fund.

The Indian High Commission told RNZ it had set up an emergency centre in New Delhi for Nepal flood victims and was available to help anyone who needed support.

The High Commission said the emergency number (+64 21 539 817) is monitored frequently, and members of the community could also contact the mission through WhatsApp.

RNZ understands another New Zealander missing in the floods is Suhasini Reddy, who had moved to Australia.

Reddy's brother, Rajeev, said in a Facebook post he was trying to establish the extent of the damage around the immigration checkpoint between Nepal and Tibet and whether anyone had been able to reach higher ground.

Dinesh Khadka, former honorary consul of Nepal to New Zealand Supplied

Dinesh Khadka, former honorary consul of Nepal to New Zealand, said the checkpoint had been completely swept away in the flooding, and nobody had been able to contact anyone who was in the area.

Khadka said there was no further information about the five missing New Zealanders.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said New Zealand was offering consular support in Nepal and was prepared to "surge" more resources if needed.

He did not have any further information about the five New Zealanders missing "apart from to say that we've got consular support in there

engaging with authorities".

Luxon also acknowledged the thousands of Nepali people living in New Zealand.

"Having spoken to some members of the Nepalese community this morning, you know, there are many families here in New Zealand that are going through high levels of anxiety, understandably, because they're losing, they've lost loved ones at home as well," he said.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon RNZ / Nick Monro

RNZ contacted the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade for an update regarding the missing New Zealanders.

"MFAT is aware of five New Zealanders believed to be in the impacted region and whose whereabouts have yet to be established," a spokesperson from the ministry said.

"Consular officials are providing support to the families of those individuals. For privacy reasons, MFAT cannot confirm the names of the New Zealanders affected."

World.title: Penrith go top after spiteful clash that all but ends Canterbury's finals hopes
World.content:
Canterbury's NRL finals hopes are hanging by a thread after a 24-10 loss to Penrith, who moved within reach of a top-two finish at Western Sydney Stadium.

Second-rower Liam Martin bagged a double as the Panthers moved back to the top of the ladder on Friday night.

A shaky start to the year has left the Bulldogs playing catch-up on the top eight for most of 2026, and they could be officially out of the finals picture by Saturday night.

If North Queensland and South Sydney win their respective round-26 games, they will become the last two teams to book their finals spots.

To play finals from here, the Bulldogs need to beat Brisbane next week and hope the Cowboys lose their last two games, both of which are at home against bottom-nine sides.

The Bulldogs also need ninth-placed Manly to lose to the Warriors in the last round of the regular season after the Sea Eagles kept alive their slim hopes of making the eight by thumping the last-placed Dragons 44-10 at Brookvale Oval earlier on Friday.

Look back at all the action in our live blog below, and check out all the stats in the full Score Centre.

World.title: Min Woo leads after flying start at Tour playoff finale
World.content:
The Chef is cooking up a storm in the Tour Championship kitchen.

Min Woo Lee, nicknamed The Chef, had the world's leading golfers eating out of his hand with an 8-under-par 62 on Friday (AEST) at East Lake.

It was good enough to lead the exclusive field at the season-ending tournament in Atlanta, with nearest challengers Viktor Hovland, Collin Morikawa and Chris Gotterup two behind.

World number one Scottie Scheffler is among a four-player group at 5-under, while Australian Adam Scott (66) is one further back.

Lee made an electrifying start in his Tour Championship debut, which no-one saw coming, after two lowly finishes — tied 55th and 47th — to begin the PGA Tour playoffs.

"Very average two weeks the last two weeks. It was probably the saddest I've been on the golf course, which is not good," Lee said.

"We're really lucky to be out here and play some good golf to get into the playoffs. It just felt so hard."

With runner-up finishes this year at Pebble Beach and the Scottish Open, Lee was a lock to be among the top 30 players who get a shot at the playoffs title, the $US10 million ($14 million) prize and a five-year exemption on the PGA Tour.

Lee coined his nickname after his popular catchphrase "let him cook" went viral.

He had the right recipe on Friday, taking advantage of the rain-softened course to post eight birdies — four on each nine including the last — to match his career-low best total on the Tour.

Former world number one and 2013 Masters champion Scott also hit his straps.

The Tour Championship is special to Scott, who won the tournament in 2006.

The Queenslander has been ultra-consistent since, with a consecutive major championship streak of 101 straight starts that makes him only the second player in the history of professional golf to achieve the feat.

Scott produced five birdies with a lone bogey, leaving him tied ninth.

Scheffler started his day with a 2 metre par putt and never came close to another bogey in his round of 65.

He is number one in the Tour playoff rankings and picked up a $23 million bonus last week, but that doesn't matter at East Lake as under the current format any of the 30 players who win the Tour Championship are deemed to be the playoffs champion.

Rory McIlroy, the only three-time playoffs champion, opened with a 68.

AAP

World.title: Marathon runner felt part of identity 'stolen' after losing national record
World.content:
Hours after seeing his national record broken by two seconds at the Gold Coast marathon, Andy Buchanan was sitting in his hotel room reflecting.

He was raw, 'going through the feels', and brutally honest as he articulated what it felt like to have something intangible, yet still his, taken from his grasp.

"I saw it pop up, new Australian record, and it just hit me like a thousand cement trucks," Buchanan said on his YouTube channel at the time.

"That's a huge run from Haftu [Strintzos], good on him. Obviously, the record was going to be broken at some stage.

"It feels like something's been stolen, I feel like that was a big part of my identity the last year."

His disappointment ran even deeper, having finished 18th in the half marathon the day before.

That was nearly two months ago, and when he was introduced as the former Australian record holder at the media launch for Sunday's Sydney Marathon, he visibly winced.

The pain has not disappeared, but the attitude to banish it is stronger.

"I hated that weekend up on the Gold Coast," he said.

"I raced poorly on Saturday and Haftu come out and ran so, so well and broke my record.

"But that's OK, that's what records are there for and it actually wasn't that deep and I just needed to move on.

"I'm still the same person with or without the record. I'm really eager to get it back but it's not that deep."

Going the distance

The record was unattainable for an Australian man for decades.

Rob de Castella's mark stood for 36 years, before Brett Robinson's breakthrough in 2022, then Buchanan in 2024, and now Strintzos.

And while it is unlikely to fall again on Sydney's tricky, hilly course, Buchanan will be the fastest Australian man in the elite field, headlined by reigning world champion, Tanzania's Alphonce Simbu.

They will be amongst more than 40,000 entrants in Sydney's second year as one of the world's eight marathon majors.

Buchanan (left) alongside several of the Australian entrants in the elite field for the Sydney Marathon. (Supplied: Sydney Marathon)

It is Buchanan's first marathon at home, and first since London in April last year.

"I had a stress reaction in my femur, and then I tried to get back for World Champs and then re-injured it, tried to get back for Valencia, re-injured it," he said.

"So it's just the same injury three times, which was very frustrating, but you've just got to try and learn something from every injury, and I think I've learned something, but we'll find out."

And as the second fastest male marathon runner in Australian history, the 35-year-old was always destined to go the distance.

"Growing up as a schoolkid, my parents were marathon runners back before running was cool," he said.

"And I grew up thinking the normal family holiday was to go to Gold Coast or go to Adelaide or go to Hobart or Perth, watch your parents run a marathon, then you get to spend a week or two around that state.

"But I'm very thankful for my parents that I got to have that upbringing.

"I fell in love with the marathon just by watching people at 30k and seeing the pain they were going through, and you'd see the same people then crossing the line at 42k and it's such a unique thing."

Pashley leading Australian women

The women's field also boasts the current world champion, Kenya's Peres Jepchirchir, while Ellie Pashley is vying to be the first Australian across the line — a title which pockets $30,000 for men and women.

The Tokyo Olympian won the Ballarat Marathon in April, her first after the birth of her second child.

Ellie Pashley is an Olympic marathon runner and a mother of two. (ABC News: Darryl Torpy)

"I'm really excited to be honest. I think time off from the sport really grows your hunger to get back into it," she said.

"Watching last year, seeing the course, seeing the race amongst the Australian women, I was really pumped to try and get a spot in the race this year and I'm excited to be a part of it."

And she is trying not to measure herself against some of Australia's other leading female marathoners.

"I feel like it takes me a while to get back after having a baby," Pashley said.

"I think some of the Australian women make it look fairly easy with how incredibly they run so soon after childbirth.

"I feel like I'm still building back up and I hope I'm a little bit fitter than I was in Ballarat.

"There's always a few hiccups along the way when you have young children with illness and things like that. But I'm feeling fitter and I'm hoping to give a good time."

Caitlin Scott won her debut marathon in Melbourne last year. (Nike Melbourne Maraton Festival)

Caitlin Scott, 29, is one of the other leading Australian women, having only made her marathon debut in Melbourne last year.

"I feel like I'm quite green and inexperienced as a marathon runner, so I'm really excited for Sunday … just to give the distance another crack and see what we can do," she said.

World.title: The secret of Wests Tigers remarkable NRLW rebirth
World.content:
Traditionally, Wests Tigers have found wins hard to come by in the NRLW.

The joint venture has endured difficult times since it entered the competition three years ago.

Before this season they'd won just five of their 29 matches and never more than two in a single campaign.

They entered 2026 on the back of consecutive wooden spoons and most pundits predicted more of the same.

But Craig Sandercock's side has emerged as the success story of the season, winning six of eight matches thus far — more than they've won in the rest of their existence combined — to sit third on the ladder with three rounds remaining.

Only Brisbane and the Sydney Roosters, the two premiership favourites, have managed to lower their colours, and their most recent win, a one-point triumph over Newcastle courtesy of a last-minute field goal in an instant classic, showed just how far they've come.

According to backrower Shaylee Bent, who joined the club this season from Gold Coast, losing such games used to be a Tigers trademark.

"I'll be honest, they'd finished bottom of the table two years in a row and from playing them they could be in the fight but they'd always lose late," she said.

"They never had the experience to win the moments that really count.

"The girls who have been here in the past, they have all the potential in the world but now they have those experienced players around them they can do what they're best at.

"That clarity lets them be good at what they're good at."

Bent is playing some of the best football of her career at the Tigers. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

Bent is one of those experienced players, having played in three grand finals and for New South Wales and Australia during her career.

Along with fellow recruits such as halfback Raecene McGregor and lock forward Holli Wheeler, she's helped spearhead a turnaround that has the Tigers on the brink of their first ever NRLW finals series.

In doing so, Bent is playing the best football of her life — better than anything she produced on the more star-studded rosters she enjoyed at St George Illawarra and Gold Coast when she was a New South Wales and Jillaroos regular.

She's scored as many tries this season as in her last four years combined and is putting up career highs for run metres per game, tackles per game, line breaks and tackle busts.

Bent says she's taken it on herself to be a leader for the young Tigers side and the responsibility clearly agrees with her.

"I'm proud of myself for getting involved more. When I've been on good teams with good players around me I've let them take the hard runs, take the runs to win the game and things like that," she said.

"But I've found what works for me here.

"I'm in a team where I don't have all those names around me. I have to be a leader and I'm loving it. I love being that energy bunny and hopefully there's a ripple effect."

The addition of Bent and Wheeler, who Bent cites as one of the greatest influences on the team's all-effort mentality, has rounded out a strong pack that includes wrecking machine Sarah Togatuki and ageless wonder Kezie Apps.

Apart from former Dally M winner and three-time NRLW champion McGregor, the rest of the roster is filled mainly with up-and-comers who went through those hard times and are now daring to dream of something greater.

"They might not have the experience of players like Kezie, but they aspire to be like her and we're still growing together," Bent said.

"We have so much young depth and in the years to come they're going to be where we are.

"Sandy isn't just prepping them to play for one week. He's developing them."

The Tigers are fixing to be a club that relies on local juniors, but that development isn't restricted to youngsters.

Caitlin Turnbull is one of Wests Tigers biggest success stories. (Getty Images: Brett Hemmings )

Caitlin Turnbull, who made her NRLW debut last year at 25, has experienced another strong season at fullback, and rugby union convert Faythe Manera is enjoying success as a backline utility in her first season in league as the club's equal-top scorer.
