Tech.title: Best Laptops (2026): My Top Recommendations After Testing Hundreds
Tech.content:
I’ve been reviewing laptops for well over a decade, sometimes testing more than 30 devices per year. They aren’t all winners, and many should be avoided, no matter how slick the marketing or cheap the discount. Good news: It’s my job to recommend laptops that fit your budget and won’t make you regret your purchase six months later. These are my favorite laptops that I’ve tested myself and would highly recommend you buy.

For more guidance, also see my recommendations in specific categories, such as the Best MacBooks, Best Gaming Laptops, Best Chromebooks, Best Budget Laptops, Best Windows Laptops, and Best 2-in-1 Laptops. My guide on How to Choose a Laptop may also help if you’re undecided.

Updated August 2026: I’ve updated my recommendations after testing the Dell XPS 13, Alienware 15 Gaming Laptop, and Lenovo LOQ 15 Essential.

The Laptops I Recommend Most

When friends or family ask what laptop to buy, I always start with the MacBook Air. It is far more powerful than its compact size suggests. It’s a shame about the recent $200 price increase from $1,099 to $1,299, but even at that new price, it remains my top pick because it nails the big picture. Everything from the trackpad to the speakers is of the highest quality, and it delivers all the performance and battery life the average person needs.

With the latest M5 chip, its GPU matches the M3 Pro MacBook Pro, easily handling everything from gaming to video editing. That’s not at all what the MacBook Air is designed for, but the performance is there when you want to dabble. It’s what makes it feel like a do-it-all machine, all contained in a fanless chassis that’s still one of the thinnest laptops you can buy. Oh, and did I mention it’ll last well over a full workday away from the wall socket and perform just as well on battery as when plugged in? In almost every aspect, it’s the gold standard.

While the lower price of the new MacBook Neo might be tempting, the MacBook Air is the better choice for anyone working at a computer all day. With its superior performance, extra memory, faster storage, and Thunderbolt ports, you will never have to question if you have the right tool for the job. (And unless you already know you need a MacBook Pro, you probably don’t.)

Speaking of price, I have to mention the new Dell XPS 13 next. It's primarily being talked about as a budget laptop, thanks to its $699 starting configuration. But that model only comes with 8 GB of RAM, which presented some performance limitations when I tested it. Dell, fortunately, sells an upgrade model with 16 GB of RAM for $899, which is otherwise identical. Both models have the same gorgeous screen, which is not only sharp, bright, and color-accurate, but also includes a 120-Hz refresh rate, which makes animation and motion on the device look super smooth. The XPS 13 is filled with features like that, which don't normally end up in a laptop at this price.

While it doesn't have what I'd call powerhouse performance, the Intel Wildcat Lake chip inside gets the job done. Don't try to play games on it, though. That translates to great, all-day battery life, competitive with the MacBook Air. The XPS 13 is especially good for those who want a compact laptop. Because of the tiny bezels, it's still one of the best laptops to work on a plane with. But even beyond that, it's just the best laptops you can buy under $1,000 right now. You'll probably just want to avoid that 8 GB model. Beyond the memory situation, the only real caveat is the lack of a headphone jack.

If you want a Windows laptop that looks and feels high-end, I would point you to the OmniBook Ultra 14. It might be the prettiest Windows laptop you can buy right now. The device is beautifully built and incredibly sturdy, with a thin chassis, an oversized haptic trackpad, and polished metal edges. I also appreciate the three Thunderbolt 4 ports split between both sides for convenient charging, as well as the surprisingly good speakers. I tested the high-end model, which features a fast Snapdragon X2 Elite, 32 GB of RAM, and a gorgeous 2880 x 1800 OLED display. The screen offers near-perfect colors, excellent brightness, and astounding HDR performance. It doesn’t get much better than this. It's usually quite expensive, but we're finally starting to seem discounts that drop it to a more reasonable price. There's also an Intel model with a very efficient and powerful chip that would also be a good choice. I'd go with whichever is cheaper at the current moment.

And lastly, for something with a larger screen, I'd recommend the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 5x. It serves as a particularly good alternative to the 15-inch MacBook Air, coming in at a much lower cost. These days, you can buy the upgraded model with the 2560 x 1600 OLED display (and 165-Hz refresh rate) for $1,000, on sale at Amazon. While it's slightly thicker than the MacBook Air, it leaves more room for extra ports including HDMI, UBS-A, and an SD card slot. And while the Snapdragon X2 Plus isn’t quite an M5 killer, I was happy with the performance and battery life provided.

Cheap Laptops That Are Actually Good

While “cheap” means something different to everyone, the best budget laptops generally fall under $750. This is where Windows truly shines, offering great specs for less money. Thanks to the latest processors from Qualcomm and Intel, these laptops now offer battery life that rivals Apple. The best affordable laptop I’ve checked out is the HP OmniBook 5. The model I tested has a Snapdragon X processor, 16 GB of RAM, 512 GB of storage, and a 14-inch OLED screen. Discounts fluctuate frequently, but right now you can buy that configuration directly from HP for $650. That’s a killer deal.

I also recently tested the new HP OmniBook 3, which uses the same chip as the OmniBook 5. It frequently sells for less than the OmniBook 5 by at least a $100 or so. HP is selling this configuration of the 14-inch model for just $543. While the OmniBook 3 is a good alternative, the OmniBook 5 is much thinner and looks more modern. Neither laptop has a particularly great touchpad, though, which is easily the biggest flaw in both laptops. Between the two, the OmniBook 5 is the better buy if you can afford it.

The MacBook Neo is Apple’s new entry-level laptop. It initially started at an aggressive $599, but that price has recently been raised to $699. Even at that price, the laptop shines when it comes to the display. It offers the best screen you can find at this price, bringing the macOS experience to an unprecedented value, even at $699 (or $799 for the 512 GB model). Apple clearly gave priority to the front-of-screen experience, delivering a premium feel across the display, build quality, and keyboard. While the 8 GB of RAM, outdated ports, and slower SSD are notable drawbacks—making the MacBook Air a better choice for remote workers—the Neo is the most premium-feeling laptop available for students, travelers, and casual users.

Given how good some of these budget laptops are, it’s a bit harder to find a place for Chromebooks. The standout option is still the Lenovo Chromebook Plus 14. It’s the most premium Chromebook available, with an OLED screen, 16 GB of RAM, and battery life that rivals the MacBook Neo. Its price just keeps going up, though, now up to $849. That’s far too expensive for what you get.

Instead, I recommend the Acer Chromebook Plus 516, which is the best of the cheaper Chromebooks. While it’s a bit thick and the screen isn’t the sharpest (especially for a 16-inch laptop), it’s the best laptop you can buy for under $500, and it occasionally dips down to $349. Acer didn’t skimp on the quality of the touchpad, either, which I appreciate. Windows laptops are about to get much stronger in this category, however, just as higher-priced Chromebooks will be seemingly phased out over time and replaced by the upcoming Googlebooks. Personally, I wouldn't spend more than $500 for a Chromebook and would instead opt for one of the cheaper HP OmniBooks mentioned above if you're already spending close to this price.

Powerful Laptops for Those Who Need It

While the laptops above are great for the average person, content creators and gamers need extra performance. For the former, the 16-inch M5 Max MacBook Pro is the ultimate choice. It combines immense power with surprising portability and fantastic battery life—a rare feat. The M5 generation is the most impressive yet, with a greatly expanded GPU and significantly boosted on-device AI processing thanks to a more efficient Neural Engine and faster memory bandwidth. While it is one of the most powerful AI laptops available, the MacBook Pro isn’t for everyone; it is built specifically for professional creatives and engineers running heavy, demanding applications. It’s become more expensive in 2026, but there’s still nothing quite like it on the market.

There are a number of Windows alternatives to the MacBook Pro, including the Asus ProArt P16 and Lenovo Yoga Pro 9i. And while these are both powerful, they take an old-school approach to performance, using hot-and-heavy discrete graphics cards that significantly reduce the battery life to achieve that level of performance. We'll probably need to wait for Nvidia's anticipated RTX Spark laptops for a true MacBook Pro competitor later this year. The Dell XPS 14 takes a different approach, ditching the discrete GPU for Intel’s new X7 or X9 chip (also known as B390 or Intel Arc graphics). The results are seriously impressive, replicating the performance of an RTX 4050 without the downsides of using a discrete GPU. Moreover, the Dell XPS 14 has a level of polish in its design really seen only on MacBooks—even surpassing them in some areas. The more affordable configurations with the Core Ultra 5 or 7 don't have as strong of graphics, but you still get the premium design and excellent battery life.

The most common use for laptop performance, however, is for playing games. If you plan on booting up any graphically intensive games more than a couple of times a week, you will want a dedicated gaming laptop. After testing dozens over the past year, the Alienware 15 Gaming Laptop is my current recommendation. At $1,200 for the RTX 5050 model or $1,350 for the upgrade RTX 5060, this is the best deal in gaming laptops right now.

It performs well, though its strongest quality compared to the competition is how robust and beautiful the exterior chassis is. Most gaming laptops around this price are eyesores. The main downside to the Alienware 15 is the screen, which has some noticeably bad color reproduction. The visuals have a desaturated look that annoys me, which is common on these budget gaming laptops.

The Lenovo LOQ 15 with the RTX 5060 has been my top pick for affordable gaming laptops throughout most of the year, as it has been the cheapest way to get decent gaming performance without any major compromises to the laptop. It has a much better display than the Alienware 15, for example. However, it's recently gone up by hundreds of dollars in price, which is frustrating. Its high-quality display still makes it stand out, though, and it's worth the couple hundred extra dollars in my book.

There’s a whole world of gaming laptops outside the budget tier, though. I’ve tested an assortment of options, and I always come back to the Razer Blade 14 and Razer Blade 16. Portable, minimalist, and extremely well-made, they have rightfully earned their reputation as the MacBooks of PC gaming—along with the MacBook Pro–like price tag. Their sleek design means they work just as well for school or work as they do for gaming, without the bulk of a traditional gaming laptop. While there are more powerful options out there, nothing quite matches the Razer Blade.

Tech.title: He Scraped All of Their Art for AI. Now He’s Collaborating on a Tool to Help Them
Tech.content:
Since early 2023, photographer Jingna Zhang and a small crew of volunteers have worked tirelessly to maintain an image-sharing social media and portfolio app called Cara. So far, it has attracted about 1.5 million artists. What drew them to the platform? A shared opposition to the unauthorized use of their work to train AI models and a desire to publicize their art while avoiding exploitation by Big Tech.

But while Cara filters out AI images and offers protective features—including Glaze, a tool meant to mask the style of the images picked up by scrapers in order to disrupt AI mimicry—preventing scrapes themselves is nearly impossible. And just this month, beginning on August 13, Cara was subjected to three major scrapes, which spiked its server fees and alarmed creators who had migrated there from platforms like Instagram, where all content is explicitly available to Meta as training data.

The first of these incidents came to light when the individual responsible posted a 12-terabyte archive of 12 million works from Cara—more or less its entire library of publicly available images—on the subreddit r/DefendingAIArt. “It was a fun project,” wrote the redditor, MandarinDawnPoppy994, in his since-deleted post, saying the process cost him less than $10.

“We actually found out about it through our users tagging us,” Zhang tells WIRED, since the scraper was “gloating and looking for other people to join him to do something with the dataset on Reddit,” sparking a fierce debate across AI-related forums about the ethics of what he had done. “I just feel it's targeted and very hurtful,” she adds, noting that “laws are not caught up on” protections against such data harvests, meaning that scrapers can often justify it as technically legal. (Zhang is separately part of two ongoing class actions brought by visual artists, one against Stability AI, Midjourney, and others and the second against Google, alleging that the companies’ image generator tools were trained on their copyrighted work.)

In a surprising turn of events, however, the person who grabbed all the art off Cara would turn out to regret his stunt and agree to collaborate with Zhang on a new open-source tool to protect artists.

In the meantime, unfortunately, other scrapers continued to take advantage of Cara’s vulnerabilities and minimal resources. While a number of AI proponents objected to going after Cara, a few were apparently emboldened by MandarinDawnPoppy994 to carry out what Zhang sees as “copycat” attacks.

A second scraper pulled about 8.5 million links from Cara, as well as metadata like usernames, titles, and tags, and uploaded these to Hugging Face, the AI developer platform. After Hugging Face was bombarded with takedown requests, it responded in a statement that while it would issue a notice to the user, “CaptiveDreamer,” to remove the personal metadata, it could not do the same for the URLs, since “no copies of the artworks are hosted here,” and the links “point to the copies the artists published on Cara.” The company concluded that “further copyright reports on the same basis will not change this outcome.”

Finally, on August 22, a third scraper obtained 123,000 images from Cara, along with text posts and user bios that included personal information, sharing it all on a site called Academic Torrents. Zhang then launched a GoFundMe for legal fees, setting a goal of $120,000, explaining that the money would go toward exploring any and all strategies of defending Cara through cyber and copyright laws. As of Thursday, she has raised more than $100,000, and she says Cara is actively looking for any additional legal assistance.

Tech.title: Inside Meta’s Push to Put Robots to Work in Data Centers
Tech.content:
Meta is testing robots that can plug in cables, reset servers, and handle other tasks inside its data centers, according to several current and former workers familiar with the projects. The ongoing effort, which has not been previously reported, may eventually allow Meta to operate its rapidly expanding data center footprint with fewer humans, keeping labor costs in check as its spending on AI infrastructure soars.

Meta is using robots and related hardware from several different vendors, including Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB, according to the same workers, who asked to remain anonymous because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media. Kinova and ABB declined to comment. Watney didn’t respond to requests for comment.

In one experiment, Meta is evaluating whether a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm could be used for power cycling, or cutting off electricity to servers. The company is also testing a different robot to swap networking cables. One Meta data center worker estimates that if it’s successful, the bot could replace up to 80 percent of some people’s workloads. “We thought those of us performing the physical tasks were safe for a while, but not anymore,” says the worker. “It’s coming for us all, unfortunately.”

At some facilities, Meta quietly adopted another, relatively simple robot. It looks like a finger—or perhaps a pointy stick—that can press the power button on a Mac Mini or other device to restart it when remotely prompted by a human.

Meta declined to comment on the testing described in this story. Company spokesperson Francis Brennan said in a statement that Meta is investing heavily in training and hiring workers to build and operate its data centers. “America is in the middle of its biggest infrastructure boom since World War II and there’s a major shortage of skilled workers to fill the roles; we need more workers, not fewer,” he said.

But at a conference last year, Eric Xu, senior manager for robotics at Meta, said the company’s “long-term goals” are to put robots in data centers, arguing they could speed up incident response, monitor the environment, and handle preventative maintenance. “We believe more collaboration and research will be needed, but we have to start otherwise we don't have a chance to do this,” he said.

Until recently, robots largely weren’t well suited for the delicate work happening in data centers. They were expensive, and in earlier trials in the industry, sometimes crushed servers while attempting simple tasks, a person briefed on the experimentation says. But the hardware has gotten cheaper, and the AI models powering robots are now far more capable than they were a few years ago. Several startups are currently working to build commercial robots capable of assembling servers, swapping parts, and replacing wires.

Got a Tip? Do you currently work at a data center or have previously and want to talk about what's happening in the industry? We'd like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at peard33.24

Robots could offer more consistent output at a lower cost than human labor, especially in less populous regions where data centers are plentiful but qualified workers are scarce. Proponents also rally behind a pro-worker message: Like AI agents promise to do for knowledge workers, they argue robots could take on data center technicians’ most repetitive and dangerous tasks while freeing them to focus on more complex challenges. Longer term, getting workers out of the picture could make it more feasible to run data centers underwater, in space, or in other environments potentially inhospitable to living, breathing species.

Tech.title: The Easiest Ways to Share Anything Between Android and iOS
Tech.content:
Whisper it quietly, but certain bricks in Apple’s walled garden might be getting taken away.

Thanks to some recent upgrades added to Android by Google, it's now easier than ever to share files between an iPhone and an Android phone, without installing any new apps (though that's still an option too).

So if you need to send a photo, contact card, web link, or anything else, these are the options you have available. As is often the case with Android, they may vary depending on the make and model of your handset, though you should find at least one of these methods works for you.

Share Files via AirDrop

This is the big one: Google recently figured out a way to add support for AirDrop—Apple's previously closed-off, device-to-device sharing protocol—to newer Pixel phones. It doesn't appear that Apple was involved in the process, but the company hasn't gotten in Google's way since, and the functionality has been rolled out to other phones (including the recent Pixel and Galaxy handsets).

Some prep work may be required. On Samsung phones, you need to open Settings, then choose Connected devices > Quick Share and enable Share with Apple devices—though there's no such toggle switch on Pixel phones—it'll just work right away. It needs enabling on iOS too: From Settings, tap General > AirDrop, and Everyone for 10 Minutes.

An iPhone appearing as a sharing option on a Samsung Galaxy device. Photograph: David Nield

With that done, whenever you tap the share button anywhere in any Android app, you can choose Quick Share from the resulting pop-up panel to communicate with a nearby iPhone. The iPhone should show up in the available devices, so select it to start the transfer—which will still need to be accepted on the iPhone.

It will work the other way too, starting from AirDrop on an iPhone, as long as the Android device is set up to receive from any other device. From Settings, tap either Connection preferences (Google Pixel phones) or Connected devices (Samsung Galaxy phones), then select Quick Share > Who can share with you.

Share Files via QR code

Google hasn't stopped with AirDrop on Android. It has also recently pushed out a QR-code-based option for sharing from Android to iOS. It's a bit more clunky than AirDrop, but it'll work no matter what kind of Android phone you've got.

Again, you need to go through Quick Share, which pops up as an option whenever you try to share something in Android—no matter what the app or item you want to share. You won't see an iPhone appear if you don't have the AirDrop functionality, but you should see a Use QR code option on the right, under Share with iPhone and other devices, which after a few moments shrinks down to just a QR code symbol.

Tech.title: XGIMI Vibe One Battery-Powered Projector Review (2026)
Tech.content:
The fact that a battery-powered, Google-certified, Netflix-streaming, Full HD LCD projector can cost less than $250 is remarkable. The fact that it’s actually pretty good verges on preposterous. The XGIMI Vibe One manages both, which is great news you’re looking to project your next bingeable series just about anywhere.

This portable projector weighs only 3.1 pounds and measures 12.1 by 5.3 by 4.5 inches. It’s the size and shape of one of those sadistic mini foam rollers you'd find at the gym, but with a useful handle. This handle rotates 160 degrees to serve as a stand, letting you tilt the image from wall to ceiling without needing a separate tripod. The Vibe One also doubles as a portable LED lamp and Bluetooth speaker.

This petite projector is obviously not in the same league as a hugely powerful (and much more expensive) all-in-one model like the enormous Nebula X1 Pro, but is it still worth buying?

Lights, Camera, Action

WIRED’s favorite projectors include the similarly cylindrical but wired XGIMI MoGo 3 Pro ($379), and the brand's fully portable XGIMI MoGo 4 ($399) that boasts a 2.5-hour battery life, 450 ISO lumens of brightness, and the cutest key fob-style remote control.

Of those three, the Vibe One is definitely the runt of the XGIMI litter, with its simple plastic casing and toned-down specifications, but it is one of the cheapest Full HD, battery-powered projector on the market, undercutting the smaller but similarly powerful Nebula Capsule 3 ($530).

I’m a fan of XGIMI’s industrial design, and the brand has worked wonders here given the obvious budget constraints. My review sample was a muted cream, but the brand also offers a more playful blue and yellow option, and both come with stickers for customization.

Tech.title: I Asked 100 Companies for My Data. I Got Deletion Notices Instead
Tech.content:
I filed a request with McDonald’s earlier this month to access all of the personal data the fast food company collected about me, and I received a stunning 515-page report a few days later that detailed my app interactions in granular detail and predicted I would never stop eating there.

Under the California Consumer Privacy Act, I have the legal right to request access to information from large companies that collect personal data. So I was curious what others might have on me, and I spent the next week filing more than 100 requests.

The CCPA went into effect in 2020, and three of its key provisions are the right to opt out of the selling of personal information, the right to delete that info, and the right to request a copy for yourself.

I focused solely on the latter—access requests—to better understand what data is being collected. Most companies must list two ways for you to file. These are often via a web form, phone number, or email address, as designated in their privacy policy. After you submit a request, companies can take 45 days to complete it.

My experience placing these data access requests was incredibly time-consuming, from finding the right filing methods to verifying my identity multiple times. Most exasperating during this process were the companies that either responded to my access requests with messages concerning the deletion of information, which I explicitly said not to do, or refused to process the request through a method listed in their privacy policy.

Consumer advocates I spoke with were upset with how these requests were handled. “That's crazy,” said Ben Winters, director of AI and privacy at the Consumer Federation of America. “That's not an acceptable status quo.” Winters sees these examples as exhibiting the weaknesses of policy frameworks that rely on companies to act responsibly and in good faith.

In accordance with WIRED’s policies, I am disclosing that I used generative AI to draft bureaucratic emails and update my tracking spreadsheet as part of this report. I wrote the body of this article mainly by hand in my scratch notebook.

One of the first errors came from Crunchbase, known for its database about tech startups. I emailed my access request to its privacy address on August 17. My message laid out the rights I wanted to exercise and included a direct request not to erase anything: “I am not requesting deletion at this time. Please do not treat this as a deletion request.” I received a reply two days later from a Crunchbase support representative.

“Thanks so much for your patience. Your account has been permanently deleted from Crunchbase. Please let me know if you need anything else!” the message read in full.

I followed up via email almost immediately, reiterating that I wanted data access, not data deletion. “Your Crunchbase user account was deleted. Other data located on Crunchbase was not deleted,” read the follow-up support response explaining what happened. If I wanted to have a Crunchbase account, I would have to reregister.

When I reached out to Crunchbase for comment, a spokesperson blamed the mistake on a “processing error” and said that the company would proceed with my original access request as filed. The spokesperson also claimed the misclassified response came from “a person on our customer success team” and not a generative AI tool.

My interactions with BeenVerified, a searchable database that gathers public records, also encapsulate my friction-filled experience placing these access requests.

I emailed BeenVerified’s dedicated CCPA compliance address on the morning of August 19. It laid out that I was a California resident placing an access request, not a deletion request. You’ll never guess what happened next.

Tech.title: There Are So Many Conspiracy Theories About Dolly Parton and Vaccines
Tech.content:
Conspiracy theories surrounding singer and philanthropist Dolly Parton’s recent death have flooded the internet, referencing everything from satanic rituals to cloning. But one conspiracy theory has dominated all the others: the claim that Parton’s death was caused by “turbo cancer” brought on by the Covid vaccine.

There is no evidence to support the claim that Parton’s death had anything to do with the vaccine. Parton, 80, died after “a short battle with cancer,” her family said in a statement. In May, Parton shared that she was responding well to treatment related to her immune system and digestive system.

In 2020, the singer donated $1 million to fund research in support of the vaccine. The following year, she filmed herself getting the vaccine, singing an adapted version of her hit song Jolene before receiving the shot. “Vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, I'm begging of you, please don't hesitate," Parton sang in a video.

Now, a number of influential right-wing conspiracy theorists and MAGA-aligned pundits have spent the past few days claiming—or, in many cases, suggesting—that the vaccine killed Parton.

“Was Dolly Parton yet another Covid vaccine victim?” far-right radio host Wayne Allyn Root, who recently interviewed President Donald Trump on his show, wrote on X. "She took the vaxx on TV. She changed the name of her hit song 'Jolene Jolene' to 'Vaccine, Vaccine.' She encouraged fans to get it. Now she's dead of cancer. This sounds like another case of 'turbo cancer. RIP Dolly.” (Earlier this month, Root urged Trump to declare a national emergency during the midterms when he had the president on his show. “Let me just say, stranger things have happened, OK?” Trump responded.)

Tech.title: Only a Few Days Left to Get Signalis and Big Walk on PlayStation Plus
Tech.content:
September is almost here, and that means PlayStation Plus subscribers only have a few days left to grab August’s free games on the service. People online rave about Signalis, and Dying Light 2 has generally favorable reviews on Metacritic. Big Walk seems like a fun, cartoony co-op game that many people should enjoy for its silliness and puzzles. And all PlayStation Plus subscribers can play these games now until the end of August.

PlayStation Plus, which is Sony’s version of Xbox Game Pass, offers a large, constantly expanding library of games. Subscribers can choose from the Essential, Extra and Premium tiers, each with unique perks and benefits. Starting at $11 a month, the plans give subscribers access to monthly games and rewards, and each month, all subscribers can access a handful of games at no additional charge.

If you subscribe to PlayStation Plus, here are the games you can play at no additional cost until Aug. 31.

Signalis

Some folks on Reddit call this game a “Resident Evil game that’s secretly a Silent Hill game that’s actually a love story,” which should pique the interest of many horror game enthusiasts. You play as Elster, a humanoid android called a Replika, who is searching for her lost partner and missing dreams in a dystopian solar system. You’ll explore a derelict spaceship, fight nightmarish creatures and solve puzzles along the way with limited resources. Maybe play this survival horror game with the lights on.

Big Walk

This goofy-looking game from the makers of Untitled Goose Game is all about solving puzzles, cooperation and talking. Set off with your friends in a wide world filled with puzzles and adventure, and that’s just half the fun. The other half is hanging out with your pals as you all watch a sunset, or stealing your friends’ binoculars and kicking them over a cliff. It’s all in good fun.

Dying Light 2 Stay Human: Reloaded Edition

This game takes place about 20 years after the original and – spoiler – the virus that turns people into zombies has nearly won. You play as one of the last survivors, who is tasked with delivering goods and news between settlements. But really, you’re looking for your sister in all the chaos. The only issue is you’ve got hordes of zombies to get through. Use parkour and brutal weapons to get through the undead and survive another day.

For more on PlayStation Plus, here’s what to know about the gaming service and a rundown of PS Plus Extra and Premium games added in July. You can also check out the latest and upcoming games on Xbox Game Pass.

Tech.title: What Meta’s All-New Social Media Guidelines Promise to Change for Teen Users
Tech.content:
The fallout of an $18 billion lawsuit against Meta, announced on Wednesday, is already here. A new announcement from Meta is designed to meet the terms of the settled lawsuit while helping to prevent teen social media addiction.

In its post, Meta outlined a series of changes to both Instagram and Facebook that will apply only to those under 18. Most of the changes were required as part of the lawsuit settlement, notably the creation of daily limits and night mode controls for teens, as well as the adoption of age-assurance measures to help prevent cheating the system. As part of the agreement, Meta has denied any wrongdoing.

There’s been worldwide pushback against teens and children using social media, including the EU restricting access to social apps for kids under 13, and Australia banning apps like Instagram for anyone under 16. But some advocates worry Meta’s changes won’t be enough to fully protect teens.

In an interview with Democracy Now on Thursday, attorney and co-director of the AI Now research institute, Amba Kak, said the changes don’t address the platform’s architecture, which is designed to addict teenagers with features like infinite scroll. “It’s the business model of surveillance advertising, where it is the optimization of engagement and attention at any cost,” Kak said. “And I think if we don’t get at those root cause fixes, we’re going to be stuck playing whack-a-mole.”

A representative from Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Time limits for kids

Chief among the upcoming changes to Instagram and Facebook are time limitations for teens. A new default time limit will set the social media scrolling time to 2 hours a day for those under 18, and it can only be extended by parents.

An additional night mode will block most access to content such as feeds, stories, explore mode and reels between midnight and 6 a.m. and a school mode will mute notifications between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m.

Meta is also adding a feature to give 15-minute warnings to teens if they’ve been on the apps for an extended period of time, as well as 60-minute and 90-minute warnings they’re daily allotment is running down. To further reduce constant scrolling, autoplay for videos and clips will also be turned off by default, but like most features, it can be adjusted by parents.

Protection against toxic content

Meta is also implementing a number of changes intended to reduce toxicity and obsession with social media. By default, teens won’t see likes and reactions on posts, including their own. They’ll also be restricted from seeing certain content, such as cosmetic surgery and “extreme makeup” filters, although it’s not clear how far those limitations will extend (for example, a filter that adds dog ears).

Meta is adding age-appropriate content restrictions, but it remains vague on the details. While using movie ratings and parent feedback to build filters, the company fails to explain how this applies to social media posts or provide examples of blocked content.

In addition, teens will have the option to choose a non-algorithm version of their feeds that won’t be personalized by any Meta recommendations (which I also want for my own account).

Hazy tools for age verification

A new age-assurance strategy is also coming to Instagram and Facebook, but it’s unclear how it will work.

“We’re investing in even stronger technology to proactively catch accounts that may belong to under-13s,” Meta said on its blog. “We’re also strengthening the technology we use to identify accounts that may be between the ages of 13 and 17.”

Meta didn’t provide any details on how this tech would work, what it would look for or how it would flag accounts. I also asked about any appeals process for those incorrectly tagged, but Meta didn’t respond to my request.

It’s possible Meta will be using AI scan to profile context, account activity and visual cues to raise red flags, but there’s not much clarity otherwise.

Rolling out changes

The proposed changes were approved by a judge on Thursday, and Meta will roll out the first protections in the coming months, with the rest to follow afterward, although the exact timeline isn’t clear. As required by the agreement, Meta will also establish an independent social media research foundation to share “consented” user data in an effort to support teen well-being.

In its post, Meta said, “The fact is that teens move fluidly between dozens of apps a day. All platforms should empower parents and support teens by putting the same measures in place … we urge TikTok and YouTube to join us and state attorneys general in adopting this new standard.”

Other platforms have not responded to this call-out.

Tech.title: 1 in 6 VPNs Track Your Location, According to New Report From Proton
Tech.content:
Using a virtual private network is a surefire way to keep your information private when browsing the internet. But a new report from Proton, released on Wednesday, exposes some major holes in that concept.

A VPN is a tool that encrypts your internet behavior and hides your IP address and physical location, with the goal of keeping your identity and identifying information secure. But 64 of the VPN apps downloaded in the US, Proton found, are owned by Chinese companies and contain trackers that collect all sorts of user information, including device IDs, network information, device models and mobile carrier data.

And 25% of the apps in question were found to actively track your location.

Data from millions of VPN users is going to China

In June alone, these apps were downloaded over 13 million times.

Narrowing down the numbers further, Proton found that 31 of those Chinese-owned VPNs use shell companies registered in jurisdictions such as Singapore, Hong Kong and the UK to further hide their identities.

An authoritarian government like China’s could use this information to track a person’s location. So if a public official, someone in law enforcement, a journalist or even someone attending a protest was using one of these VPNs for safety, this flaw would expose them to potential threats.

It should be clear that China isn’t the only country where companies harvest the data these apps collect, but it’s near the top of the list. Israel, Russia and the Five Eyes countries — Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the UK and the US — all have companies collecting tracking data from millions of people.

Stronger privacy guardrails are needed

Transparency is a big issue here, with a load of bad VPN apps being readily available for download through Apple and Google. Proton’s report points out that both companies require developers to submit their own paperwork to verify their apps, with little verification (and no independent audits) being done on Apple’s or Google’s part. Apple and Google didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

This lack of guardrails in the verification process makes it hard to decipher which virtual private network apps protect your privacy and do what their policies promise and which are virtually doing the opposite.

“Proton’s report is yet another example of why it’s so important to know who’s behind your VPN and what data they’re collecting,” CNET Senior Writer Attila Tomaschek said. “It’s also another reminder that just because a VPN app is popular in Apple’s or Google’s app marketplaces, it doesn’t necessarily mean that the VPN app is safe to use.”

If you’re looking for a VPN, Tomaschek points to VPNs like Proton and ExpressVPN, which regularly rank near the top of CNET’s VPN recommendations. Each virtual private network is put through a rigorous testing process that includes a thorough examination of the app’s privacy policy, transparency reports, audits, corporate structure and legal jurisdiction.

When all else fails, avoid any VPN that is murky about any of those key principles. “Instead, opt for a trustworthy VPN that is crystal clear about where it’s based, who’s behind it and how it protects user privacy,” Tomaschek said.

Tech.title: Complaints Pile Up for Popular Meal Kit Services Amid Missing Ingredients and Poor Customer Service
Tech.content:
Weeks after fulfillment issues began at Marley Spoon following its former food supplier’s bankruptcy filing, customers are speaking out about their negative experiences with the Martha Stewart-backed meal kit brand.

(Full disclosure: CNET has tested Marley Spoon several times. We liked it so much, it landed on our list of the best services and earned an Editors’ Choice award before the fulfillment issues began.)

Sylvia Turcotte, who has been a Marley Spoon customer for over six years, told CNET that she and her husband have loved the brand’s offerings for years and would even mark certain recipes as “restaurant quality” when they were worthy and often served them to dinner guests.

Then, in July, issues began with her regular deliveries: melted ice, warm protein and questionable produce. In August, a box that was supposed to contain 27 ingredients was missing 21.

“Needless to say, I did not cook Marley [Spoon] that week,” Turcotte said. “What I do not understand is why the powers that be have not suspended the meal plan until they get their logistics straightened out. Instead, they are ruining their brand.”

Other Marley Spoon customers shared additional disappointing experiences, including receiving boxes missing protein and receiving no response from customer service when inquiring about damaged or incomplete boxes.

Marley Spoon’s transition

Marley Spoon’s transition to a new supplier has been rocky. Corin Cesaric/Zooey Liao/CNET

In April, Marley Spoon’s previous food supplier, FreshRealm, which also supplied Blue Apron, filed for bankruptcy. CNET later confirmed that Misfits Market would be taking over fulfillment for both brands.

Marley Spoon has offered customers credit toward their next order when a problem occurs.

Best Meal Kits, as Tested by CNET See at CNET

The transition has been rocky, with Misfits Market spokesperson Ken Shuman previously saying the company has “compressed what’s typically a 10- [to] 12-month transition into under 10 weeks,” and “an operational transition at that speed has real challenges, and the biggest one has been inventory.”

“Customers who experience missing items or other issues with their order are encouraged to contact Marley Spoon’s Customer Care team directly through the Help Center,” a spokesperson told CNET. “While credits may be automatically issued in some cases, the team will review the individual circumstances and determine the appropriate resolution, including a refund.”

When I inquired to customer service about a refund instead of credit for missing ingredients, I did not hear back on two occasions. The Marley Spoon customer service phone number directs you to the website or app.

However, Marley Spoon previously shared a statement regarding the fulfillment issues, which read in part, “We take this very seriously and are working around the clock to ensure our customers receive their boxes on time, with the correct, high-quality ingredients they expect from Marley Spoon.”

Stewart remains affiliated with the brand, with select recipes of hers featured every week, her team confirmed to CNET. However, they added that the “delivery and fulfillment operations are managed independently.”

While some loyal customers have said they want to help the brand weather the storm, others have told CNET they’ve decided to cut their losses and cancel their subscriptions entirely. When a subscription is canceled rather than paused, any accrued credits are lost.

“I love Marley Spoon,” Turcotte said. “I hope they can solve their issues.”

Blue Apron

Blue Apron faces similar challenges

Similar issues have plagued Blue Apron recently. In a previous statement to CNET, Blue Apron said in part that the company is “temporarily focusing our menu on what we’re confident we can deliver, adding quality checks before boxes ship, and making progress with our partners to fix what’s broken.”

On social media, after the company released a statement about the service disruptions, customers echoed complaints made about Marley Spoon, particularly about a lack of response from customer service.

“I’ve been a customer since 2012,” one commenter wrote. “[Blue Apron] has taught me how to cook, and I love it dearly. But these last two weeks have been challenging. This week we received a box of condiments, a bag of spinach, a card for a steak recipe (I’m a vegetarian) but no steak and not one complete recipe to cook.”



Blue Apron responded to the comment, saying it would reach out via direct message to handle the situation.

Tech.title: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Telescope Is About to Start Its Cosmic Survey
Tech.content:
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is ready for its trip to Florida so that it can get launched into space. NASA

After nearly a decade in development, NASA’s next big telescope is almost ready to travel into space. The agency has set Sunday as the launch date for the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. This places the project approximately eight months ahead of its original schedule and, according to NASA leadership, significantly under budget.

NASA is getting some assistance from SpaceX for this launch. The telescope is being taken into space by a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, where it’ll separate and head to its final location while the SpaceX rocket returns to Earth.

With the launch just a few days away, the telescope should be pretty close to ready to go. That includes detailed inspections to verify it sustained no damage during transit. Engineers also loaded 290 gallons of hydrazine to fuel the telescope and conducted several dress rehearsals in preparation for the launch.

The destination for the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point, located about 1 million miles from Earth on the far side of the sun. The region is a gravitational sweet spot that allows spacecraft to maintain a relatively stable position while orbiting the sun alongside Earth.

With its wider field of view, the Roman telescope promises to see quite a lot of the universe. NASA

How to watch the Nancy Grace Roman Telescope launch

The launch is set to take off from Launch Complex 39A at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sunday at 7:26 a.m. ET/4:26 a.m. PT. NASA is livestreaming the event, with coverage beginning at 6:20 a.m. ET, and it’ll include a post-launch news conference starting at 9:30 a.m. ET with a media Q&A session.

NASA is streaming it across all its social platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, Twitch, YouTube and X. The agency says the launch is also watchable on NASA Plus, Amazon Prime and Discovery Plus. Netflix isn’t mentioned on NASA’s list, but it won’t hurt to check the day of the launch to see if it’s streaming there as well.

It’s quite an early launch for a Sunday, so if you’re a late sleeper or a churchgoer, you may have to wait until later to watch it back.

What is the Nancy Grace Roman Telescope looking for?

The telescope is named after astronomer Nancy Grace Roman, NASA’s first female executive and an instrumental voice in the planning and construction of the Hubble Space Telescope.

The two telescopes share more than just a connection to Roman. Both use 2.4-meter mirrors and can produce images with similar sharpness. But Roman is designed to see much more of the sky at once, capturing images at least 100 times larger than Hubble’s. The observatories also specialize in different wavelengths of light: Hubble observes ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light, while Roman focuses on visible and infrared wavelengths.

The Roman Telescope can see as much of space in just two images as the Hubble does in over 400. NASA

NASA envisions Roman and Hubble working hand in hand. Roman will scan enormous swaths of the sky, uncovering objects and phenomena that can later be examined in greater detail by Hubble. By combining Roman’s panoramic surveys with Hubble’s more focused observations, astronomers hope to build a richer picture of the cosmos.

During its mission, Roman is expected to observe more than 100 billion stars and billions of galaxies, detect tens of thousands of supernovae and transmit nearly 1.4 terabytes of scientific data to Earth every day.

Tech.title: Human, Beware: The Secrets We Tell AI Chatbots Aren’t Private
Tech.content:
Are people oversharing sensitive information with AI? Short answer: yes.

A new survey called The AI Privacy Problem by DuckDuckGo Research said about a third of people are sharing secrets with chatbots that they don’t share with friends, family and medical professionals. The number rises to 56% among self-described AI enthusiasts. Researchers also found that 43% of parents reveal things to AI that they don’t tell the most trusted people in their lives, including their kids.

Though the survey didn’t specify what kind of personal information is shared with AI, past reports have shown that we often turn to chatbots for help with physical and mental health issues, financial advice, parenting questions and marital problems.

The problem isn’t about seeking help. The problem is losing control over what happens with the data after it’s shared in chats. Companies can use your private info to train their AI systems. Law enforcement can get it through subpoenas. And if you’re using AI chatbots at work, your employer can likely access your chat history, too.

AI companies try to convince people that chatbots are trusted confidantes, but that’s a false narrative, the DuckDuckGo report said.

“These messages all rest on one assumption: That these chats are private. In most cases, that just isn’t true,” researchers said.

In fact, the survey found that many respondents didn’t realize how their chatbot data could be used or accessed or that they didn’t know about settings to prevent their information from being recorded or stored. When it comes to protecting their data, nearly 40% of respondents had no trust in companies and nearly 50% had no trust in the US government.

Privacy risks of large language models

Many of us know that companies bombard us with targeted, personalized online ads. If you run a Google search for vacuums, you’ll see vacuum ads pop up on your screen. If you search for Mediterranean cruises, you’ll surely get cruise ads on YouTube (owned by Google). Companies also buy, sell and share our social media data to help guide their advertising.

But AI data-sharing goes well beyond being the focus of selling you products. If you provide sensitive information to a chatbot, it could be revealed or exposed. A researcher at Wake Forest University found that AI agents, which use LLM data to perform autonomous tasks, can sometimes leak data, either maliciously or unintentionally.

Your conversations with AI chatbots don’t disappear into the ether. Unless you opt out, the AI system will record and save them for future use, such as additional training for the AI model. Last year, hundreds of chats on Anthropic’s chatbot Claude appeared in Google search results.

One main concern with LLMs is data memorization, said AI expert Uttara Ananthakrishnan, assistant professor at the University of Washington’s Foster School of Business. “When someone asks the same question as someone else, it is possible that the LLM gives them exactly the same answer it gave someone else,” Ananthakrishnan told CNET. “The LLM might not know that the answer contains information that someone can use to identify someone else.”

Cops can use chat data

What you say in a “private” chat could also wind up in court or part of a police investigation. Companies with AI models such as Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini) and OpenAI (ChatGPT) are legally required to turn over chat data if subpoenaed by law enforcement or the US government. Only 25% of DuckDuckGo survey respondents knew this. As MemX, an AI memory agent, stated starkly in a blog post: “A conversation with a mainstream chatbot is a business record, not a confidential consultation.”



It’s already happened several times. ChatGPT transcripts were used during a double murder investigation in South Carolina earlier this year and in the Palisades arson case last year. A Snapchat AI conversation was used as evidence in a 2024 murder trial.

As OpenAI founder and CEO Sam Altman said on a podcast earlier this year, “If you go talk to ChatGPT about your most sensitive stuff and then there’s like a lawsuit or whatever, we could be required to produce that.”

Employers can use chat data

Free speech isn’t really free in the worker-employer relationship. Companies can fire you over your social media posts, and they can also access your AI accounts if you’re using them at work under certain circumstances, like if your access is based on the company’s enterprise account.

And putting company info in a private chat, even on your personal account, is a major no-no, although a survey earlier this year showed that two in five workers did just that.

Some big companies, such as Walmart, Delta, T-Mobile, Chevron and Starbucks, are even using AI to gauge worker positivity — or toxicity. These AI systems scan employee messaging platforms such as Slack or Teams, looking for clues in keywords and sentences, in what is called “emotion AI.”

Some companies also want workers to put their Slack messages in public channels so their AI systems can use those chats for further model training.

Chat data can be used for training

More than half of the DuckDuckGo survey respondents did not know (or were not sure) that their chatbot conversations were used for AI training. Nearly three in five were “uncomfortable” with that, and 30% were “very uncomfortable.”

Boiled down, AI training is the process of feeding massive amounts of data into an AI system so it can recognize patterns, make decisions and solve problems — basically, match or exceed what humans can do. That data can include published materials, video and audio recordings out in the world, as well as your chats.



A 2025 Stanford study showed that six companies fed user chat data back into their AI systems for further training — Amazon (Nova), Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini), Meta (Meta AI), Microsoft (Copilot) and OpenAI (ChatGPT). Not all of them have opt-out options.

AI chatbots provide a false sense of intimacy and perhaps confidentiality, said the University of Washington’s Ananthakrishnan.



“Users interact with these tools as sounding boards, sharing unfiltered thoughts, sensitive health queries, and vulnerable personal dilemmas that they would likely never type into Google,” Ananthakrishnan told CNET. “People are deeply uneasy about their most intimate, conversational thoughts being ingested into a system where they could inadvertently become public record.”

Use chatbots securely and privately

We aren’t advocating you run and hide from chatbots, but there are ways to maximize your privacy if and when you use them. Many chatbots have settings you can deploy that will prevent them from being stored on company servers to be used as an AI model training.

In an explainer, CNET reporter Blake Stimac gives a complete breakdown of how to turn off data sharing for Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT and Grok. With Meta, it’s more of a request than an opt-out.

There are also ways to keep your chatbot experiences as safe as possible: Treat chats as “public environments,” don’t overshare your mental state and regularly export your data to see what information the AI has stored about you.

For greater privacy, there are chatbots that run only offline and locally — in other words, not on any cloud servers. Those include Jan.ai, Ollama, LM Studio, PrivateGPT and GPT4All.

Tech.title: Adobe Photoshop Adds a Whole New AI Editing Mode
Tech.content:
Adobe is giving Photoshop users more AI tools for their work belt. A new feature called AI Assisted Editor lets you do a variety of things with your images using merely natural language prompts. It’s not replacing the traditional Pro Editor; it’s just another option.

Adobe also announced several other new features on Thursday — a light adjustment layer for more lighting controls, Instruct Edit with Masks for prompt-based editing, and Markup to let you visually communicate edits by drawing on an image.



Adobe has been busy with new AI wrinkles in the past several months. AI Assistant arrived in March to enable editing with conversational commands, and in June, the company added AI assistants to Photoshop, Premiere Pro, InDesign, Illustrator and Frame.io. Earlier this month, OpenAI and Adobe teamed up to integrate dozens of photo- and video-editing capabilities into ChatGPT.

AI Assisted Editor is currently being tested in the beta version of Photoshop, which costs $23 per month.

AI Assisted Editor keeps it simple

When you open Photoshop, you will see two editing interface options: AI Assisted and Pro Editor. AI Assisted is the new feature announced Thursday, and Pro Editor is Photoshop’s classic workspace offering manual control over layers, adjustments and editing tools.

Photoshop masters are likely comfortable with Pro Editor, but less-experienced users might gravitate toward AI Assisted for simpler editing.

If you go with AI Assisted, you can use a natural language prompt bar to request edits and changes. A vertical tool bar includes seven functions, including prompt to edit (using natural language prompts), remove background, generative expand (extend image dimensions), generative remove (eliminate unwanted objects), generative fill (add, replace, or remove content), generative upscale (increase image resolution) and AI markup (annotate images).



The Prompt to Edit function could be the biggest game changer. You can change out the image entirely with a natural language prompt. Maybe you’ve got an image of someone sitting on a beach, but want them in the mountains. A prompt of “Put this person on a hiking trail in the mountains” could do the trick.

More new Photoshop features

Adobe also announced three other new options for what the company called “more precise, sharper editing.” The light adjustment layer lets you toggle through several lighting controls — exposure, contrast, highlights, shadows, whites and blacks.

Photoshop’s Light Adjustment Layer lets you toggle between several adjustments.

With the Instruct Edit with Masks function, you can simply describe the edits you want in the masked areas — have the person smile, put the bird in flight, open the blue door — instead of having to mark every area on the image that you want to edit.

With the markup tool, you can draw on an image to tell the AI your changes. You might circle a building and tell the AI to make it brown, or maybe draw an arrow to where you want a certain object. Adobe says markup is a way of being more precise with the AI to avoid any ambiguity that might occur if you instead used text prompts.

Tech.title: The Powerful Stealth AI Model ‘Ox Alpha’ Is Now GLM-5.3-Flash, and You Can Use It
Tech.content:
The anonymous Ox Alpha AI model that popped up on OpenRouter, the unified AI platform, last week has been claimed by the Chinese company Z.ai. Now officially known as GLM-5.3-Flash, the model is both powerful and cheap, challenging the capabilities and cost of popular models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

When it was first teased, Ox Alpha became the most popular model for the week on OpenRouter and all of its traffic was served through Chinese-made AI chips. After it was confirmed to be the company behind the new model, Z.ai’s stock price soared, Bloomberg reports.

Ox Alpha was described as a “frontier model built for efficient coding, sustained agentic work, and real-world production use,” according to an OpenRouter post on X. In a follow-up post, the platform confirmed that the provider wouldn’t train on your prompts.

Z.ai’s GLM family are open-weight models, where core components are publicly released, allowing anyone to download and use them. (That’s different from open-source AI models, which make all pieces of the model available, including the source code, weights, and training data.) Weights for GLM-5.3-Flash are available on Hugging Face, another unified AI platform.

Being open-weight puts the GLM family in contrast to closed-weight models from big US developers like OpenAI and Anthropic. Open-weight models, which are popular among Chinese companies, have been the subject of heated debate in the US because of the potential that users will change or misuse them. But big American companies, including OpenAI, have come out in support of open ecosystems. Meta recently said it would release the weights of a previously closed model, Muse Spark 1.2.

Like other recent AI models, GLM-5.3-Flash has enhanced agentic capabilities, such as using a browser and a computer, allowing the model to navigate web pages and open and interact with desktop apps.

How can you access the GLM-5.3 Flash?

In an announcement post on X, Z.ai said the new model is available across all official platforms. The easiest and most direct way to access the model is to subscribe to one of Z.ai’s GLM coding plans, which start at $18 a month. The model will also provide 3x the usable quota of GLM-5.3.

Because GLM-5.3-Flash is open-weight, you can also download it and use it on your own hardware — no paying for subscription or API costs. Although it might require some hefty computing power to do so, as the model weights themselves tip the scales at more than 300GB.
